title: A workflow for the next laboratory
A workflow for the next laboratory
text:
The workflow you can reuse



Five steps in order: find, check, analyse, explain and reproduce, with the source, inputs, output and a backup saved throughout.



Find the data and the project folder without “recent files”. Check rows, units, missing values and the independent unit.
Analyse with a plot of individual units first. Explain size, spread or uncertainty, and a limitation.
Reproduce: restart, render, and back up.


Every station today exercises part of this chain. Ask students which step they found hardest during the mini-study and start there.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Practice stations: start where you are weakest
text:
Practice stations: start where you are weakest



Files: download, unzip, find and inspect files in the terminal.
R: repair a broken analysis and rerun it.
Meaning: explain units, spread, uncertainty and limits.
Report: render your Day 23 report from a fresh session.
Remote: log in and transfer a file, if the service is available. Otherwise note it as still to do.





Practice branches into four stations: files (locate and inspect), R (repair and rerun), meaning (units and limits) and report (render and share).




Everyone should eventually do files, R and meaning. Remote access is practised when the real service works; finishing the local stations does not complete the remote task.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
text:
Repair a broken analysis
seedling <- read_csv("seedlings.csv")
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm + initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$Growth_mm)
What is wrong?

Path: the file is in data/: "data/seedlings.csv".
Names: seedling versus seedlings; growth_mm versus Growth_mm (R is case sensitive).
Meaning: growth is final minus initial. P01: 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm.
Packages: library(readr) and library(dplyr) must come first.


Let students find the problems before revealing them. The last one is the most important: code can run without error and still compute the wrong biology. Checking one row by hand catches it.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Explain before calculating: spread and units
text:
Explain before calculating: spread and units



Two groups can share a mean and still differ in spread: both have mean 14 mm, SD 1 and 6 mm.
A larger SD is not automatically bad technique; organisms vary.
One plant with 100 cells measured is still one independent plant.
A missing value is not zero: zero invents a measurement.





Two toy groups with the same mean but very different spreads of individual values.




These are questions from Station 3 of the practical. Ask students to explain each in one sentence to a neighbour before checking the answers.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Explain before calculating: uncertainty and range
text:
Explain before calculating: uncertainty and range



Estimate 3 mm, 95% interval −2 to 8 mm. Does that show no effect?
No. The interval includes zero and effects in both directions: the study cannot tell. Report the uncertainty.
A reading above the highest calibration standard: flag it, dilute, measure again.
A positive leaf-area slope: an association, not proof that changing area changes mass.





An estimated difference of 3 mm with a 95 percent interval from −2 to 8 mm that spans zero.




Supplied numbers, not computed from the course data. Avoid “not significant, so no difference”. The calibration and association items revisit Days 19 and 20.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
text:
Investigate a high value



Algae data: reference culture A11 = 41.7 mg, the largest value in the file.
The data dictionary records a spill for A19, but nothing wrong with A11.
So A11 stays in the primary result.
To see how much it matters, make a separate object:

algae_without_a11 <- filter(algae,
  culture_id != "A11")




Algae biomass by group with group means; reference culture A11 at 41.7 mg is circled as a recorded value with no evidence of an error.




Start from the imported algae object (library(readr), library(dplyr), read_csv(“data/algae.csv”)). Do not edit the CSV. A high value is a question to investigate, not permission to remove it.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: How much does A11 change the result?
text:
How much does A11 change the result?



Primary (all available): reference 28.20, supplement 33.92 mg; difference 5.72 mg.
Sensitivity check (A11 omitted): reference 26.97 mg; difference 6.95 mg.
The supplement mean does not change; the reference n drops from 12 to 11.
Report the primary result. Label the check “A11 omitted without evidence of error”.
Three different issues: A19 missing, A11 high but recorded, and the study’s simplifying assumptions.





The observed supplement-minus-reference difference is 5.72 mg with all available data and 6.95 mg when A11 is omitted; the diagnostic does not replace the primary analysis.




Record the steps in reports/final-investigation.txt. After rendering, check that the main figure and inline numbers come from the primary data, not from a diagnostic object left in memory.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
section: Hand the work over and test it
text:
Hand the work over and test it


Write instructions a stranger could follow:

the question, and what one row means;
where the raw data are, what blank cells mean;
which report to render, and what it should show.

Then test them: extract the project into a new folder, follow your own instructions, and fix anything unclear.




A recipient uses the source and data to reach a tested project, without needing the author’s memory.




A successful render does not supply the meaning: the reader still needs units, counts and a limitation in the HTML. If the instructions change, make a new clearly named package and test that one too.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
text:
Questions for your next lab
Ask these before analysing any new dataset:

What does one row represent, and what was independently assigned?
What are the units, and what do blank cells mean?
Which figure shows the individual observations and answers the question?
Where are the raw data, the source, the output and the backup?

Write them, with your workflow, in reports/next-lab.txt.

Asking these questions is a sign of competence, not of not knowing. Encourage students to add one question of their own that they would ask a lab teacher.

title: A workflow for the next laboratory
text:
Summary

The workflow is the same for every dataset: find, check, analyse, explain, reproduce.
Check one row by hand: code can run and still compute the wrong biology.
Missing is not zero; high is not automatically wrong; keep the primary result and label any sensitivity check.
An interval that includes zero means “uncertain”, not “no effect”.
A report is finished when someone else can render it from a fresh copy and understand it.

After this course: use this project and reports/next-lab.txt in your later lab courses and thesis work. Start every new dataset with the questions on the previous slide.
Now: open the Day 25 exercises. Leave with your primary report, the labelled A11 check, reports/final-investigation.txt, a tested handover, reports/next-lab.txt and reports/readiness-review.txt.

In the readiness review, students list three things they can now do reliably and two that need more practice, with a concrete next practice task. Remote login and transfer stay listed as pending if the real service was not used.

title: From a question to a report
From a question to a report
text:
Choose one study


Duckweed (default)

20 flasks, randomly given extra nutrient or control.
Outcome: dry biomass after seven days, mg.
Compare with the Welch test from Day 17.
Report: duckweed-report.Rmd

Organic alternative

12 synthesis runs, standard or modified protocol.
Outcome: product yield, %.
Descriptive comparison, no test.
Report: organic-study.Rmd





Two study options: duckweed biomass in flasks, or collected-product yield from synthesis runs.




Duckweed is a small floating aquatic plant. The organic study needs no chemistry: the maximum possible product mass is supplied. If students made organic-report.Rmd on Day 15, they keep it and use Save As for organic-study.Rmd.

title: From a question to a report
section: Write the plan before the code
text:
Write the plan before the code


Save in reports/study-decisions.txt:

Question, in one sentence.
Independent unit: what was randomly assigned?
Outcome and units, and how it is calculated.
Missing values: which, and what you will do.
Plot, and the direction of the comparison (e.g. nutrient − control).





The analysis goes from the question to the independent unit and data, then to a description; inference needs extra model assumptions.




The plan takes a few lines and prevents most errors later. For the organic route, say explicitly that no confidence interval or test is added.

title: From a question to a report
text:
Count the independent units



Duckweed: the flask is the unit. The many fronds in one flask share its water and nutrients.
Organic: the synthesis run is the unit. Weighing one product three times is still one run.
More readings of the same unit do not add replicates (Day 14).





Four flasks with many fronds each are four units; four synthesis runs with repeated weighings are four units.




Ask students to say the unit out loud before they calculate anything. This is also the first question to ask a lab teacher about any new dataset.

title: From a question to a report
section: Import, check, and keep the missing flask
text:
Import, check, and keep the missing flask


library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
duckweed <- read_csv("data/duckweed.csv",
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(duckweed)
available <- duckweed |>
  filter(!is.na(biomass_mg))

Expect 20 rows, 20 unique flask_ids, labels control and nutrient.
F17 was spilled: 10 control + 9 nutrient measurements available.





Twenty flasks were started, ten per group; F17 in the nutrient group was spilled, leaving 19 measurements.




A zero for F17 would invent a very low biomass and drag the nutrient mean down. Keep the raw table unchanged; the available object makes the exclusion visible. Record checks as findings (“20 rows, 1 missing: F17, spilled”), not as “data were checked”.

title: From a question to a report
text:
Plot the flasks, then compare


nutrient <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "nutrient")
control <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "control")
comparison <- t.test(nutrient$biomass_mg,
                     control$biomass_mg)

Means: nutrient 39.63 mg, control 32.28 mg.
Nutrient − control: 7.35 mg, 95% CI 2.27 to 12.44 mg, Welch p ≈ 0.007.
The groups overlap: F11 (nutrient) is below several controls.





Individual duckweed biomass values by group with group means as diamonds; nutrient flasks are higher on average but the groups overlap.




The order of the two vectors sets the direction: nutrient minus control. The interval concerns the mean difference, not 95% of flasks. The low control F08 (19.8 mg) has no recorded error, so it stays.

title: From a question to a report
section: Organic route: compare yields, not grams
text:
Organic route: compare yields, not grams



Runs started at different scales, so compare percentages:
yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
Check Y01 by hand: 100 × 0.62 / 1.00 = 62 %.
Means: standard 68.67 %, modified 77.00 % (SD 4.32 and 3.74 percentage points).
Difference: 8.33 percentage points, modified − standard. No test needed.





Individual product yields for six standard and six modified runs, with group means as diamonds.




8.33 percentage points is not an 8.33% relative increase. Higher yield does not show higher purity: purity was assumed, not measured.

title: From a question to a report
section: Write a result paragraph someone can check
text:
Write a result paragraph someone can check
Include: direction and size with units, available n, the spread or overlap, the uncertainty if you estimated it, and one limitation.
“Nutrient flasks had on average 7.35 mg more dry biomass than controls (95% CI 2.27 to 12.44 mg; Welch, p ≈ 0.007; 9 nutrient and 10 control flasks). F17 was spilled and has no measurement.”







Faulty draft
Repair




“There were 20 biomass results.”
20 flasks, 19 measurements; F17 missing.


“The nutrient plants all grew more.”
The groups overlap; the mean is higher.


“The SD is the error in the treatment effect.”
SD is spread of flasks; the CI is uncertainty in the difference.


“p is the probability that nutrients work.”
p assumes no difference and asks how surprising the data are.




Ask students to point at the code line or table that produced every number in their paragraph. Rewrite the meaning, not only the strength of the wording (“proves” to “suggests” is not enough).

title: From a question to a report
section: Practise on fresh data: algae cultures
text:
Practise on fresh data: algae cultures



data/algae.csv: 24 cultures, reference or supplement; A19 was spilled.
Available: 12 reference + 11 supplement.
Means: 28.20 mg and 33.92 mg: supplement − reference ≈ +5.72 mg.
The largest single culture, A11 (41.7 mg), is in the reference group: a higher mean does not mean every culture is higher.
Putting 0 for A19 would drop the supplement mean to 31.09 mg: wrong.





Individual algae biomass values for reference and supplement cultures with group means marked; the groups overlap and the highest value is a reference culture.




This is a short script, algae-transfer.R, and a memo in reports/algae-transfer.txt, not a second full report. The culture is the unit; its many cells are not replicates. Day 24 reproduces this script in a fresh folder; Day 25 looks more closely at A11.

title: From a question to a report
section: Before you finish: the report must run on its own
text:
Before you finish: the report must run on its own

Packages and import at the top of the report.
Checks and calculations, with findings written down.
Plot of individual units and a small summary table.
Comparison in the stated direction, and the result paragraph.
Restart R, render, and read the HTML as a stranger would.

Keep data/ unchanged and outputs in output/. If something fails, write down where.

The report must not depend on objects created in the console. Paths are relative to the project root. A complete first version today is the goal; Day 24 will expose hidden dependencies.

title: From a question to a report
text:
Summary

One question, one independent unit, one outcome with units: write them down first.
Missing is not zero: report started and available counts (20 flasks, 19 measured).
Plot the individual units before any summary or test.
State the direction (nutrient − control) and report size, uncertainty, n and a limitation.
The report must render from a fresh R session using only its own code.

Next (Day 24, reproduce and share): can someone else run your report in a fresh copy of the project and get the same result?
Now: open the Day 23 exercises. Leave with duckweed-report.Rmd (or organic-study.Rmd) and its HTML, reports/study-decisions.txt, and the algae script and memo.

Remind students to save a note of anything that failed. These files are the input for Day 24.

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
The parts of a computer



Disk (SSD): slow but permanent. Saved CSVs, scripts and reports live here.
RAM: fast, temporary working space. Everything in R’s Environment pane lives here.
CPU: carries out the calculations, using data that are in RAM.
A file is read from disk into RAM before R can work with it.





Saved data are read from storage into working memory and processed by the CPU.




Typical student laptop today: 8–16 GB RAM, 256 GB–1 TB SSD. Disk is many times larger than RAM. Ask students to find their own numbers in the practical (Settings → About, or About This Mac). Avoid detail about caches, buses or clock speeds.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
section: CPU cores, and what a GPU is
text:
CPU cores, and what a GPU is



A CPU has a few cores; each can work on a separate task. parallel::detectCores() counts them.
A GPU has thousands of simple cores doing the same small calculation at once.
GPUs are used for images, video and deep learning (for example protein-structure prediction).
This course runs on the CPU. You will hear about GPUs later; you do not need one here.





A CPU drawn with eight large cores beside a GPU drawn with hundreds of tiny cores.




The drawing is schematic: real GPUs have thousands of cores. Ordinary R code uses one core at a time unless it is written to use more. A bigger computer with many cores helps when a job can be split into independent pieces, for example analysing many samples separately. That returns tomorrow.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
Programs and processes



A program is an installed file on disk, such as RStudio.
A process is a running copy of it, using CPU and RAM now.
Task Manager (Windows) or Activity Monitor (Mac) lists processes and the RAM each uses.
Look for rsession or R: that is where your data are.





One application saved on storage can be launched as running processes using memory and CPU.




Demonstrate: open Task Manager or Activity Monitor, find the R process, run x <- rnorm(1000000) and show its memory grow by about 8 MB; then rm(x) and gc(). The operating system does not always show memory as released straight away; that is normal. Closing RStudio ends the process; the program remains installed.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
Closing R empties its RAM



Objects in the Environment pane are in RAM. Restart R and they are gone.
Saved files (data, scripts, .Rmd, outputs) stay on disk.
That is why we restart R and render from saved files: a result only in RAM cannot be checked or repeated.





Closing a running process clears its working session while the saved note persists on storage.




Connect to week 2: Session → Restart R, then run the script from the top. The figure uses an editor note; R objects behave the same way. The habit of rendering in a fresh session exists because of this RAM/disk split.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
How many bytes?



One DNA letter in a text file takes 1 byte, one grey pixel takes 1 byte, and one number in R takes 8 bytes.


A byte = 8 bits = one of 256 patterns. 1 kB = 1,000 bytes; 1 MB = 1,000,000; 1 GB = 1,000,000,000.

Three numbers carry the whole lecture: a letter of text is 1 byte, a pixel in an 8-bit grayscale image is 1 byte, and a number in R is 8 bytes. We use decimal units (1 MB = one million bytes), as disk makers do. Some programs use 1,024-based units; the difference does not matter for rough estimates.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
section: Estimate a table before you load it
text:
Estimate a table before you load it



A grid of 10 columns and one million rows needs 1,000,000 times 10 times 8 bytes, which is 80 MB, plus working space.


RAM ≈ rows × numeric columns × 8 bytes. Plan for 2–3× that: R makes copies while it works.

Work through the arithmetic aloud: one million times ten is ten million numbers; times eight is eighty million bytes; that is 80 MB. Working space: filtering, mutate and plotting create new objects alongside the old one. The 2–3× factor is a rule of thumb, not an exact law.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
Check the rule in R
x <- rnorm(1000000)
format(object.size(x), units = "MB", standard = "SI")     # "8 MB"

set.seed(21)
n <- 100000
big <- data.frame(matrix(round(rnorm(n * 10, mean = 20, sd = 4), 1), ncol = 10))
format(object.size(big), units = "MB", standard = "SI")   # "8 MB"
write_csv(big, "output/big-measurements.csv")
file.size("output/big-measurements.csv") / 1e6            # 4.79



Object
Prediction
R says




1,000,000 numbers
8 MB
8,000,048 bytes


100,000 rows × 10 columns, in R
8 MB
8.0 MB


same table as CSV
≈ 5 MB (5 characters per value)
4.79 MB


data/seedlings.csv: file / object
tiny
592 bytes / 6,968 bytes




object.size() = bytes in RAM; file.size() = bytes on disk.
For a 24-row table, R’s bookkeeping is bigger than the data. The rule is for large tables.


Students run exactly this code in the practical, so the numbers match theirs. The extra 48 bytes for x are a fixed header. The seedlings tibble is 6,968 bytes because column names, types and the read_csv column specification are stored alongside 96 values.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
section: A CSV stores numbers as text
text:
A CSV stores numbers as text



The text 25.7 with a comma is 5 bytes, the same number in R is 8 bytes, and a long decimal written as text is 19 bytes.


One character = one byte. Rounded values make a CSV smaller than its R object; long decimals make it larger.

A CSV does not store numbers, it stores digits, a decimal point, commas and line endings. 25.7 followed by a comma is five characters. R stores every number in 8 bytes whatever its digits. Unrounded output, such as rnorm values written with all digits, can take 18–19 characters per value.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
section: File size is not RAM size
text:
File size is not RAM size



Rounded numbers: CSV 4.8 MB, in R 8.0 MB.
Add a unique ID per row (S000001, …): CSV only 5.6 MB, in R 14.4 MB. Each different text value costs about 64 bytes.
One million unrounded numbers: CSV 18.6 MB, in R 8.0 MB.
Repeated labels (treated / control) stay cheap: R stores each different text once.





Measured file sizes on disk and object sizes in R for three generated tables: 4.8 versus 8.0 MB, 5.6 versus 14.4 MB, and 18.6 versus 8.0 MB.




All values were measured in R with set.seed(21). The ID column alone is 6.4 MB in RAM but 0.8 MB on disk (8 characters per ID). Lesson: do not read the file size and assume the same RAM; estimate from rows, columns and column types instead.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
section: DNA is text: one byte per letter
text:
DNA is text: one byte per letter


dna <- readLines("data/dna.txt")
nchar(dna)                  # 40
file.size("data/dna.txt")   # 41
bases <- strsplit(dna, split = "")[[1]]
table(bases)  # A 11, C 9, G 9, T 11

40 letters + a line ending = 41 bytes.
Human genome: 3.1 billion letters ≈ 3.1 GB as text.
Split into separate letters in R, each costs 8 bytes: ≈ 25 GB.





The 40-letter course file takes 41 bytes; the human genome as text takes about 3.1 GB, and about 25 GB as separate letters in R.




The sequence in data/dna.txt is invented. strsplit returns a list; [[1]] takes its first element. In R, object.size(dna) is 152 bytes and object.size(bases) is 592 bytes: separate letters cost 8 bytes each. Genome tools store sequences compactly and read them piece by piece rather than loading everything as one R vector.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
section: An image is a grid of numbers
text:
An image is a grid of numbers



Each pixel is a brightness, 0 (black) to 255 (white): 1 byte in an 8-bit file.
data/pixels.csv: 8 × 8 = 64 pixels; 24 are above 100.
A camera image of 2048 × 2048 = 4,194,304 pixels:

file: 4.2 MB;
in R: × 8 bytes = 33.6 MB;
100 time-lapse images in R: 3.4 GB.






The 8 by 8 table of brightness values in pixels.csv and the same values displayed as a grey image.




In R: pixels <- as.matrix(read_csv(“data/pixels.csv”)); sum(pixels > 100) gives 24. A colour image has three values per pixel (red, green, blue), so three times as many bytes. Many microscope cameras store 16-bit images (2 bytes per pixel); the R estimate stays 8 bytes per value.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
How big is biology data?



Sizes on a log scale from 592 bytes for seedlings.csv to 24 GB for a single-cell table, with a dashed line at 16 GB laptop RAM.


Single-cell RNA-seq: 30,000 genes × 100,000 cells × 8 bytes = 24 GB, more than a 16 GB laptop, before any working space.

Each step on the axis is a factor of 100. The course data sit at the far left; real experiments can be millions of times larger. Real single-cell tools store mostly-zero tables compactly, but the plain estimate shows the scale of the problem and why such analyses usually run on bigger computers.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
When RAM runs out



Swapping: the computer moves parts of RAM to the much slower disk. Everything crawls, even the mouse.
R stops: Error: cannot allocate vector of size …, or the session crashes and the Environment is lost.
Estimate first. If 2–3× the estimate is near your RAM: use fewer rows or columns, a compact format, or a bigger computer.





A 24 GB object does not fit in 16 GB of RAM; the computer swaps to disk or R stops with an error.




Do not demonstrate this on a laptop in class; it can freeze the machine. Remind students that the operating system, browser and RStudio already use several GB, so a 16 GB laptop may have much less free. The bigger computer is tomorrow’s topic.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: How a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
Summary







Idea
Key fact




CPU
does the calculations; a few cores


RAM
fast, temporary; R objects live here; emptied when R closes


Disk
slow, permanent; files live here


GPU
thousands of simple cores; images, deep learning; not needed here


RAM for a table
rows × numeric columns × 8 bytes; plan 2–3×


File vs object
CSV text: 1 byte per character; can be smaller or larger than in R


Scale
genome ≈ 3.1 GB as text; 2048² image ≈ 33.6 MB in R; single-cell table ≈ 24 GB



Next (Day 22, remote computer): log in to a bigger computer, move a project there, render, and bring the result back.
Now: Open exercises · Quiz. Leave with data-size.R, output/big-measurements.csv and reports/data-size.txt.

Check that students have recorded their own laptop’s RAM: they will compare it with the remote computer tomorrow.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: The problem: a reading is not a concentration
text:
The problem: a reading is not a concentration



Unknown samples gave absorbance 0.310, 0.520 and 0.900.
On its own, 0.520 means nothing: another instrument, reagent batch or day gives a different reading for the same sample.
Six standards of known concentration, 0 to 10 mg/L, were measured with the samples (data/calibration.csv).
A standard is a calibration point, not a biological replicate.





Six standards of known concentration from 0 to 10 mg/L next to an unknown sample whose concentration we want.




The standards set the scale for this run of the instrument. That is why they are measured each time, in the same run as the unknowns.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Which variable goes on which axis?
text:
Which variable goes on which axis?



We prepared the concentration and measured the absorbance.
So concentration goes on x and absorbance on y:
absorbance = intercept + slope × concentration
Intercept: the fitted reading at 0 mg/L, a background signal (the blank S1 read 0.041).
Slope: the increase in absorbance per 1 mg/L.
The line does not have to pass through every point.





Six prepared standards with absorbance rising from 0.041 to 0.687, and the fitted straight calibration line.




The direction is deliberate: the measured quantity is the response. Later we rearrange the same line to get concentration. Fitting concentration on absorbance would be a different regression and is not used here. The nonzero intercept is a background reading: do not force the line through zero just because zero concentration sounds like nothing.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
text:
Fit the line in R
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
standards <- read_csv("data/calibration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
calibration_fit <- lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l, data = standards)
coef(calibration_fit)
#>        (Intercept) concentration_mg_l
#>         0.03957143         0.06488571

~ reads “explained by”: response on the left, the prepared variable on the right.
Line: absorbance ≈ 0.0396 + 0.0649 × concentration.
Slope units: absorbance per mg/L. Every extra 1 mg/L adds about 0.065 to the reading.


lm() is the same function students use again tomorrow for a biological association. coef() returns the intercept and slope; [1] and [2] select them. Keep the full-precision values in R; round only in the prose.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
text:
Check the residuals



Residual = observed − fitted reading, in absorbance units.
S1: 0.041 − 0.0396 = +0.0014: just above the line.
All six lie within ±0.008 of the line, on both sides, with no curved pattern.
Six standards are limited evidence: the line is checked only between 0 and 10 mg/L.





Residuals of the six standards scatter within about 0.008 absorbance units of zero, without a curved pattern.




residuals(calibration_fit) gives the same values as the hand calculation. Look for curvature (a smile or frown shape) or one point far from the others. A residual is a difference in absorbance, not a concentration error and not a p-value.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
text:
Read the line backwards


Rearrange the line:
concentration = (absorbance − intercept) / slope

U2 read 0.520 → (0.520 − 0.0396) / 0.0649 ≈ 7.40 mg/L.
U1 read 0.310 → 4.17 mg/L.
These are point estimates; the standards and the readings both carry uncertainty that we do not calculate here.





A reading of 0.520 is traced across to the calibration line and down to about 7.40 mg/L.




Trace with a finger: across from the measured reading to the line, then down to concentration. The input is measured; the output is estimated. Use the unrounded coefficients in the calculation.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
text:
Estimate only inside the standards
unknowns <- read_csv("data/unknowns.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
intercept <- coef(calibration_fit)[1]
slope <- coef(calibration_fit)[2]
unknowns <- unknowns |>
  mutate(within_range = absorbance >= min(standards$absorbance) &
                        absorbance <= max(standards$absorbance),
         concentration_mg_l = if_else(
           within_range, (absorbance - intercept) / slope, NA_real_))



sample_id
absorbance
within_range
concentration_mg_l




U1
0.310

4.17

0.900

The standards read 0.041 to 0.687. U3 is above the highest standard, so it gets NA instead of a number.
The row stays in the table with its reading, so the reason for the missing estimate is visible.


& requires both conditions. NA_real_ is a numeric missing value. This is the table saved as output/day19-unknowns.csv in the practical.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
text:
Why not just calculate U3?



The formula happily returns 13.3 mg/L for U3.
But no standard was measured above 10 mg/L. The line might bend there: many assays flatten out at high concentration.
A number you can calculate is not a number you can support.
Report U3 as “above the calibration range” and measure it again, diluted.





U3’s reading of 0.900 lies above every measured standard, outside the range checked by the calibration.




The calibrated range is evidence, not an inconvenience to bypass. Saturation at high concentration is common in absorbance assays; we do not need to know why to respect the range.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Bring a high sample into range by dilution
text:
Bring a high sample into range by dilution


A separate sample was too concentrated, so a new measurement was made:

1.00 mL of sample plus solvent up to 10.00 mL total → dilution factor 10.00 / 1.00 = 10.
The diluted reading, 0.520, is inside the standards → 7.40 mg/L diluted.
Original ≈ 7.404 × 10 ≈ 74.04 mg/L.

The in-range reading is what was measured; the original concentration is calculated from it and the recorded volumes.




The new diluted reading 0.520 gives 7.40 mg/L, and multiplying by the factor 10 gives an original estimate of 74.04 mg/L.




“10.00 mL total” does not mean adding 10 mL of solvent to 1 mL of sample. This is a separate example, not a new reading for U3: U3 still needs its own new measurement. Assume no substance is lost. The uncertainty of the volumes and the calibration is ignored in this simple point estimate.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: Pitfall: rounded coefficients change the answer
text:
Pitfall: rounded coefficients change the answer



Rounding to two decimals gives intercept 0.04 and slope 0.06.
Reading 0.310: 4.17 mg/L with the full coefficients, 4.50 mg/L with the rounded ones.
Reading 0.520: 7.40 versus 8.00 mg/L.
Calculate from coef(calibration_fit); round only the final number you write.





Inverse estimates for readings 0.310 and 0.520 are higher when the coefficients are rounded to two decimals than with the full coefficients.




The slope is small, so rounding it from 0.0649 to 0.06 changes it by about 8 percent, and every estimate with it. This is a deliberate diagnostic; students try it in the practical with round(intercept, 2) and round(slope, 2) in a separate expression. More decimals in a report are not more precision either.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
section: A new instrument needs its own line
text:
A new instrument needs its own line



A second instrument: six standards 0 to 5 mg/L (data/calibration-transfer.csv).
Its own fit: intercept 0.0216, slope 0.1001 per mg/L. The old coefficients do not apply.
X1 read 0.270 → 2.48 mg/L, inside the standards (0.024 to 0.525).
X2 read 0.700 → above range: keep the row, flag it, measure again diluted.





On the second instrument’s calibration, X1 at 0.270 lies within the standard readings and X2 at 0.700 lies above all of them.




Fit as transfer_fit with its own coefficient objects so the main report is not silently changed. Putting 2.48 mg/L back into the forward equation returns 0.270: a useful check of the algebra, but it reuses the same line, so it does not validate the calibration.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
text:
Write the result
“Absorbance increased linearly with concentration across six standards from 0 to 10 mg/L (slope 0.065 absorbance units per mg/L; residuals within ±0.008). Sample U1 was estimated at 4.17 mg/L and U2 at 7.40 mg/L. U3 (absorbance 0.900) was above the highest standard and needs to be diluted and measured again.”







Misreading
Better




“The line fits well, so any concentration is fine.”
Only between the lowest and highest standards.


“U3 is 13.3 mg/L.”
U3 is above the calibration range: no estimate.


“The intercept should be zero.”
It is the background reading; do not force it.


“7.40 mg/L is exact.”
It is a point estimate; uncertainty is not calculated here.




Ask students which code produces each number in the paragraph. They should be able to point at coef(), residuals() and the unknowns table.

title: Turn an instrument reading into a concentration
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Standard
Solution of known concentration, measured in the same run as the samples


Direction
Prepared concentration on x, measured absorbance on y: lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l)


Coefficients
Intercept 0.0396 (background); slope 0.0649 absorbance per mg/L


Residual
Observed − fitted reading; look for curvature or one point far away


Inverse
(absorbance − intercept) / slope: U1 4.17, U2 7.40 mg/L


Range
Estimate only between the lowest and highest standard; U3 → NA with a reason


Dilution
New in-range reading × factor; 1 → 10 mL gives ×10 (7.40 → 74.04 mg/L)


Precision
Calculate with full coefficients; round only the reported result


New instrument
New standards, new fit (slope 0.1001 per mg/L for the transfer data)



Next (Day 20, association): the same lm() on two measured biological variables, where neither was set by us.
Now: open the Day 19 exercises. Make calibration-report.Rmd with the line and residual plots, the slope with units and the range-checked unknowns; save output/day19-unknowns.csv and both figures, then render.

The exercises continue with the rounding diagnostic, the dilution table and an independent transfer-calibration.Rmd for the second instrument.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
text:
About this lecture
On Day 16 the treated seedlings grew 6.22 mm more on average than the controls. But a second experiment with 24 new seedlings would give a different number. How much should we trust 6.22 mm? Almost every results section you will read or write answers this with three numbers: an estimate, a 95% confidence interval, and a p-value.

The estimate is the observed treated-minus-control difference in means, with units and a direction.
The confidence interval is a range of population differences compatible with the data, under the model.
The p-value asks how surprising the data would be if the true means were equal.
Welch’s test (t.test in R) produces all three for two independent groups, without assuming equal spread.

This is a reading and writing day: we do not derive the t formula. We learn to run the test, read every number, and write a result sentence that is correct.

Motivate from the reader’s side: students will meet “mean difference 6.2 mm (95% CI 2.7 to 9.7; p = 0.002)” in every paper and every lab report they mark or write. The aim today is that they can produce that sentence from R and explain each part, including what it does not mean. Continuity: Day 16 set up the comparison and the direction; today adds uncertainty. Day 18 changes the design to paired measurements.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
text:
The problem: groups overlap



Treated mean 21.49 mm, control mean 15.28 mm, 12 plants each.
Difference: 6.22 mm (treated − control).
But the dots overlap: several control plants grew more than several treated plants.
Plants vary. A different random set of 24 would give a different difference.

Question: is 6.22 mm a stable feature of the treatment, or could chance variation between plants produce a gap like this?




The two seedling groups overlap despite a higher treated mean.




Use the figure saved in comparison.Rmd on Day 16. Point at an individual control plant above the treated mean. The inferential question concerns the population mean difference under the study’s conditions, not whether every treated plant beats every control. This is the motivation for the whole day: a difference observed in one sample is a starting point, not a conclusion.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Check the design before any test
text:
Check the design before any test
Welch’s test fits this study because:

Independent units: each plant is its own unit, randomly allocated to a group.
One value per plant: growth = final − initial, computed once.
Unequal spread is allowed: treated SD 4.87 mm vs control SD 3.19 mm is fine for Welch.

A test cannot repair the design:

Repeated readings of the same plant are not extra plants (Day 14).
Before/after on the same plant needs a paired analysis (Day 18).
In very small samples, look at the dots for strong skew or a single dominating value; keep genuine unusual values and ask for advice if the simple model looks unsuitable.


State the assumptions in biological terms, not as a ritual. Welch’s version does not assume equal population variances, which is why it is the default in R. It does assume independence, and nothing in the output will warn you if that is violated. Random allocation is what lets us interpret a difference as a treatment effect within these conditions.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Run the comparison in the direction we named
text:
Run the comparison in the direction we named
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
treated <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "treated")$growth_mm
control <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "control")$growth_mm

comparison <- t.test(treated, control,
                     var.equal = FALSE,          # Welch: spreads may differ
                     alternative = "two.sided",  # a difference in either direction counts
                     conf.level = 0.95)
comparison

The first vector minus the second: here treated − control. The order of arguments sets the sign.
var.equal = FALSE is already the default; writing it makes the method visible to a reader.
Save the result as an object so you can extract numbers: comparison$conf.int, comparison$p.value.


This builds on Day 16’s comparison.Rmd, which already creates the treated and control vectors. Students should run it, not copy numbers from the slide. Emphasise naming the direction in words before running the code, so that the sign of the output is a check rather than a surprise.

text:
Reading the output

Sample sizes are not printed: get them from your data (12 and 12).
The interval and estimate carry mm; t, df and p have no unit.


Ask students to annotate their own printout with exactly these four columns: quantity, value, units, meaning. The difference of means is not printed directly; it is the subtraction of the two printed means. Do not spend time on the t formula; the important skill is knowing which number answers which question and which carry units.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: The estimate and its confidence interval
text:
The estimate and its confidence interval

The estimate 6.22 mm and 95 percent confidence interval 2.70–9.73 mm are shown against zero difference.
Estimate 6.22 mm; 95% CI 2.70 to 9.73 mm.
Zero marks “no difference between population means”. This interval lies entirely above zero.
The interval is about the mean difference, not about individual plants: it does not contain 95% of plants.


Units and sign matter. Read the interval as: population mean differences from about 2.7 to 9.7 mm are compatible with these data under the model. Values near zero are not well supported; neither are differences of 15 mm. Students often read every interval as a spread of individuals; the next two slides separate those ideas.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
text:
What “95%” refers to



Imagine repeating the whole experiment many times, each time computing a new interval.
The true difference is fixed. The intervals move from study to study.
A 95% procedure covers the truth in about 95% of repeats — under its assumptions.
We do not know whether our one interval is one of the hits.





Illustrative repeated studies produce intervals around separate estimates; the true difference is fixed.




This is a conceptual illustration, not additional seedling experiments. Some intervals miss the fixed truth; that is part of what 95% means. The probability statement is about the procedure, not about this particular interval. Avoid “there is a 95% probability the true value is in this interval” — under this frequentist framework the truth is fixed and either inside or not.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Spread among plants is not the difference interval
text:
Spread among plants is not the difference interval

Individual measurements and the estimated mean-difference interval answer different questions.
Left: individual growth values. Spread here is natural variation between plants (SD).
Right: uncertainty in the treated − control mean difference (CI).
Before reading any error bar, ask: which quantity, and on which axis? A figure caption must say.


Students frequently read any bar as individual spread or any bar as a confidence interval. Ask them to identify the axis and the summarised object in each panel before interpreting. Link back to Day 13: if you draw whiskers, define them.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
text:
What the p-value conditions on


Definition: if the two population means were equal (and the assumptions held), how often would a statistic be at least this extreme, in either direction?

Here p ≈ 0.0015: rarely.
The shaded tails lie beyond the observed |t| = 3.70.

It is not:

the probability that the null hypothesis is true;
the probability that the treatment works;
a measure of how large the effect is.





The Welch equal-means reference distribution shades both tails beyond the observed statistic magnitude.




The reference curve uses the actual Welch statistic and approximate degrees of freedom. It is not a distribution of possible treatment effects. The key phrase is “if the means were equal”: the p-value is computed under that model. Two-sided means both tails count. A large biological effect and a tiny one can both give small p-values with enough data, which is why the estimate and interval must be reported too.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Direction is a choice; reversing it flips the interval
text:
Direction is a choice; reversing it flips the interval


reverse <- t.test(control, treated)
comparison$conf.int   #  2.70   9.73
reverse$conf.int      # -9.73  -2.70
comparison$p.value    #  0.0015
reverse$p.value       #  0.0015

Same data, opposite sign: control − treated.
The two-sided p-value is unchanged.
Keep the direction you stated in advance as the reported result; save the check in a separate object.





The same comparison in opposite directions produces reflected confidence intervals.




This is not a new experiment, only the same contrast described in the other direction. The function’s argument order determines the sign, not an object name such as treatment_effect. Using a separate object keeps the primary result intact in the report.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: What makes an interval wider or narrower?
text:
What makes an interval wider or narrower?





The 90%, 95%, and 99% intervals use identical observations but different widths.


Confidence level: 90% → 3.31 to 9.12; 99% → 1.41 to 11.02 mm. More coverage requires a wider interval. Keep 95% as the stated analysis.




Main and transfer study intervals differ in estimate and width while also having different spreads and sample sizes.


Data: width depends on sample size and spread together. The transfer study (9 per group) has a narrower interval than the main study (12 per group) because its plants vary less.


Changing conf.level does not change the observed means; it changes how wide the procedure must be to achieve its long-run coverage. On the right, do not teach “bigger n always gives a narrower interval” when spread also differs: transfer SDs are about 1.9 and 2.5 mm against 4.9 and 3.2 mm in the main study.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
text:
When the interval includes zero

An illustrative 2 mm difference has a 95% interval from −1 to 5 mm, covering zero and both directions.
Illustrative small study: estimate 2 mm, 95% CI −1 to 5 mm.
Both a small harmful and a moderate helpful effect remain compatible with the data.
Including zero is not proof of no effect. “Not significant” means inconclusive here, not equal.


These are illustrative numbers, not output from the course data. Ask students what positive and negative differences remain inside the range. A common error in student reports is writing “the treatment had no effect” from p > 0.05; the honest statement is that this study could not determine the direction.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Write a result, not a threshold label
text:
Write a result, not a threshold label
Good: “Treated seedlings grew on average 6.22 mm more than controls (95% CI 2.70 to 9.73 mm; Welch two-sided test, p ≈ 0.0015; 12 plants per group).”
Then one sentence on biological size and one on design limits.







Misreading
Better




“The null hypothesis has probability 0.0015.”
Under equal means and the assumptions, a statistic this extreme is rare.


“The result is significant.” (alone)
Give estimate, units, interval and p.


“p is small, so the effect is large.”
Size comes from the estimate and interval, not from p.


“p > 0.05, so there is no difference.”
The data are inconclusive about direction.




Random allocation supports a causal comparison within these study conditions, but p alone never establishes causality or generalisation beyond them. Encourage a sentence on biological relevance: is 6 mm over a week a lot for a seedling of about 20 mm? Precision of wording is part of the analysis, not editing afterwards.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
section: Worked example: a second class’s study
text:
Worked example: a second class’s study
transfer <- read_csv("data/seedlings-transfer.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
new_treated <- transfer |> filter(treatment == "treated") |> pull(growth_mm)
new_control <- transfer |> filter(treatment == "control") |> pull(growth_mm)
transfer_test <- t.test(new_treated, new_control)
transfer_test



Quantity
Value




Plants per group
9 and 9


Estimate (treated − control)
4.21 mm


95% CI
1.95 to 6.47 mm


Welch p-value
0.0012



“Treated seedlings grew 4.21 mm more on average (95% CI 1.95–6.47 mm; Welch, p ≈ 0.0012; 9 per group).”

Use transfer from its own saved import and growth calculation in transfer-comparison.Rmd, not leftover console objects. Have students write the result sentence before showing the last line. Point out the estimate is smaller than the main study’s, yet the interval is narrower: less plant-to-plant variation.

title: How uncertain is the difference?
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Estimate
Treated − control difference of means, in mm; direction set by argument order


Welch’s test
Two independent groups; spreads may differ; t.test(x, y)


Design first
Independence and one value per unit; a test cannot repair design


95% CI
Range of mean differences compatible with the data; procedure covers the truth in ~95% of repeats


CI vs SD
CI is uncertainty in the mean difference, not spread of plants


p-value
How extreme the data would be if means were equal — not P(null), not effect size


CI includes 0
Inconclusive about direction, not proof of equality


Reporting
Estimate + units + CI + test + p + n, then size and limits in words



Next (Day 18, paired observations): when each plant is measured twice, the two readings are not independent, and the analysis must keep each pair together.
Now: open the Day 17 exercises. Add the method, estimate, interval, sample sizes and p-value to comparison.Rmd, keep the individual-point plot, restart R, and render.

Recite the result sentence once more as the model answer. The exercises extend comparison.Rmd and transfer-comparison.Rmd; the rendered HTML should be understandable without R’s printout. Students should check direction and units in the rendered output, not only in the console.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
Tell the reader what was measured
text:
One question, one evidence trail


Question: how does seven-day growth vary among plants, and between control and treated seedlings?

Input: data/seedlings.csv, 24 plants in separate pots, 12 per group, lengths in mm.
Source: descriptive-report.Rmd at the project root.
Output: an HTML file that anyone can open.
Each step can be traced to the one before it: question → data → code → result.





A biological question leads to the measured data file, which leads to a rendered report.




The supplied measurements are simulated; plants received control or a nutrient treatment, and the formulation is unspecified. An organic-yield report may replace this context but is not an extra required report. If the teacher asks for the repaired Day 11 data instead, the report must say so and carry 23 usable growth values through all counts.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Give each part of the report a job
text:
Give each part of the report a job



Question: one or two sentences: what and why.
Data and methods: input file, independent unit (one plant), outcome and units, checks, how growth was calculated.
Results: a table with n, mean, median and SD; a figure with individual plants and means; a caption.
Interpretation and limitation: what the numbers show, in words, and what they cannot show yet.





A short report divided into question, data and methods, results with a figure, and interpretation and limitation.




Distinguish methods (what was done) from results (what was found). A caption names the unit and the symbols. The interpretation describes direction, variation and limits; it does not repeat all printed output.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Data and methods: show the checks
text:
Data and methods: show the checks
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
anyDuplicated(seedlings$plant_id)   # 0: each plant ID appears once
seedlings |> count(treatment)       # control 12, treated 12
sum(is.na(seedlings$initial_mm))    # 0 missing
sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm))      # 0 missing
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

These are Day 11’s checks, now inside the report: a reader sees what was checked and the result.
anyDuplicated() returns 0 when there is no repeated ID; a positive number is the position of the first repeat.
In the text: “24 plants (12 per group), no missing lengths, growth = final − initial length (mm).”


Include only checking output that helps the reader; keep the code in the source either way. If the repaired Day 11 file is used, the methods must state the source and that P06 is unavailable, and every count must use 23 usable growths.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Results: a table and a figure that agree
text:
Results: a table and a figure that agree


group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
    mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(group_summary, digits = 2,
  caption = "Growth by treatment; lengths in mm.")

knitr::kable() prints a tidy table, rounded to 2 decimals.
The table is made by code: if the data change, the table changes too.





Individual growth measurements as small dots, with red diamonds marking the control mean of 15.28 and the treated mean of 21.49 millimetres.


Reuse the Day 13 figure: plants as dots, means as diamonds, a caption with n and units.


Control: n 12, mean 15.28, median 15.65, SD 3.19 mm; treated: n 12, mean 21.49, median 20.85, SD 4.87 mm. A caption must make clear that SD describes spread among plants; this report has no confidence intervals. Do not paste a screenshot of the Environment pane.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Interpretation: claims at the level of the evidence
text:
Interpretation: claims at the level of the evidence


Supported: “Treated plants grew a mean of 21.5 mm and controls 15.3 mm (n = 12 each). Treated plants also varied more (SD 4.9 vs 3.2 mm), and the groups overlap.”







Weak sentence
Repair




“The results were good.”
Name the pattern and its size.


“The treated group had more error.”
“Treated plants varied more (SD 4.9 mm).”


“Every treated plant grew more.”
False: the groups overlap.







Measured plants support a sample description; a further jump to a universal cause is crossed out.


We described the sample. Estimating how uncertain the difference is comes in week 4.


The smallest treated plant grew 12.2 mm, less than most controls, so “every treated plant” fails. “The computer removed the bad values” is another weak sentence from the exercises: say which value was changed and which source evidence justified it. In the organic alternative, a higher mean yield does not establish greater purity or a better method in general.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Every number has a visible origin
text:
Every number has a visible origin



A reader should be able to trace each number in the text back to a saved input and a chunk of code.
Inline R puts a calculated value straight into a sentence. In the source:
We measured `r nrow(seedlings)` plants.
renders as “We measured 24 plants.”
The object must be created earlier in the report. The sentence still needs units and meaning.





A saved input CSV feeds analysis chunks, which produce the table and the prose in the report.




The literal inline code is shown with escaped characters so this slide does not try to run it. When students render their report, the inline expression is calculated. In the exercises they add two inline values: one count and one mean or SD.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Keep the report where its paths work
text:
Keep the report where its paths work



Save descriptive-report.Rmd at the project root, beside data/ and output/.
Then "data/seedlings.csv" means the same file on every computer that has the project.
A path like C:/Users/anna/Downloads/... works only on Anna’s laptop.
Render from the R Console, putting the HTML into reports/:

rmarkdown::render("descriptive-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")




The report source sits at the project root beside its data and output folders; a personal absolute path would not move with the folder.




Knitting resolves relative paths from the report’s own folder, so moving the .Rmd into reports/ would break data/ paths. The output_dir argument places the HTML in reports/ while the source stays at the root. Never put a render call inside the report itself: a report must not try to render itself.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Render from files, not from memory
text:
Render from files, not from memory



Restart R, then render. The report must load its own packages, import its data and create every object.
An object that exists only in your Environment pane is not part of the report; on another computer it is missing.
Best test: copy the project to a new folder, render there. Record any failure, fix it, rerun.
A .Rproj file does not contain the data. The CSV must travel with the report.





A fresh session rebuilds the new HTML from the saved data and saved report source; old console objects are not an input.




Installation commands belong in setup, not in an analysis that should run repeatedly. If rendering fails, read the first meaningful error and the chunk name. A rendered report on a supervisor’s computer is the real test.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Adapt the structure to a new study, not the old conclusion
text:
Adapt the structure to a new study, not the old conclusion


The second class’s data, data/seedlings-transfer.csv, go into transfer-description.Rmd.

18 plants, 9 per group; treated mean 17.87 mm (SD 1.94), control 13.66 mm (SD 2.53).
Here the treated plants vary less, the opposite of the first study.
Replace imports, counts, numbers, captions and sentences together. A new title on an old report is still the old report.





In the transfer study, treated plants have a higher mean growth than controls but their points are less spread out.




If students used the transfer data in earlier scripts, they recreate its objects inside the new report rather than relying on the Environment pane. A sentence copied from the first report (“treated plants varied more”) would now be false.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
section: Two reviews before you hand it in
text:
Two reviews before you hand it in


Reader review (code closed, HTML only)

What was the question?
What is one unit, and how many were there?
Which file, which outcome, which units?
What do the dots and diamonds mean?
What is the main pattern and its main limitation?


Analyst review (source open)

Does every number match a table or chunk?
Is n the number of usable values?
Were all transformations written in code?
Does it render after restarting R, in a fresh folder?
Is there a change log: issue, correction, rerun?


Remove a redundant printout before you remove a unit label or a limitation.

The exercises include a revision log in reports/day15-revision.txt. The organic alternative has 12 runs, six per protocol, with yields in percent and SD in percentage points; the same reviews apply.

title: Tell the reader what was measured
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Structure
Question → data and methods → results (table + figure) → interpretation and limitation


Input
Name the file; show checks for IDs, labels, missing values; state n (24 plants, 12 per group)


Results
Table from code (knitr::kable()), figure with plants and means, caption with n and units


Claims
Describe the sample (means 21.5 vs 15.3 mm, overlap, SD); no tested effect yet


Lineage
Every number traceable to data and code; inline R for counts and means


Location
.Rmd at project root; render from the Console with output_dir = "reports"


Fresh session
Restart R and render; test in a new folder; the data travel with the report


New study
Adapt the structure; replace every number, caption and sentence



Next (Day 16, comparisons): turn the description into a comparison: state the question, the direction (treated − control) and the independent units before calculating a difference.
Now: open the Day 15 exercises. Leave with descriptive-report.Rmd (or organic-report.Rmd) and its rendered HTML, with the data needed to render it.

No hypothesis test is required today. Avoid spending the session on cosmetic formatting while inputs or interpretation remain unclear.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
Summarise without hiding the observations
section: The problem: means alone hide the plants
text:
The problem: means alone hide the plants



Left: only the two group means, 15.28 and 21.49 mm.
Right: the same means with the 24 plants behind them.
Now you can see that the groups overlap, that one treated plant grew only 12.2 mm, and that two treated plants grew about 30 mm.
You can also count the plants: 12 per group.





Left panel shows two group means alone; right panel shows the same means together with the individual plant growth values, which overlap between groups.




Ask which panel lets a reader check the claim “treated plants grew more”. With the points, they can see it is true of the means but not of every plant. The point plot does not need to be cluttered: a small horizontal jitter separates overlapping dots without changing their measured heights.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: A summary is a new, smaller table
text:
A summary is a new, smaller table



seedlings: 24 rows, one per plant.
group_summary: 2 rows, one per treatment.
The two summary rows are not two new plants; they describe groups.
Keep both tables. The plant table feeds the individual points; the summary feeds the mean markers.





Twenty-four plant measurements on the left are compressed into two group summary values on the right.




Show both objects in the RStudio Environment pane and compare their dimensions. Summarising deliberately throws away detail; that is why we keep the plant-level table for plotting and for any later test.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: One row per group with group_by() and summarise()
text:
One row per group with group_by() and summarise()
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_plants = n(),
            n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
            mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")



treatment
n_plants
n_observed
mean_mm
median_mm
sd_mm




control
12
12
15.28
15.65
3.19


treated
12
12
21.49
20.85
4.87




group_by(treatment): do the next step separately for each treatment. summarise() returns one row per group.
n() counts rows (plant records); sum(!is.na(growth_mm)) counts usable measurements (! means “not”).
.groups = "drop" leaves an ordinary table. Check one mean by hand: mean(filter(seedlings, treatment == "control")$growth_mm).


Start day13-groups.R with library(readr), library(dplyr) and library(ggplot2), as in the practical. Read the pipe aloud: take seedlings, then group by treatment, then summarise. The names on the left of = become column names. The values in the table are rounded for display; the object keeps full precision.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: Always report how many plants contributed
text:
Always report how many plants contributed



In the complete file both groups have 12 plants and 12 growths.
Summarise the repaired Day 11 file (output/seedlings-cleaned.csv) and control has 12 plants but 11 growths: P06 is unknown.
Its control mean is 15.21 mm, not 15.28 mm: a different set of plants contributed.
That is why the table has both n_plants and n_observed. A reader needs the n next to every mean.





In the repaired file both groups keep twelve plant records, but one control plant has no usable growth value, leaving eleven.




Missingness changes the contributing count without inventing a zero. The counts belong beside the summaries, not hidden in an undocumented filter. The control SD in the repaired file is 3.34 mm.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: Plot the plants, then add the means
text:
Plot the plants, then add the means


group_plot <- ggplot(seedlings,
    aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(
    width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 13),
    alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = group_summary,
    aes(x = treatment, y = mean_mm),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 18,
    size = 4, colour = "darkred") +
  labs(x = "Treatment",
       y = "Change in seedling length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()




Individual growth measurements as small dots, with red diamonds marking the control mean of 15.28 and the treated mean of 21.49 millimetres.



First layer: plants from seedlings. Second layer: means from group_summary.
height = 0: dots move sideways only; their measured heights never change.



inherit.aes = FALSE means the second layer gets its own mapping, because group_summary has no growth_mm column. The seed makes the jitter identical each time the script runs. Ask students to find one plant above and one below each mean.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: If you draw whiskers, say what they are
text:
If you draw whiskers, say what they are



These whiskers show mean ± SD: how much plants vary around the mean.
Another figure’s whiskers may show a confidence interval (Day 17): how uncertain the mean is. They can look identical.
A caption that says only “error bars” leaves the reader guessing.
Fine choice for today: show the points and the means, no whiskers.





Diamonds with whiskers show mean plus or minus sample standard deviation beside the individual plant measurements.




Ask: what could a reader infer from a caption that simply says “error bars”? Too little. The treated whisker is longer because the treated SD (4.87 mm) is larger than the control SD (3.19 mm). The CI comes later in the course with a different meaning.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: A histogram shows the shape of a distribution
text:
A histogram shows the shape of a distribution


ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = growth_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 4,
    boundary = 0, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ treatment, ncol = 1)

Growth is cut into 4 mm bins; bar height = number of plants in each bin.
facet_wrap() gives one panel per group on a shared axis.
A histogram shows shape and gaps, but not individual plants or their identities.





Separate histograms show the counts of control and treated growth values in four-millimetre bins on a common axis.




The vertical axis counts plants, not a biological response. With 12 plants per group, every bin has only a few plants. In the treated panel, the two plants near 30 mm form their own bar.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: The bin width shapes the picture
text:
The bin width shapes the picture



The same 12 control values with bins of 2, 4 and 6 mm.
With 2 mm bins there appear to be gaps and peaks; with 6 mm the shape looks smooth.
Nothing about the plants changed: only a display choice.
With small samples, describe only features that survive several bin widths, and state the bin width you used.





The same twelve control growth values drawn as histograms with bin widths of 2, 4 and 6 millimetres look noticeably different.




The same caution applies to axis ranges: stretching the vertical axis can make a difference look larger or smaller without changing a single measurement. Compare figures by reading their axes, not their visual impression. Invite students to compare the dot plot with all three histograms.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: Write a caption the reader can check
text:
Write a caption the reader can check


Weak: “Treatment makes everything larger; error is shown.”
Better: “Seven-day growth (mm) of individually potted seedlings. Each dot is one plant (n = 9 per group); diamonds are group means. No error bars are shown.”
A caption names:

the unit (one plant) and outcome with units;
what each symbol means;
the n, and what any whiskers represent.





Point plot of the transfer study: dots are individual plants and diamonds are group means, nine plants per group.




The figure is from the second class’s study (data/seedlings-transfer.csv), which students summarise independently in the exercises. “Everything larger” is contradicted by the overlap; “error” is undefined. Ask students to repair a weak caption in three specific places.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
section: Save the table and the figure as files
text:
Save the table and the figure as files
write_csv(group_summary, "output/growth-summary.csv")
ggsave("output/growth-summary.png", plot = group_plot, width = 6, height = 4)

A CSV stores the numbers; a PNG stores the picture. The object in R is neither until you save it.
Use different file names for each study, e.g. output/day13-transfer-summary.csv.
Reader test: close RStudio, open the PNG and CSV from the file manager. Can you find one plant, a mean, the units and the n?


After saving, ask students to find the two ordinary files in a file manager and say which application could open each. Restarting R and rerunning the script confirms the outputs come from the script and the raw data.

title: Summarise without hiding the observations
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Summary table
group_by() + summarise(): one row per group; 2 rows are not 2 new plants


Counts
n() counts records, sum(!is.na()) counts usable values; report n with every mean


Seedlings
Control 15.28 mm (SD 3.19), treated 21.49 mm (SD 4.87), 12 each


Points + means
Plant table for dots, summary table for diamonds; jitter sideways only


Whiskers
Mean ± SD and a confidence interval look alike: always say which


Histogram
Counts per bin; with small n the bin width changes the apparent shape


Caption
Unit, outcome and units, symbols, n, meaning of any whiskers


Outputs
CSV for numbers, PNG for figures, both regenerated by the script



Next (Day 14, replicates and uncertainty): what counts as an independent plant, and how much a mean would change if we repeated the sampling.
Now: open the Day 13 exercises. Leave with day13-groups.R, output/growth-summary.csv, output/growth-summary.png and a caption.

The organic-yield option in the practical reuses exactly the same steps (group_by(protocol)), with SD in percentage points; it replaces, not adds to, the repaired-seedling summary. No test is introduced today.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
Check the measurement, then calculate
section: The problem: one slip changes the result
text:
The problem: one slip changes the result



In the export, plant P21’s final length is 4.38. The source notebook says 43.8 mm: the value was typed in centimetres.
Left as it is, P21 “grew” −19.2 mm.
That one cell pulls the treated mean from 21.49 mm down to 18.21 mm.
R prints both numbers with the same confidence. Only a check against the source tells them apart.





Treated growth values with P21 left as 4.38 (one point far below zero, group mean 18.21 mm) and with P21 corrected to 43.8 mm (group mean 21.49 mm).




This is the motivation for the whole day. Ask: if this mean went into a report, who would notice? Usually nobody, until a reviewer or a repeat experiment disagrees. The treated means are computed after the other documented repairs (labels, P18, duplicate). The correction of P21 is justified by the notebook entry, not by the fact that the value looks small.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: What is wrong with this export?
text:
What is wrong with this export?


The study has 24 plants; data/seedlings-messy.csv has 25 rows.

P01 appears twice: one plant, two identical rows.
Treatment is written control, Control and treated (with a trailing space).
P18’s initial length is the text 18.7 mm.
P21’s final length is 4.38 (centimetres).
P06 has no final length.

data/field-notes.txt records what actually happened for each case.




One plant, P01, produces two identical file records that point to the same measured plant.




Open the CSV in a text editor first so students see the raw characters. A repeated ID is a question, not automatically an error: in a design with one row per time point, repeated IDs are expected. Here the protocol says one row per plant, and the field notes confirm that the second P01 row is an import duplicate.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Keep the original; repair in a script
text:
Keep the original; repair in a script



Never edit the raw CSV by hand. Keep it exactly as received.
Make each repair in day11-cleaning.R and write a new derived file.
For every changed value, the trail is: observation → evidence → action → check.
Then you, a supervisor or a reviewer can see each change, why it was made, and rerun it.





Preserve the raw CSV, explain the changes in a repair script, and recreate a separate clean CSV.




A hand-edited spreadsheet loses the record of what was changed. A script is a record: the comments say which source note justified each line. In the exercises students write output/cleaning-notes.txt with one line per problem: plant, observation, evidence, action.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Inspect the entries as text first
text:
Inspect the entries as text first
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
raw <- read_csv("data/seedlings-messy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), trim_ws = FALSE)
dim(raw)                                   # 25 rows, 4 columns
unique(raw$treatment)                      # "control" "Control" "treated" "treated "
raw |> count(plant_id) |> filter(n > 1)    # P01 appears twice

col_character() reads every column as text, so 18.7 mm and 4.38 stay visible instead of being guessed or turned into missing values.
trim_ws = FALSE keeps the trailing space in "treated "; the default would hide it.
count() finds repeated IDs. Then look at both P01 rows in full before deciding anything.


Demonstrate the printed output and point at the quoted “treated” value. We are not asking beginners to memorise importer options; explain why these options help inspect this particular file. If two rows shared an ID but disagreed in a measurement, they would need investigation, not arbitrary deletion.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: A suspicious value is a question, not a verdict
text:
A suspicious value is a question, not a verdict



4.38 is not wrong because it is small. It is wrong because the notebook records 43.8 mm.
"18.7 mm" becomes the number 18.7 only after we confirm the unit is millimetres.
A very small or large value without source evidence stays in the data. Plants really do vary.
If you cannot decide, ask the person who recorded it, and note the open question.





Rulers show the same length expressed as 43.8 millimetres and 4.38 centimetres; only the source notebook justifies correcting P21.




The field notes end with: “A low or high measurement by itself is not sufficient reason to change or exclude it.” Read that sentence aloud. Deleting inconvenient biological values to make a result look cleaner is a serious error in research. A confirmed transcription slip is different.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
text:
Unknown is different from zero



P06’s final length was not recorded. Keep it as NA (not available).
A zero would claim the plant shrank to nothing: growth −24.7 mm (its initial length was 24.7 mm).
That invented value pulls the overall mean from 18.49 mm to 16.69 mm.
Do not copy a value from another file to fill the gap either. Report the plant as missing.





The overall mean growth is 18.49 mm when P06 is kept as missing, and 16.69 mm when its final length is invented as zero.




A measured zero growth would mean that initial and final readings were equal: a real observation. A missing value means we do not know. Spreadsheets sometimes turn blanks into zeros on export; always check how missing values are coded. In the exercises students make a separate object wrong_zero_example to see this effect, and keep it apart from the corrected table.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
text:
The repair, step by step
cleaned <- raw |>
  mutate(treatment = tolower(trimws(treatment)),                       # P03, P15 labels
         initial_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P18", "18.7", initial_mm),  # unit text removed
         final_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P21", "43.8", final_mm)) |>   # notebook value
  distinct() |>                                                         # identical P01 row
  mutate(initial_mm = parse_double(initial_mm),
         final_mm = parse_double(final_mm),
         growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

trimws() removes edge spaces; tolower() makes Control into control.
if_else() changes one identified record only, never “every small value”.
distinct() removes rows that are identical in every column; we use it only because the P01 rows are identical and the notes confirm the duplicate.
P06 stays missing: parse_double() keeps the blank as NA.


Each line maps to one sentence in the field notes; ask students to say which. distinct(plant_id, .keep_all = TRUE) would silently keep one of two disagreeing records and is not used here. The raw object and the CSV on disk are unchanged.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Count records and usable measurements separately
text:
