Count records and usable measurements separately


nrow(cleaned)                 # 24 plants
sum(is.na(cleaned$growth_mm)) # 1 unknown
mean(cleaned$growth_mm)       # NA
mean(cleaned$growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
                              # 18.49 (23 plants)

NA from mean() is R telling you a value is unknown. Good.
na.rm = TRUE gives the mean of the 23 available growths. Report it as such: “n = 23 of 24 plants”.





Both groups retain twelve plant records; one control plant lacks a usable growth value, giving 11 available control growths and 12 treated.




Ask students to predict both mean calls before running them. The first returns NA; the second is about 18.49 mm across 23 available growth values, both groups combined. Control has 12 records but 11 usable growths. Removing a missing value inside a mean does not remove it from the report.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: Save, read back, and check the file on disk
text:
Save, read back, and check the file on disk
write_csv(cleaned, "output/seedlings-cleaned.csv")
check_copy <- read_csv("output/seedlings-cleaned.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(check_copy)                      # 24
anyDuplicated(check_copy$plant_id)    # 0: no repeated ID
sum(is.na(check_copy$growth_mm))      # 1: P06
check_copy |> count(treatment)        # control 12, treated 12

An object in the Environment pane is not the file a colleague receives. Check the saved file.
Then restart R and rerun the whole script: the raw CSV still has 25 rows, the derived CSV has 24. That difference is expected and documented.


The output folder already exists in the course project. Restarting R is the test that the script, not leftover console work, produces the file. Students also write output/cleaning-notes.txt describing each change and the value left unknown.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
section: A new file is a new source to check
text:
A new file is a new source to check


A second class sends data/seedlings-transfer.csv: 18 plants, 9 per group.
Before importing, write down what you expect: what one row is, which ID must be unique, column names, units, allowed labels. Then check and record what you observe.

No source note reports an error in this file, so no correction is justified.
An unusual value: inspect it, keep it, and ask the recorder.





Initial against final length for the eighteen transfer plants, coloured by control and treated group; a new study needs its own checks.




The data dictionary in data/README.md gives the meanings and units. The checks are the familiar ones: nrow, unique IDs, unique labels, missing values, numeric types, and whether final minus initial can be calculated. Students record what they observed, not just “passed”. Their handover must state that no correction was supported.

title: Check the measurement, then calculate
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Inspect first
Read as text (col_character(), trim_ws = FALSE); unique(), count() reveal labels and repeated IDs


Evidence
A value is changed only when a source record supports it, never because it looks odd


Raw file
Never edited; repairs live in a script that writes a separate derived file


Duplicates
Compare all fields and the design; distinct() only for confirmed identical rows


Missing
Unknown stays NA; a zero is a claim (P06 would “grow” −24.7 mm)


Counts
24 plant records, 23 usable growths; report the n behind every mean


Check
Read the saved file back; restart R and rerun the script



Next (Day 12, variation): with a table we can trust, we describe how much individual plants differ from each other, not only their average.
Now: open the Day 11 exercises. Leave with day11-cleaning.R, output/seedlings-cleaned.csv and your cleaning notes.

Ask for one sentence: which source fact justified each change, and which measurement stayed unknown? The exercises add the cleaning notes, the effect of the P21 slip and of an invented zero, and a check of the transfer file.

title: A report that runs its calculations
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
text:
Copied numbers go stale



Top: numbers copied by hand into Word stay old when the data are corrected. Bottom: a rendered report is rebuilt from the corrected data.



Copy and paste: every correction means finding and retyping every affected number and figure.
R Markdown: correct the data, render again, and text, numbers and figures all agree.


Ask who has had to redo a figure in a lab report after a correction. The point is not that Word is bad for writing; it is that results should come from the analysis, not from memory or the clipboard.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: One source file, one readable report
text:
One source file, one readable report



report.Rmd is the source: your text plus R code. You edit this.
Rendering runs the code and writes report.html: text, results and figures.
The HTML is a reading copy. Edits made there are lost at the next render.
Keep the .Rmd, the data and the HTML together.





An R Markdown source with text and code is rendered into an HTML report containing a plot.




Open the supplied report.Rmd next to its rendered HTML. The source alone does not contain the CSV; it only names it.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
text:
Inside an .Rmd file


---
title: "Seedling growth"
output: html_document
---

## Question

How much did the seedlings grow?

```{r import}
library(readr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
```



Header between the --- lines: title and output format.
Text as you would write it. ## Question is a heading.
Code chunk between ```{r} and ```. import is the chunk’s label; each label must be unique.
# outside a chunk makes a heading; inside a chunk it starts an R comment.



The supplied template has this structure. Students should not have to type the fences from memory; copy from the template. The .Rmd stays in the project root so that data/seedlings.csv points to the data.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
text:
Render it


Save, then click Knit. Or type in the Console:
rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd",
                  output_dir = "reports")

Never put this line inside the report: a report must not render itself.
output_dir puts the HTML in reports/; the .Rmd stays in the project folder.





The report source, the original data and the HTML output have different roles and are kept together.




Knit may put the HTML next to the source instead; find the actual file rather than assuming. rmarkdown::render calls the render function from the rmarkdown package without loading the whole package.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Chunks run from top to bottom
text:
Chunks run from top to bottom



Rendering runs chunks in order, like a script from the top.
A plot of growth_mm must come after the chunk that calculates it.
library() and the import go first.
Installing packages is setup, not part of the report.





Loading packages and importing come first, then calculating growth, then plotting and interpreting.




In the exercises students move a plot chunk above the calculation on purpose, read the error, and move it back.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
text:
The report starts from nothing



Knit starts a fresh R session. Objects you made in the Console do not exist there.
So every import and calculation the report needs must be written in the report.
The test: restart R, then render. If it works, the report is complete.





An object in your interactive R session does not exist when the report is rendered in a fresh session.




A report that only works after some Console typing cannot be reproduced by anyone else. The direct render() call can see Console objects, which is why the course always says “restart R, then render”.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
text:
Put calculated numbers into sentences


In the text of the .Rmd:
There are `r nrow(seedlings)` plants.
The HTML reads: There are 24 plants.

Import the 18-plant transfer study instead, and it reads 18. No retyping.
But words you typed yourself, such as “twelve per group”, do not update. Reread the text when the data change.





The number in the sentence is calculated from the imported table.




Inline R removes stale copied numbers, but it cannot fix a description of the wrong study. The transfer-report exercise asks students to search their source for “24” and the old filename.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
text:
A figure with a caption
```{r growth-figure, fig.cap="Each point is one independently potted seedling."}
ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 8)) +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)")
```


Reuse the plotting code from Day 8; add library(ggplot2) to the first chunk.
The caption says what the figure shows. A sentence below it says what you see in it.


Code can stay visible in these first reports so the method is easy to inspect. The caption names the unit of observation; the prose interprets.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: When rendering stops: read the first error
text:
When rendering stops: read the first error


The message names the chunk. Check, in order:

Is the package loaded (library()) before use?
Are file and column names spelt exactly right?
Is the object made in an earlier chunk?
Are all chunk labels unique, every fence closed?

Change one thing, render again.




Two chunks both labelled import stop the render; giving them different labels fixes it.




In the workshop copy students break one thing at a time (duplicate label, misspelt file, plot before calculation), record the message and the repair in reports/render-recovery.txt, and restore a working render each time. Recovery, not memorising messages.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
section: Sharing the .Rmd alone is not enough
text:
Sharing the .Rmd alone is not enough



The report reads data/seedlings.csv. Someone who gets only report.Rmd cannot render it.
Share the project folder: .Rproj, .Rmd, data/, output/, reports/, with the same layout.
A screenshot or a shortcut does not replace the data file.





Rendering the HTML needs both the report source and its input data file.




The last exercise copies the project to another folder and renders it from there. Moving the .Rmd into reports/ would break its relative data path.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: A report that runs its calculations
text:
Summary







Idea
Key fact




Why
Results come from the data at every render; no copied numbers that go stale


Source and output
Edit report.Rmd; report.html is a reading copy, rebuilt at each render


Parts
Header between ---; text; code chunks between fences, each with a unique label


Render
Knit, or rmarkdown::render() in the Console, never inside the report


Order
Chunks run top to bottom: packages, import, calculation, then plot


Fresh session
The report must contain every step; restart R, then render to test


Inline R
`r nrow(seedlings)` puts a calculated number in a sentence; typed words still need checking


Errors
Read the first error and its chunk label; change one thing at a time


Sharing
.Rmd plus data in the same project layout



Next (Day 10, first report): write a short report that answers a biological question and that someone else can rerun.
Now: open the Day 9 exercises. Leave with report.Rmd (question, methods, labelled figure, interpretation) and its rendered HTML, rendered again after restarting R.

Start the exercises by rendering the unchanged template, so there is a known working baseline. Extended work: report-workshop.Rmd with deliberate errors, transfer-report.Rmd for the 18-plant study, and render-recovery.txt.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: Why not just open it in a spreadsheet?
text:
Why not just open it in a spreadsheet?



Day 1: a spreadsheet turned the gene name SEPT2 into the date 2-Sep.
Size limits fail silently too. The old .xls format stops at 65,536 rows; in 2020 this hid about 16,000 positive COVID-19 tests in the UK.
read_csv() reads the file and leaves it unchanged on disk. Every check, such as the number of rows, is a line in your script.





An old .xls sheet holds at most 65,536 rows; the rows beyond the limit are not saved, without any warning.




The data were not wrong; the container was too small and nothing warned anyone. In R, the size of a table is checked with one line (dim), which we do shortly.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: A file on disk, a table in memory
text:
A file on disk, a table in memory



As on Day 1, a CSV is plain text: a header line with column names, then one line per row.
read_csv() reads it and creates a table object in R’s memory.
Changing the object does not change the file. Changing the file does not change the object until you import again.





read_csv reads the saved seedling file into a 24-row, four-column object in R memory.




Same disk versus memory distinction as week 1 and Day 6. Open seedlings.csv in a text editor once so students see the commas. The raw file stays exactly as supplied all course.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: First: is R looking in the right folder?
text:
First: is R looking in the right folder?


getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")

getwd() should print your project folder, not data.
The second line should print TRUE.
data/seedlings.csv is a relative path: it starts from the project folder, so it works on a classmate’s computer too.





The course project folder contains data with seedlings.csv, next to output and reports.



If you get FALSE: open introcomputing.Rproj from the extracted folder. Do not paste your personal path into the code.

Common causes of FALSE: working inside the ZIP preview, an extra folder level from extraction, or a different project open. Fix by opening the right project, not by writing C:/Users/anna/… into every line.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
text:
Import and inspect


library(readr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
dim(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
str(seedlings)


library(readr) loads the importer. Installed once; loaded in every new session.
head() shows the first 6 rows only, not the whole table.
dim(): 24 rows, 4 columns.
str(): plant_id and treatment are text (chr); the lengths are numbers (num).



read_csv returns a tibble, a kind of table. show_col_types = FALSE only hides a message; it does not replace looking at the types with str(). Have students copy column names from names() rather than typing from memory.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
text:
What does one row mean?



One row is one plant. P01: control, 25.7 mm at the start, 44.3 mm seven days later.
Two lengths in one row are the same plant measured twice, not two plants.
plant_id and treatment are labels; the _mm columns are measurements.
The file does not say “mm” or “seven days”: that comes from data/README.md.





Plant IDs and treatments are labels; initial and final lengths are numeric measurements in millimetres.




Read P01’s row aloud. The header is not an observation. Units, random allocation and the fact that the data are simulated are all in the data dictionary, not in anything R can compute.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
text:
One column, one vector
seedlings$initial_mm
length(seedlings$initial_mm)    # 24
mean(seedlings$initial_mm)      # 22.47

$ picks one column by name and gives a vector, like those on Day 6.
24 values: one per plant. The header is not counted.
The mean initial length is 22.47 mm. Always give the unit: R only sees numbers.
This mean mixes both groups, so it says nothing yet about the treatment.


Ask students to say the result as a full sentence with unit and what was averaged. Comparing the groups is Day 8 and week 3.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
text:
Missing is not zero


mean(c(10, NA, 20))                # NA
mean(c(10, NA, 20), na.rm = TRUE)  # 15
mean(c(10, 0, 20))                 # 10
sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm))     # 0

NA = not available: no reading exists.
na.rm = TRUE leaves it out: mean of two values.
Writing 0 instead invents a plant of zero length.





Leaving out one unavailable reading gives a mean of 15; a genuine zero gives a mean of 10.




R refuses to give a mean when a value is NA unless asked: it will not pretend all values are known. In a report, say how many values were missing and why if known. seedlings.csv is complete; the messy version on Day 11 is not.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
text:
Worked example: a second study


transfer <- read_csv("data/seedlings-transfer.csv",
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
dim(transfer)                       # 18 4
tail(transfer)
length(unique(transfer$plant_id))   # 18
table(transfer$treatment)           # 9 9
sum(is.na(transfer$final_mm))       # 0




The transfer study has 18 plants, nine per group.




A new name, transfer, so the 24-plant seedlings table is not overwritten.
18 rows, 18 distinct IDs, 9 per group, nothing missing: what the study description promises.


tail shows the last rows; head alone could hide problems at the end. unique() counts distinct IDs; repeated IDs would prompt investigation here because the design has one row per plant. Random allocation is stated in the design, not visible in the rows.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
section: A plausible table can still be the wrong one
text:
A plausible table can still be the wrong one



Two studies can have the same column names. Both import without errors.
Check the numbers against the description: 24 plants or 18? 12 or 9 per group?
Same for a lab table: solutions.csv has 6 rows, 5 columns. Mass (g) and molar mass (g/mol) are both numbers, but adding them is meaningless.





Two study folders hold measurement tables with similar columns, one with 24 and one with 18 plant records.




A wrong file with a plausible name produces plausible output. A numeric type tells you R can do arithmetic, not that the arithmetic makes sense; the dictionary says what each column means.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
text:
Write down what you checked
A useful import note gives evidence, not just “checked”:

data/seedlings-transfer.csv: 18 rows × 4 columns, 18 distinct plant IDs, 9 control and 9 treated, no missing lengths. Lengths in mm, seven days apart (from data/README.md). Simulated teaching data.


Facts from R: rows, columns, types, IDs, group counts, missing values.
Facts from the dictionary: units, what one row is, how plants were allocated.


The practical asks for reports/transfer-import-audit.txt and reports/solutions-import-audit.txt. Unusual values prompt questions, never silent deletion.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Read a table without losing its meaning
text:
Summary







Idea
Key fact




Why code, not a spreadsheet
read_csv() leaves the file unchanged; spreadsheets can silently convert or drop data (row limits)


File vs object
The CSV stays on disk; the imported table lives in R’s memory


Relative path
data/seedlings.csv from the project folder; check with file.exists()


Inspect
dim(), names(), str(), head(), tail(): 24 × 4 for seedlings.csv


Rows and columns
One row = one plant; IDs and groups are labels; lengths are measurements in mm


Missing
NA is not 0; na.rm = TRUE leaves it out of that calculation; report how many


Meaning
Units and design come from data/README.md, not from R



Next (Day 8, transform and plot): calculate each plant’s growth as a new column and draw a figure where every point is a plant.
Now: open the Day 7 exercises. Leave with day07.R, which imports and inspects seedlings.csv and leaf-mass.csv and runs from the top after a restart.

The extended exercises inspect the 18-plant transfer study and solutions.csv and save two short audit notes in reports/.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Meet R and RStudio
Meet R and RStudio
text:
Two programs: R and RStudio



R calculates.
RStudio is the window you work in. It starts R for you.
Four panes: Editor, Console, Environment, Files / Plots / Help.
The Editor shows saved files. The Console is a conversation with R.





RStudio has four panes: the Editor for saved files, the Console where R runs instructions, the Environment listing objects in memory, and Files, Plots and Help.




Open RStudio on the projector and point at each pane in turn. The arrangement can be changed, so name panes by their job. The Editor only appears once a file is open.

title: Meet R and RStudio
text:
Open the course project



Open your extracted introcomputing-course folder.
Double-click introcomputing.Rproj.
Top right should say introcomputing.

R now works inside this folder, so data/seedlings.csv is found: the relative paths from Day 2.




Double-clicking introcomputing.Rproj opens RStudio with the course folder as working folder; getwd ends in introcomputing-course and file.exists for data/seedlings.csv is TRUE.




Demonstrate from the file manager, not from RStudio’s recent list. Type getwd() and file.exists(“data/seedlings.csv”) in the Console. If a student gets FALSE: check the project name in the corner; look for a ZIP preview or an extra nested folder level, as on day 1.

title: Meet R and RStudio
section: Console or terminal? Look at the prompt
text:
Console or terminal? Look at the prompt



The R Console answers 44.3 minus 25.7 with 18.6 but does not know pwd; the shell knows pwd but answers 44.3 minus 25.7 with command not found.


> waits for R. $ waits for the shell. An error in the wrong window means move the instruction, not the computer is broken.

RStudio also has a Terminal tab next to the Console. It is a shell, like the one from days 3 and 4 (on Windows it may not be the Ubuntu shell). In this course R goes in the Console; shell commands stay in the usual terminal. Let students deliberately type pwd in the Console once to see the message.

title: Meet R and RStudio
text:
A first calculation


In the Console:
44.3 - 25.7
[1] 18.6
P01 grew from 25.7 mm to 44.3 mm: 18.6 mm.


[1] marks the first value printed. It is not part of the answer.
A + prompt means R waits for the rest. Finish the line, or press Esc.
Try P02: 32.3 − 24.3 gives 8.



Everyone types this, not only watches. Then show the + prompt by typing “44.3 -” and Enter, and how Esc brings back >. Numbers are from data/seedlings.csv (simulated).

title: Meet R and RStudio
section: A supplied plot of all 24 seedlings
text:
A supplied plot of all 24 seedlings


seedlings <- read.csv("data/seedlings.csv")
plot(seedlings$initial_mm, seedlings$final_mm,
     xlab = "Initial length (mm)",
     ylab = "Final length (mm)")

One point per plant: 24 points.
seedlings appears in Environment: 24 obs. of 4 variables.
Up is final length, not growth.





Scatter plot of final against initial length for the 24 simulated seedlings, one point per plant.




Paste the code; do not explain <-, $ or read.csv yet (days 6 and 7). The first line only works because the project is open. Click seedlings in the Environment pane to show the table viewer and point out that this is a view: the CSV file is unchanged. Ask: what is one point? Does the y-axis show growth?

title: Meet R and RStudio
section: Where we are heading: a report
text:
Where we are heading: a report

A rendered HTML report: title and question with data and methods on the left; a table of growth by group and a plot of individual plants on the right.Open report.Rmd and click Knit. R runs the saved instructions on data/seedlings.csv and writes report.html: question, code, table and plot.

Demonstrate live. The table shows 12 control and 12 treated plants, with mean growth 15.28 and 21.49 mm. Do not teach the syntax now; the point is that the whole report is rebuilt from saved files. Students write their own first report on day 10. If Knit fails with a missing package, use the installation line from the setup page.

title: Meet R and RStudio
text:
Memory goes, files stay



Save a note as reports/day05-notes.txt.
Quit RStudio; reopen through introcomputing.Rproj.
The Environment is empty. seedlings is gone.
The note, report.Rmd and report.html are still there.





The seedlings object in R’s memory is gone when R quits, while data/seedlings.csv, report.Rmd, report.html and the saved note remain on disk and can be read again.



That is why we will save instructions in files: Knit again and everything comes back.

Connect to day 1 (saved means you can close and reopen) and to week 2: an object made only in the Console disappears; a saved script or report can make it again. Day 6 starts with exactly this.

title: Meet R and RStudio
text:
Summary

R calculates; RStudio is where you work.
Open the course through introcomputing.Rproj so data/... paths work.
> is R (Console); $ is the shell (terminal).
Objects live in memory; files are saved on disk.
A report is rebuilt from saved instructions and data with Knit.

Next (Day 6, R basics): calculations, named objects and vectors, saved in a script.
Now: open the Day 5 exercises. Leave with reports/day05-notes.txt, and report.html if Knit worked.

Anyone whose project does not open or whose Knit fails should get setup help before day 6; week 2 starts from an open project.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Same folders, another window



The terminal is a window where you type. The shell is the program that reads and runs what you type.
Windows: open Ubuntu. Mac: open Terminal.
Nothing new is stored. The terminal shows the same folders as the file manager, described in words instead of icons.





A file-manager window and a terminal listing show the same practice folder.




Show the workspace in both interfaces side by side. On Windows, Ubuntu has its own home folder, separate from the Windows Documents folder; this week we deliberately work in the Ubuntu home. The R project stays in Documents.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Read the prompt before typing



The terminal prompt, the cd command and the practice destination have different roles.



The prompt (anna@laptop:~$, or ending in % on a Mac) means “ready”. Do not type it.
Then comes the command (cd), then its argument: what it acts on (practice).
Press Enter to run it.


The username in the prompt is only an example. Distinguish the command from its argument now. An option such as -p in mkdir -p changes how a command behaves; -l in ls -l asks for a longer listing.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Where am I? What is here?
text:
Where am I? What is here?


cd
mkdir -p introcomputing-shell/practice
cd introcomputing-shell
pwd
ls


cd alone takes you to your home folder.
mkdir -p makes the folder, and its parent if needed.
pwd prints where you are, e.g. /home/anna/introcomputing-shell.
ls lists what is here. You should see practice.


Run one line at a time and read what each line prints.

Pause after pwd and ask several students what their path ends with. The beginning differs per person (/home/anna, /Users/anna); the end should be introcomputing-shell. Browser Downloads may be elsewhere: we are not working there.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Move down, and back up


cd practice
mkdir seedlings
mkdir observations
cd seedlings
pwd
cd ..
pwd

.. means the folder one level up; ~ means your home folder.
Before each pwd, predict how the path will end.





cd moves into child folders; cd .. returns to the parent folder.




Expected endings: /practice/seedlings, then /practice. cd only moves into folders that already exist; it does not create anything.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Each window has its own location
text:
Each window has its own location



explorer.exe . (Ubuntu on Windows) or open . (Mac) opens the current folder in the file manager. The . means “here”.
Clicking into a folder there does not move the terminal. Check with pwd.
Two terminal windows can also stand in different folders.





Two terminal windows keep separate current folders.




Open a second terminal and run pwd in both. These opening commands are local conveniences; on a remote computer there is no file manager to open.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Silence often means success



ls in an empty folder prints nothing. The folder exists; it is just empty.
Many commands, such as mkdir, print nothing when they work.
A real problem prints a message: read it.





ls in the empty observations folder prints no names before the next prompt appears.




Run ls inside observations, then contrast with cd no-such-folder on the next slide. The terminal is not a chat: it does not confirm success unless asked.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: When a command fails, you stay put
text:
When a command fails, you stay put


cd no-such-folder
pwd
cd ~/introcomputing-shell

The error says the folder does not exist. You are still where you were.
Check spelling and capitals: Observations is not observations on Ubuntu.
Lost? cd ~/introcomputing-shell brings you back.





A failed cd leaves the current folder unchanged.




Ubuntu distinguishes upper and lower case; a default Mac disk often does not. Match the real spelling anyway so the work transfers to other computers. Do not teach deleting or “repairing” anything to recover from a typo; ask “where am I and what is here?” (pwd, ls).

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Spaces split a name in two
text:
Spaces split a name in two



The shell splits what you type at spaces. mkdir field notes makes two folders.
Quotes keep the words together: mkdir "field notes".
Easier: use names without spaces, such as field-notes.





Unquoted mkdir field notes creates two folders; quoted “field notes” creates one.




Demonstrate only in the practice folder. Ask students how many folders each line creates before running it.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Keys that save typing

Tab completes a file or folder name. Type cd pra, press Tab.
Up arrow brings back the previous command. Read it before pressing Enter.
Ctrl+C stops a running command or clears a half-typed line. It does not copy.
Copy and paste in the terminal: Ctrl+Shift+C / Ctrl+Shift+V (Ubuntu), Command+C / Command+V (Mac).

Tab completion also prevents typos: it only completes names that really exist.

Show each key live. Students who press Ctrl+C to copy and see their command disappear will remember this slide.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
section: Worked example: a route between neighbours
text:
Worked example: a route between neighbours


You are in results/notes and want inputs:
cd ../../inputs
pwd

Up once to results, up again to the workspace, then into inputs.
A route only works from the starting folder it was written for. Write down the start too.





From notes, the route to inputs goes up two levels and then into inputs.




This is the route challenge in the exercises. Have students draw the tree and predict before running. If they run the same route from a different folder it fails or lands somewhere else: that is the point.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Check yourself

You run cd seedlings. Did any file move?
ls prints nothing. Did it fail?
cd Observations gives an error. Where are you now?
Which of pwd, ls, mkdir, cd creates something?


Answers: 1 no, only the shell’s current folder changed; 2 no, the folder is empty (an error would print a message); 3 where you were before; 4 only mkdir. pwd and ls look, cd moves.

title: The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Summary

The terminal shows the same folders as the file manager, in words.
pwd tells you where you are; ls what is there.
mkdir makes a folder; cd moves you (.. up, ~ home). Moving changes nothing on disk.
No output is often success; an error message tells you what went wrong, and you stay where you were.
Quote names with spaces, or avoid spaces.

Next (Day 4, inspect and unzip): use the terminal to unpack an archive of laboratory files and look inside them.
Now: open the Day 3 exercises. Leave with the introcomputing-shell workspace and navigation-notes.txt in it: your pwd path, the route back from home, and three commands with their meanings.

The exercises add a command log (prediction, result, correction) and a route challenge. Students who cannot yet return to their workspace from anywhere need help before Day 4.

title: Kinds of files
Kinds of files
section: Download and unpack the course files
text:
Download and unpack the course files



Download the course ZIP.
Extract it (Windows: Extract All; Mac: double-click).
Move introcomputing-course to Documents.
Turn on show file extensions.

Work in the extracted folder, not inside the ZIP.




The course project folder contains data, output and reports folders; seedlings.csv is inside data.




Demonstrate once and keep it short; the exercise page has the click-by-click steps. Check that data, examples, output and reports are directly inside the folder students work in; extraction can add an extra folder level, and a second download creates “(1)” names. Ask students with OneDrive/iCloud Documents to tell you. Show the extensions setting in File Explorer and Finder.

title: Kinds of files
text:
Plain text is just characters



seedlings.csv and dna.txt open in a text editor show only letters, digits and commas; .csv, .tsv, .txt, .R, .Rmd and .md files are plain text.



seedlings.csv: a header line, then one line per plant. P01 grew 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm.
Any editor shows the same characters. R reads them directly.


Open data/seedlings.csv in Notepad or TextEdit on the projector. Point at the header and at P01. The units (mm) are in data/README.md, not in the file. Then open data/dna.txt: also plain text. Tell Mac users to set TextEdit to plain text (Settings, New Document, Plain text).

title: Kinds of files
section: A Word file is a package
text:
A Word file is a package



A .docx shown in a text editor is unreadable; renamed to .zip and extracted it is a folder of XML files such as word/document.xml and word/styles.xml.


.docx and .xlsx are ZIP packages. PDF and PNG files are not text either.

Demo: open examples/seedling-notes.docx in Notepad: “PK” and symbols. Copy it to output, rename to .zip, extract, open word/document.xml: the sentences are there between tags. On a Mac, TextEdit renders .docx files as documents; use File, Open, Options, “Ignore rich text commands”, or rename a copy to .txt. Optionally open the PDF and PNG in the editor: they start with %PDF and PNG.

title: Kinds of files
text:
Same table: CSV or Excel



seedlings.csv stores only values; seedlings.xlsx also stores a coloured header, a growth formula and a second sheet.


We keep data as CSV: every program reads it, and nothing is hidden.

Open examples/seedlings.xlsx in Excel or LibreOffice: show the formula in E2 (=D2-C2, displayed 18.6) and the “notes” sheet. Then open data/seedlings.csv in the spreadsheet: values only. Formatting and calculations belong in R code, where every step is written down.

title: Kinds of files
text:
Spreadsheets can change your data



Opening a gene list in Excel turned SEPT2 into 2-Sep and MARCH1 into 1-Mar.


Never save raw data from a spreadsheet. Close it without saving.

Open examples/genes.csv in a text editor, then in Excel. Excel may show dates; LibreOffice in our test left the names alone, so the figure is the backup. Ziemann et al. (2016, Genome Biology) found such errors in about 1 in 5 papers with supplementary Excel gene lists. HGNC renamed SEPT and MARCH genes in 2020 (SEPTIN2, MARCHF1), but older files still use the old names.

title: Kinds of files
text:
Swedish Excel writes a different “CSV”



The same rows in the course CSV and in a Swedish-Excel CSV, which uses semicolons between values and decimal commas such as 25,7.


Look at a CSV in a text editor before you analyse it.

Relevant here at Umeå: Excel set to Swedish saves “CSV” with semicolons, because the comma is the decimal sign. Open examples/seedlings-semicolon.csv. R’s read.csv stops with “more columns than column names”; read.csv2 reads it. Reading data into R comes later in the course.

title: Kinds of files
text:
Word “improves” your text



The same R line in a text editor uses straight quotes and works; in a word processor it has curly quotes and R reports an error.


Write code, data and notes in a text editor (later, RStudio), not in Word.

Compare the last line of examples/seedling-notes.txt and examples/seedling-notes.docx. Word’s autocorrect replaced the straight quotes. Paste the curly version into R if R is installed: Error: unexpected input. TextEdit on a Mac is also a word processor by default: Format, Make Plain Text before saving, otherwise you get an .rtf file.

title: Kinds of files
text:
Extensions are labels



Renaming seedlings.csv to seedlings.xlsx leaves plain text that Excel refuses; renaming notes.docx to notes.zip works because it was a ZIP all along.


Renaming changes the name, not the contents. Converting needs Save As.

Ask: what is inside seedlings.xlsx after renaming? The same commas and numbers. The extension tells the computer which program to use; it does not convert anything. That is also why extensions must be visible.

title: Kinds of files
section: Keep the original; work on a copy
text:
Keep the original; work on a copy



Copying the raw CSV into output creates a separate practice file while the original stays in data.


Copy data/seedlings.csv to output/seedlings-practice.csv. Experiment only on copies.

The original is what was measured. If a spreadsheet changes the copy, start again from the original. Demonstrate the copy in the file manager; tomorrow’s exercises use this file.

title: Kinds of files
text:
Save a plain-text note



An edited note is saved to disk and then reopened from its folder.


Save reports/day01-notes.txt. Check that the name ends in .txt, not .rtf. Close the editor, then reopen the note from its folder.

Mac: Format, Make Plain Text before saving. With extensions hidden, a note can end up as notes.txt.rtf without anyone noticing. Unsaved text is lost when the editor closes; a saved file stays on disk. Tomorrow students start by finding this note.

title: Kinds of files
text:
Check yourself

You open a .docx in Notepad and see PK and symbols. Is it broken?
Which file can R read directly: seedlings.csv or seedlings.xlsx?
A gene list shows 1-Mar. What happened?
A CSV line reads P01;control;25,7;44,3. Where does it come from?


Answers: 1 no, it is a ZIP package; 2 seedlings.csv (plain text); 3 a spreadsheet turned MARCH1 into a date; 4 Excel set to Swedish (or another language with decimal commas). Ask students to check 1 on their own computers.

title: Kinds of files
text:
Summary

Plain text (.csv, .txt, .R, .Rmd, .md) is just characters: any editor shows it, R reads it.
.docx and .xlsx are ZIP packages; PDF and images are not text either.
An .xlsx adds formatting, formulas and sheets. We keep data as CSV.
Spreadsheets can change data (gene names to dates) and write “CSV” with semicolons.
Word turns " into “ ”. Write code in a text editor.
An extension is a label. Renaming does not convert.

Next (Day 2, folders and paths): writing down exactly where a file is.
Now: open the Day 1 exercises. Leave with reports/day01-notes.txt, reports/file-types.txt and output/seedlings-practice.csv.

The exercises have the detailed click sequence. The independent task sorts every file in the course folder into plain text or not. Students who could not extract the course folder need help before Day 2.

title: Week 5 revision — reproduce and transfer
text:
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.
Topic quizzes: computers and data size · remote work · small study · reproduction · consolidation.

Q1. Name the location, not just the filename
Your report rendered remotely, but local Downloads is empty. What should you check? Does closing the SSH terminal necessarily delete saved remote output?






Hint





Rendering, transferring, and locating the received copy are separate actions.









Answer





Locate the output on the remote computer, then check whether it was transferred and to which destination. A remote desktop is not automatic synchronisation. Closing SSH ends a session, not saved files, subject to the service’s storage policy. Whether a running process continues depends on the service.




Q2. Where does R keep its objects?
You load a table with read_csv(), calculate growth in the console, and then restart R. Which of these still exist: the CSV file, the object in the Environment pane, the saved script? Which part of the computer holds each?






Hint





RAM is fast but temporary; the disk is slower but permanent.









Answer





The CSV file and the saved script survive: they are on disk. The object was in RAM and disappears when R restarts. This is why reports are rendered from saved files in a fresh session.




Q3. Will it fit?
Estimate the RAM needed for a table with 1,000,000 rows and 10 numeric columns. How much free RAM would you plan for? Would a single-cell table of 30,000 genes × 100,000 cells fit on a 16 GB laptop?






Hint





One number in R takes 8 bytes. 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes; 1 GB = 1,000 MB.









Answer





1,000,000 × 10 × 8 = 80,000,000 bytes = 80 MB; plan for about 2–3 times that (160–240 MB) as working space. The single-cell table needs 30,000 × 100,000 × 8 bytes = 24 GB before working space, more than a 16 GB laptop has: use a subset or a bigger (remote) computer.




Q4. Available duckweed measurements
Twenty independent flasks were started, ten per allocation. Nutrient flask F17 spilled before weighing. How many available biomass observations are there, and why is replacing the missing value by zero inappropriate?






Hint





Start with ten per group, then account for the documented spill.









Answer





There are 10 control and 9 nutrient observations, 19 in total. Zero would invent a known biomass; unavailable and absent biomass are different meanings. Retain the original row, report the loss, and make the comparison conditional on the observed data and missingness limitation.




Q5. A percentage difference needs its units
In the supplied alternative, percentage yield is 100 × collected mass / supplied maximum mass, with matching mass units. Protocol means are 68.67% and 77.00%. Is their difference an 8.33% relative increase? Does it establish greater purity?






Hint





Subtracting two percentages gives a difference in percentage points.









Answer





The modified-minus-standard difference is 8.33 percentage points. A relative percentage change would divide by the starting mean and multiply by 100; it is a different quantity. Greater yield alone does not establish greater purity, safety, sustainability, or general superiority. Product purity was an explicit simplifying assumption in this numerical exercise, not a measured finding.




Q6. Share a recipe, not only its output
A reader receives your HTML but cannot update the analysis for new data. What else should be in the shared project? Why test extraction in a new location?






Hint





HTML displays a result; source and inputs are needed to update it.









Answer





Include the .Rmd source, actual input CSV, dictionary, project file, required output folder if used, and a short README naming packages and the file to render. Testing a new location detects dependencies on personal absolute paths or missing files. The .Rproj does not contain the dataset. A fresh session detects hidden interactive objects. Include only the study files.




Q7. What does successful reproduction establish?
Your report renders successfully from the shared source and input. Does that prove the design and interpretation are correct, or provide a backup against losing your only disk?






Hint





Test reproduction, scientific validity, and backup separately.









Answer





It establishes that the supplied work regenerates the result in the tested environment. A flawed analysis can be reproducible. Scientific validity still needs the design, assumptions, checks, and reasoning. Backup is a separate action: keep a retrievable copy using supported separate storage.




Q8. Checks have limits
The received table has the same filename, byte size, row count, and column names as the source. Does this prove that every measurement matches? What would you check in a small transfer audit before making a stronger claim?






Hint





A changed value can leave a table’s dimensions unchanged.









Answer





No. A changed value can occupy the same number of characters, and tables can have identical dimensions but different contents. Inspect the intended saved input, verify named records and missing values, and compare the contents using the supported method. Record the actual source and destination locations. Check saved contents rather than an unsaved editor buffer.




Q9. File size is not object size
A CSV of 100,000 rows × 10 numbers rounded to one decimal is 4.79 MB on disk. Is the loaded object in R larger or smaller? What happens to the object and the file when a unique text ID such as S000001 is added to every row?






Hint





In a CSV, one character is one byte; in R, one number is 8 bytes. Each different text value in R carries its own bookkeeping.









Answer





Larger: 100,000 × 10 × 8 bytes = 8.0 MB, because a value such as 19.3, takes only 5 bytes as text. With the ID column the object grows to 14.4 MB (6.4 MB for the IDs) but the file only to 5.59 MB. Check with object.size() and file.size() rather than assuming the file size equals RAM.




Q10. DNA and images as bytes
data/dna.txt holds 40 letters and is 41 bytes. Estimate the human genome (about 3.1 billion letters) as a text file. Then estimate one grayscale camera image of 2048 × 2048 pixels as an 8-bit file and as numbers in R.






Hint





One letter or one 8-bit pixel is 1 byte; one number in R is 8 bytes. The 41st byte of dna.txt is the line ending.









Answer





The genome is about 3.1 GB as text. The image has 4,194,304 pixels: about 4.2 MB as an 8-bit file and 33.6 MB as numbers in R.




Q11. A fresh dataset requires fresh counts
The algae table has 24 independent cultures, twelve per allocation. A19 in the supplement group spilled before weighing. Its available group means are 28.20 mg for reference and 33.91818 mg for supplement. Give available n and the observed supplement-minus-reference difference. Must supplement contain the largest single observation?






Hint





One supplement outcome is unavailable; subtract reference mean from supplement mean.









Answer





Available n is 12 reference and 11 supplement, 23 in total. The directed difference is 33.91818 - 28.20 ≈ 5.72 mg. A higher group mean does not require every value to be higher: reference culture A11 at 41.7 mg is the largest individual observation. Describe both the centre and observations.




Q12. A sensitivity check does not justify deletion
Omitting A11 lowers the algae reference mean to 26.97273 mg and increases the observed difference to about 6.95 mg. No source record identifies A11 as an error. Which result should be primary, and how should the other be labelled?






Hint





Ask whether the source record supports an exclusion.









Answer





Keep the all-available-measurements result primary: about 5.72 mg. The other is a diagnostic sensitivity calculation with an explicitly changed sample and no independent evidence for exclusion. Reweighing preferences or a more convenient p-value cannot justify removing a recorded observation. A19 remains a distinct missing measurement; omitting A11 does not repair that loss.




Q13. Rendering can miss the more serious fault
In a disposable report copy, an input is temporarily renamed. In another copy, the prose claims that every enrolled duckweed flask had a measured outcome. Which fault should stop rendering, and which may render successfully?






Hint





A missing input can stop execution; software can reproduce false prose.









Answer





The unchanged input path should fail when its required file is unavailable. Restore its exact name/path, rerun, and compare the result. The false prose can render successfully because software does not automatically validate the claim. It contradicts the documented missing F17 measurement. Check scientific meaning as well as execution; keep intentionally faulty copies out of the final package.




Q14. Is this a rounding difference or a different analysis?
One memo gives a mean of 33.91818 mg and the report displays 33.92 mg. Another report gives 34.32 mg. What should be investigated, and why should you check the input and calculation before changing display precision?






Hint





Round 33.91818 to two decimal places, then compare it with both displayed values.









Answer





33.92 is the first value rounded to two decimal places. 34.32 is not explained by that rounding. Check the saved input, available counts, group selection, outcome definition, and calculation, then confirm which rendered file was opened. Changing the number of displayed digits cannot repair a different input or an unrecorded exclusion. Retain full-precision values for subsequent calculations.




Q15. The receiver has the old README
You made report-share-v1.zip, extracted it into receiver-v1, and then added a missing unit to report-share/README.txt. The README in receiver-v1 still lacks the unit. What happened, and how do you give your colleague the corrected version? Is the ZIP on your laptop also your backup?






Hint





A ZIP is a snapshot of the folder at the moment it was made.









Answer





Neither the old ZIP nor its extracted copy changes when you edit the source folder. Make report-share-v2.zip from the folder that contains report-share, extract it into a new folder such as receiver-v2, check that the unit is there, and send v2. The ZIP is not a backup: it sits on the same disk as the original, so keep a copy on separate supported storage as well.



Return to day 25 consolidation and save your next-lab workflow with the reference pages.

title: Quiz: recover and check a complete workflow
text:
Exercises · Weekly revision
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A seedling’s initial length is 25.7 mm and final length is 44.3 mm. Repair this outcome calculation:
growth_mm = final_mm + initial_mm






Hint





Growth here means final length minus initial length.









Answer





growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm, giving 18.6 mm.




Q2. An estimated treatment-minus-control difference is 3 mm with a 95% confidence interval from −2 to 8 mm. Does this establish that the treatment has no effect?






Hint





The interval includes zero and values on both sides of it.









Answer





No. The estimate is positive, but the interval includes decreases and increases. Report the estimate and uncertainty rather than claiming equality.




Q3. The algae reference mean is 28.20 mg and supplement mean is 33.91818 mg. Omitting the largest reference value, A11, changes its mean to 26.97273 mg. Calculate both supplement-minus-reference differences. Which should be primary if A11 has no documented error?






Hint





Compare the unchanged supplement mean with each reference mean.









Answer





All available observations: about 5.72 mg. Omitting A11: about 6.95 mg. Keep the all-available result primary; label the other as a sensitivity check with a changed sample, not an established correction.




Q4. A summary shows 33.91818 mg; a rendered report shows 33.92 mg. Another report shows 34.32 mg. Which discrepancy is ordinary rounding, and what would you check for the other?






Hint





Round the first value to two decimal places.









Answer





33.92 mg is ordinary rounding. Investigate 34.32 mg by checking the saved input, available counts, group selection, exclusions, outcome calculation and which output file was opened.

title: Quiz: reproduce and share a report
text:
Lecture · Exercises · Weekly revision
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A report uses an object imported only in the R console. Which check is most likely to expose this dependency?

Change the plot colour.
Restart R and Knit from the saved source.
Rename the HTML.







Hint





Restarting clears interactive session objects.









Answer





(ii). The report should create its objects in its own chunks. Add the import before the analysis that uses it.




Q2. A share folder contains introcomputing.Rproj and duckweed-report.html. Is that enough to recalculate the analysis for new data? What is missing?






Hint





A project file sets context; HTML displays a result.









Answer





No. Include the .Rmd source, actual input CSV, dictionary, required output folder, and README naming packages and the file to render. The .Rproj does not contain the dataset.




Q3. In a disposable project copy, the input CSV is renamed but the report still requests its old path. In another copy, only the prose is changed to falsely say every duckweed flask had a measured outcome. Which fault should stop rendering?






Hint





Software can encounter an unavailable input without recognising a false scientific sentence.









Answer





The unchanged path to the renamed input should cause a file error. The false prose may render successfully, so counts and interpretation also need review.




Q4. A report renders correctly after extraction into a new folder. Which claim follows?

The source and supplied inputs regenerate the result in the tested environment.
The scientific interpretation is proved correct.
The ZIP protects against losing the only disk.







Hint





Reproduction, scientific validity and backup are separate checks.









Answer





(i). Successful reproduction is evidence about the tested source, inputs and environment. Design and interpretation still need review, and disk loss needs a separately stored backup.




Q5. You make report-share-v1.zip, then correct a sentence in report-share/README.txt. A colleague extracts v1. Do they see the correction?






Hint





A ZIP stores the folder as it was when the ZIP was made.









Answer





No. Make a new, newly named ZIP (report-share-v2.zip), extract it into a new folder, and check that the corrected sentence is there before sending it.




Q6. You run unzip report-share-v1.zip -d receiver-v1. Where is duckweed-report.Rmd, and why?






Hint





The ZIP was made from the folder report-share/.









Answer





At receiver-v1/report-share/duckweed-report.Rmd. Extraction keeps the packed folder, so it adds one level inside the destination. Open receiver-v1/report-share/introcomputing.Rproj to test it.




Q7. You run zip -r report-share-v1.zip report-share/ from Documents, the folder that contains report-share. Where is the ZIP saved, and why is that better than saving it inside report-share?






Hint





Where is the new ZIP saved?









Answer





In Documents, beside report-share, because a new ZIP is saved in the current folder. A ZIP kept inside the folder it packs would be packed into the next ZIP, which would then contain an old copy of itself.

title: Quiz: a small biological study
text:
Exercises · Weekly revision
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Twenty duckweed flasks were independently allocated to control or nutrient conditions, ten each. F17 in the nutrient group spilled before weighing. What is the experimental unit, and how many biomass measurements are available per group?






Hint





Fronds in one flask share a treatment allocation.









Answer





The flask is the independent unit. There are 10 control and 9 nutrient biomass measurements, 19 in total.




Q2. Which code preserves the documented unavailable measurement when selecting observations for a biomass plot?

Replace its biomass by zero.
Keep the original table and create available <- filter(duckweed, !is.na(biomass_mg)).
Delete every nutrient flask.







Hint





Keep the raw record and distinguish missing from measured zero.









Answer





(ii). The plotting object contains available measurements, while the original table retains F17 and its missing value. State the unavailable count in the caption.




Q3. You run t.test(nutrient$biomass_mg, control$biomass_mg). Which directed difference does its confidence interval describe?






Hint





For two supplied vectors, the comparison follows first minus second.









Answer





Nutrient mean minus control mean. A positive difference means the nutrient group has the larger mean biomass.




Q4. For a synthesis run, percentage yield is defined as 100 × collected mass / supplied maximum mass, with both masses in grams. A run collects 1.17 g from a supplied maximum of 1.50 g. Calculate its yield. Does this measure purity?






Hint





Divide matching mass units before multiplying by 100.









Answer





100 × 1.17 / 1.50 = 78%. This is yield under the supplied assumptions; it is not a purity measurement.




Q5. Protocol means are 68.67% and 77.00%. Express modified minus standard in the correct units. Is this the same as relative percentage change?






Hint





Subtracting percentages gives a difference on the percentage scale.









Answer





The difference is 8.33 percentage points. Relative change would divide that difference by the standard mean and multiply by 100, giving about 12.13%. These answer different questions.

title: Quiz: work on another computer
text:
Exercises · Weekly revision
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. After connecting with SSH, which command shows your current folder on the remote computer?

hostname (ii) pwd (iii) exit (iv) getwd()







Hint





hostname names the machine. getwd() belongs in R.









Answer





(ii), pwd. It prints the working directory of that shell. hostname identifies the answering machine; exit ends the shell session.




Q2. A report rendered remotely, but your laptop’s Downloads folder is empty. Which step should come first?

Reinstall R. (ii) Render five more copies. (iii) Locate the remote output and check the transfer destination.







Hint





Rendering and transferring are separate actions.









Answer





(iii). Find the saved output on the remote computer, check whether it was transferred, and locate that destination on the laptop.




Q3. Two project copies both contain reports/receipt.txt. You edit and save the laptop copy. Must the remote copy change too? What should you inspect before sending it?






Hint





A shared filename does not establish shared storage.









Answer





No. Separately copied folders need a new transfer unless a configured sharing service updates them. Open the saved contents of the intended source and receiving copy; record their locations.




Q4. A received algae table has 24 rows and 23 available biomass measurements, matching the source. Does this establish that every recorded biomass is identical?






Hint





Two values can contain the same number of characters while differing numerically.









Answer





No. These are useful structural checks, but a changed value can leave both counts unchanged. Compare saved contents or named records using the supported method before making a stronger claim.




Q5. What happens to saved remote files when you run exit in an SSH shell? Does the same answer guarantee that a running R process continues?






Hint





A saved file and a running process are different things.









Answer





The shell connection ends; saved files remain subject to the service’s storage policy. Whether a running process continues depends on the service and how it was started.

title: Quiz: how a computer works, and data size
text:
Exercises · Weekly revision
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Match each part to its job: CPU, RAM, disk, GPU.

keeps saved files when the computer is off; (b) does the calculations, with a few cores; (c) fast, temporary working space for running programs; (d) thousands of simple cores for images and deep learning.







Hint





Ask which part loses its contents when R closes.









Answer





CPU (b), RAM (c), disk (a), GPU (d). R objects live in RAM; CSV files, scripts and reports live on disk.




Q2. You make growth <- final_mm - initial_mm in the console, then restart R. Is growth still there? What should you do so the result can be repeated?






Hint





Restarting R ends the process that held its RAM.









Answer





No: the object was in RAM and is gone. Save the code in a script or R Markdown report (and save outputs with write_csv() if needed), so the result can be recreated from files on disk.




Q3. Estimate the RAM needed for a table with 500,000 rows and 20 numeric columns. How much free RAM would you plan for?






Hint





rows × columns × 8 bytes, then 2–3 times that for working space.









Answer





500,000 × 20 × 8 = 80,000,000 bytes = 80 MB. Plan for roughly 160–240 MB free.




Q4. In a CSV, the value 25.7, takes 5 bytes. In R, the number takes 8 bytes. A CSV of short rounded numbers is 4.8 MB. Is the loaded object larger or smaller than the file? What if the values had 15 or more digits each?






Hint





A CSV uses one byte per character; R uses 8 bytes per number whatever its digits.









Answer





Larger: our 4.8 MB file became an 8.0 MB object. With long values (about 19 characters each, including the comma) the CSV is larger than the object: one million such numbers made an 18.6 MB file but an 8.0 MB object.




Q5. The human genome has about 3.1 billion letters. How large is it as a plain text file? Roughly how large would it be in R stored as separate letters at 8 bytes each?






Hint





One letter in a text file is one byte. 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes.









Answer





About 3.1 GB as text, and about 3.1 × 8 ≈ 25 GB as separate letters in R: too big for most laptops.




Q6. A camera image has 2048 × 2048 grayscale pixels. How large is it as an 8-bit file (1 byte per pixel), and as numbers in R?






Hint





First count the pixels: 2048 * 2048.









Answer





4,194,304 pixels: about 4.2 MB as a file and 33.6 MB in R (8 bytes per pixel).




Q7. A single-cell RNA-seq table has 30,000 genes × 100,000 cells. Will it fit in the RAM of a 16 GB laptop? What happens if you try anyway?






Hint





30000 * 100000 * 8 / 1e9 gives GB.









Answer





No: it needs about 24 GB before working space. The computer starts swapping to disk and everything crawls, or R stops with “cannot allocate vector” or crashes. Use a subset, a more compact format, or a bigger computer (Day 22).

title: Day 20 — A biological association
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 20 — A biological association
text:
Today’s question
Do larger leaves have more dry mass, and how much more per cm² of leaf? Leaf area is easy to measure from a photo, while dry mass means drying and weighing the leaf, so a relation between the two is useful in plant ecology. You fit a line with the same lm() as on day 19, but this time neither variable was set by us: both were measured on leaves as they were found.
data/leaf-mass.csv contains one leaf from each of 18 plants, with its area (leaf_area_cm2) and dry mass (dry_mass_mg); see data/README.md. The data are simulated.
Save today: association-report.Rmd and its HTML, output/day20-leaf-line.png, and transfer-association.Rmd with its HTML. Create association-report.Rmd at the project root and put the code below into it.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
text:
Plotting leaf mass against area

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

leaves <- read_csv("data/leaf-mass.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
leaf_plot <- ggplot(leaves, aes(x = leaf_area_cm2, y = dry_mass_mg)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Leaf area (cm²)", y = "Leaf dry mass (mg)") +
  theme_minimal()
leaf_plot
range(leaves$leaf_area_cm2)

Larger leaves tend to be heavier, but leaves of similar area still differ in mass by several mg. The areas range from 2.96 to 14.68 cm².

title: Day 20 — A biological association
text:
How much mass per cm²?
Use lm() to find out how much dry mass goes with each extra cm² of leaf area:

leaf_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_cm2, data = leaves)
coef(leaf_fit)

leaf_plot <- leaf_plot +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(leaf_fit)[1], slope = coef(leaf_fit)[2],
              colour = "steelblue")
leaf_plot
ggsave("output/day20-leaf-line.png", leaf_plot, width = 6, height = 4)




One leaf from each of eighteen plants, with the fitted dry-mass relationship.


The slope is 4.11 mg per cm²: in these plants, a leaf with 1 cm² more area had on average about 4.11 mg more dry mass. The intercept, 9.48 mg, is where the line would cross zero area. No leaf has zero area and the smallest one measured is 2.96 cm², so the intercept only positions the line.
Because leaf area was not assigned to the plants, the line describes how area and mass go together in this sample. Older or better-lit plants might have both larger and heavier leaves, so the line does not show that making a leaf larger would add 4.11 mg.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: What mass does the line predict for an 8 cm² leaf?
text:
What mass does the line predict for an 8 cm² leaf?
Use the two coefficients to find out the fitted mass at 8 cm²:

coef(leaf_fit)[1] + coef(leaf_fit)[2] * 8

The answer is 42.36 mg: the average mass the line expects for leaves of that size. Single 8 cm² leaves will be somewhat lighter or heavier. A leaf of 80 cm² is far outside the measured areas; the formula would give 338 mg, but nothing tells us that the line continues that far.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Which leaves lie far from the line?
text:
Which leaves lie far from the line?
Use residuals() to find out how far each leaf lies above or below the line:

leaves <- leaves |>
  mutate(fitted_mass_mg = fitted(leaf_fit),
         residual_mg = residuals(leaf_fit))

leaf_residual_plot <- ggplot(leaves, aes(x = leaf_area_cm2, y = residual_mg)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Leaf area (cm²)", y = "Observed − fitted mass (mg)") +
  theme_minimal()
leaf_residual_plot




Individual dry-mass residuals around the leaf-area relationship.


Check one by hand: A01 has area 2.96 cm² and mass 21.19 mg, the line predicts 9.48 + 4.11 × 2.96 = 21.64 mg, so its residual is −0.45 mg, just below the line. The largest residuals are A17 (8.42 mg below) and A14 (6.31 mg above). The points lie on both sides of zero without a curve, so a straight line is a fair summary.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Does one leaf decide the slope?
text:
Does one leaf decide the slope?
A18 is the largest leaf, at the end of the range, where one point can tilt a line the most. Use a second fit without A18 to find out how much the slope depends on it:

without_a18 <- leaves |> filter(plant_id != "A18")
sensitivity_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_cm2, data = without_a18)
coef(leaf_fit)
coef(sensitivity_fit)

Without A18 the slope is 4.065 instead of 4.110 mg per cm², a small change, so the conclusion does not hinge on one leaf. Nothing in the records says A18 was measured wrongly, so it stays in the main result; the second fit is only a check, and you label it as one.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
text:
The association report
In association-report.Rmd, describe the study (one leaf from each of 18 plants, area and dry mass measured, nothing assigned), show the plot with the line and the residual plot, and answer three questions in the conclusion:

What association did you see?
What does the slope mean, in numbers with units?
What would this study need in order to show that leaf area causes mass?

Add one sentence about the A18 check, restart R and render.






Hint: a slope sentence





“Within the measured range of 2.96 to 14.68 cm², each additional 1 cm² of leaf area was associated with about 4.11 mg more dry mass on average.” Avoid “making the leaf larger causes …”, because area was measured, not changed.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
section: Does the slope change if area is in mm²?
text:
Does the slope change if area is in mm²?
1 cm² is 100 mm². Use mutate(leaf_area_mm2 = 100 * leaf_area_cm2) and a new fit, unit_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_mm2, data = leaves), to find out whether changing the unit changes the line.






Answer





The slope becomes 0.0411 mg per mm², 100 times smaller, while the intercept and every fitted mass stay the same: max(abs(fitted(leaf_fit) - fitted(unit_fit))) is essentially zero. The number changes with the unit; the relation between the leaves does not. Always write the unit next to a slope.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
text:
Did larger seedlings stay larger?
In the second seedling study, data/seedlings-transfer.csv, each of 18 plants was measured at the start and seven days later. Create transfer-association.Rmd and use lm(final_mm ~ initial_mm, data = transfer) to find out how strongly a seedling’s final length goes with its initial length. Colour the points by treatment, add the combined line, and make a residual plot.






Answer check





Initial lengths range from 20.0 to 28.8 mm. The slope is 0.51: a seedling 1 mm longer at the start was on average about 0.5 mm longer at the end. A seedling starting at 24 mm has a fitted final length of 40.0 mm. The colours show that the treated plants lie mostly above the line, so the treatment adds to the pattern. This is a different question from day 17’s, which compared mean growth between the randomly allocated groups; that comparison remains the way to judge the treatment.

title: Day 20 — A biological association
text:
Week 4 in one table
At the end of association-report.Rmd, add a table comparing the four analyses of this week, for use in later lab courses:









Question
Design
Day
What R gives




Did treated plants grow more?
Two independent groups
16–17
Mean difference, Welch CI and p-value


Did each plant’s rate change?
Same plants measured twice
18
Mean change, paired CI and p-value


What concentration is in my sample?
Prepared standards
19
Calibration line, estimate within range


Do two measurements go together?
Two variables measured on each unit
20
Slope with units, residuals

title: Day 20 — A biological association
text:
Check your understanding

Is the slope measured in mg, cm², or mg/cm²? mg/cm².
Does a strong relationship show that one variable causes the other? No; here area was measured, not changed.
Would 18 leaves from one plant give 18 independent units? No; leaves of the same plant share its conditions.

Leave with: association-report.Rmd, its HTML, output/day20-leaf-line.png, and transfer-association.Rmd with its HTML.
