title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
Today’s question
A spectrophotometer reports an absorbance, a number without units, but you want to know the concentration of your sample in mg/L. To translate one into the other, you measure standards, solutions of known concentration, and fit a straight line through their readings. What are the concentrations of three unknown samples that read 0.310, 0.520 and 0.900?
The standards in data/calibration.csv cover 0 to 10 mg/L, and the unknowns are in data/unknowns.csv. Both are simulated; see data/README.md. No chemistry is needed beyond the idea of a concentration.
Save today: calibration-report.Rmd and its HTML, output/day19-unknowns.csv, both figures, and transfer-calibration.Rmd with its HTML. Create calibration-report.Rmd at the project root and put the code below into it.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
Plotting the standards
We prepared the concentrations and measured the absorbance, so concentration goes on the x-axis and absorbance on the y-axis:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

standards <- read_csv("data/calibration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
calibration_plot <- ggplot(standards,
                          aes(x = concentration_mg_l, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Known concentration (mg/L)", y = "Absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()
calibration_plot

The six readings rise from 0.041 to 0.687 almost along a straight line. We describe that line as absorbance = intercept + slope × concentration. The intercept is the reading at zero concentration, a background signal; the slope is how much the absorbance rises for each extra mg/L.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
Fitting the line
Use lm() to find out the intercept and slope of the line that fits the standards best:

calibration_fit <- lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l, data = standards)
coef(calibration_fit)

lm() fits a linear model: ~ separates the response on the left from the variable that explains it on the right, and coef() returns the fitted intercept and slope. The R documentation for lm describes more options, but we only need this straight line.
You should get an intercept of 0.03957 and a slope of 0.06489 per mg/L: each extra mg/L adds about 0.065 to the absorbance. The intercept is not zero, because even the blank standard reads 0.041; leave it in the line rather than forcing the line through zero. Add the line to the plot:

calibration_plot <- calibration_plot +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(calibration_fit)[1],
              slope = coef(calibration_fit)[2], colour = "steelblue")
calibration_plot

[1] and [2] pick the first and second coefficient.



Prepared standards and their fitted calibration line.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: How close are the standards to the line?
text:
How close are the standards to the line?
A residual is a measured reading minus the reading the line predicts at that concentration. A positive residual means the standard lies above the line. Use residuals() to find out whether the line misses any standard badly, or bends away from them:

standards <- standards |>
  mutate(fitted_absorbance = fitted(calibration_fit),
         residual = residuals(calibration_fit))
standards

residual_plot <- ggplot(standards,
                        aes(x = concentration_mg_l, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Known concentration (mg/L)", y = "Residual absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()
residual_plot




Deviations of standard readings from the fitted line, in absorbance units.


Check the first standard by hand: 0.041 − 0.0396 = +0.0014, just above the line. All six residuals lie within ±0.008, on both sides of zero and without a curved pattern, so a straight line describes the standards well between 0 and 10 mg/L. Nothing was measured outside that range.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
Concentrations of the unknowns
Turning the line around gives concentration = (absorbance − intercept) / slope. Use it to find out the concentration of each unknown, but only where its reading lies between the lowest and highest standard:

unknowns <- read_csv("data/unknowns.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
intercept <- coef(calibration_fit)[1]
slope <- coef(calibration_fit)[2]

unknowns <- unknowns |>
  mutate(within_range = absorbance >= min(standards$absorbance) &
                        absorbance <= max(standards$absorbance),
         concentration_mg_l = if_else(
           within_range, (absorbance - intercept) / slope, NA_real_))
unknowns
write_csv(unknowns, "output/day19-unknowns.csv")

& requires both conditions to be true, and if_else() gives a missing value, NA_real_, where the reading is out of range. U1 is 4.17 mg/L and U2 7.40 mg/L. U3 reads 0.900, above the highest standard (0.687). The formula would give 13.3 mg/L, but no standard was measured there and many assays level off at high concentrations, so U3 gets NA. In the lab, it would be diluted and measured again.
In calibration-report.Rmd, explain what a standard is, show both plots, give the slope with its units (absorbance per mg/L), report U1 and U2, and explain why U3 has no estimate. Save the figures with ggsave(), restart R and render.






Hint: which way round is the model?





We prepared concentration and measured absorbance, so absorbance is the response: lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l). We then rearrange that line to get a concentration. lm(concentration_mg_l ~ absorbance) is a different line.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
A diluted sample
A different sample read far above the standards, so 1.00 mL of it was diluted with solvent to a total of 10.00 mL and measured again. The diluted solution read 0.520. Assuming nothing is lost during dilution, its concentration is ten times lower than the original’s. Use the calibration line and the dilution factor 10.00 / 1.00 to find out the concentration of the original sample, and add the calculation to your report.






Hint and answer check





diluted_absorbance <- 0.520
dilution_factor <- 10.00 / 1.00
diluted_mg_l <- (diluted_absorbance - intercept) / slope
original_mg_l <- diluted_mg_l * dilution_factor
c(diluted_mg_l = diluted_mg_l, original_mg_l = original_mg_l)
The diluted solution is 7.40 mg/L, so the original is 74.04 mg/L. This works because 0.520 is a new reading inside the standards. It does not give a value for U3, which would need its own dilution and reading.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
Does rounding the coefficients matter?
A report might print the line as absorbance = 0.04 + 0.06 × concentration. Use round(intercept, 2) and round(slope, 2) in a separate calculation to find out what U1 would come out as if someone used these rounded numbers.






Answer





With the full coefficients U1 is 4.17 mg/L; with the rounded ones it is 4.50 mg/L, 8% too high (and U2 becomes 8.00 instead of 7.40). The slope is a small number, so rounding it to 0.06 changes it a lot. Calculate with intercept and slope, and round only the result you write in the text.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
A second instrument
Another instrument was calibrated with six standards from 0 to 5 mg/L (data/calibration-transfer.csv), and two samples, X1 and X2, were measured on it (data/unknowns-transfer.csv). Create transfer-calibration.Rmd with its own import, plot, residual plot and fit, using new object names such as transfer_standards and transfer_fit. Use its line to find out the concentrations of X1 and X2, keeping the range check.






Answer check





The new line has intercept 0.0216 and slope 0.1001 per mg/L, so the old line does not apply to this instrument. The standards read 0.024 to 0.525. X1 (0.270) is 2.48 mg/L; X2 (0.700) is above the standards and gets NA, to be diluted and measured again. Putting 2.48 back into the line, intercept + slope * 2.48, returns 0.270: a quick check that the algebra is right.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
Check your understanding

What does a positive residual mean? The standard reads higher than the line predicts.
Does a good fit from 0 to 10 mg/L support an estimate at 100 mg/L? No; only between the lowest and highest standard.
Are the concentration estimates exact? No; the standards, the readings and the fitted line all carry some uncertainty, which we have not calculated.

Leave with: calibration-report.Rmd, its HTML, output/day19-unknowns.csv, both figures, and transfer-calibration.Rmd with its HTML.
Next: Day 20 — A biological association.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
text:
Today’s question
Ten plants had their leaf photosynthesis measured, then the light was increased and the same ten plants were measured again. Did their photosynthesis rate go up, and by how much? Because every plant appears twice, we compare each plant with itself: a paired design.
The file data/paired.csv holds simulated rates in micromoles of CO₂ per square metre per second, written µmol m⁻² s⁻¹; see data/README.md. Before was always measured first, and after second.
Save today: paired-report.Rmd and its HTML, output/day18-changes.png, and paired-transfer.Rmd with its HTML. Copy the root report.Rmd to paired-report.Rmd and put the code below into it.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Is every plant in the table once?
text:
Is every plant in the table once?

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

paired <- read_csv("data/paired.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
paired
anyDuplicated(paired$plant_id)

You should see ten rows, one per plant, each with a before and an after value. anyDuplicated() returns 0, meaning that no plant identifier appears twice. The identifier is what tells us which two readings belong together. Here they already share a row; if the readings came in two separate files, you would match them by plant_id before subtracting, never by row position.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: How much did each plant change?
text:
How much did each plant change?
Use mutate() to find out how much the rate of each plant changed:

paired <- paired |>
  mutate(change_umol_m2_s = after_umol_m2_s - before_umol_m2_s)

paired |>
  select(plant_id, before_umol_m2_s, after_umol_m2_s, change_umol_m2_s)
mean(paired$change_umol_m2_s)

Check the first plant by hand: L01 went from 5.87 to 6.95, an increase of 1.08. All ten changes are positive, from 1.08 to 4.17, and the mean change is 1.983 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. The plants started at quite different levels (5.20 to 8.81), but taking each plant’s own change removes those differences.
Plot the changes, so a reader can see every plant:

change_plot <- ggplot(paired, aes(x = plant_id, y = change_umol_m2_s)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Plant identifier", y = "After − before (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹)") +
  theme_minimal()
change_plot
ggsave("output/day18-changes.png", change_plot, width = 6, height = 4)




Each point is one plant’s after-minus-before change; the dashed line marks no change.


L02 rose by 4.17, much more than the others. Nothing in the records says it was measured wrongly, so it stays in the analysis.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: How uncertain is the mean change?
text:
How uncertain is the mean change?
A paired t-test estimates the mean change and its 95% confidence interval:

paired_comparison <- t.test(paired$after_umol_m2_s,
                            paired$before_umol_m2_s,
                            paired = TRUE,
                            alternative = "two.sided")
paired_comparison

paired = TRUE tells R that the first value in each vector belongs to the same plant, and so on. With after first and before second, the estimate is after minus before: a mean change of 1.98, 95% CI 1.25 to 2.71 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, p = 0.00017. The interval describes the mean change; individual plants changed by anything from 1.08 to 4.17. There are ten independent units here, the plants, not twenty readings.
A paired t-test is the same as testing the ten changes against zero. Use t.test(paired$change_umol_m2_s, mu = 0) to find out whether it gives the same estimate, interval and p-value. It does: it is the same analysis written differently, not a second piece of evidence.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
text:
What can this experiment show?
The rate went up in every plant. But the light changed and time passed between the two readings, because every plant was measured before, then after. Acclimation during the day or drift in the instrument could also raise the readings, and a small p-value cannot separate these from the light. A better experiment would add plants that are measured twice without any change in light.
In paired-report.Rmd, write the question, the ten plants measured twice, the ID check, the change plot, the test result in the after-minus-before direction, and this limitation. Restart R and render.






Hint: check the direction with one plant





L01’s change should be +1.08. The same order, after then before, belongs in the mutate() line and in the two vectors given to t.test(); if the estimate is −1.98, one of them is reversed.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Why not analyse before and after as two groups?
text:
Why not analyse before and after as two groups?
Use t.test(paired$after_umol_m2_s, paired$before_umol_m2_s), without paired = TRUE, to find out what happens if you ignore the pairing and treat the readings as two separate groups of plants, as on day 17.






Answer





The estimate is the same, 1.98, but the interval widens to 0.74 to 3.23. The differences between plants (some start at 5, some at 9) stay in the calculation and blur the change. The design decides the test: these are the same plants, so the paired analysis is the right one.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: What happens if the pairs get mixed up?
text:
What happens if the pairs get mixed up?
A common mistake is to sort the before column and the after column separately, for example in a spreadsheet. Find out what that does: make a separate object, keep paired unchanged, and compare the two.

wrong_sorted <- paired |>
  mutate(before_umol_m2_s = sort(before_umol_m2_s),
         after_umol_m2_s = sort(after_umol_m2_s),
         change_umol_m2_s = after_umol_m2_s - before_umol_m2_s)
mean(wrong_sorted$change_umol_m2_s)
sd(paired$change_umol_m2_s)
sd(wrong_sorted$change_umol_m2_s)
t.test(wrong_sorted$after_umol_m2_s, wrong_sorted$before_umol_m2_s, paired = TRUE)







Answer





The mean change is still 1.983, so the mean cannot reveal the mistake. But the SD of the changes falls from 1.02 to 0.50, and the p-value becomes about 0.0000006. Sorting matched the smallest reading with the smallest, not each plant with itself, so these “changes” belong to no real plant. A smaller p-value from broken pairs is simply wrong. Sorting the whole table by plant_id is safe, because rows move together.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Three plants: how much can they tell us?
text:
Three plants: how much can they tell us?
A teaching example measured three plants, D1, D2 and D3, before and after a change in light: before 5, 8 and 6, after 7, 9 and 9 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. Create paired-transfer.Rmd and enter the values as a table:
demo <- data.frame(plant_id = c("D1", "D2", "D3"),
                   before_umol_m2_s = c(5, 8, 6),
                   after_umol_m2_s = c(7, 9, 9))
Use a change column and t.test(..., paired = TRUE) to find out whether three plants are enough to tell that the rate went up. Add a change plot with a zero line, a short interpretation, and a note that these are illustrative values, kept separate from the ten-plant study. Render it.






Answer check





The changes are +2, +1 and +3: mean 2, SD 1. The 95% interval for the mean change is −0.48 to 4.48 (p = 0.07). All three plants went up, yet the interval includes zero, because three pairs say very little about plants in general. The honest conclusion is “uncertain”, not “no effect”. More plants would narrow the interval; measuring the same three plants again would only show how repeatable the instrument is.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
text:
Check your understanding

How many independent units are in paired.csv? Ten plants, not twenty readings.
Can two unrelated groups of plants be paired by putting them side by side? No; a pair is the same plant measured twice.
Does the small p-value show that light caused the increase? No; light and time changed together.

Leave with: paired-report.Rmd, its HTML, output/day18-changes.png, and paired-transfer.Rmd with its HTML.
Next: Day 19 — A calibration line.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text:
Today’s question
On day 16 the treated seedlings grew on average 6.22 mm more than the controls. A second experiment with 24 new seedlings would give a different number, so how much should we trust 6.22 mm? Today you add a Welch two-sample t-test to comparison.Rmd. It gives the two numbers that every results section reports next to an estimate: a 95% confidence interval and a p-value.
Open comparison.Rmd and run its chunks, so that seedlings, treated and control exist. The study design is described in data/README.md.
Save today: comparison.Rmd and its HTML, day17-checks.R, and an updated transfer-comparison.Rmd with its HTML.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Does the Welch test fit this study?
text:
Does the Welch test fit this study?
Each value in treated is the growth of one plant, and each value in control is the growth of another plant. The plants were randomly allocated to the two groups, so the groups are independent, which is what Welch’s test needs. The treated plants vary more (SD 4.87 mm) than the controls (SD 3.19 mm); that is fine, because Welch’s test does not assume equal spread. Look at the day 16 plot once more for a single plant far away from all others. There is none here, so the test can go ahead.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text:
Running the test

comparison <- t.test(treated, control, var.equal = FALSE,
                     alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)
comparison

t.test() subtracts the second vector from the first, so the result describes treated minus control, the direction we chose on day 16. var.equal = FALSE selects Welch’s method (it is also R’s default; writing it shows the reader which test you used), alternative = "two.sided" counts a difference in either direction, and conf.level = 0.95 asks for a 95% interval. The R documentation for t.test lists all arguments.
You should see, among other lines:
t = 3.7012, df = 18.986, p-value = 0.001517
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.700984 9.732349
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y
 21.49167  15.27500

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text:
Reading the output









R prints
Value
Units
Meaning




mean of x, mean of y
21.49, 15.28
mm
Mean growth of treated and control plants


(subtract them)
6.22
mm
The estimate: treated − control


95 percent confidence interval
2.70 to 9.73
mm

t, df

Used to calculate the p-value

How surprising the data would be if the means were equal



Read the result in this order. The estimate says that treated plants grew 6.22 mm more on average in our sample. The confidence interval says that population mean differences from about 2.70 to 9.73 mm fit the data; because the whole interval lies above zero, the data point to more growth with the treatment. The interval is about the mean difference, not about single plants: several control plants grew more than several treated plants. If the whole experiment were repeated many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true difference.
The p-value answers a narrower question: if treated and control plants had the same mean growth, how often would a difference at least this large appear by chance? About 0.15% of the time, so rarely. This is not the probability that the treatment has no effect, and it says nothing about whether 6 mm matters for a seedling of about 20 mm. That judgement needs the estimate and biology.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Writing the result in the report
text:
Writing the result in the report
Use $ to take numbers out of the result instead of retyping them, so the report stays correct if the data change:

mean(treated) - mean(control)
comparison$conf.int
comparison$p.value

In comparison.Rmd, add a Methods sentence (two independent groups, growth = final − initial, treated minus control, Welch two-sample t-test) and a Results paragraph such as:

Treated seedlings grew on average 6.22 mm more than controls (21.49 mm versus 15.28 mm, 12 plants per group; 95% confidence interval 2.70 to 9.73 mm; Welch two-sample t-test, p = 0.0015).

End with one sentence on the biological size of the difference and one on the limits of this small simulated study. Keep the individual-point plot. Restart R and render.






Hint: what if an interval includes zero?





Zero means “no difference in mean growth”. An interval from, say, −1 to 5 mm contains both small negative and moderate positive differences, so the study cannot tell the direction. Report it as inconclusive, not as “no effect”.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Does the order of the groups matter?
text:
Does the order of the groups matter?
In a new script, day17-checks.R, use t.test(control, treated) to find out whether swapping the two groups changes the conclusion.






Answer





The interval becomes −9.73 to −2.70 mm: the same numbers with the opposite sign, because it now describes control minus treated. The p-value stays 0.0015. The data have not changed, only the direction in which we describe them, so keep the treated-minus-control version in the report.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text:
How sure is “95% sure”?
In day17-checks.R, use t.test(treated, control, conf.level = 0.90) and conf.level = 0.99 to find out how the range of plausible differences changes when you ask for more or less confidence.






Answer





90%: 3.31 to 9.12 mm. 95%: 2.70 to 9.73 mm. 99%: 1.41 to 11.02 mm. The more confident you want to be that the interval contains the true difference, the wider it must be. The means do not change. Keep 95% in the report: choose the level before you look, not after.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text:
Correcting wrong sentences
Each of these sentences, all common in student reports, contains one error. Write a corrected version of each in day17-checks.R as a comment.

“There is a 0.15% probability that the treatment has no effect.”
“95% of treated plants grew between 2.70 and 9.73 mm more.”
“Another study found a 2 mm difference with a 95% interval of −1 to 5 mm, so the treatment does nothing.”







Answer






The p-value is calculated assuming equal means: if the means were equal, a difference this large would appear in about 0.15% of experiments.
The interval is for the mean difference, not for individual plants.
The interval includes zero but also differences of up to 5 mm, so the study could not determine the direction. It is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text:
A second class’s data
Another class repeated the experiment with nine plants per group (data/seedlings-transfer.csv; you summarised it on day 16 in transfer-comparison.Rmd). Use t.test(new_treated, new_control) to find out whether treated plants also grew more in this study, and how precisely the difference is estimated. Create the two vectors from transfer the same way you created treated and control, then add the test and a results sentence to transfer-comparison.Rmd and render it.






Answer check





Mean growth was 17.87 mm (treated) and 13.66 mm (control): a difference of 4.21 mm, 95% CI 1.95 to 6.47 mm, Welch p = 0.0012. This interval is narrower than the first study’s (7.0 mm wide against 4.5 mm), even though each group has three plants fewer, because these plants vary much less (SD 1.94 and 2.53 mm against 4.87 and 3.19 mm). Precision depends on both sample size and spread.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text:
Check your understanding

Which numbers have units of mm: the difference, the interval, or the p-value? The difference and the interval; a p-value has no unit.
Does the SD of a group describe the uncertainty in the difference? No; SD describes how much single plants vary.
If all treated plants had grown in one shared pot and all controls in another, would this test still fit? No; the plants would no longer be independent units.

Leave with: comparison.Rmd and its HTML reporting the estimate, interval, p-value and sample sizes; day17-checks.R; and transfer-comparison.Rmd with its HTML.
Next: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text:
Today’s question
Does the nutrient treatment change how much a seedling grows? Last week you described the plants. Today you turn that description into a comparison: you decide what to compare and in which direction, look at the plants, calculate the difference between the group means, and prepare the report that day 17 extends with a statistical test.
Open introcomputing.Rproj and use the complete data/seedlings.csv; the study is described in the data dictionary.
Save today: comparison.Rmd and its HTML, output/day16-growth.png and output/day16-plan.txt.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: The question, the unit and the direction
text:
The question, the unit and the direction
The outcome is growth, final minus initial length in millimetres. The unit is one plant in its own pot, randomly allocated to a group, so there are 12 independent plants per group. Each plant was measured twice, but its two lengths give one growth value, so it counts once.
We compare mean growth of treated plants minus mean growth of control plants. A positive difference then means the treated plants grew more. Deciding the direction before calculating keeps the code, the numbers and the sentences in the report consistent.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text:
Growth in the two groups
Use group_by() and summarise() to find out how many plants are in each group and how much they grew:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mm = mean(growth_mm),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm), .groups = "drop")
group_summary

Each group has 12 plants. The control mean is 15.28 mm (SD 3.19 mm) and the treated mean 21.49 mm (SD 4.87 mm).

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text:
Looking at the plants

growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 16)) +
  labs(x = "Treatment group", y = "Growth over the study period (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot




Individual growth values in the supplied simulated dataset. The slight horizontal displacement separates overlapping dots.


The treated plants sit higher on average, but the groups overlap: the largest control plant (18.7 mm) grew more than the smallest treated plant (12.2 mm). So the treated group grew more on average, not every treated plant.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Would another experiment give the same difference?
text:
Would another experiment give the same difference?
No. Twelve other plants per group would give another difference, because plants vary. Even if the treatment did nothing, two groups of plants would rarely have exactly equal means. Day 17 asks how large a difference chance alone could produce, and for that we need three terms.
The null hypothesis is that mean growth would be the same under both conditions if we could grow very many plants. The alternative is two-sided: a difference in either direction counts, and we decide this now, before seeing any test. A p-value says how often a difference at least as extreme as ours would arise if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the treatment works, and it does not tell you how large the effect is.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text:
Preparing comparison.Rmd
Save a copy of the root-level report.Rmd as comparison.Rmd, also in the project root so its data/ paths work, and keep your earlier reports.

Write the analysis plan at the top of the report and in output/day16-plan.txt: the question, the outcome and its unit, the unit (one plant), how plants were allocated, and the direction (treated − control).
Add the import, group_summary and the plot. Use group_by(treatment) and summarise(mean(initial_mm)) to find out whether the groups started at the same size. Controls started slightly longer (23.0 mm against 21.9 mm), which is why growth, not final length, answers the question.
Add the treated, control and observed_difference code. Reverse the subtraction in a separate line to find out what changes: only the sign (−6.22 mm). Keep treated − control as the result you report.
Use min(treated) and max(control) to find out whether every treated plant grew more than every control plant. It did not: 12.2 mm is less than 18.7 mm. Write the results as a statement about means.
Write a results paragraph with n, both means with SDs, the difference with its direction and unit, and the overlap. End with what is still open: how uncertain the difference is. Save the figure with ggsave("output/day16-growth.png", growth_plot, width = 6, height = 4) and render the report.







Hint: a surprising sign





Print mean(treated) and mean(control) separately. A negative difference from mean(control) - mean(treated) describes the reverse comparison, not a different biological result. Calling an object treatment_effect does not change its sign; the order of the subtraction does.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text:
A second class’s data
The second class’s experiment, data/seedlings-transfer.csv, has 18 plants, nine per randomly allocated group, measured seven days apart. Did their treated plants also grow more? Create transfer-comparison.Rmd in the project root with the same question and direction.

Import the file, check it (18 rows, no repeated ID, no missing values) and calculate growth. T01 grew 15.0 mm; check it by hand.
Use group_by() and summarise() with n(), mean() and sd() to find out how much each group grew, and save the table as output/day16-transfer-summary.csv. Control: 9 plants, mean 13.66 mm (SD 2.53 mm). Treated: 9 plants, mean 17.87 mm (SD 1.94 mm).
Calculate the difference, treated − control. You should get 4.21 mm, smaller than the 6.22 mm of the first study. Different plants, grown by a different class, give a different estimate; whether the two differences are really different is not something we can judge yet.
Suppose this class had grown all treated plants in one tray and all controls in another. In two sentences in the report, say how many independently treated units each group would then have (one tray) and why measuring more plants in those trays would not help. Render from a fresh session; day 17 adds the test to this report.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text:
Check your understanding






Can we conclude that every treated plant grew more?





No. Look at the dots: the largest control plant grew more than the smallest treated plant. The treated plants grew more on average.









Are 12 plants measured twice 24 independent replicates per group?





No. The two measurements belong to the same plant and are combined into one growth value. Each group has 12 independent plants.









Does the difference of 6.22 mm tell us how uncertain it is?





No. That depends on how much plants vary and how many there are, which is what the Welch test on day 17 uses.



Leave with: comparison.Rmd, its rendered HTML, and output/day16-growth.png.
Next: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
text:
Review questions from the week. See the statistics reference for definitions.
Topic quizzes:

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
text:
1. Mean, variance, and SD
Three growth measurements are 12, 14, and 16 mm. What are the mean, sample variance, and sample SD? Show the units.






Worked answer





Mean = 14 mm. Deviations are −2, 0, and 2 mm; squared deviations sum to 8. Divide by n − 1 = 2 to obtain sample variance 4 mm². Its square root is sample SD 2 mm. SD describes spread among these measurements, not the uncertainty in their mean.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 2. A common shift and a unit conversion
text:
2. A common shift and a unit conversion
If every measurement above gains 10 mm, what happens to mean and SD? If the original lengths are converted from mm to cm, how do mean, SD, and variance change?






Answer and check





Adding 10 shifts the mean to 24 mm but leaves SD at 2 mm, since deviations from the mean are unchanged. Dividing lengths by ten gives mean 1.4 cm, SD 0.2 cm, and variance 0.04 cm². Variance scales by the square of the conversion factor.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 3. An unusual number is a question, not proof of an error
text:
3. An unusual number is a question, not proof of an error
The messy table contains final length 4.38 for P21. What permits correcting it to 43.8 mm? What should happen to the unavailable final measurement for P06?






Answer and check





The supplied source notes confirm a transcription/unit error and give 43.8 mm. The unusual value alone would not justify multiplying by ten. P06 remains missing because there is no supported replacement in this exercise. Preserve the raw file and record repairs in code; zero would invent a measurement.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
text:
4. Rows versus available measurements
After the confirmed identical duplicate is removed, the repaired table has 24 plants and one unavailable growth value in the control group. How many plant records and available growth measurements are there per group?






Answer and check





There are 12 control and 12 treated plant records, but 11 control and 12 treated available growth measurements. The complete clean seedling file used later is a separate teaching dataset with 12 available per group. State which file the analysis uses so its counts match the results.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 5. More readings or more independent units?
text:
5. More readings or more independent units?
One treated plant is measured twelve times. A second study independently assigns twelve plants to treatment. Are these equivalent sources of information about differences among plants?






Answer and check





No. Repeated readings of one plant may reveal measurement consistency but do not create twelve independently treated plants. The design determines the experimental unit. Likewise, reweighing one synthesis run does not create more independently prepared runs.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 6. Spread of observations versus spread of sample means
text:
6. Spread of observations versus spread of sample means
The supplied simulation draws means from samples of four or sixteen plants from the same fixed toy population. Why can the means of sixteen spread less without changing the population’s individual SD?






Answer and check





The source measurements stay the same. A mean averages independent sampling variation, so repeated means based on more observations typically vary less. The SD among repeated sample means describes sampling variability of an estimate; it is not SD among individual plants. A precise estimate can still be biased or based on an inappropriate design.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 7. A duplicate identifier needs a design check
text:
7. A duplicate identifier needs a design check
A file has two rows with the same plant ID. Is deleting one automatically justified? How does the answer differ between one row per plant and one row per time point?






Answer and reasoning





No. First establish the intended row meaning and compare the complete records. In the supplied messy exercise, an identical duplicate import is confirmed by source notes. In a repeated-time design, the same plant ID can legitimately recur. Different readings attached to one ID require investigation, not arbitrary deletion.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 8. What did the invented zero do?
text:
8. What did the invented zero do?
P06 initially measured24.7 mm and has no final reading. A student substitutes final length0. What growth does this calculate, and why is it different from retaining NA?






Answer and reasoning





It invents −24.7 mm growth. NA states that growth cannot be calculated from the available record; zero final length asserts a measured final size. Omitting an explicitly counted missing value in an available-case mean does not authorise making up a zero measurement.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 9. Same mean, different spread in a new source
text:
9. Same mean, different spread in a new source
The transfer study has a larger treated mean but a smaller treated SD. Is that inconsistent? What should the axis and summary table say?






Answer and reasoning





It is consistent: centre and individual spread describe different features. Use seven-day growth in mm, available n=9 per group, and the actual group summaries. Centre and spread need separate descriptions.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
section: 10. Read the units after a transformation
text:
10. Read the units after a transformation
A vector has SD 2 mm and variance 4mm². What happens to SD and variance if every value is divided by 10 to express cm? What if10 mm is added to every value instead?






Answer and reasoning





Conversion gives SD 0.2 cm and variance 0.04cm². A common additive shift changes the mean but neither deviations nor SD/variance. The physical spread did not diminish merely because its unit changed.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
text:
11. Two simulation settings
One run draws 12 values for each mean and repeats that400 times. Another draws 12 values and repeats1000 times. Did the second acquire more independently measured plants or reduce the sample size of each mean?






Answer and reasoning





Neither. The source observations and 12 draws per sample stay fixed. More repetitions give a more stable picture of the simulated sampling distribution. Increasing the number of independent draws per estimated mean is a different change from collecting more simulation repetitions.

title: Week 3 revision — measurements and variation
text:
12. Repair a descriptive conclusion
A report says: “The higher group mean proves every treated plant improved; the SD is the 95% uncertainty.” Repair the two errors without adding a test.






Answer and reasoning





A greater observed mean can coexist with overlapping individuals, so describe the group tendency and observations. SD describes individual spread, not a95% confidence interval. A descriptive report should state outcome, units, n, centre, spread and limits rather than inventing inferential or universal claims.



Return to the descriptive report, or continue to comparisons.

title: Quiz: A descriptive report
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Which input gives 24 complete plant growth values: seedlings.csv or the repaired seedlings-messy.csv? What should a report state?






Hint





The repair exercise retains one unavailable final measurement.









Answer





seedlings.csv has 24 complete growth values. The repaired messy input has 24 plant records but 23 observed growths. State the input and report available sample sizes consistent with it.




Q2. A report says “Treated plants had a higher mean, so every treated plant outgrew every control.” What should you inspect, and how would you revise it?






Hint





A group mean summarises observations without ordering every pair of plants.









Answer





Inspect the individual-point plot for overlap. Report the larger observed mean with its units and sample sizes, while noting individual variation and overlap between groups.




Q3. What should the Methods and figure caption identify so a reader can understand the growth summary?






Hint





How were measurements obtained, and what does one point represent?









Answer





Identify the independent plant, treatment groups, initial/final readings seven days apart, growth = final − initial in mm, input file, relevant data checks, available n, and plotted symbol meanings. Label SD as individual spread.




Q4. Your HTML renders only while objects remain in the RStudio Environment. Which action tests and repairs this?

Save a screenshot.
Restart R and render, adding missing imports/calculations to the source.
Rename the HTML.







Hint





The source should create every object needed by later chunks.









Answer





(ii). A fresh-session render reveals hidden dependencies. Include loading, import, checks, derived variables, summaries, and plots in the saved workflow.




Q5. A report reads data from /home/sam/Downloads/plants.csv. Why might a copied project fail? Give a more portable layout.






Hint





A personal absolute path points outside the copied project.









Answer





That path may not exist elsewhere. Keep data inside the project, for example data/seedlings.csv, and use that relative path from the report at project root. Test the complete copy in a newly located folder.

title: Quiz: Independent units and sampling
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. One plant is measured twelve times with a ruler. How many independently treated plants does this provide? What can the repeated readings help assess?






Hint





Separate the unit assigned to treatment from repeated measurement of it.









Answer





One plant. The repeats help assess measurement consistency; they do not create twelve independent plants.




Q2. Treatment is assigned to whole trays, with twelve plants in each tray. Which is the treatment unit?

A ruler reading.
Each plant independently.
A tray.







Hint





All plants in a tray receive the same allocation together.









Answer





(iii), a tray. Plants within it share the treatment unit and potentially the environment. More independently allocated trays are needed for independent tray-level replication.




Q3. The supplied simulation draws from one fixed source distribution. Will means of samples of sixteen usually spread more or less than means of samples of four? Does the source SD change?






Hint





Distinguish variation among observations from variation among estimated means.









Answer





The sixteen-draw means usually spread less. The stored source values and their SD stay unchanged.




Q4. What do the 400 values in means_16 represent?

400 newly measured plants.
Means of 400 simulated samples, each with sixteen draws.
Sixteen means from samples of 400 plants.







Hint





Read the outer repetition count and inner sample size separately.









Answer





(ii). replicate(400, mean(sample(..., size = 16, replace = TRUE))) calculates 400 means. The draws simulate sampling; they are not new measurements.




Q5. You increase simulation repetitions from 400 to 1000 while retaining sixteen draws per sample. Does this have the same effect as increasing plants per sample? What does set.seed() control?






Hint





One setting changes how well the simulated distribution is represented; the other changes what each estimate averages.









Answer





No. More repetitions give a more stable picture of the same sampling distribution; more independent draws per mean typically narrow it. set.seed() sets the random generator state so the simulated sequence can be reproduced.

title: Quiz: Group summaries and figures
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A table has 24 plants in two treatment groups. After group_by(treatment) |> summarise(mean_mm = mean(growth_mm)), how many rows should the summary have? What does one row mean?






Hint





A grouped summary produces one result per group.









Answer





Two rows, one per treatment. Each row describes a group; it is not an additional plant observation.




Q2. Which table supplies each layer in a plot showing individual dots and group-mean diamonds?






Hint





The individual layer and summary layer have different observational levels.









Answer





The plant-level table supplies individual dots. The grouped summary table supplies one mean diamond per treatment.




Q3. Why use horizontal jitter with height = 0 for a growth dot plot?






Hint





The vertical position encodes the measured growth.









Answer





Horizontal jitter separates overlapping dots without changing their measured growth heights. Vertical jitter would move the displayed measurements.




Q4. A histogram looks two-peaked with bins 2 mm wide and one-peaked with bins 6 mm wide. What can you conclude about the two peaks?






Hint





Small-sample histogram shape depends on how nearby values are grouped.









Answer





The apparent two-peak detail is sensitive to bin choice. Compare the individual points and describe broad features that remain stable rather than claiming two biological populations from this display alone.




Q5. A caption says “Bars show error.” What information is missing? If the figure has only individual dots and mean diamonds, what should its caption say?






Hint





Identify the plotted quantity, units, observation unit, and symbol meanings.









Answer





An error bar must specify its quantity, such as SD or a confidence interval. For this figure, state that dots are individual plants, diamonds are group means, and growth is measured in mm; include available sample sizes. There are no error bars to describe.

title: Quiz: Mean, variance, and SD
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. For growth values 12, 14, and 16 mm, calculate the mean, sample variance, and sample SD, with units.






Hint





The squared deviations from 14 are 4, 0, and 4. Sample variance divides their sum by \(n-1\).









Answer





Mean 14 mm; sample variance \((4+0+4)/2 = 4\) mm²; sample SD \(\sqrt{4}=2\) mm.




Q2. What will this return, and why?
mean(c(10, 10, 10, 100))
median(c(10, 10, 10, 100))






Hint





The mean uses every value; the median uses the ordered middle values.









Answer





The mean is 32.5 and median 10. The large value strongly affects the mean; neither result is an arithmetic error.




Q3. A vector has mean 14 mm and SD 2 mm. What happens when 10 mm is added to every value? What happens when the original values are divided by ten to express centimetres?






Hint





A common addition leaves deviations unchanged. Unit conversion rescales both measurements and their deviations.









Answer





Adding 10 mm gives mean 24 mm, SD 2 mm. Converting the original values gives mean 1.4 cm, SD 0.2 cm and variance 0.04 cm².




Q4. Two groups have the same mean but SDs of 1 and 6 mm. Which statement is supported?

The second group has greater observed spread.
Every second-group plant is larger.
The second group was measured incorrectly.







Hint





SD describes variation among observations, not its cause.









Answer





(i). The observations in the second group vary more around their mean. SD alone does not identify biological or measurement causes.




Q5. A synthesis run collects 0.62 g from a supplied maximum of 1.00 g. Percentage yield is 100 * collected / maximum. What is the yield? If another run yields 70%, how many percentage points higher is that?






Hint





Use the supplied ratio, then subtract the percentages.









Answer





62% yield; 70% is 8 percentage points higher. The difference is not an 8% relative increase.

title: Quiz: Check and repair data
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. The file is intended to have one row per plant. It has 25 rows but 24 unique plant IDs. What should you inspect before removing a row?






Hint





Compare every field in the repeated records and consult the source notes.









Answer





Inspect the repeated ID’s full records and the source notes. Here both P01 records are identical and the recorder confirms an import duplicate. In a time-series table, a repeated plant ID could be legitimate.




Q2. P21 has a final length of 4.38. Which evidence justifies changing it to 43.8 mm?

Other plants are larger.
The correction increases the group mean.
The original source record gives 43.8 mm.







Hint





A surprising value suggests a check; it does not specify the correct value.









Answer





(iii). The source record supports this correction. Size or a preferred result alone does not establish an error.




Q3. P06 started at 24.7 mm and its final measurement is missing. What growth would replacing the missing final value with zero produce? What should the cleaned table retain?






Hint





Growth is final minus initial. A missing value states that the measurement is unavailable.









Answer





It would invent \(0 - 24.7 = -24.7\) mm growth. Retain NA for final length and growth; there is no supported replacement.




Q4. After repair there are 12 plant records in each group, with one control growth unavailable. What are the available growth sample sizes?






Hint





Count observed values separately from enrolled plant records.









Answer





11 controls and 12 treated plants have observed growth. Both groups still contain 12 plant records. sum(!is.na(growth_mm)) counts available growths.




Q5. Which files allow you to reproduce and explain a repair?

Only the cleaned CSV.
Raw CSV, source notes, and repair script.
A screenshot of RStudio.







Hint





A reproducible repair needs both its input and the reasons for changing it.









Answer





(ii). The script regenerates derived data from the original, and the source notes explain the correction evidence.

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
text:
Today’s question
What can we honestly say about seedling growth from these measurements? Today you write a short report that answers that question for a reader who was not in the room: what was measured, how growth was calculated, what the figure shows, and what we cannot conclude yet. It uses everything from days 6–9, and it must render on a fresh R session so that anyone can rerun it.
Open the project, open report.Rmd, and use Save As to save a copy as first-report.Rmd in the project folder, so the data/ paths keep working. The rendered HTML can go into reports/.
Save today: first-report.Rmd and its HTML.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
text:
What a reader needs
A short report has four parts, each answering one question a reader has:

Question and data: what did you want to know, and what was measured?
Methods: how did you get from the file to the result?
Results: what does the figure show, and which numbers matter?
Interpretation: what do the results mean, and what can they not tell us?

The study is described in data/README.md: 24 seedlings in separate pots, 12 randomly allocated to a nutrient treatment and 12 to a control, each measured at the start and after seven days, in mm. The nutrient is not specified, and the data are simulated. Put these facts in your first section; the reader cannot see the dictionary.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
text:
Methods and simple checks
Write the method in words a biologist understands: “Growth was calculated as final minus initial length for each plant, in mm.” That says more than “we used mutate()”. The code goes in the report too, so the calculation can be rerun:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

Then use three short checks to find out whether the data are complete and plausible, and report the answers:

nrow(seedlings)
sum(is.na(seedlings$growth_mm))
range(seedlings$growth_mm)

There are 24 plants, no missing growth values, and growth ranges from 8.0 to 30.8 mm. So every plant was measured, and every plant grew.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: The figure, and what to say about it
text:
The figure, and what to say about it
Use the growth-by-treatment plot from day 8, with every plant as a point, growth in mm on the y-axis, and a caption saying that each point is one independently potted plant.
Then describe it. Good sentences say something specific that the reader can see in the figure:

“Growth varied among plants in both groups.”
“Treated plants tended to grow more: controls grew 8.0–18.7 mm and treated plants 12.2–30.8 mm, but the groups overlap.”

Two sentences go too far. “Every treated plant grew more than every control” is false: P17 (treated) grew 12.2 mm, less than most controls. “The treatment works” needs an estimate of how uncertain the difference is, which comes in week 4. A fair limitation is that this is one small, simulated study.
mean(seedlings$growth_mm) gives 18.4 mm, but that mixes both groups, so it does not answer whether they differ. Group means come in week 3.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
text:
Writing the report
Write the four sections in first-report.Rmd:

Question and data: the question, the design (number of plants, groups, random allocation, simulated data) and what one row is.
Methods: how the file was read and growth calculated, in words, with the code chunk and its relative path, and the unit.
Results: the labelled figure and the three checks. Use inline code for at least one number, such as the number of plants.
Interpretation: the pattern, the variation among plants, and one limitation.

Restart R and render from the Console (not inside the report):

rmarkdown::render("first-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")

If it fails, start from the first error and add whatever the report is missing.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
text:
Leaf area and leaf mass
Does a larger leaf also weigh more? The file data/leaf-mass.csv has one leaf from each of 18 plants, with its area in cm² and its dry mass in mg. In a script leaf-first-look.R, read it into leaves and draw a scatter plot with leaf_area_cm2 on the x-axis and dry_mass_mg on the y-axis, with units in the axis labels.
The points lie close to a rising line: leaves from 2.96 to 14.68 cm² weigh from 21.19 to 71.33 mg, and larger leaves are heavier. No treatment was applied here; the plot shows that the two measurements go together in these plants.






Hint: adapting the plot





Start with leaves <- read_csv("data/leaf-mass.csv", show_col_types = FALSE), then reuse the ggplot() code from day 8 with the new table, the new columns, new axis labels and geom_point() without jitter.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
section: Reading your report as a stranger
text:
Reading your report as a stranger
Open the HTML in a browser, without looking at the .Rmd, and read it as someone who has never seen the data. Note every problem and how you fixed it in reports/report-revision.txt.

Can you find the question, the input file, the number of plants, the two groups, the unit, and what one point in the figure is? Add whatever is missing to the .Rmd, not to the HTML, which is replaced at every render.
Take three sentences from your interpretation and find, for each, the figure, number or dictionary fact that supports it. Rewrite any sentence nothing supports, such as one claiming every treated plant grew more.
If you have two figures (initial versus final length, and growth by group), keep the one that answers your question. For “did treated plants grow more?” that is growth by group, because its y-axis is growth.
Restart R, render again, and check that the HTML shows your corrections.







Hint: a description or a conclusion?





“In this sample, treated plants tended to grow more, but the groups overlap” can be checked against the points. “The treatment always increases growth” goes far beyond 24 simulated plants. Before week 4, describe the pattern, the overlap and the limits of the study.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
text:
A second, smaller brief
Write a second short report, laboratory-brief.Rmd in the project folder, about one of these tables, with the same four sections:

The 18-plant transfer study (data/seedlings-transfer.csv): did treated plants grow more in the second class’s experiment? There are 18 plants, 9 per group, and T01 grew 15.0 mm.
The solution recipes (data/solutions.csv): what concentration does each recipe give? Use 1000 * (mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol) / (final_volume_ml / 1000) for mmol/L. Each substance gives 50, 100 and 150 mmol/L. The masses differ between the substances because glucose molecules are heavier than sodium chloride, so the same concentration needs more grams.

For either choice:

Say what one row is: one plant, or one recipe. For the recipes, define mole and molar mass as on day 6.
Check the table’s size, column types and missing values, and report them.
Calculate growth or concentration, make one labelled figure, and save it with a derived table as output/laboratory-brief-...png and .csv.
Write the interpretation with one limitation for this study: for plants, the small sample and overlap; for recipes, that the values follow from a formula, not from measured variation.
Restart R and render. Then copy the brief with its data and .Rproj to a practice folder, render it there, and note the folder in report-revision.txt.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
text:
Completion check
Open your HTML in a browser. Can you find the question, the units, what one dot is, and the main limitation? Then restart R and check that the saved .Rmd renders.






Self-check





The .Rmd contains the imports, the growth calculation and the plot. The HTML reads sensibly without the code. There is no personal path such as C:/Users/anna/Desktop anywhere in the source.



Keep: first-report.Rmd, its HTML, and leaf-first-look.R if completed. Next: what happens when a laboratory table is imperfect?
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
text:
Today’s question
You have code that calculates growth and draws a figure. How do you hand that to someone as a readable report, without copying numbers and pictures into a Word file by hand, where they go out of date as soon as the data change? An R Markdown report is one file, ending in .Rmd, that holds your text and your R code. Rendering it runs the code and produces an HTML page with the text, the results and the figures together. When the data change, you render again.
(These course webpages are made with Quarto, a close relative. You only need R Markdown.)
Save today: report.Rmd and its rendered HTML.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
text:
The report template
Open the project and click report.Rmd in the Files pane. Keep it in the project folder, next to data/, so that data/seedlings.csv still points to the data; moved into reports/, the same path would point to a folder that does not exist.
A minimal report looks like this:
---
title: "Seedling growth"
output: html_document
---

## Question

How much did the seedlings grow during the observation period?

```{r import}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
```

There are `r nrow(seedlings)` plants in the dataset.

```{r mean-growth}
mean(seedlings$growth_mm)
```

Growth is final minus initial length, measured in millimetres.

It has three kinds of content. The header, between the two --- lines, sets the title and says the output is an HTML page. Ordinary text is written as is; ## Question makes a heading. A code chunk starts with three backticks and {r} and ends with three backticks; the word after r, such as import, is the chunk’s label, and every label must be different. The sentence with `r nrow(seedlings)` is inline code: when the report is rendered, R replaces it with the number of plants, 24.
A # means different things in the two places: in the text it makes a heading, inside a chunk it starts an R comment.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
text:
Rendering the report
Save the file and click Knit. R starts a fresh session, runs the chunks from top to bottom, and writes an HTML page that opens in a viewer. You can do the same from the Console:

rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")

rmarkdown::render uses the render() function from the rmarkdown package. output_dir = "reports" puts the HTML in reports/; the .Rmd stays where it is. Knit may put the HTML next to the .Rmd instead, so look for the file rather than assuming where it went. Never put the render line inside the report itself: the report would try to render itself.
Because rendering starts fresh, the report must contain every step it needs: library() lines, the import and the calculations. Something you only typed in the Console does not exist when the report is rendered.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
text:
A figure with a caption
Load ggplot2 in the first chunk, and add the growth plot from day 8 in its own chunk. fig.cap gives the figure a caption:
```{r growth-figure, fig.cap="Each point is one independently potted seedling."}
ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 8)) +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)")
```

The caption says what the figure shows. Below it, write a sentence saying what you see, for example that growth varies within both groups and the groups overlap.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
text:
Your first report

Render the supplied template before changing anything, to find out whether your setup works. An HTML page should open. If it does not, fix that first.
Change the title and the question to your own words and render again.
Put the import, the growth calculation and the labelled growth figure in chunks, in that order. If the template creates the same object twice, keep one.
Write a short methods paragraph: what one row is (one plant), how growth was calculated, and in which unit.
Misspell a column name on purpose, e.g. growth_m, and render. Find the chunk label in the error message, fix the spelling, and render again.
Restart R (Session → Restart R) and render once more. It works, because the report contains every step it needs.







Hint: rendering stops





Read the first error and the chunk label it names. Is the package loaded with library() before its functions are used? Are the data imported before the calculation? Are the file and column names spelt exactly? Does every chunk have an opening and a closing fence? When you ask for help, include the error text.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
text:
When rendering stops
Errors are easier to fix once you have seen them on purpose. Save a copy of your report as report-workshop.Rmd, in the project folder, and break it in three ways, one at a time. Each time, note in reports/render-recovery.txt what you changed, the first line of the error, and how you fixed it; then fix it and render again before the next break.

Give two chunks the same label to find out what R says. It stops with a message about a duplicate chunk label and names the label.
Misspell the CSV file name in the import, e.g. data/seedling.csv, to find out what a missing input looks like. The error says the file does not exist. An object of the same name left in your Console does not help, because rendering starts fresh.
Move the plot chunk above the chunk that calculates growth_mm. The error says growth_mm (or seedlings) was not found: chunks run from top to bottom, so a figure can only use what earlier chunks made.

Finally, open the HTML in a browser next to the .Rmd. The .Rmd is the recipe you edit; the HTML is the reading copy, and changes made to it are lost at the next render. The measurements themselves are in data/seedlings.csv.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: A report for the second class’s data
text:
A report for the second class’s data
Use Save As to make transfer-report.Rmd, in the project folder, for the 18-plant study in data/seedlings-transfer.csv. The point is a report that describes that study and nothing else.

Change the import to data/seedlings-transfer.csv and call the table transfer. Keep the library() lines and the growth calculation in the report.
Use inline code to state the number of plants, so the report itself finds out how many there are. The HTML should say 18.
Rewrite the question, methods and caption for this study: 18 plants, 9 per group. Add the growth-by-group figure and the initial-versus-final figure from day08-transfer.R, each with a caption saying what one point is and what the y-axis measures.
Restart R and render. Then search the .Rmd for 24 and for seedlings.csv. Every hit is a sentence or line that may still describe the other study; fix any that do.
Find out whether the report works in another place: copy transfer-report.Rmd, introcomputing.Rproj, the data folder and empty output and reports folders into a new practice folder, open that copy’s .Rproj and render there. If something is missing, note it in render-recovery.txt.

The finished transfer report describes 18 plants, 9 per group, none missing, and T01 grew 15.0 mm.






Hint: the HTML still says 24





A number typed into the text does not change when the data change. Replace it with inline code such as `r nrow(transfer)`, and check that the import really reads the transfer file.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
text:
Check your understanding






Which files do you keep?





The .Rmd source, its input data and the HTML. The HTML is convenient to read, but only the .Rmd can make it again.









Why not just type the number of plants into the sentence?





A typed number stays the same when the data change. Inline code recalculates it at every render.



Keep: your saved report.Rmd and a successfully rendered HTML report. Next: write your first complete short report.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Today’s question
How much did each seedling grow, and did the treated plants grow more than the controls? The table only holds the start and end lengths, so today you calculate growth as a new column, pick out the plants and columns you need, and draw a figure in which every plant is a point. All of it is code in a script, so a corrected value later only means running the script again.
Start a script called day08.R in the project folder.
Save today: day08.R, output/seedling-growth.png and output/seedling-growth.csv.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Growth as a new column

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
head(seedlings)

dplyr and ggplot2 are packages, like readr on day 7. mutate() adds a column calculated from the others, here final minus initial length for each plant, and we store the result under the old name seedlings. The table in R now has a fifth column; the CSV file on disk is unchanged. Check the first plant by hand: P01 grew 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm.
Growth and final length answer different questions. final_mm says how big a plant ended up; growth_mm says how much it changed. A plant that started big can end big and still have grown little.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Choosing plants and columns
filter() keeps the rows (plants) that meet a condition, and select() keeps the columns you name:

control_plants <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "control")
growth_table <- select(seedlings, plant_id, treatment, growth_mm)

control_plants has 12 rows, the control plants. growth_table has all 24 rows but only 3 columns. Note the double ==: it asks “is this equal?”, while <- stores. "control" is in quotes because it is a text label and must be spelt exactly as in the data.
Several steps can be chained with the pipe |>, which passes the table on to the next function. Use it to find out how many control plants grew more than 15 mm:

longer_control <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "control") |>
  filter(growth_mm > 15)
nrow(longer_control)

Read it as “take seedlings, then keep the controls, then keep those that grew more than 15 mm”. 7 of the 12 control plants did. If a chain gives a surprising answer, run it one step at a time.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Did longer seedlings end longer?
ggplot() draws a figure from a table. aes() says which column goes where:

size_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = initial_mm, y = final_mm,
                                  colour = treatment)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Initial seedling length (mm)",
       y = "Final seedling length (mm)",
       colour = "Treatment") +
  theme_minimal()
size_plot

Each point is one plant, coloured by its group. + adds a part to the figure: geom_point() draws the points, labs() names the axes with their units, and theme_minimal() gives a plain background. A + at the end of a line tells R that the instruction continues on the next line.
The points form a loose cloud: seedlings that started longer ended only slightly longer on average. The treated points (final lengths up to 54.8 mm) sit mostly above the controls. But this figure shows final size, not growth.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Growth in each group
To answer the question about growth, put the group on the x-axis and growth on the y-axis:

growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 8),
             alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot

Points with similar values would hide each other, so jitter moves them a little sideways. height = 0 makes sure no point moves up or down, so every growth value stays exactly as measured, and seed = 8 makes the sideways spread the same every time you run it.



Growth of each seedling by treatment; the groups overlap.


The controls grew between 8.0 and 18.7 mm and the treated plants between 12.2 and 30.8 mm. Treated plants tended to grow more, but the groups overlap: P17 (treated, 12.2 mm) grew less than most controls. Whether a difference of this size could be chance is a question for week 4; today we describe what we see.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Saving the figure and the table
text:
Saving the figure and the table

ggsave("output/seedling-growth.png", plot = growth_plot,
       width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 150)
write_csv(growth_table, "output/seedling-growth.csv")

ggsave() writes the figure as a PNG image, and write_csv() writes the table as a CSV file, both into the project’s output/ folder. An existing file with the same name is replaced without asking, so never write into data/. Open both files from the file manager to check they are there.






Hint: a plot or file is missing





Assigning a plot to a name does not show it; type the name, e.g. growth_plot, to print it. If saving fails, dir.exists("output") should say TRUE. If R says a column is not found, check names(seedlings) and rerun the mutate() line.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Your own figures
Add these to day08.R.

Calculate P02’s growth by hand and compare it with the table: 32.3 − 24.3 = 8.0 mm, the smallest growth in the experiment.
Use filter() and select() to make a table treated_growth with only the treated plants’ IDs and growth, and save it as output/treated-growth.csv. It has 12 rows and 2 columns.
Draw initial length against growth, with both axes labelled in mm, to find out whether plants that started longer also grew more. They did not: if anything, the longer seedlings grew slightly less. Or do the yield task below.
Restart R and run the whole script. The saved files should be recreated and still open.


Alternative: which protocol gives a better yield?
The file data/organic-recovery.csv records twelve runs of a chemical synthesis, six with a standard and six with a modified protocol. For each run, theoretical_mass_g is the largest possible product mass and isolated_mass_g the dry product collected, both in g; assume the product is pure. Runs started at different scales, so compare percentage yields rather than masses:

organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
organic <- mutate(organic,
                  yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
head(organic)

The first run, Y01, collected 0.62 g of a possible 1.00 g: 62%. Draw a plot with protocol on the x-axis and yield_percent on the y-axis, labelled “Isolated product yield (%)”, using the same jitter as above, to find out which protocol gave higher yields. The standard runs gave 62–74% and the modified runs 72–82%. Save the table as output/organic-yields.csv and the plot as output/organic-yields.png.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
A second class’s data
Day 7’s 18-plant study in data/seedlings-transfer.csv asks the same question with new plants. Start day08-transfer.R and repeat the workflow there.

Read the file into transfer, add growth_mm with mutate(), and check one plant by hand: T01 grew 40.3 − 25.3 = 15.0 mm. The table still has 18 rows: adding a column does not remove plants.
Make transfer_growth with ID, treatment and growth (18 rows), and transfer_treated with the treated plants only (9 rows).
Draw initial against final length, and initial against growth, to find out whether plants that started longer grew more in this study. They ended longer, but they grew less: two figures of the same plants, two different answers, because the y-axes measure different things.
Draw growth by group with the jitter from above. The controls grew 10.8–17.4 mm and the treated plants 15.0–21.4 mm, so again the groups overlap. Try changing only width in position_jitter(): the points move sideways, but no growth value changes.
Save output/transfer-growth.csv, output/transfer-treated.csv, output/transfer-growth.png and output/transfer-size.png. Below the growth figure in your script, write a comment that could serve as its caption: what one point is, what the y-axis measures in which unit, and what you see.







Hint: the treated table has the wrong number of rows





Filter on the label, treatment == "treated", spelt exactly as in the data. There should be 9 rows; check table(transfer$treatment).
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Which dilutions are possible?
A stock is a solution of known concentration. To dilute it, you take some stock and add liquid until you reach the final volume you want; the amount of dissolved substance stays the same. So the stock volume you need is
stock volume = target concentration × final volume / stock concentration.
With both concentrations in mmol/L and the final volume in mL, the stock volume comes out in mL. The file data/dilutions.csv lists four requested dilutions.

Work out D02 by hand first: stock 500 mmol/L, target 50 mmol/L, final volume 50 mL gives 50 × 50 / 500 = 5 mL of stock. Then read the file into dilutions and use mutate() to add stock_volume_ml for every row. You get 2.5, 5, 10 and 100 mL.
D04 asks for 100 mL of stock to make 50 mL of solution, which is impossible. Its target, 200 mmol/L, is stronger than its stock, 100 mmol/L, and adding liquid can only make a solution weaker. Add a column that flags this: possible_by_dilution = target_mmol_l <= stock_mmol_l (<= means “less than or equal to”). It is TRUE for D01–D03 and FALSE for D04.
Save the whole table, D04 included, as output/dilution-check.csv, so the impossible request stays on record. Then use filter(possible_by_dilution) to keep the three possible ones and plot their final volume against stock volume, both in mL. The points lie on a straight line, because for the same stock and target the stock volume is proportional to the final volume.
In reports/dilution-interpretation.txt, explain in two or three sentences why D04 is impossible, and the difference between “bring to 50 mL in total” and “add 50 mL of liquid”.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Check your understanding






Which function selects plants, and which selects measurements?





filter() keeps rows, so it selects plants. select() keeps columns, so it selects variables such as growth_mm.









Why keep the raw table when you have growth_mm?





Growth is calculated from the recorded lengths. Keeping them lets anyone check the calculation, for example P02: 32.3 − 24.3 = 8.0 mm.



Keep: day08.R, your derived tables and figures in output/. If you chose the yield task, keep the two organic-yields files as well. Next: put explanation and code in one report.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report
