title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text:
Today’s question
On day 6 you typed plant lengths by hand. The real experiment has 24 seedlings, and their lengths are in data/seedlings.csv. Can we bring that table into R unchanged, and check that it holds what we think it holds: 24 plants, two groups, two lengths each?
The study is described in the data dictionary, data/README.md: 24 seedlings in separate pots, 12 randomly allocated to a nutrient treatment and 12 to a control, each measured at the start and after seven days, in millimetres. These are simulated teaching data. Keep the dictionary open; R can count rows, but only the dictionary tells you what a row means.
Open introcomputing.Rproj and create a new script, day07.R, in the project folder.
Save today: day07.R.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
section: Is R looking in the right folder?
text:
Is R looking in the right folder?
Use getwd() and file.exists() to find out whether R can see the seedling file:

getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")

getwd() prints the folder R is working in, which should be your project folder, not data. The second line should print TRUE. The path data/seedlings.csv starts from the project folder, so the same line works on a classmate’s computer, even though their full path is different.






Hint: file.exists() says FALSE





You have probably opened a different project, a project inside a ZIP preview, or a folder with an extra level from extraction. Open introcomputing.Rproj from the folder where data, output and reports sit side by side. Do not paste your own full path into the code; it would break on every other computer.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text:
Reading the CSV into R
The readr package provides read_csv(), which reads a CSV file into a table. A package is a collection of extra functions. It is installed once (see the software setup page) and loaded with library() in every new R session.

library(readr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
dim(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
str(seedlings)

The table is now an object called seedlings in R’s memory; the file on disk is unchanged. head() shows its first six rows. dim() gives 24 rows and 4 columns, so all 24 plants arrived. names() lists the columns, plant_id, treatment, initial_mm and final_mm, and str() shows their types: plant_id and treatment are text (chr), the two lengths are numbers (num). show_col_types = FALSE only hides a message; it does not check anything for you.
Read the first row aloud: plant P01, in the control group, was 25.7 mm at the start and 44.3 mm seven days later. Each row is one plant and each column one variable. The two lengths in a row are the same plant measured twice, so the table describes 24 plants, not 48.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text:
One column at a time
$ takes one column out of the table as a vector, like those you made on day 6:

seedlings$initial_mm
length(seedlings$initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$initial_mm)

There are 24 initial lengths, one per plant, and their mean is 22.47 mm. The unit comes from the dictionary: the file only contains numbers. This mean mixes both groups, so it says nothing yet about the treatment.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text:
Missing values
When a measurement was never made, R shows NA, “not available”. It is not a zero: a seedling of length 0 mm is a different thing from a seedling nobody measured.

mean(c(10, NA, 20))
mean(c(10, NA, 20), na.rm = TRUE)
mean(c(10, 0, 20))

The first mean is NA, because R will not pretend it knows the missing value. na.rm = TRUE asks R to leave it out, which gives 15 from the two values that exist. Writing 0 instead gives 10, from three values, one of which was invented. When you leave missing values out, say how many there were.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text:
The seedling table
Add each step to day07.R with a short comment giving the answer.

Use tail(seedlings) to find out which group the last plant, P24, belongs to. It is treated, with lengths 22.4 and 44.7 mm.
Use sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm)) to find out how many plants have no final length. The answer is 0: is.na() gives TRUE for each missing value and sum() counts them.
The file data/leaf-mass.csv comes from a different study. Read it into an object called leaves, and use dim(), names() and the dictionary to find out what one row is. It has 18 rows and 3 columns: one leaf from each of 18 plants, with its area in cm² (leaf_area_cm2) and dry mass in mg (dry_mass_mg).
Restart R (Session → Restart R) and run day07.R from the top. Everything should come back, and the CSV files are still exactly as supplied.







Hint: could not find function "read_csv"





Run library(readr) first; after a restart it has to be run again. If R says there is no package called readr, install it as on the setup page. For column names, copy them from names(seedlings): initial_mm works, initial does not.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text:
A second class’s data
Another class repeated the experiment with 18 seedlings, in data/seedlings-transfer.csv. According to the dictionary, it has the same columns, 9 plants per group, and lengths in mm measured seven days apart. Before you use someone else’s table, check that it matches that description. Create day07-inspection.R for this part.

Read the file into a new object, transfer, so that your seedlings table is not overwritten. Use dim() to find out how many plants it has: 18 rows, 4 columns.
Use length(unique(transfer$plant_id)) to find out whether any plant appears twice. unique() keeps each ID once, so 18 distinct IDs in 18 rows means every row is a different plant.
Use table(transfer$treatment) to find out how many plants are in each group: 9 control and 9 treated, as promised.
Use sum(is.na()) on both length columns to find out whether any length is missing (none is), and range() to find out whether the lengths look like seedlings in mm: initial 20.0 to 28.8 mm, final 36.0 to 46.2 mm.
Write what you found in reports/transfer-import-audit.txt, as sentences someone else can check. For example: “data/seedlings-transfer.csv: 18 rows × 4 columns, 18 distinct plant IDs, 9 control and 9 treated, no missing lengths. Lengths in mm, seven days apart (from the dictionary).”







Hint: transfer$initial gives NULL





The column is called initial_mm. Copy names from names(transfer). If your note says 24 plants, you have looked at seedlings, not transfer.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text:
Solution recipes
The file data/solutions.csv lists six solutions that we will calculate with later. Each row gives a solution ID, the dissolved substance (solute), its mass in g, its molar mass in g/mol, and the final volume in mL. As on day 6, a mole is a unit of amount of substance and the molar mass says how many grams one mole weighs.

Read the file into solutions. Before running str(), predict which columns are text and which are numbers, then check. solution_id and solute are text; the other three are numbers.
Use dim(), unique(solutions$solute) and sum(is.na()) to find out how many solutions there are, which substances, and whether anything is missing: 6 rows, 5 columns, two substances (sodium-chloride and glucose), nothing missing.
Use range() on mass_g and molar_mass_g_mol to find out how far each varies: masses from 0.2922 to 2.7024 g, molar masses 58.44 and 180.16 g/mol. Both columns are numbers, but they measure different things, so adding a mass to a molar mass would be meaningless.
Save reports/solutions-import-audit.txt: the size of the table, what each column means and its unit, and the rule you will use later: amount (mol) = mass / molar mass, concentration = amount / final volume in litres.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text:
Check your understanding






Why is the header not a plant?





The header line holds the column names. dim() counts only the 24 data rows.









Why can R not tell whether the lengths are in mm or cm?





The file contains only names and numbers. Units are written in the dictionary, by people. That is why the column names end in _mm.









Why does day07.R also work in a classmate’s project folder?





It uses the relative path data/seedlings.csv, which starts from whatever project folder is open, not a path containing your user name.



Keep: day07.R. Next: calculate growth and draw a figure.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
text:
Today’s question
A seedling was 20 mm long at the start of an experiment and 37 mm long at the end. How much did it grow, and how much did three, then four, plants grow? Today you write the answer as a saved R script, so that you can run the whole calculation again whenever a value changes. The measurements are simulated teaching data.
Open the course project by double-clicking introcomputing.Rproj, as on day 5. Keep the R reference sheet open while you work.
Save today: day06.R in the project folder.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
text:
A first calculation
Type these lines in the Console, pressing Enter after each:

37 - 20
37 / 20

R prints [1] 17 and [1] 1.85. The [1] only numbers the first value printed. The two answers say different things about the plant: it grew 17 mm, and its final length is 1.85 times its initial length. The ratio has no unit, because mm divided by mm cancels. Both calculations are correct; which one you want depends on your question.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: A script that remembers the calculation
text:
A script that remembers the calculation
Choose File → New File → R Script and save it as day06.R in the project folder. Write these lines in the script:

# Measurements are lengths in millimetres.
initial_mm <- 20
final_mm <- 37
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm

Put the cursor on the first line and click Run (or press Ctrl+Enter, or Cmd+Enter on a Mac) to run it, then run each following line the same way. <- stores the value on its right under the name on its left, so read growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm as “store final minus initial under the name growth_mm”. The names appear in the Environment pane, and the last line prints 17. A line starting with # is a comment for people; R skips it.
Names must be typed exactly: growth_mm and Growth_mm are different names. Saving the script and running it are separate actions. Saving writes the instructions to disk; running creates the objects in R’s memory. That is why the script is what you keep: the objects disappear when R stops, and the script makes them again.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
text:
Three plants at once
c() combines several values into a vector, so one name can hold the lengths of three plants. Replace the single values in your script with:

initial_mm <- c(20, 22, 19)
final_mm <- c(37, 40, 34)
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm
mean(growth_mm)
length(growth_mm)

R subtracts position by position, so the plants grew 17, 18 and 15 mm. mean() and length() are functions: a name followed by brackets, with the values to work on inside. The mean growth is about 16.67 mm, and length() counts 3 plants. The subtraction only makes sense because both vectors list the same three plants in the same order.
Use a comparison to find out which plants grew more than 16 mm:

growth_mm > 16

The answer, TRUE TRUE FALSE, says that the first two plants did and the third did not. Plant labels are text and go in quotes, plant_id <- c("P01", "P02", "P03"); "20" in quotes is text too, not a number. To read about a function, type ?mean in the Console and look at the Description and Examples.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: How much did four plants grow?
text:
How much did four plants grow?
Continue in day06.R. Write a comment above each part saying what it calculates and in which unit.

A fourth plant grew from 21 to 39 mm. Add it to both vectors and use length() to check that each now has 4 values. The growth values are 17, 18, 15 and 18 mm, with a mean of 17 mm.
Use division to find out how many times longer each plant became, and store the result as length_ratio. The values are about 1.85, 1.82, 1.79 and 1.86. Plants 2 and 4 both grew 18 mm, but plant 2 has the smaller ratio because it started longer (22 mm against 21 mm). If you prefer chemistry, do the product-yield calculation below instead.
The first plant was re-measured: its final length is 38 mm, not 37. Predict which growth value changes, then edit the script and run it from the top. The first growth value becomes 18; the others stay the same.
Find out whether your script is complete: save it, choose Session → Restart R, and run all lines from the top. You should get the same results, because everything the calculation needs is in the script.


Alternative: how much product was collected?
In a chemical synthesis, starting materials are turned into a product. For this simulated example the largest possible product mass is given: 1.00 g, stored as theoretical_mass_g. The dry product collected weighs 0.62 g, stored as isolated_mass_g; assume it is pure. The percentage yield is the collected mass as a percentage of the largest possible mass:

theoretical_mass_g <- 1.00
isolated_mass_g <- 0.62
yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
yield_percent

The yield is 62%; the gram units cancel. Change the collected mass to 0.70 g and run the lines again to find out the new yield: 70%.






Hint: object not found, or a + prompt





Error: object 'growth_mm' not found means R has no object with that name yet. Check the spelling and capitals, then run the line that creates it. A line in the editor does nothing until you run it. If the Console shows + instead of >, R is waiting for the end of a line: check quotes and brackets, or press Esc.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: When a stored result goes stale
text:
When a stored result goes stale
In a spreadsheet, a cell with a formula updates itself when its inputs change. An R object does not. Create a new script, day06-extended.R, to see what that means and why the order of plants matters.

Write initial_mm <- 20, final_mm <- 37 and growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm, and run them. Then set final_mm <- 39 and print growth_mm without rerunning the subtraction. It still says 17, because growth_mm holds a number, not a formula. Rerun the subtraction and it says 19. Add a comment explaining this.
Recreate the three-plant vectors from above. Suppose the final lengths had been typed in a different order, c(34, 37, 40). Store them as final_wrong and use final_wrong - initial_mm to find out what growth R reports: 14, 15 and 21 mm instead of 17, 18 and 15. R gives no warning, because both vectors still have three values; only you know which plant each position belongs to.
Use division by 10 to convert the correct growth from mm to cm, and store it as growth_cm. Compare mean(growth_mm) and mean(growth_cm): 16.67 mm and 1.667 cm, the same growth in different units. Keep the original vector; give the converted one its own name.







Hint: R recycled my vector





If one vector is shorter than the other, R may reuse its values to fill the gap and give a result of the wrong length, sometimes with only a warning. Check both lengths with length() before subtracting.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
text:
How concentrated is the solution?
The same habit, every input named with its unit, works for laboratory calculations. A solution is a substance dissolved in a liquid. A mole (mol) is a unit of amount of substance, and the molar mass says how many grams one mole weighs (g/mol). The concentration in mol/L is the amount of substance divided by the final volume of solution in litres. All the values below are supplied.
Add this to day06-extended.R to find out the concentration of 0.2922 g sodium chloride (molar mass 58.44 g/mol) in a final volume of 100 mL:

mass_g <- 0.2922
molar_mass_g_mol <- 58.44
final_volume_ml <- 100
amount_mol <- mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol
final_volume_l <- final_volume_ml / 1000
concentration_mmol_l <- 1000 * amount_mol / final_volume_l
concentration_mmol_l

The amount is 0.005 mol in 0.100 L, so the concentration is 50 mmol/L (1 mmol is one thousandth of a mol). Keeping each step separate lets you check each conversion on its own.

Predict what happens if you double the mass to 0.5844 g, then check: the concentration doubles to 100 mmol/L.
Restore the mass and double the final volume to 200 mL instead. The same amount is now spread over twice the volume, so the concentration halves to 25 mmol/L.
Use the same lines to find out the concentration of 0.9008 g glucose (molar mass 180.16 g/mol) in 100 mL. It is also 50 mmol/L: a glucose molecule is heavier, so the same number of moles weighs more.
Save reports/calculation-check.txt with the formula in words, the conversion factors you used, and your three results. Then restart R and check that day06-extended.R reproduces them.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
text:
Check your understanding






What survives restarting R: an unsaved object or a saved script?





The saved script. Objects live in R’s memory and disappear when R restarts; run the script again to recreate them.









Why is mean(plant_id) not useful?





Plant IDs are labels that name plants, not measurements. An average label has no meaning: R returns NA with a warning.









What must be true before two vectors are subtracted position by position?





They must have the same length and list the same plants in the same order.



Keep: day06.R, with the four-plant example and comments about units. Next: import a whole table.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
text:
Try each question before opening its answer. Use your file manager, terminal, and terminal reference to check actions as well as words.
Topic quizzes: 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
text:
1. Plain text or not?
You open seedlings.csv, seedlings.xlsx and report.Rmd in Notepad or TextEdit (plain-text mode). Which show readable text, and which file could R read directly as a table?






Answer and check





seedlings.csv and report.Rmd are plain text: only characters, readable in any editor. seedlings.xlsx shows PK and unreadable symbols, because it is a ZIP package of XML files. R reads seedlings.csv directly; that is why the course keeps data as CSV.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 2. A relative path needs a starting place
text:
2. A relative path needs a starting place
From introcomputing-course, the path data/seedlings.csv works. From inside reports, why does the same path ask for a different location?






Answer and check





A relative path starts at the current folder. From reports it asks for reports/data/seedlings.csv, not the neighbouring data folder. Return to the project root, then locate data/seedlings.csv. The file did not move; your starting location changed. In a shell, use pwd to identify that starting place.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 3. Predict a pipe and a saved extract
text:
3. Predict a pipe and a saved extract
The supplied samples.tsv has a header plus four records: two control and two treated. The header does not contain treated. What does this print, and does the second command change the source manifest?
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt






Answer and check





The first command prints a line count of 2. grep sends matching lines through the pipe to wc. The second saves matches to treated-samples.txt; it does not change samples.tsv. > replaces any previous contents of the destination. This is literal text matching, not interpretation of treatment groups or chemical classes. It could also match untreated if that word occurred.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
text:
4. Copy, move, and extract
What remains after copying notes.txt to notes-copy.txt? How is moving the original different? Does opening a ZIP preview necessarily mean its files have been extracted into an ordinary project folder?






Answer and check





A copy leaves the original and makes another file. A move changes the original’s location or name. A ZIP preview is a view of an archive; use extraction to create the ordinary folder and files needed for the project. Locate the actual extracted .Rproj, rather than opening one inside an archive preview.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 5. A path on someone else’s laptop
text:
5. A path on someone else’s laptop
Anna’s code reads /Users/anna/Documents/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv. Why does it fail on Ben’s laptop, and which path works for both?






Answer and check





The absolute path contains Anna’s username, so the folder does not exist on Ben’s laptop. The relative path data/seedlings.csv, read from the project folder, works on any computer that has the project.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 6. The same filename on two computers
text:
6. The same filename on two computers
You see report.html in a remote desktop. Is it automatically in your laptop’s Downloads folder? Would a ZIP stored beside the original be a separate backup against losing the laptop?






Answer and check





No to both. Remote access is not automatic file transfer, and identical names can refer to separate copies. Use the supported transfer route and name the destination. A ZIP on the same disk is a convenient sharing package; use supported separate storage for protection against losing that disk.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
section: 7. Gene names and Swedish CSV files
text:
7. Gene names and Swedish CSV files
A gene list opened and saved in Excel shows 2-Sep where SEPT2 used to be. A classmate’s “CSV” contains P01;control;25,7;44,3. What happened in each case?






Worked answer





Excel turned the gene symbol into a date, and saving made it permanent; about one in five papers with Excel gene lists had such errors (Ziemann et al. 2016). The second file was saved by Excel set to Swedish, which uses semicolons between values and decimal commas. Look at data files in a text editor, and close raw data in a spreadsheet without saving.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
text:
8. Two terminal windows
Shell A is inside day03/readings while Shell B is in the workspace root. You run cd .. in Shell A. What changes in Shell B?






Worked answer





Nothing automatically changes in Shell B. Each shell has its own current directory. Check pwd in both windows. The folders themselves did not move, and changing a shell location does not move an independent file-manager window.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
text:
9. Quote the intended argument
You want one folder called field notes. Compare mkdir field notes with mkdir “field notes”. Which command expresses the intended single name?






Worked answer





The quoted command groups both words into one argument and creates one named folder. The unquoted command normally supplies two names and creates two folders. Practise only in the disposable workspace, then use ls and the graphical view to inspect what actually exists.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
text:
10. A surprising grep count
In a copy of the four-record manifest, S01 is labelled untreated; S03 and S04 are treated. How many records match grep -F treated, and does that count establish three treatment allocations?






Worked answer





There are three literal text matches because untreated contains treated. It does not establish three treated plants. Inspect the selected IDs and use the study description to understand labels. The unchanged source manifest still has two treated records.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
text:
11. A manifest path fails
The manifest lists measurements/S04.csv, but the copied folder contains S04-renamed.csv. Should you delete the record, change its measurement, or investigate identity?






Worked answer





Investigate. In the deliberate classroom rename, the file contents still identify S04 and 39.8 mm, and the known rename supports restoring its filename. In a real ambiguous case, obtain source evidence.

title: Week 1 revision — files and computers
text:
12. Console or terminal?
You type pwd in RStudio’s Console and get Error: object 'pwd' not found. Then you type 44.3 - 25.7 in the terminal and get 44.3: command not found. What went wrong, and where does each instruction belong?






Worked answer





Each instruction went to the wrong program. pwd is a shell command and belongs in the terminal, at a $ prompt. 44.3 - 25.7 is R and belongs in the Console, at a > prompt, where it gives 18.6 (P01’s growth in mm). Neither error means the computer is broken.



Return to day 5 exercises to practise in RStudio, or continue to week 2.

title: Quiz: Meet R and RStudio
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. What is the difference between R and RStudio?






Hint





One calculates; the other is the window you work in.









Answer





R is the program that runs calculations. RStudio is the application around it, with an editor, the Console, and panes for files, plots and objects. RStudio starts R for you.




Q2. Where should each instruction run: pwd, grep -F treated samples.tsv, and 44.3 - 25.7?






Hint





Look at the prompt: > waits for R, $ waits for the shell.









Answer





Run pwd and grep in the terminal’s shell. Run the subtraction in the R Console, where it gives 18.6 mm for the supplied plant lengths.




Q3. You type pwd in the R Console and see Error: object 'pwd' not found. Is R broken?






Hint





Which program read the instruction?









Answer





No. R does not know shell commands. Type pwd in the terminal instead.




Q4. file.exists("data/seedlings.csv") prints FALSE. What should you check first?






Hint





A relative path starts from the folder R is working in.









Answer





Check that the course project is open (its name in RStudio’s top-right corner) and that it is the extracted folder in which data, output and reports sit next to introcomputing.Rproj. getwd() shows the folder R is working in.




Q5. The supplied plot has initial length across and final length up, both in mm, with one point per plant. How many points should there be for the course seedlings, and does the vertical axis show growth?






Hint





Read what each axis measures before interpreting it.









Answer





24 points, one per plant. The vertical axis shows final length. Growth is final minus initial length for each plant.




Q6. After you quit and reopen RStudio, seedlings is gone from the Environment pane, but report.Rmd and report.html are still in the Files pane. Why?






Hint





Memory versus saved files.









Answer





seedlings was held in R’s memory, which is cleared when R stops. The .Rmd and .html are files saved on disk. Knitting report.Rmd again rebuilds the whole report from the saved data file.

title: Quiz: Inspecting an archive
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. What differs between unzip -l lab-data.zip and unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data?






Hint





The -l and -d options have different roles.









Answer





-l lists entries without extracting them. The second command extracts ordinary files into lab-data. Both leave the ZIP available.




Q2. A manifest has one header line and four sample lines, each ending with a newline. Two samples are labelled treated; the header lacks that word. What do these commands print?
wc -l samples.tsv
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l






Hint





The first counts all lines; the second counts only matching lines.









Answer





The counts are 5 and 2. Five lines represent four samples plus a header.




Q3. In a practice manifest, S01 is untreated, S03 and S04 are treated, and S02 is control. How many records match grep -F treated? Are they all treated samples?






Hint





Literal text matching also finds a search word inside a longer word.









Answer





Three records match: S01, S03, and S04. untreated contains treated, so a text match is not the same as selecting a treatment category.




Q4. What does grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt change if the destination already exists?






Hint





Consider both the input and the redirection destination.









Answer





It replaces treated-samples.txt with the matching lines. The distinct input samples.tsv stays unchanged. Redirection needs a separate destination because > can truncate a file before reading starts.




Q5. The manifest names measurements/S04.csv, but a practice copy contains S04-renamed.csv. What evidence would support restoring its name?






Hint





A similar filename alone does not prove sample identity.









Answer





In this exercise the rename was deliberate and known. Check the file’s recorded sample ID and 39.8 mm measurement against the source, restore S04.csv, and recheck the manifest path. An unexplained discrepancy would need source evidence.




Q6. The organic-laboratory inventory has a header and four sample rows; O02 and O03 are labelled ester, and no other line contains that word. What does grep -F ester inventory.tsv | wc -l print, and what has grep selected?






Hint





The pipe counts the matching lines.









Answer





2. grep selected the lines whose text contains ester; the chemical class comes from the supplied labels, not from grep.

title: Quiz: The terminal
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. You are in route-challenge/results/notes. The folder inputs is directly inside route-challenge. Which command reaches it?

cd ../inputs (ii) cd ../../inputs (iii) cd inputs







Hint





Draw the route back to the folder containing both results and inputs.









Answer





(ii). The first .. reaches results; the second reaches route-challenge. From there, enter inputs.




Q2. What differs between mkdir field notes and mkdir "field notes"?






Hint





How many destination arguments does the shell read in each command?









Answer





The first creates two directories, field and notes. The second creates one directory whose name contains a space: field notes.




Q3. A terminal is in practice. You run cd missing-folder, and the shell reports that the folder does not exist. What does pwd show afterwards?






Hint





Did the requested change of directory succeed?









Answer





The path to practice. A failed cd leaves the current working directory unchanged. Use ls to inspect the names that actually exist.




Q4. Two terminal windows are in the same directory. In the first, you run cd seedlings. Does the second window move too? Have any files moved?






Hint





Distinguish a shell’s current location from the stored folder tree.









Answer





Each shell has its own working directory, so the second stays where it was. cd changes a shell’s location; it moves no files or folders.




Q5. Which command creates a directory: pwd, ls, mkdir readings, or cd readings? What do the other three do?






Hint





Which commands inspect storage, and which change a location?









Answer





mkdir readings creates the directory. pwd prints the current directory; ls lists its entries; cd readings enters an existing directory.

title: Quiz: Folders and paths
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. In the course project, data and reports are both directly inside introcomputing-course. Is reports inside data? What is their parent folder?






Hint





Draw the tree with indentation.









Answer





No, they are neighbours. Their parent is the project folder, introcomputing-course.




Q2. Which of these paths is absolute and which is relative: /Users/anna/Documents/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv and data/seedlings.csv?






Hint





Where does each path start?









Answer





The first is absolute: it starts at the top of the disk (/). The second is relative: it starts from an agreed folder, here the project folder.




Q3. From the project folder, data/seedlings.csv finds the measurements. From inside reports, where does the same path point?






Hint





A relative path starts from the current folder.









Answer





To a data folder inside reports, which does not exist. Go up to the project folder first (written ../data/seedlings.csv from reports).




Q4. Anna’s R code reads C:\Users\anna\Documents\introcomputing-course\data\seedlings.csv. Ben runs it on his laptop. What happens, and what should Anna write instead?






Hint





Which part of the path is specific to Anna’s laptop?









Answer





It fails, because Ben’s laptop has no folder C:\Users\anna. Anna should write the relative path data/seedlings.csv, which works for anyone who opens the project folder.




Q5. You move the folder practice/map-a into practice/map-b. Does note.txt inside it change? What is its new path from the project folder?






Hint





Compare the contents of the file with its location.









Answer





The contents stay the same; only the location changes. The new path is practice/map-b/map-a/note.txt.




Q6. You add a sentence to a note, close the editor and choose Don’t save. What is in the file when you reopen it?






Hint





Where does unsaved text live?









Answer





The last saved version, without the new sentence. Unsaved text lives in working memory and disappears when the program closes; saved text is on disk.

title: Quiz: Kinds of files
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Which of these are plain-text files: seedlings.csv, report.Rmd, seedling-notes.docx, dna.txt, seedlings.xlsx?






Hint





Which of them would show readable words and numbers, and nothing else, in Notepad or TextEdit?









Answer





seedlings.csv, report.Rmd and dna.txt are plain text. seedling-notes.docx and seedlings.xlsx are compressed ZIP packages that need a word processor or spreadsheet program.




Q2. You open a .docx file in a text editor and see PK followed by strange symbols. Is the file damaged?






Hint





What is a .docx file really, underneath?









Answer





No. A .docx is a ZIP package of XML files, so a text editor shows raw bytes. Copy it, rename the copy to .zip and extract it: the text is in word/document.xml.




Q3. The first lines of a CSV are:
plant_id,treatment,initial_mm,final_mm
P01,control,25.7,44.3
How many plant records are shown? How much did P01 grow?






Hint





The first line names the columns. Growth is final length minus initial length.









Answer





One plant record; the header is not a plant. P01 grew 44.3 - 25.7 = 18.6 mm.




Q4. Name two things an Excel file can store that a CSV file cannot. Why does this course still keep data as CSV?






Hint





Think of what you saw in examples/seedlings.xlsx.









Answer





Formatting (bold or coloured cells), formulas, and several sheets. CSV stores values only, but any program, including R and a text editor, can read it, and what you see is exactly what is stored.




Q5. A gene list contains SEPT2 and MARCH1. A colleague opens it in Excel, saves it, and sends it on. What may have gone wrong?






Hint





What do SEPT and MARCH look like to a spreadsheet?









Answer





Excel may have turned them into dates such as 2-Sep and 1-Mar, and saving made that permanent. About one in five published papers with Excel gene lists contained such errors (Ziemann et al. 2016). The genes are now called SEPTIN2 and MARCHF1.




Q6. A classmate’s CSV contains the line P01;control;25,7;44,3. What is different from the course file, and where does such a file come from?






Hint





Look at what separates the values, and at the decimal sign.









Answer





Values are separated by semicolons and decimals use a comma (25,7 instead of 25.7). Excel set to Swedish (and many other European languages) saves “CSV” this way. Programs expecting commas will split the rows in the wrong places, so always look at a CSV in a text editor first.




Q7. You paste read.csv(“data/seedlings.csv”) from a Word document into R and get Error: unexpected input. Why?






Hint





Look closely at the quote marks.









Answer





Word replaced the straight quotes " with curly quotes “ ”, which R does not understand. Write code in a text editor or RStudio.




Q8. You rename seedlings.csv to seedlings.xlsx. Is it now an Excel file?






Hint





Does renaming rewrite the contents?









Answer





No. The contents are still plain text with commas; only the label changed, and Excel will refuse to open it. Converting a format needs a program that rewrites the file, such as Save As.

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
text:
Start with the biological question and the independent experimental unit. Neither a large table nor a small p-value can repair a design with no independent replication.
An interval around the mean does not describe where 95% of individual plants will fall. Adding technical repeats of the same plant does not add independent plants to the sample size.

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
text:
The two comparisons taught here
Independent groups: separate plants/pots allocated to control and treatment. Use a guided Welch two-sample t-test for the difference in mean growth. Define the direction before reporting it, such as treated minus control.
Paired observations: the same plant before and after a change. Compute after minus before within each plant, then analyse the differences. Correctly matching identifiers is essential; row order in two files is not evidence of matching pairs.
Both approaches need independent experimental units or pairs. For small samples, inspect unusual observations and strong skew. A test is conditional on its assumptions; you are not learning an automatic test-selection algorithm.
A p-value is the probability, under the null model and its assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Report the estimated difference, its units, confidence interval, sample sizes, and a biological interpretation. A small p-value does not establish a large or causal effect; a large one does not establish equality.

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
text:
A straight line
In lm(y ~ x, data = table), the intercept is fitted y at x = 0 and the slope is the fitted change in y for a one-unit increase in x. The slope’s units are y-units per x-unit. The residual is observed y minus fitted y.
For calibration, standards have known x values; invert the fitted line to obtain an unknown concentration from its signal, only within a supported range. This simple calculation provides a point estimate, without full uncertainty propagation. For an observational biological association, the slope does not establish what would happen if we intervened to change x.
See week 3 and week 4 for worked examples.

title: Glossary: words we use in this course
text:
Word
Meaning here




File
A named, saved collection of information, such as text, measurements, or a picture


Folder / directory
A container organising files and other folders


File system
The way an operating system stores and organises files and directories


Path
An address locating a file or directory on a particular computer


Extension
A filename ending such as .csv, .R, .Rmd, or .html, indicating its intended format


Home directory
The starting personal folder for an account on a computer


Working directory
The folder relative paths currently start from


Operating system
Software managing the computer and the applications running on it


CPU
The processor that carries out instructions


RAM / memory
Working storage used by running programs; save work to persistent files


Process
A running instance of a program


Bit / byte
A bit is 0 or 1; a byte contains eight bits, with 256 possible patterns


Terminal
A window or interface through which you interact with a shell


Shell
A program interpreting commands such as cd and ls


Console
In this course, usually the R interface that reads R expressions


Local / remote
On your current laptop / on another computer reached over a network


SSH
A secure connection to a remote shell


Remote desktop
A graphical session on a remote computer


Archive
A package containing files and folders, for example a ZIP


CSV / TSV
Text tables whose fields are separated by commas / tabs


Object
A named value held in an R session


Function
A named operation applied to inputs, such as mean()


Argument
An input or setting given to a function or command


Package
A collection of R functions and related resources


Observation
A recorded measurement or set of measurements; not necessarily an independent replicate


Experimental unit
The independently allocated entity, such as a pot or culture flask


Technical replicate
A repeated measurement of the same underlying sample


Missing value
A measurement that is unavailable; represented by NA in R


Raw data
The original supplied measurements, preserved without overwriting


Theoretical mass
In the organic practice, the supplied maximum possible product mass for a run


Isolated mass
In the organic practice, the dry product collected, assumed pure for the simplified calculation


Percentage yield
100 × isolated mass / theoretical mass, using the same mass units


Percentage point
A difference on a percentage scale: 70% minus 60% is 10 percentage points


Derived data
Values calculated or cleaned from the originals with documented code


Render / Knit
Run a report’s code and combine results with its text to create a document


Reproducibility
Being able to regenerate a result from its stated inputs, code, and environment

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
text:
We will use a terminal to give the computer short written instructions. On Windows we use Ubuntu, a version of Linux, through Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). Mac users can use the Terminal application already on their Mac.
You do not need to understand the commands yet. This page gets you ready for the first exercises. Installation help will be provided during the course.
crumbs: Windows: install Ubuntu / Mac: open Terminal

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
text:
Windows: install Ubuntu

1. Prepare
Save your work: installation may require restarting your computer. You need an internet connection and permission to install software. On a university-managed computer, ask the teaching team if administrator access is unavailable.
Use Windows 11 for this setup. Microsoft’s installation command also supports Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) or later; if you have an older system, ask for help choosing a supported course environment.


2. Open PowerShell as administrator
Open Start, type PowerShell, right-click Windows PowerShell, and choose Run as administrator. Accept the Windows permission prompt.
PowerShell is a Windows command window. We use it for installation; later Linux exercises belong in Ubuntu.


3. Install
In PowerShell, type this command and press Enter:
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
Wait for it to finish and restart the computer if requested. This installs Ubuntu alongside your Windows applications using WSL.
These steps follow Microsoft’s WSL installation instructions.


4. Open Ubuntu and create your Linux account
After restarting, open Start, search for Ubuntu, and open it. First startup may take a little time.
When asked, choose a Linux username, for example anna, using lowercase letters. Then choose a password and enter it again when prompted. This is a separate account from your Windows account.
Nothing appears while you type the password, not even dots. This is normal. Type it and press Enter. Keep the password somewhere secure; do not send it to a teacher or include it in a screenshot.
When setup finishes, you should see a line ending in a prompt, often $. The prompt means Ubuntu is waiting for a command. Do not type the $ itself.
The account and password behaviour is described in Microsoft’s environment setup guide.


5. Check Ubuntu
In Ubuntu, run these commands one at a time:
whoami
pwd
uname -s
whoami should show your Linux username. pwd shows your current folder, usually /home/ followed by your username. uname -s should print Linux.
To check WSL itself, open PowerShell and run:
wsl --list --verbose
Look for an Ubuntu entry with 2 in the VERSION column. A running or stopped state is normal. If your installation shows version 1, bring it to the setup session so we can help check it.


6. Opening Ubuntu next time
Open Ubuntu from Start. You normally do not need administrator mode for course exercises. Closing its window does not delete your saved files.
crumbs: Windows: install Ubuntu / Mac: open Terminal

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
text:
Mac: use Terminal directly
Open Finder, then Applications → Utilities → Terminal. You can also search for Terminal with Spotlight. You do not need to install Ubuntu.
Run the same three commands:
whoami
pwd
uname -s
Your home folder is usually /Users/ followed by your username, and uname -s prints Darwin, the underlying macOS system. That is expected. macOS is not Linux, but the basic commands we use work in both environments. A prompt ending in % is also normal on a Mac.
Commands labelled Ubuntu only, such as apt, do not belong in Mac Terminal.
crumbs: Windows: install Ubuntu / Mac: open Terminal

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
section: First exercise: a folder you can find again
text:
First exercise: a folder you can find again
On Windows use Ubuntu; on Mac use Terminal. Run one line at a time:
cd
mkdir -p introcomputing/first-session
cd introcomputing/first-session
pwd
ls

cd on its own takes you to your home folder.
mkdir -p creates the named folders if they do not already exist.
cd introcomputing/first-session moves into that folder.
pwd prints its full location, called its path.
ls lists what is inside. A new, empty folder produces no listed filenames.

Now see the same folder in a graphical file manager:
Windows — run in Ubuntu:
explorer.exe .
Mac — run in Terminal:
open .
The dot means “the folder I am in now”. The file-manager window and the terminal are showing the same place in two different ways.
Close the terminal, reopen it, and find your folder again:
cd ~/introcomputing/first-session
pwd
Here ~ is shorthand for your home folder. Being able to return to saved work is part of being ready, even when the folder is still empty.

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
section: Windows and Ubuntu have different home folders
text:
Windows and Ubuntu have different home folders
On Windows, Ubuntu’s /home/anna is different from Windows’ C:\Users\anna. A file downloaded by your Windows browser does not automatically appear in your Ubuntu home folder. For terminal exercises, use the Ubuntu home folder we just created. We will practise locating downloads and transferring files together.
You can reach Ubuntu files through explorer.exe ., or by entering \\wsl$ in File Explorer’s address bar and opening your Ubuntu distribution. See Microsoft’s guide to Windows and Linux file systems.
R and RStudio will have separate setup instructions. You do not need to install them inside Ubuntu to complete this page.

If something goes wrong







What you see
What to do




Windows asks for an administrator password you do not have

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
text:
R performs calculations. RStudio is the application in which we write code, inspect results, and make reports. Install both on your laptop, or use the supported remote applications when access details are provided.
These steps are for native Windows or macOS applications. Windows students do not need to install a second copy of R inside Ubuntu/WSL. The Linux command-line setup is a separate page.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
text:
1. Install R
Go to CRAN’s R downloads and choose your operating system. On Windows choose the base installation, then the standard installer. On Mac choose the installer matching your Mac’s processor and supported macOS version; About This Mac identifies the processor. If the choices are unclear, bring your computer to the setup session. Install R before RStudio.
R is available for Windows, macOS, and Linux through the R Project and CRAN.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
text:
2. Install RStudio Desktop
Download the free RStudio Desktop installer from Posit. Choose your operating system, install it, then open RStudio. You do not need to purchase a product or create a cloud account. Check the download page’s current system requirements if your computer is older. RStudio requires an R installation, as explained in Posit’s download guide.
Find the Console pane. Its prompt is usually >. Type:
2 + 3
Press Enter. The result should be [1] 5. The [1] labels the first element printed; it is not part of your answer or something you type.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
text:
3. Install the small package set
Packages add functions to R. In the R console, run this once while connected to the internet:
install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "rmarkdown", "knitr"))
Wait until the prompt returns. Keep installation commands out of your analysis and report: they change the computer’s setup and need not run every time. Load packages in each new analysis session using library().
If asked to compile packages from source on Windows or Mac, ask for help using the available binary packages. Installing compilers is not a course exercise.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
section: 4. Download and extract the course folder
text:
4. Download and extract the course folder
If you extracted the course folder during day 1, reuse it and continue with step 4 below.

If you do not already have it, download course-files.zip.
Find it in your browser’s downloads, then show it in the file manager.
On Windows, right-click and choose Extract All; on Mac, double-click the ZIP. Move the extracted introcomputing-course folder to a place you can find again, such as Documents. Extract the whole folder, not a single file.
Inside the extracted folder, open introcomputing.Rproj in RStudio. A ZIP preview in Windows is not an extracted project.

Your folder should look like this:
introcomputing-course/
├── introcomputing.Rproj
├── report.Rmd
├── START-HERE.txt
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── seedlings.csv
│   └── ...
├── output/
└── reports/
The .Rproj file tells RStudio which folder is this project. Data remain ordinary files inside it. In the R console run:
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")
The first result should end with introcomputing-course; the second should be TRUE. data/seedlings.csv means “inside the data folder of this project”. Keep this relative path so the project works in another location too.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
section: 5. Check packages and the first report
text:
5. Check packages and the first report
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
packageVersion("rmarkdown")
If these commands finish without an error, open report.Rmd from RStudio’s Files pane and click Knit. A report with a table and a growth plot should appear. Its data are simulated. You will learn to explain and modify this report in week 2; you are checking the installation now.
R Markdown uses Pandoc to make the output document; RStudio supplies it. You do not need a PDF/LaTeX installation for our HTML reports. R Markdown’s installation documentation describes these dependencies.

text:
If something goes wrong







Symptom
First check




RStudio cannot find R
Check that R installed successfully before RStudio.


“There is no package called …”
Run the package installation line in the R console, then load the package again.


file.exists() is FALSE
Open the extracted .Rproj; look for an extra nested folder after extraction.


The console shows + instead of >
An expression is unfinished. Press Esc and check closing quotes or brackets.


Knit reports “object not found”
The report needs code creating the object; an object made only in the console is insufficient.


An installation or permissions error persists
Save the exact error and use the setup session; the remote route is an alternative once available.



Please show the exact error and the step you reached. Do not send passwords or authentication codes. On a managed computer, use the approved software route with support from the teaching team.
