title: Data Analysis in Life Sciences
text:
A five-week introduction to computing for biologists. You will learn what is inside your data files, how to work in a terminal, and how to use R to turn biological measurements into figures, statistics and reports that anyone can re-run. No programming experience is needed.
Start with the course introduction slides: why spreadsheets are not enough for biological data.

title: Data Analysis in Life Sciences
text:
The five weeks



Week
Biological question
What you will do




1 — Files and the terminal
What is in our data files, and where are they?
Tell plain text from Word and Excel files, write paths, use a terminal, unpack and search lab data, meet R


2 — R and reports
How much did the seedlings grow?
Import a table, calculate growth, plot it, and render an R Markdown report


3 — Variation
How much do individual plants differ?
Check data, summarise groups, understand mean, SD, and replicates


4 — Comparisons and lines
Did the treatment work? How do two measurements relate?
Estimate a difference with uncertainty, analyse pairs, fit a calibration line and an association


5 — Bigger data and reproducibility
Can someone else repeat our analysis?
Estimate how much memory data need, use a remote computer, run a small study, and reproduce and share it



Each topic in the left menu has Lecture (slides), Exercises, and a Quiz. More about outcomes and weekly checkpoints: About the course.

title: Data Analysis in Life Sciences
text:
Getting started

Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal.
Install R and RStudio, then open your project.
Download the course project and laboratory archive.
Working on a remote Linux computer. Connection details will be added when the course environment is confirmed.

Then begin with Day 1: kinds of files. Keep the terminal reference, R reference, statistics reference, and glossary at hand.

title: About the course
text:
Data Analysis in Life Sciences is a five-week introduction to computing for biologists. It starts with the kinds of files your data come in and ends with an analysis that someone else can re-run from the raw data. The aim is that in later lab courses and in your thesis you analyse data in R rather than by hand in a spreadsheet. The course introduction slides explain why.
No previous experience with the terminal, programming, or statistics is assumed. All course datasets are simulated teaching data.

title: About the course
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do

Tell plain-text data files from Word and Excel files, find files by their path, and estimate how much memory a dataset needs.
Inspect and organise lab files with a few command-line tools, locally and on a remote Linux computer.
Import biological measurements into R, check them, calculate new variables, summarise groups, and make labelled plots.
Describe variation with mean, variance and SD, and tell the spread of individual plants from the uncertainty of an estimate.
Use a t-test and a straight-line fit, reporting effect size, uncertainty, units, and limitations.
Write an R Markdown report that renders from its saved data and code.

The course does not cover database searching, sequence alignment, or omics analysis; those come in later courses.

title: About the course
text:
Weekly checkpoints







Week
By the end of the week you can




1 — Files and the terminal
Open a data file as plain text, give its path, find it in the terminal, and run a first calculation in R


2 — R and reports
Import a table, calculate growth, plot it, and render a report from its source


3 — Variation
Check a messy table, summarise groups, and explain SD versus uncertainty


4 — Comparisons and lines
Estimate a difference with a confidence interval, analyse paired data, and fit a calibration line


5 — Bigger data and reproducibility
Estimate a dataset’s memory needs, work on a remote computer, and reproduce a small study from a fresh folder

title: About the course
section: Three places where you type commands
text:
Three places where you type commands








Where
Typical commands
What it acts on




Terminal on your laptop (Ubuntu or Mac Terminal)
pwd, ls, unzip
Files and programs on your laptop


R Console in RStudio
mean(), read_csv(), ggplot()
R objects, and files R can reach


Remote terminal after ssh
pwd, ls, supported remote commands
Files and programs on the remote computer



A folder called data exists on many computers. When something cannot be found, first check which computer and which folder you are in.

title: About the course
text:
What to keep
Keep the raw data unchanged. Save your R code and .Rmd files, not only screenshots or printed numbers, and keep generated figures and HTML reports next to their source. The downloads page has the course folder and a working report template.
Some exercises offer a chemistry-lab alternative to the biology example; choose one. Each gives every definition, quantity, unit and formula you need, so no chemistry course is required.

title: About the course
text:
Getting help
Note the exact error message, the line or chunk that produced it, the file name, and whether you were working locally or remotely. Never include passwords or login codes in a help request.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
text: We will also use HPC2N or another remote Linux environment. A remote computer is a computer you connect to over the network. Your laptop displays the session; the remote computer runs the programs and stores the files you save there.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
text:
Two ways to work remotely








Connection
What you see
What you use it for




SSH
A terminal on the remote computer
Navigate folders and run commands.


Remote desktop
A graphical workspace on the remote computer
Use a file manager and the applications provided for the course.



Both give access to a remote environment. Whether they share exactly the same files depends on how the service is configured; the course instructions will identify the folders to use.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
text:
What SSH means
SSH is a way to log in securely to another computer. The usual command has this shape:
ssh your-username@remote-computer-address
This is an explanation of the shape, not a working course command. We will supply the actual address and explain any additional authentication steps.
On Windows you can start SSH from Ubuntu; on Mac use Terminal. Once connected, commands such as pwd and ls act on the remote computer. Use exit to leave the SSH session and return to your local shell.
The first connection may ask you to trust the remote computer’s host key. Follow the course’s verification instructions before accepting it. Password prompts may show no characters while you type. Never share passwords or authentication codes.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
section: Always ask: which computer am I using?
text:
Always ask: which computer am I using?







Question
Why it matters




Is this terminal local or remote?
It determines where commands run.


Which folder am I in?
pwd gives the location on that computer.


Where did I save the data or report?
Saving remotely does not automatically create a laptop copy.


Where is RStudio running?
R needs access to files in its own environment.



A browser download on your laptop, a file in local Ubuntu, and a file on HPC2N can be three separate copies. Identical filenames do not make them the same file. Opening a remote desktop does not automatically transfer your laptop’s files.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
section: What we will practise when access is ready
text:
What we will practise when access is ready

Sign in using the supplied instructions and identify the remote computer.
Use pwd and ls, create a practice folder, and locate a supplied dataset.
Leave the SSH session with exit, then reconnect and find the folder again.
Open the supported remote desktop and find the designated course files.
Transfer a small file using the supported route and identify both copies.
Open the provided R environment and locate a rendered report.

These are small introductory exercises. Instructions about where programs may run and how to end the remote-desktop session will accompany the service details.

title: Course files and datasets
text:
All datasets are simulated teaching examples. Downloading a file is the start of the workflow: find it, extract it if needed, and place it where you can return to it. Read the project setup guide for step-by-step help.



Download
Used for
What it contains




course-files.zip
R practicals, weeks 2–5
An RStudio project, all datasets and dictionaries, a working report.Rmd, and output folders


lab-data.zip
Command line, week 1
A README, a sample manifest, four small measurement files, and field notes


organic-lab.zip
Alternative command-line practice
Supplied organic sample labels, a product-recovery table, README, and dictionary; no prior chemistry needed


Starter R Markdown
Inspect or replace the template
The same working first report supplied in the project ZIP


Data dictionary
Understand the biological design
Units, identifiers, missing values, and independent experimental units



Keep the extracted introcomputing-course folder together. All .Rmd reports should be saved in its root, beside introcomputing.Rproj, so paths such as data/seedlings.csv mean the same thing throughout the course.
The shell practice archive is separate. On Windows, the Ubuntu home folder and your normal Windows Documents folder are different locations. A remote computer is another location again. Transfer files explicitly between these locations.
The course project also includes data/organic-recovery.csv, for short organic laboratory transfer exercises. It supplies the maximum possible and collected product masses, with the calculation defined in each exercise. Choose a transfer option where a lesson offers it.
The expanded practice uses six further CSV files included in the project ZIP: seedlings-transfer.csv, solutions.csv, dilutions.csv, calibration-transfer.csv, unknowns-transfer.csv, and algae.csv. The data dictionary supplies designs, definitions, units, and the meaning of missing values. Use each exercise’s stated input file, not the result from a different instrument run or study.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
text: These examples assume that you opened the extracted course .Rproj file. Use RStudio’s R console for R, not a terminal waiting for shell commands. Save reusable code in an R script or your .Rmd report.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
text:
Objects and functions
lengths_mm <- c(12, 15, 18)
mean(lengths_mm)
sd(lengths_mm)
length(lengths_mm)
<- assigns a value to a name. c() combines values into a vector. mean() computes an arithmetic mean, sd() a sample standard deviation, and length() the number of elements. Text needs quotes, as in "control". R is case-sensitive: Length and length are different names.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
text:
Import, inspect, and calculate
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
nrow(seedlings)
glimpse(seedlings)

seedlings <- seedlings |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
|> means “take this result and pass it to the next function”. mutate() adds or changes columns. A calculation creates a derived measurement; it does not change the original CSV unless you explicitly write a file.
treated <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "treated")

summary_table <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mm = mean(growth_mm), sd_mm = sd(growth_mm),
            .groups = "drop")
== compares values; it does not assign. filter() selects rows. group_by() tells summarise() which groups to summarise. For missing data, report both available and missing counts rather than silently dropping records.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
section: A plot and an exported file
text:
A plot and an exported file
growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 7)) +
  labs(x = "Allocation", y = "Seven-day growth (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot
ggsave("output/growth.png", plot = growth_plot, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 150)
write_csv(summary_table, "output/growth-summary.csv")
The + joins layers in a ggplot. Horizontal jitter separates overlapping points; height = 0 preserves their measured values. ggsave() needs an output folder that already exists; the course project includes one.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
text:
Missing is not zero
x <- c(10, NA, 20)
is.na(x)
sum(is.na(x))
sum(!is.na(x))
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
NA denotes an unavailable value. na.rm = TRUE computes from available observations; it does not justify missingness or replace a report of how many were missing. The mean here is 15 from two available values.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
text:
Error recovery







Message or symptom
Check




“object not found”
Spelling, case, and whether the line creating it ran


“could not find function”
Whether the right package was loaded


“cannot open file”
Project, path, filename case, and local versus remote computer


Console prompt is +
Unfinished quotes/brackets; press Esc and fix the expression


Report fails but console works
An object or package may exist only in your interactive session



Use ?mean, ?t.test, or ?lm to open R’s help for a named function. Ask for help with the exact error and the smallest relevant code, without credentials.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
text:
Use Ubuntu on Windows, Terminal on Mac, or the terminal provided remotely. Type commands after the prompt ($ or %). They act on the computer to which the current shell belongs. Type pwd whenever you are unsure where you are.
Some commands overwrite existing files. Practise in the course workspace and read the destination name before pressing Enter.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
text:
Paths and punctuation
~                        your home folder on this computer
.                        the current folder
..                       the parent folder
data/seedlings.csv       a relative path from the current folder
/home/anna/course        an example absolute path on Linux
cd .. moves one level up. A filename containing spaces needs quoting, for example less "field notes.txt". Use simple filenames with hyphens or underscores in your own work. Use Tab to complete names and the up arrow to recall a command. Ctrl+C interrupts a running command; it is not the copy shortcut.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
text:
A pipe connects programs
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
grep outputs matching lines. The | passes those lines to wc as input. There is no intermediate saved file. In our manifest, the answer is 2 because two records contain treated. This count is meaningful because each record is one line and the header does not contain the search term.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
text:
Redirection saves output
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt
The > writes to a file instead of the screen and replaces existing contents at that path. >> appends. The search does not parse a table or understand treatment groups: it matches text. It would also match untreated if that label occurred in the file.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
text:
Connect graphical and terminal views
In Ubuntu on Windows, explorer.exe . opens the current folder in File Explorer. On a Mac, open . opens it in Finder. These are local conveniences, not remote file-transfer commands. The remote desktop and file-transfer instructions will identify the supported remote route.
See week 1 for guided practice and remote access for the local/remote distinction.

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
section: Which kind of file holds the measurements?
text:
Which kind of file holds the measurements?
Did seedlings grow differently after a nutrient treatment? The measurements are simulated teaching data from 24 seedlings in separate pots, 12 treated and 12 controls, each measured at the start and after seven days; data/README.md describes the study. Before we analyse them we look at the file they are stored in. Some files are plain text, which any program can read. Others, such as Word and Excel files, are packages that only particular programs understand, and spreadsheets can even change the data. No programming today.

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
text:
Downloading the course folder

Download the course files.
In the browser’s downloads list, choose Show in folder (Windows) or Show in Finder (Mac). The file is usually in Downloads.
Extract the ZIP: on Windows, right-click course-files.zip and choose Extract All; on Mac, double-click it.
Move the extracted folder introcomputing-course into Documents and work there, never inside the ZIP. It contains the folders data, examples, output and reports, and the files report.Rmd and introcomputing.Rproj.







I see two course folders. Which should I use?





Extraction can create an extra outer folder, and downloading twice gives names ending in (1). Open folders until you find the one that directly contains data, output and introcomputing.Rproj, and use that one. Ask before deleting the other.









My Documents folder is in OneDrive or iCloud





Tell the teacher. A cloud-managed Documents folder can show a file (with a cloud icon) that is not yet on the laptop, so we check that the course files open with the network turned off.



The ending of a filename, such as .csv or .docx, is its extension. File managers often hide it, so turn it on: in Windows File Explorer choose View → Show → File name extensions; in Mac Finder choose Finder → Settings → Advanced → Show all filename extensions.

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
text:
A plain-text editor
A text editor shows exactly the characters stored in a file, with no formatting. On Windows, use Notepad: right-click a file and choose Open with → Notepad. On Mac, use TextEdit, set to plain text under TextEdit → Settings → New Document → Plain text. TextEdit tries to display Word files as documents, so to see what is really inside a file use File → Open, click Options and tick Ignore rich text commands. Later in the course, RStudio will be our text editor.

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
text:
What is inside seedlings.csv?
Open data/seedlings.csv in the text editor to find out how much plant P01 grew. The first lines are:
plant_id,treatment,initial_mm,final_mm
P01,control,25.7,44.3
P02,control,24.3,32.3
The first line is a header that names the columns, and each following line describes one plant. P01 started at 25.7 mm and ended at 44.3 mm, so it grew 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm. Nothing else is in the file: only letters, digits, commas and line breaks. Such a file is plain text, and a CSV (“comma-separated values”) file is a table written as plain text. Every editor shows the same characters, and R can read them directly.
Plain text works for anything that can be written as characters. Open data/dna.txt and you see a DNA sequence of the letters A, C, G and T. The plain-text files you will meet in this course are:








Extension
What it holds
Example




.csv, .tsv
tables (commas or tabs between values)
data/seedlings.csv


.txt
notes, DNA sequences
data/dna.txt, data/field-notes.txt


.md
documentation, with simple marks such as # for headings
data/README.md


.R, .Rmd
R code, and R Markdown reports
report.Rmd

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
section: What is inside a Word file?
text:
What is inside a Word file?
The folder examples holds the same short note about the experiment as seedling-notes.txt and as seedling-notes.docx, saved by a word processor. Open both in the text editor (not in Word) to find out where the Word file keeps the text. The .txt shows the note; the .docx starts with PK followed by unreadable symbols, because a .docx file is a compressed ZIP package.
To look inside, copy examples/seedling-notes.docx into output, rename the copy seedling-notes.zip (accept the warning) and extract it. Inside the folder word, open document.xml in the text editor. The sentences of the note are there, surrounded by tags such as <w:p> and <w:t> that mark paragraphs and text. The package holds 16 files, among them styles.xml with fonts and headings and docProps/core.xml with the author and dates, and Word puts them together when it opens the document.






TextEdit shows the formatted note instead of PK





Use File → Open → Options → Ignore rich text commands. If that does not help, copy the .docx into output, rename the copy to end in .txt, and open the copy.



Excel files (.xlsx) are packages of the same kind. PDF files and pictures are not text either: open examples/seedling-notes.pdf and examples/seedlings-plot.png in the text editor, and the first characters, %PDF and PNG, tell programs which format follows.

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
section: The same table as CSV and as Excel
text:
The same table as CSV and as Excel
Open examples/seedlings.xlsx in a spreadsheet program (Excel or LibreOffice Calc) to find out what an Excel file stores beyond the measurements. It holds the same 24 plants as data/seedlings.csv, plus a bold, coloured header row, a column growth_mm whose cells are formulas (click E2 and you see =D2-C2 while the cell shows 18.6), and a second sheet called notes.
A CSV file can store none of these: it holds values only, one table per file. That is why this course keeps data as CSV. Any program can read it, including R and a text editor, and what the text editor shows is exactly what is stored. Formatting and calculations belong in R code, where every step is written down; a coloured cell is information that R never sees.

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
section: Can a spreadsheet change the data?
text:
Can a spreadsheet change the data?
Open examples/genes.csv in the text editor and then in Excel to find out what Excel does to the gene symbols SEPT2 and MARCH1. Excel guesses that they are dates and shows 2-Sep and 1-Mar. If the file is saved, the gene names are replaced for good. (LibreOffice usually keeps the names; the lecture slides show what Excel does.) Ziemann and colleagues (2016) found such errors in about one in five published papers that had gene lists as Excel files, and in 2020 the human gene naming committee (HGNC) renamed these genes, for example to SEPTIN2 and MARCHF1, partly for this reason. Older data files still use the old names.
Then open examples/seedlings-semicolon.csv in the text editor and compare it with data/seedlings.csv:
plant_id;treatment;initial_mm;final_mm
P01;control;25,7;44,3
This is how Excel saves “CSV” on a computer set to Swedish (and many other European languages): the comma is the decimal sign, so semicolons separate the values. A program that expects commas splits these rows in the wrong places, so look at every CSV in a text editor before analysing it.
For this course: if you look at raw data in a spreadsheet, close it without saving.

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
text:
Text editor or word processor?
A word processor (Word, Pages, Google Docs) is made for formatted documents and changes what you type. Compare the last line of the two notes from examples to find out what Word did to a line of R code:
seedling-notes.txt:   seedlings <- read.csv("data/seedlings.csv")
seedling-notes.docx:  seedlings <- read.csv(“data/seedlings.csv”)
Word replaced the straight quotes " with curly quotes “ ”. R understands only straight quotes, so code copied from the Word file stops with Error: unexpected input. Write code, data and notes for analysis in a text editor, and later in RStudio. TextEdit on Mac is a word processor too unless you choose Format → Make Plain Text before saving; otherwise it saves a formatted .rtf file.

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
text:
Renaming and file extensions
Renaming a file changes its name, not its contents. Renaming the .docx to .zip worked because the file was a ZIP package all along. Renaming seedlings.csv to seedlings.xlsx does not make an Excel file, and Excel refuses to open it because the contents are still plain text. Changing a format needs a program that rewrites the file, such as Save As with another format.

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
section: A practice copy of the measurements
text:
A practice copy of the measurements
The files in data stay exactly as supplied, so that you can always start again from what was measured. Copy data/seedlings.csv into output and rename the copy seedlings-practice.csv, checking that the name still ends in .csv. Open the copy in a spreadsheet program to see the same 24 plants as a table, then close it without saving. Tomorrow’s exercises use this copy.

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
text:
Your first plain-text note
Create a new plain-text file in the text editor (on Mac, Format → Make Plain Text) and write a few sentences: what one row of data/seedlings.csv describes and in which units, one thing an .xlsx file can store that a .csv file cannot, and why raw data should not be saved from a spreadsheet. Use Save As to save it as day01-notes.txt in reports, and check in the file manager that the name ends in .txt and not .txt.txt or .rtf. Then close the editor, go to reports in the file manager and open the note again to check that your last sentence was saved.

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
section: Which files in the course folder are plain text?
text:
Which files in the course folder are plain text?
Open each file in the text editor to find out which files in the course folder R could read directly. Check every file in data and in examples, and report.Rmd, introcomputing.Rproj and START-HERE.txt in the project folder, without changing or saving any of them. Write the result in a new plain-text file reports/file-types.txt, one line per file, with the kind of program meant to open each file that is not plain text:
data/seedlings.csv       plain text   table, commas between values
examples/seedlings.xlsx  not text     spreadsheet program (ZIP package)
If a file shows only readable words and numbers, it is plain text; if it starts with PK, %PDF or PNG and then unreadable symbols, it is not.






Check your list





Plain text: every file in data, report.Rmd, introcomputing.Rproj (a few RStudio settings written as text), START-HERE.txt, and in examples the files README.txt, seedling-notes.txt, genes.csv and seedlings-semicolon.csv. Not plain text: seedling-notes.docx (word processor), seedlings.xlsx (spreadsheet), seedling-notes.pdf (PDF reader) and seedlings-plot.png (image viewer).

title: Day 1 — Kinds of files: plain text, Word and Excel
text:
Check your understanding






You open a .docx file in Notepad and see PK and strange symbols. Is the file broken?





No. A .docx is a compressed ZIP package of XML files, so Notepad shows its raw bytes, while Word unpacks the package and shows the formatted document.









A colleague sends a gene list as .xlsx and MARCH1 appears as 1-Mar. What happened?





A spreadsheet converted the gene symbol to a date when the list was opened and saved, and the name cannot be recovered from the date. Ask for the original file.









You rename seedlings-practice.csv to seedlings-practice.txt. What changed?





Only the name. The file still holds the same commas and numbers, and a text editor shows the same contents.



Save today: reports/day01-notes.txt, reports/file-types.txt and output/seedlings-practice.csv.
Next: folders and paths.

title: Day 2 — Folders and paths
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 2 — Folders and paths
text:
Where is yesterday’s note?
Open the file manager and find day01-notes.txt by opening folders, not through the editor’s list of recent files, and write down the folders you opened, in order. That list is the note’s address. Today we learn to write such addresses down precisely, so that you, a classmate and R can all find the seedling measurements.

title: Day 2 — Folders and paths
text:
The project as a tree
A folder can contain files and more folders, so a project can be drawn as a tree in which indentation shows what is inside what:
introcomputing-course/
├── introcomputing.Rproj
├── report.Rmd
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   └── seedlings.csv
├── examples/
├── output/
│   └── seedlings-practice.csv
└── reports/
    ├── day01-notes.txt
    └── file-types.txt
The drawing leaves out most supplied files. data and reports are neighbours: neither is inside the other, and their parent folder is introcomputing-course. That folder is the project folder (also called the project root), the starting point for everything in the project.
In the file manager, open reports, go up to its parent and enter data, and watch the address bar in Windows File Explorer. In Finder, choose View → Show Path Bar to see the route at the bottom of the window.

title: Day 2 — Folders and paths
text:
Paths
A path lists the folders on the route to a file, separated by / (or \ on Windows), and ends with the filename. Your username and the location of Documents will differ from these examples:
Windows: C:\Users\anna\Documents\introcomputing-course\data\seedlings.csv
Mac:     /Users/anna/Documents/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv
Linux:   /home/anna/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv
Read a path from left to right: start at the top of the disk (/, or the drive C:\ on Windows) and open each folder in turn.
Find out the full path of seedlings.csv on your own laptop. On Windows, select the file and choose Copy as path; on Mac, right-click it, hold the Option key and choose Copy “seedlings.csv” as Pathname. Paste the path into a text file. It should end in introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv, with your own username near the start.

title: Day 2 — Folders and paths
text:
Absolute and relative paths
The paths above are absolute: they start at the top of the disk and give the whole route. A relative path starts from a folder you have agreed on. From the project folder, data/seedlings.csv means “enter data, then find seedlings.csv”. From inside reports, the same words ask for a data folder inside reports, which does not exist. The folder from which a program reads relative paths is its working directory; tomorrow the terminal will tell us its working directory, and later RStudio will start in the project folder.
The absolute path contains your username and the place you chose for the folder, so it differs on every laptop. The relative path data/seedlings.csv is the same for everyone who has the project folder, which is why our R code will use relative paths.

title: Day 2 — Folders and paths
section: Finding files from different starting folders
text:
Finding files from different starting folders
Use the file manager to find out which route leads from reports to the practice copy output/seedlings-practice.csv. You have to go up to the project folder first, because output is a neighbour of reports, not inside it.
Then make a place for notes: create a folder practice in the project folder, with field-notes and figures inside it, and copy yesterday’s note into field-notes under the name seedling-observations.txt. Write down its relative path from the project folder, close the file manager, and follow your path to open the note again. The path is practice/field-notes/seedling-observations.txt.
Names made of simple letters, numbers and hyphens, such as seedling-observations.txt, say what a file holds and are easy to type in the terminal and in R. Spaces and å, ä, ö cause trouble there.

title: Day 2 — Folders and paths
text:
Saved and unsaved work
While you type, the text lives in the computer’s working memory, which is cleared when the program closes. Saving writes the text to a file on the disk, where it stays after the program closes or the computer is switched off. Use the copy practice/field-notes/seedling-observations.txt to see the difference. Add “The plants were measured twice.”, save, close and reopen: the sentence is there. Then add “This line is not saved.”, close the editor and choose Don’t save: after reopening, that line is gone. Some editors save automatically or restore unsaved text; what counts is what is in the saved file.

title: Day 2 — Folders and paths
text:
Files on other computers
A path describes a place on one computer. A cloud folder (OneDrive, iCloud) may keep a copy elsewhere and synchronise it. Later in the course you will log into a remote Linux computer whose folders are separate from your laptop’s, even if the names look the same, so a file is there only after you have copied it there. For the same reason, a second copy on the same laptop is not a backup: keep important work in the university’s supported storage as well.

title: Day 2 — Folders and paths
section: What happens to a path when a folder moves?
text:
What happens to a path when a folder moves?
Use the practice folder to find out which written routes break when a folder is moved. Create practice/map-a and practice/map-b, and put a copy of your note in map-a as note.txt. In a new plain-text file reports/day02-map.txt, write two routes to note.txt: one from the project folder, and one from inside map-b, which must first go up to practice. Write down how you expect both routes to change, then move map-a into map-b with the file manager, follow the routes and correct them. Open note.txt to see whether its contents changed.
Finally, add to reports/day02-map.txt a small tree of the project folder with data, output, reports and practice, and the relative path from the project folder to seedlings.csv.






Hint: going up





From inside map-b, the route to map-a goes up one level to practice and then down into map-a. In the terminal tomorrow, “up one level” is written ...









Check your routes





Before the move, the note is at practice/map-a/note.txt from the project folder, and at ../map-a/note.txt (up to practice, then into map-a) from inside map-b. After the move, it is at practice/map-b/map-a/note.txt from the project folder and at map-a/note.txt from inside map-b. The contents of note.txt are unchanged; only its location changed. The path to the measurements is data/seedlings.csv.

title: Day 2 — Folders and paths
text:
Check your understanding






From the project folder, what is the relative path to yesterday’s note?





reports/day01-notes.txt. From inside reports, its name alone is enough, day01-notes.txt, because the starting point changed while the file stayed put.









Why does R code in this course use data/seedlings.csv rather than C:\Users\anna\…?





The absolute path works only on Anna’s laptop. The relative path works on any computer that has the project folder, as long as R starts in that folder.



Save today: reports/day02-map.txt and the practice folder.
Next: navigate these folders in a terminal.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Today’s question
Can you move around your folders by typing instead of clicking? The computers that hold large biological data, such as a sequencing facility’s server, usually have no desktop: you log in and type commands. Today you practise those commands on your own laptop, in a small workspace you create yourself. Tomorrow the same workspace will hold files from a laboratory exercise.
Save today: the introcomputing-shell workspace and navigation-notes.txt inside it.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Opening a terminal
Windows students open Ubuntu; Mac students open Terminal. The Windows/Mac setup page shows how. A shell is the program that reads your commands and runs them, and the terminal is the window you type them into. When it is ready, it shows a prompt, for example:
anna@laptop:~$
Your prompt will look different, and on a Mac it may end in %. Never type the prompt itself: type only the command after it and press Enter.
On Windows, Ubuntu has its own home folder, separate from your Windows Documents folder. This week we work in that Ubuntu home folder on purpose; the R project stays in Documents.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Where am I?
Use pwd (print working directory) to find out which folder the terminal is in, and ls (list) to find out what is in it:
pwd
ls
pwd prints something like /home/anna (Ubuntu) or /Users/anna (Mac): your home folder. ls lists its contents, which will differ from your neighbour’s.
Now make a workspace for this week and move into it:
cd
mkdir -p introcomputing-shell/practice
cd introcomputing-shell
pwd
ls
cd (change directory) on its own takes you home. mkdir (make directory) creates folders; the option -p lets it create introcomputing-shell and practice in one go, and it does not complain if they already exist. The last pwd should end in /introcomputing-shell, and ls should show practice.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: The same folder in the file manager
text:
The same folder in the file manager
To find out whether this is really the same folder you would click through, open it in the file manager. In Ubuntu on Windows type explorer.exe ., and on a Mac type open .. The . means “the folder I am in”. A window opens showing the practice folder: one folder, two ways of looking at it. Keep the window open.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Moving between folders
Make two folders for plant data and move down into one and back up again:
cd practice
mkdir seedlings
mkdir observations
ls
cd seedlings
pwd
cd ..
pwd
ls shows the two new folders. .. means the folder one level up, so the two pwd lines end in /practice/seedlings and then /practice. The workspace now looks like this, which you can check in the file manager:
introcomputing-shell/
└── practice/
    ├── seedlings/
    └── observations/
Now click into seedlings in the file manager and run pwd in the terminal. The terminal is still in practice: each window keeps its own location.
A command can also take an option that changes what it does. Use ls -l in practice to find out when each folder was last changed; the folder names are in the last column. Then use cd observations and ls to find out what is in the observations folder. ls prints nothing at all, because the folder is empty. Many commands work silently like this; a real problem prints a message.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
When a command fails
Go back to practice with cd .. and try cd Observations, with a capital O. On Ubuntu this fails, because Ubuntu treats Observations and observations as different names. Many Macs accept it. Always type the real spelling, so that your commands work on every computer.
Then try a folder that does not exist:
cd no-such-folder
pwd
The shell says there is no such file or directory, and pwd shows you are still where you were. A failed cd never moves you and never creates anything. When in doubt, ask “where am I, and what is here?” with pwd and ls.






Hint: I’m lost. How do I get back to the workspace?





Run cd ~/introcomputing-shell, then pwd. ~ is short for your home folder, so this works from anywhere on this computer.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Names with spaces, and keys that save typing
text:
Names with spaces, and keys that save typing
Inside practice, create a folder day03, move into it, and create two folders in it: readings and field notes. Type the second one with quotes:
mkdir day03
cd day03
mkdir readings
mkdir "field notes"
ls
ls shows two folders. Without the quotes, mkdir field notes would make two folders called field and notes, because the shell splits what you type at spaces. Quoting works, but names without spaces, such as field-notes, are easier to type.
Four keys make the terminal much less tiring:

Tab completes a name. Type cd fie and press Tab: the shell fills in field\ notes/, where the backslash keeps the space inside the name, just as quotes do. Tab only completes names that exist, so it also prevents typos.
Up arrow brings back your previous command. Read it before pressing Enter.
Ctrl+C stops a running command or clears a half-typed one. It does not copy. To copy and paste in the terminal use Ctrl+Shift+C / Ctrl+Shift+V in Ubuntu and Command+C / Command+V on a Mac.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Two terminal windows
Open a second terminal window and use pwd to find out where it starts. Then, in the first window, cd into readings and run pwd in both windows. The first ends in /day03/readings; the second is still in your home folder. Each shell has its own current folder, and moving one does not move the other.
Return the first window to the workspace with cd ~/introcomputing-shell, and reach day03 again with cd practice/day03. The first route works from anywhere, because it starts at your home folder. The second only works from introcomputing-shell: try it from inside readings and you get an error.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
A route between neighbouring folders
Inside your workspace, make a small project tree:
route-challenge/
├── inputs/
└── results/
    └── notes/
Create it with mkdir -p route-challenge/inputs route-challenge/results/notes and check it with ls in each folder.
Use cd to find a route from notes to its neighbour inputs, and check where you end up with pwd. The route is cd ../../inputs: up once to results, up again to route-challenge, then into inputs.
In the file manager, save a plain-text file navigation-transfer.txt inside route-challenge. Write down three routes, each with the folder it starts from: route-challenge to notes, notes to inputs, and inputs back to introcomputing-shell. Use .. in at least one and ~ in at least one. Then open a new terminal window and follow each route from its starting folder. If a route fails, the starting folder in your note is usually wrong. Correct the note.






Answer: the three routes






From route-challenge: cd results/notes
From notes: cd ../../inputs
From inputs: cd .. then cd .., or cd ~/introcomputing-shell from anywhere

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Check your understanding






What changes when I run cd? What stays unchanged?





Only the terminal’s current folder changes. No file or folder moves, and other windows stay where they were. pwd shows the new location.









Why can ls work without printing any names?





The folder is empty. An error would print a message.









Which of pwd, ls, mkdir readings, cd readings creates something?





Only mkdir readings. pwd and ls look, and cd moves you.



Save today: in introcomputing-shell, a plain-text note navigation-notes.txt with the full path printed by pwd, the command that brings you back from home, and three commands with what they do. You can write it in the file manager’s text editor.
Next: open an archive of laboratory files.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
Which seedlings received the treatment?
A lab group has sent you lab-data.zip. Its README says it holds four seedling pots, two control and two nutrient-treated, each measured once after seven days, with lengths in millimetres. A table called a manifest (samples.tsv) lists each sample’s ID, its treatment and the file holding its measurement. Today you use the terminal to find out which samples were treated and whether they are longer than the controls.
This is a small, separate practice dataset with four samples; the 24-plant dataset comes back on day 5 in R. The data are simulated.
Save today: treated-samples.txt, working/manifest-practice.tsv and working/observations.txt, all inside the extracted lab-data folder.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
section: Getting the archive into your workspace
text:
Getting the archive into your workspace
Download lab-data.zip with your browser. The download lands in your Downloads folder, which is not where your terminal works. In the terminal, run cd ~/introcomputing-shell and then open that folder graphically with explorer.exe . (Ubuntu on Windows) or open . (Mac). Copy the ZIP into it with the file manager, then run ls in the terminal: lab-data.zip should be listed.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
What is in the archive?
Use unzip -l to find out what the lab group sent before unpacking anything:
unzip -l lab-data.zip
The listing shows eight files: README.txt, samples.tsv, four measurement files measurements/S01.csv to S04.csv, and two short field notes. -l only lists; nothing has been extracted yet. Now extract into a folder of your choice and read the README:
unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data
cd lab-data
less README.txt
-d lab-data names the destination folder. Extraction makes ordinary files you can open and leaves the ZIP as it was. In less, Space moves down and q returns to the prompt.






Hint: unzip asks whether to replace a file





You have extracted into lab-data before. Answer n, look at the existing folder in the file manager, and extract into a fresh name such as lab-data-2 instead. Then use that name in cd.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
How many samples are there?
Use head and wc -l to find out how many samples the manifest describes:
head -n 3 samples.tsv
wc -l samples.tsv
head -n 3 shows the first three lines: a header naming the columns (sample_id, treatment, file), then S01 and S02. wc -l counts lines and prints 5: one header plus four samples. The columns are separated by tabs, which is what TSV (tab-separated values) means; a CSV uses commas.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
Which samples were treated?
Use grep to find out which samples received the treatment:
grep -F treated samples.tsv
grep prints every line that contains the search text; -F means plain text, not a pattern. You should see two lines, S03 and S04. The header and the control lines do not contain the word, so they are not printed.
grep matches text, not meaning: a line saying untreated would also match, because it contains treated. Always look at the lines it selected, not only at how many there are.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
section: Saving and counting the treated samples
text:
Saving and counting the treated samples
Save the treated lines to a file, and count them with a pipe:
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt
less treated-samples.txt
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
> sends the output into treated-samples.txt instead of the screen. The manifest is read and stays unchanged. The vertical bar | is a pipe: it passes grep’s lines straight to wc -l, which prints 2.
> replaces whatever the destination file contained before, so never put the input file after it: grep … samples.tsv > samples.tsv can empty the manifest before grep reads it.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
Are the treated seedlings longer?
The manifest’s file column says where each measurement is. Use head on those files to find out how long the treated and control seedlings were:
head measurements/S03.csv
head measurements/S04.csv
head measurements/S01.csv
head measurements/S02.csv
Each file has one header line and one value. The treated seedlings are 42.4 mm (S03) and 39.8 mm (S04); the controls are 32.1 mm (S01) and 35.2 mm (S02). Both treated seedlings are longer than both controls. With two pots per group that is a hint, not a result; the 24-plant dataset in week 2 is where we start answering the question properly.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
section: A practice copy of the manifest
text:
A practice copy of the manifest
You will want a copy of the manifest you can change without risking the original. Make one in a working folder and give it a clearer name:
mkdir working
cp samples.tsv working/samples-copy.tsv
mv working/samples-copy.tsv working/manifest-practice.tsv
ls working
ls
cp makes a second file; mv renames (or moves) it. ls working shows only manifest-practice.tsv, and ls shows that the original samples.tsv is still there. Both cp and mv silently replace an existing file with the destination name, so check names first.
Then use the file manager to create working/observations.txt with your answers from today: how many samples there are and why wc -l says 5, which two were treated, their lengths, and which file holds S04’s measurement.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
When untreated also matches
A colleague’s version of the manifest labels S01 as untreated instead of control. Use your practice copy to find out what grep -F treated selects then.

Copy working/manifest-practice.tsv to working/search-trap.tsv. Open only this copy in a text editor and change S01’s control to untreated.
Predict, then run grep -F treated working/search-trap.tsv | wc -l.

The count is 3: S01, S03 and S04. untreated contains the text treated, so grep cannot tell the two labels apart. Running grep -F treated working/search-trap.tsv without the count shows you the S01 line and makes the problem visible. The original samples.tsv still gives 2.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
section: A measurement file that seems to be missing
text:
A measurement file that seems to be missing
When you receive data, every file the manifest names should exist. Use a copy of the folder to find out what you see when one has been renamed.

In the file manager, copy the whole lab-data folder to received-check. In received-check/measurements, rename S04.csv to S04-renamed.csv.
In the terminal, cd into received-check and try head measurements/S04.csv. It fails with No such file or directory, although the manifest still lists that path.
Use ls measurements and head measurements/S04-renamed.csv to find out which sample that file holds. It contains S04,39.8, the S04 measurement.
Because you know it is S04, restore the name with mv measurements/S04-renamed.csv measurements/S04.csv and check that head measurements/S04.csv works again.

In real data, a file whose identity you cannot confirm from its contents is a question for the lab group, not something to rename by guessing. Add the problem, the evidence and the repair to working/observations.txt.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
section: Which samples are esters? (an organic-laboratory inventory)
text:
Which samples are esters? (an organic-laboratory inventory)
This optional task uses the same commands on a different archive: a simulated inventory of four organic-chemistry samples, each with a supplied class label. No chemistry knowledge is needed.
Download organic-lab.zip, copy it into ~/introcomputing-shell with the file manager as above, and use the day’s commands to find out which samples are labelled ester and how many there are:
cd ~/introcomputing-shell
unzip -l organic-lab.zip
unzip organic-lab.zip -d organic-lab
cd organic-lab
less README.txt
grep -F ester inventory.tsv > ester-samples.txt
grep -F ester inventory.tsv | wc -l
The inventory has a header and four samples. Two match: O02 and O03. grep searched the supplied labels; it does not recognise chemical structures. The archive also contains organic-recovery.csv, which you will use for calculations later in the course.

title: Day 4 — Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
Check your understanding






Did grep change the manifest? Why does wc -l count 5 for four samples?





grep only reads the manifest; > wrote its output to a separate file. wc -l counts lines, and the manifest has one header line plus four sample lines. The saved treated-samples.txt has no header, because the header did not match.









Why list a ZIP with unzip -l before extracting it?





You see what you received, and the folder structure it will create, before any files are written. If something is missing, you can ask the sender straight away.



Save today: treated-samples.txt, working/manifest-practice.tsv and working/observations.txt in the extracted lab-data folder, and keep lab-data.zip unchanged.
Next: Day 5 — meet R and RStudio.

title: Day 5 — Meet R and RStudio
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 5 — Meet R and RStudio
text:
Today’s question
On days 1–4 you found files, moved through folders, and searched a small table in the terminal. From next week, R does the calculations and plots. Today you get to know the place where you will do that work: open the course project in RStudio, find your way around its window, run a first calculation and a supplied plot, and watch a finished report being made from saved files.
Nothing today needs to be memorised. Day 6 explains objects, names and vectors step by step; today you only need to know where to type and where to look.
You need: R and RStudio installed (see the R and RStudio setup page), and the extracted introcomputing-course folder from day 1. If installation is not finished, follow the demonstration and use setup support before day 6.
Save today: reports/day05-notes.txt.

title: Day 5 — Meet R and RStudio
text:
R and RStudio
R is the program that calculates. RStudio is the application you work in: it has an editor for saved files, a Console where R runs your instructions, and panes that show your files, plots and help. You start RStudio; RStudio starts R for you. You will rarely open R on its own.

title: Day 5 — Meet R and RStudio
text:
Opening the course project

In File Explorer or Finder, open your extracted introcomputing-course folder.
Double-click introcomputing.Rproj. RStudio opens.
Check the top-right corner of RStudio: it should say introcomputing.
In the Files pane (bottom right) you should see data, output, reports and report.Rmd.

The .Rproj file marks this folder as an RStudio project. Opening it starts R inside this folder, so short paths such as data/seedlings.csv mean “the data folder of this project”, exactly like the relative paths from day 2.
Use getwd() and file.exists() in the Console (bottom left; its prompt is >) to find out whether R can see the seedling measurements. Type each line and press Enter:
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")
getwd() prints the folder R is working in, which should end with introcomputing-course. The second line should print [1] TRUE: the file is where the analysis will look for it.






Hint: file.exists() says FALSE






Check that RStudio’s top-right corner names the project. If it says Project: (None), use File → Open Project… and choose introcomputing.Rproj.
You may have opened an .Rproj inside a ZIP preview, or a folder with an extra level (introcomputing-course/introcomputing-course/). Find the folder in which data, output and reports sit directly next to the .Rproj file, as on day 1.
Type the quotation marks. Without them R looks for an object, not a file name.

title: Day 5 — Meet R and RStudio
text:
The four panes
The RStudio window has four areas. Their arrangement can differ slightly, but their jobs are the same:







Pane
What it is for




Editor (top left; appears when a file is open)
Saved files with instructions, such as report.Rmd.


Console (bottom left)
R runs what you type after > and prints the answer.


Environment (top right)
The objects R is holding in memory right now.


Files / Plots / Help (bottom right)
The project folder, your plots, and help pages.



Next to the Console is a Terminal tab. That is a shell like the one you used on days 3–4 (on Windows it may not be your Ubuntu shell). In this course, type R in the Console and keep using your usual terminal for shell commands.
Click report.Rmd in the Files pane and it opens in the Editor. Leave it unchanged for now: the Editor shows a saved file, while the Console is a conversation with R that is not saved.

title: Day 5 — Meet R and RStudio
text:
Console or terminal?
The prompt tells you which program is waiting: > is R, $ is the shell. It helps to have seen the wrong-window messages once, so try both. In the R Console, pwd gives Error: object 'pwd' not found, because R does not know shell commands. In your terminal, 44.3 - 25.7 gives 44.3: command not found, because the shell does not do arithmetic. Neither message means that anything is broken; the instruction belongs in the other window.

title: Day 5 — Meet R and RStudio
text:
How much did P01 grow?
Plant P01 was 25.7 mm long at the start and 44.3 mm at the end. Use the Console to find out how much it grew:
44.3 - 25.7
R prints [1] 18.6: P01 grew 18.6 mm. The [1] marks the first value printed; it is not part of the answer. P02 went from 24.3 mm to 32.3 mm; R gives 8 (it does not print a trailing .0), so P02 grew much less than P01.
If you press Enter on an unfinished line such as 44.3 -, the prompt changes to + because R is waiting for the rest. Finish the line, or press Esc to get > back.

title: Day 5 — Meet R and RStudio
text:
Did longer seedlings stay longer?
Use this supplied plot to find out whether seedlings that started long also ended long. Copy the lines into the Console and press Enter:
seedlings <- read.csv("data/seedlings.csv")
plot(seedlings$initial_mm, seedlings$final_mm,
     xlab = "Initial length (mm)", ylab = "Final length (mm)")
The first line reads the measurement file into R and calls the table seedlings. The second line draws one point per plant. You do not need to understand every symbol yet: <-, names and columns are day 6 and day 7 topics.
The plot appears in the Plots pane with 24 points, one per plant. The points are widely scattered, with at most a weak upward tendency: a seedling’s starting length tells you little about its final length. seedlings now appears in the Environment pane as 24 obs. of 4 variables: 24 plants and 4 columns. Click it to see the table; the file data/seedlings.csv itself is unchanged. The first line found the file only because the project is open.
The vertical axis is final length, not growth. Which plants grew most is therefore not visible directly in this plot.






Hint: where is growth in this plot?





Each point is one plant: its initial length across, its final length up. Growth is final minus initial, the calculation you did for P01. On day 8 you will calculate growth for every plant and plot it by group.

title: Day 5 — Meet R and RStudio
section: Where the course is heading: a report
text:
Where the course is heading: a report
Did the treated seedlings grow more? The supplied report.Rmd answers that. Click its tab in the Editor and click Knit. An HTML page opens with the question, the code, a table of growth by group, and a plot of the individual plants. The table shows 12 control plants with mean growth 15.28 mm and 12 treated plants with 21.49 mm. A new report.html appears next to report.Rmd in the Files pane.
report.Rmd holds the text and the R instructions; Knit runs them from scratch on data/seedlings.csv and writes report.html. If the data change, you Knit again and the whole report updates. In week 2 you learn to read and edit this file, and on day 10 you make your own first report.






Hint: Knit fails with “there is no package called …”





The report needs a few packages. Run the installation line from the setup page once in the Console, then Knit again. If it still fails, note the exact message for setup support; you can follow the teacher’s demonstration today.

title: Day 5 — Meet R and RStudio
section: What is still there after closing RStudio?
text:
What is still there after closing RStudio?
Choose File → New File → Text File, write one line each on what the Editor, Console and Environment are for, add P01’s growth, and save it as reports/day05-notes.txt. Then quit RStudio and reopen it through introcomputing.Rproj to find out what survived.
The Environment pane is empty: seedlings lived in R’s memory, which is cleared when R stops. Your note, report.Rmd and report.html are still in the Files pane, because they are saved on disk, as on day 1. That is why next week you save your instructions in files: they make every result again.

title: Day 5 — Meet R and RStudio
text:
Check your understanding






Where should pwd, grep -F treated samples.tsv and 44.3 - 25.7 run?





pwd and grep are shell commands: run them in the terminal, at a $ prompt. 44.3 - 25.7 is an R expression: run it in the R Console, at a > prompt. It gives 18.6.









Why open introcomputing.Rproj rather than just starting RStudio?





Opening the project makes R work inside the course folder, so short relative paths such as data/seedlings.csv find the file. Without it, R may be working in another folder and report that the file does not exist.









After restarting RStudio, seedlings has gone. Is the data lost?





No. seedlings was a copy in R’s memory. The file data/seedlings.csv is still saved and can be read again.



Save today: reports/day05-notes.txt, and report.html if Knit worked.
Next: R objects, calculations, and vectors.

title: Quiz: R calculations
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. What does the last line print?
initial_mm <- 20
final_mm <- 37
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
final_mm <- 39
growth_mm

17 (ii) 19 (iii) 39







Hint





Which assignment last changed growth_mm?









Answer





(i), 17. R stored that result when the subtraction ran. Running growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm again would update it to 19.




Q2. Three plants have initial lengths c(20, 22, 19) mm and final lengths c(37, 40, 34) mm, in the same plant order. What are their growth values and mean growth?






Hint





Subtract position by position, then divide the total growth by three.









Answer





Growth is c(17, 18, 15) mm. The mean is 50 / 3, about 16.67 mm. The matching plant order makes the position-by-position subtraction meaningful.




Q3. Which survives closing a fresh R session: an object created only in the Console, or instructions saved in day06.R? How can you recreate the object?






Hint





One is in session memory; the other is a file on storage.









Answer





The saved script survives. Open it and run the instructions from the top to recreate its objects. This assumes the session workspace was not separately saved and restored.




Q4. A collected product mass is 0.62 g and the supplied maximum is 1.00 g. Using yield_percent = 100 × collected mass / maximum mass, what is the yield? What would change if the collected mass were 0.70 g?






Hint





Both masses use grams, so their units cancel in the ratio.









Answer





The yields are 62% and 70%, respectively.




Q5. Amount in mol is mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol. Concentration in mol/L is amount divided by final solution volume in litres. For 0.2922 g, 58.44 g/mol, and 100 mL final solution, what is the concentration in mmol/L?






Hint





Convert 100 mL to 0.100 L. Multiply mol/L by 1000 to obtain mmol/L.









Answer





Amount is 0.2922 / 58.44 = 0.005 mol. Concentration is 0.005 / 0.100 = 0.050 mol/L, or 50 mmol/L.




Q6. In the previous question, what happens to concentration if you double only the mass? What if you instead double only the final volume?






Hint





Mass is in the numerator; final volume is in the denominator.









Answer





Doubling mass gives 100 mmol/L. Restoring the original mass and doubling final volume gives 25 mmol/L.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Quiz: Importing and inspecting tables
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. An imported table has 24 rows and four columns. head() displays six rows. How many plants are in the full table if each row represents one plant?






Hint





A preview and the full table dimensions answer different questions.









Answer





24 plants. head() displays a preview; dim() reports the full row and column counts.




Q2. What does file.exists("data/seedlings.csv") returning TRUE establish? Does it establish that the file contains the intended study and units?






Hint





Separate finding a path from interpreting its contents.









Answer





The file exists at that path relative to R’s working directory. Inspect the table and data dictionary to establish the study, column meanings, and units.




Q3. Predict mean(c(10, NA, 20)), mean(c(10, NA, 20), na.rm = TRUE), and mean(c(10, 0, 20)).






Hint





NA represents an unavailable value; zero is an observed number.









Answer





The results are NA, 15, and 10, respectively. The available-value mean uses two observations, while the last mean uses three.




Q4. An 18-row table is described as one row per plant. It has 17 distinct plant IDs. Should you immediately delete a row?






Hint





A discrepancy is a reason to inspect the data and study description.









Answer





Investigate which ID repeats and why. A recording error, mistaken import, or different row structure could explain it. Repeated IDs can be legitimate in a repeated-measurement table, so deletion needs evidence.




Q5. A solution table contains solution_id, solute, mass_g, molar_mass_g_mol, and final_volume_ml. Which are labels, and what does the numeric type tell you about units?






Hint





Distinguish an identifier from a measured or supplied quantity.









Answer





solution_id and solute are labels. The other columns are quantities. Numeric storage alone does not supply units or justify combining different quantities; use the dictionary and formula.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Quiz: Derived tables and figures
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A plant begins at 25.7 mm and ends at 44.3 mm. What should growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm produce? Does adding this column change the source CSV?






Hint





Distinguish the derived R table from the file it was imported from.









Answer





18.6 mm. mutate() creates or changes a column in its returned table. The source CSV stays unchanged unless a separate write operation replaces it.




Q2. Which chooses rows and which chooses columns?
filter(seedlings, treatment == "treated")
select(seedlings, plant_id, growth_mm)






Hint





Ask whether the operation selects observations or variables.









Answer





filter() chooses rows meeting the treatment condition. select() chooses the two named columns.




Q3. 
What does one point represent, and why does horizontal jitter not create additional observations?






Hint





Read the vertical axis and distinguish display position from a measurement.









Answer





One point is one plant’s change in length, in mm. Horizontal jitter separates overlapping points; height = 0 keeps every growth value unchanged. The number of plants is unchanged.




Q4. Collected product is 0.62 g from a supplied maximum of 1.00 g. Another run collects 0.90 g from a maximum of 2.00 g. Using 100 × collected / maximum, which has the higher percentage yield?






Hint





Compare ratios rather than collected masses alone.









Answer





The first yields 62% and the second 45%. The larger collected mass has the smaller percentage because the starting scales differ.




Q5. Required stock volume is target concentration × final volume / stock concentration. For stock 500 mmol/L, target 50 mmol/L, and final volume 50 mL, how much stock is required? What if stock is instead 100 mmol/L and target is 200 mmol/L?






Hint





The concentrations use the same units. Compare the calculated volume with the requested total.









Answer





The first case needs 5 mL. The second formula gives 100 mL for a requested 50 mL total, so that request cannot be met by adding solvent alone. Keep and flag the impossible request.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Quiz: R Markdown reports
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Which file is the editable recipe for a report: (i) report.Rmd, (ii) report.html, or (iii) the plot shown in RStudio?






Hint





One file combines prose and code chunks.









Answer





(i). The .Rmd is the source. Rendering it produces HTML for reading; the input data remain separate files.




Q2. A report plots growth_mm before the chunk that imports measurements and calculates growth. What should be changed?






Hint





Rendering follows the document’s chunk order.









Answer





Put package loading, import, and calculation before the plot. The saved report should create every object it uses.




Q3. You created a table only in the Console. A chunk runs interactively, but the report fails in a fresh session because that table is missing. What belongs in the report?






Hint





A fresh session cannot rely on earlier manual commands.









Answer





Include the required package calls, import, and transformations in the report before their results are used. Restart R and render again.




Q4. After changing the input from 24 seedlings to an 18-seedling study, the figure updates but the methods still say 24 plants. Has the report transferred correctly?






Hint





Code output and written descriptions must refer to the same study.









Answer





No. Update the methods, question, captions, and manually written counts. Inline R can connect reported counts to the imported table, but it cannot automatically fix an incorrect study description.




Q5. You correct a caption directly in report.html. What happens when you render report.Rmd again, and where should the correction be saved?






Hint





HTML is generated from the source.









Answer





The generated HTML can overwrite the direct edit. Correct the caption in report.Rmd, render again, and inspect the resulting HTML.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Quiz: A complete first report
text:
Lecture · Exercises
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A report includes an attractive figure but gives no input filename, sample size, or definition of a point. What information should be added?






Hint





A reader needs to connect the question to the data and result.









Answer





Identify the input and study design, number of plants, what one point represents, measured quantity, and units. Include methods explaining how the plotted outcome was calculated.




Q2. A plant-growth plot shows overlapping groups, with treated observations tending higher. Which statement is supported by that description?

Every treated plant grew more than every control.
The treated observations tended to show greater growth in this sample, with overlap.
The treatment always increases growth.







Hint





A description of this sample has a narrower scope than a universal claim.









Answer





(ii). Overlap contradicts (i), and this plot alone does not establish the universal claim in (iii).




Q3. One figure has initial length on x and final length on y. Another has treatment on x and change in length on y. Which more directly addresses whether growth differs between the groups?






Hint





Identify where change in length is actually plotted.









Answer





The treatment-versus-change figure directly compares growth by group. Initial versus final length addresses a different relationship.




Q4. A concentration is calculated as 1000 × (mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol) / (final_volume_ml / 1000), in mmol/L. For glucose mass 0.9008 g, molar mass 180.16 g/mol, and final volume 100 mL, what is the result? Is a graph of these calculated cases independent evidence of a biological treatment effect?






Hint





Trace the supplied formula, then ask where its plotted values came from.









Answer





50 mmol/L. The cases illustrate a supplied calculation; they are not independent evidence of a biological treatment effect.




Q5. What check tests whether a saved report can be reproduced: (i) seeing an old figure in RStudio, or (ii) restarting R and rendering the source with its input files?






Hint





A visible old result may depend on earlier session state.









Answer





(ii). Check that the fresh render succeeds and that its figures, numbers, units, and input description agree. Rendering success alone does not prove the interpretation is correct.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

text:
Predict the result, explain it, then use R to check. The R reference is available.
Topic quizzes: 6 · 7 · 8 · 9 · 10
