title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 1. Assignment is an action when the line runs
text:
1. Assignment is an action when the line runs
You saved growth_mm <- 37 - 20 in a script but did not run it. Must growth_mm now exist in R’s memory? What are its value and units after running?






Answer and check





Saving the script does not run it. After execution, the object contains 17 mm. Restarting removes that session object, while the saved script remains. Run the source from the top to recreate the calculation.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
text:
2. Matched values in vectors
For three plants, initial lengths are 20, 22, 19 mm and final lengths are 37, 40, 34 mm. What does position-by-position subtraction assume, and what are the resulting growth values?






Answer and check





Both vectors must refer to the same plants in the same order, with compatible lengths. The growth vector is 17, 18, 15 mm. Its mean is about 16.67 mm. Correct arithmetic on unmatched plants would still answer the wrong question.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 3. A table is more than its numbers
text:
3. A table is more than its numbers
The imported seedling table has 24 rows and four columns. What identifies a plant, what units do the length columns use, and why is averaging the plant ID not a meaningful biological summary?






Answer and check





plant_id identifies the plant; the two length columns use millimetres, as specified in the dictionary. IDs label observations rather than measure a quantity, so an average ID has no interpretation. The header names columns and is not another plant. Initial and final lengths in one row belong to one plant.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
text:
4. Plot the quantity asked for
For P01, initial length is 25.7 mm and final length is 44.3 mm. Calculate growth. Does a plot with initial length on x and final length on y directly display that growth on its vertical axis?






Answer and check





Growth is 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm. The first plot’s vertical axis is final size, not change. Create growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm and plot that derived column when growth is the outcome. Label axes with the actual variables and units, and keep the original CSV unchanged.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 5. A report works in the Console but fails when knitted
text:
5. A report works in the Console but fails when knitted
The error says an object is not found. You created that object interactively before opening the report. What needs repairing, and which files should remain after a successful render?






Answer and check





Put the needed import/calculation into the report before it uses the object, and load its packages there. Keep the .Rmd source, input data, and generated HTML. Render from a fresh session. A Console call to rmarkdown::render() must not be placed inside a report that would then try to render itself.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
section: 6. Transfer choice: a fully supplied product calculation
text:
6. Transfer choice: a fully supplied product calculation
The supplied maximum product mass is 1.00 g; collected dry product is 0.62 g, assumed pure for this simplified task. Percentage yield is 100 × collected mass / maximum mass. What is the yield, and does that number independently establish the product’s purity?






Answer and check





The yield is 62%. The gram units cancel. Purity was an assumption, not a finding from this ratio. Keep the maximum and collected masses as distinct inputs; a larger raw mass is not necessarily a greater percentage when starting scales differ.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
text:
7. A stored result becomes stale
After assigning initial_mm <- 20, final_mm <- 37, and growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm, you set final_mm <- 39. What is growth_mm before and after rerunning the subtraction?






Worked answer





It remains 17 until the subtraction runs again, then becomes 19 mm. An assigned object holds its stored result; it is not a live spreadsheet formula that automatically recomputes every dependency. Save the correct order in the script and rerun from its inputs.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
text:
8. Equal lengths but wrong plants
Initial lengths are c(20,22,19). The correct final vector is c(37,40,34), but a copy has been reordered to c(34,37,40). Both vectors have length three. Is subtraction biologically justified?






Worked answer





Not by equal length alone. R subtracts positions, so the reordered copy gives 14,15,21 mm for incorrect pairs. The correct correspondence gives 17,18,15 mm. Verify identities and order as well as compatible vector lengths.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
text:
9. Audit the new input
The transfer study is supplied as 18 independent plants, nine per group. Your report still says 24 plants. Which evidence and source lines should you inspect?






Worked answer





Check the imported filename, project and object; inspect dim(), distinct plant IDs, group labels/counts and missingness. Then check inline and manually written prose against that input. The expected transfer table is 18 by 4 with 18 unique IDs, nine records per group and no missing lengths.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
text:
10. A supplied concentration calculation
Amount in mol = mass_g / supplied molar_mass_g_mol; concentration in mmol/L = 1000 × amount / final_volume_l. For 0.2922 g, 58.44 g/mol and 100 mL final volume, what is the result?






Worked answer





100 mL = 0.100 L. The amount is 0.005 mol, giving 0.050 mol/L or 50 mmol/L. Doubling only mass gives 100 mmol/L; doubling only volume gives 25 mmol/L. The quantity refers to final total solution volume, not a solvent volume before addition.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
text:
11. An impossible dilution request
The supplied rule is stock volume = target × final volume / stock concentration. A request has stock 100 mmol/L, target 200 mmol/L and final volume 50 mL. What numerical result appears, and why is it not a valid preparation recipe?






Worked answer





The formula gives 100 mL of stock, exceeding the requested 50 mL total. The target is more concentrated than the stock, so dilution by adding solvent alone cannot achieve it. Preserve the row and flag it rather than deleting it or inventing stronger stock.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Week 2 revision — R and a first report
text:
12. Source, HTML and a revision
You corrected an HTML caption directly, then rendered the R Markdown source again and the correction vanished. Where should the revision live, and what should be tested?






Worked answer





Edit the .Rmd source and render it. The HTML is a generated reading copy and can be replaced. Check the new output location, caption, units, input description and inline counts, then rerender from a fresh session with the required ordinary data files included.



Return to your first report, or continue to data quality.

title: Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
text:
Today’s question
A labmate has exported the seedling measurements from the lab spreadsheet into data/seedlings-messy.csv. Before calculating anything you want to know whether the file really holds 24 plants with sensible lengths. R will calculate a mean from any table, so the checking is up to you. Today you inspect the export, repair what the source records support, and save a cleaned copy while the raw file stays unchanged.
The study itself is described in the data dictionary. The source records for this export are in data/field-notes.txt; read them before you start.
Save today: day11-cleaning.R in the project root, output/seedlings-cleaned.csv and output/cleaning-notes.txt.

title: Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
text:
Reading every column as text
Start day11-cleaning.R with:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
raw <- read_csv("data/seedlings-messy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), trim_ws = FALSE)
dim(raw)

Normally read_csv() guesses which columns hold numbers. Here cols(.default = col_character()) reads every column as text, so an odd entry stays exactly as it was typed, and trim_ws = FALSE keeps any spaces at the start or end of a value. dim() gives 25 rows and 4 columns, although the study has 24 plants.

title: Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
section: Is any plant in the file twice?
text:
Is any plant in the file twice?
Use count() to find out which plant IDs appear more than once, then look at those rows:

raw |> count(plant_id) |> filter(n > 1)
filter(raw, plant_id == "P01")

count() counts the rows for each ID and filter(n > 1) keeps the repeated ones. P01 appears twice, and its two rows are identical in every column. The study has one row per plant, and the field notes confirm that the second row is an accidental repeat of the import, so one of them can go. In a design with one row per time point a repeated ID would be normal, which is why you compare whole rows and the design before removing anything.

title: Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
text:
Which treatment labels are used?
Use unique() to find out how the treatment was written:

unique(raw$treatment)

There are four spellings: "control", "Control", "treated" and "treated " with a space at the end. R treats them as four different groups, so a group summary would give four rows instead of two. According to the field notes, P03’s Control means control and P15’s trailing space is an export mistake.

title: Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
text:
Are the lengths plausible?
Use filter() with %in% to look at the plants the field notes mention:

filter(raw, plant_id %in% c("P06", "P18", "P21"))

%in% keeps the rows whose ID is in the listed set. P18’s initial length is the text 18.7 mm, and the notes confirm it was measured in millimetres. P21’s final length is 4.38, much shorter than its initial 23.6 mm; the source notebook records 43.8 mm, so the value was typed in centimetres. P06 has no final length, and the notes say that reading is unavailable.
A value is changed only when a source record supports the change. A small or large value on its own is not a reason, because plants really do vary.

title: Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
section: Does the cleaned table have 24 plants?
text:
Does the cleaned table have 24 plants?
Use nrow(), anyDuplicated() and sum(is.na()) to find out whether the repair left one row per plant and how many growth values are missing:

nrow(cleaned)
anyDuplicated(cleaned$plant_id)
sum(is.na(cleaned$growth_mm))
cleaned |> count(treatment)
write_csv(cleaned, "output/seedlings-cleaned.csv")

You should get 24 rows, 0 (no ID is repeated), 1 missing growth value, and 12 plants in each group. So the control group has 12 plants but only 11 usable growth values. write_csv() saves the cleaned table as a new file next to the other outputs.

title: Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
text:
Why P06 stays missing
Use mean() to find out the average growth of all plants:

mean(cleaned$growth_mm)
mean(cleaned$growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE)

The first line gives NA: one value is unknown, and R will not guess. With na.rm = TRUE (“remove NA”) R averages the 23 available values and gives 18.49 mm, which you report as the mean of 23 of the 24 plants.
Writing 0 for P06’s final length would claim a measurement nobody made. P06 started at 24.7 mm, so it would “grow” −24.7 mm and pull the overall mean down to 16.69 mm.






Hint: avoid silently losing records





Look at filter(raw, plant_id == "P01") before using distinct(). Do not use distinct(plant_id, .keep_all = TRUE): it keeps the first row for each ID and throws away a second row even when the two disagree. Disagreeing records need investigation.

title: Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
text:
Checking your repairs

Add a comment above each repair in day11-cleaning.R naming the field-note entry behind it. Then use filter(cleaned, plant_id %in% c("P06", "P18", "P21")) to find out whether those plants now have the values the notes give. You should see P18 with initial length 18.7, P21 with final length 43.8, and P06 with final length NA.
Use group_by(treatment) and summarise(mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE)) on cleaned to find out how much each group grew on average. Control gives 15.21 mm (11 plants) and treated 21.49 mm (12 plants).
How much would the P21 slip have mattered? Make a copy in which P21 keeps the typed value: slipped <- mutate(cleaned, final_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P21", 4.38, final_mm), growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm), and summarise it the same way. The treated mean drops to 18.21 mm, because P21 now “grew” −19.2 mm.
Make wrong_zero_example in the same way, with P06’s final length set to 0, and use mean(wrong_zero_example$growth_mm) to find out what the invented zero does to the overall mean. You should get 16.69 mm instead of 18.49 mm.
Use read_csv("data/seedlings-messy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) with its default settings and str() to find out what R would have made of this file without the text import. The trailing space is silently removed, so only three labels remain, and initial_mm becomes a text column (chr) because of the single 18.7 mm entry, so no mean can be calculated from it.
Write output/cleaning-notes.txt with one line per problem: the plant, what you saw, the evidence, and what you did. End with the plant whose measurement is unknown. Then restart R (Session → Restart R), rerun the whole script, and use nrow() to confirm that the raw file still has 25 rows and output/seedlings-cleaned.csv has 24.

title: Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
text:
A second class’s data
Another class has sent data/seedlings-transfer.csv: 18 seedlings, nine in each group, measured seven days apart like ours. They sent no field notes. Is the file ready to use? Start a new script, day11-transfer.R.

Use dim(), count(plant_id), unique(treatment) and sum(is.na()) to find out whether the file has one row per plant, two clean labels and complete lengths. You should find 18 rows, no repeated ID, only control and treated, and no missing values.
Use mutate() to calculate growth_mm and find out how much T01 grew. Check it by hand: 40.3 − 25.3 = 15.0 mm. Save the table with growth as output/day11-transfer-growth.csv.
Write a short handover note, output/day11-transfer-audit.txt, saying what you checked and what you found. Since nothing was wrong and there are no source records, no value was changed. If a value had looked odd, you would keep it and ask the recorder.

title: Day 11 — Can we trust this table?
text:
Check your understanding






What makes a repair justified?





A source record, such as the notebook entry for P21. A check only raises the question; the evidence answers it. A very small or large value may be real and is kept unless a record shows it was entered wrongly.









The cleaned file has 24 rows but the raw file has 25. Is something lost?





No. The extra row was the identical second P01, removed because the field notes confirm the duplicate import. All 24 plants are still there; P06 is kept with an unknown final length.



Keep: day11-cleaning.R, output/seedlings-cleaned.csv and output/cleaning-notes.txt. Next: describe variation.

title: Day 12 — How much do the plants differ?
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 12 — How much do the plants differ?
text:
Today’s question
“Control seedlings grew 15.3 mm on average” does not tell a reader whether every plant grew about 15 mm or whether some grew 8 mm and others 19 mm. Today you describe both the centre of a set of measurements and their spread, first with three small numbers you can check by hand and then with the seedlings.
Use the complete file data/seedlings.csv today, not yesterday’s repair exercise; the study is described in the data dictionary.
Save today: day12-variation.R in the project root.

title: Day 12 — How much do the plants differ?
text:
Mean and median
The mean adds all values and divides by how many there are. The median is the middle value after sorting, or the average of the two middle values when there is an even number. Use both to find out where three growth values are centred:

growth_mm <- c(12, 14, 16)
mean(growth_mm)
median(growth_mm)

Both give 14 mm. Now one value is much larger than the others:

uneven_mm <- c(10, 10, 10, 100)
mean(uneven_mm)
median(uneven_mm)

The mean is 32.5 mm and the median 10 mm. The large value pulls the mean strongly but hardly moves the median. Neither number is wrong; if the large value is a real measurement, it stays in the data.

title: Day 12 — How much do the plants differ?
section: How far is each value from the mean?
text:
How far is each value from the mean?
The deviation of a value is its distance from the mean: value minus mean. For 12, 14 and 16 mm the deviations are −2, 0 and +2 mm. They always add up to zero, because the mean sits in the middle, so their plain average cannot measure spread. Squaring each deviation removes the sign: 4, 0 and 4.

title: Day 12 — How much do the plants differ?
text:
Variance and standard deviation
The sample variance adds the squared deviations and divides by one less than the number of values. The standard deviation (SD) is the square root of the variance. Use R to find out both for the three growth values, once by the formula and once with the built-in functions:

deviations_mm <- growth_mm - mean(growth_mm)
sum(deviations_mm^2) / (length(growth_mm) - 1)
var(growth_mm)
sd(growth_mm)

The squared deviations add up to 8, and 8 / 2 gives a variance of 4 mm². The SD is 2 mm. Because the variance squares millimetres, its unit is mm², which is hard to picture; the SD is back in millimetres and can be read next to the mean. Dividing by n − 1 instead of n is the usual choice when the values are a sample, and var() and sd() do the same.
Now compare two toy groups with the same mean:

close_mm <- c(13, 14, 15)
spread_mm <- c(8, 14, 20)
mean(close_mm)
mean(spread_mm)
sd(close_mm)
sd(spread_mm)

Both means are 14 mm, but the SDs are 1 mm and 6 mm: the plants in the second group differ much more from each other.



Two toy groups share a mean of 14 mm but differ in spread. Dots are measurements; the dashed line is their common mean.

title: Day 12 — How much do the plants differ?
section: How much do the control plants vary?
text:
How much do the control plants vary?
Use the same functions on the control plants to find out their centre and spread:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
control <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "control")
mean(control$growth_mm)
median(control$growth_mm)
var(control$growth_mm)
sd(control$growth_mm)

The 12 control plants grew a mean of 15.28 mm (median 15.65 mm) with an SD of 3.19 mm and a variance of 10.18 mm². None of them grew exactly 15.28 mm: their growth ranges from 8.0 to 18.7 mm. In a report, round to what the ruler can support, for example “mean 15.3 mm, SD 3.2 mm, n = 12”.

title: Day 12 — How much do the plants differ?
section: Centre and spread in the seedlings
text:
Centre and spread in the seedlings

Write the three-row hand calculation for 12, 14 and 16 mm in a comment in day12-variation.R: each value, its deviation, its squared deviation, their sum, and the divisor n − 1. Check that it gives the same 4 mm² as var().
Use mean(), median(), var() and sd() on the treated plants to find out whether they differ from the controls in centre, in spread, or in both. You should get 21.49 mm, 20.85 mm, 23.67 mm² and 4.87 mm: the treated plants grew more and varied more.
Use the same four functions on c(12, 14, 26) to find out what one unusually tall plant does to each summary. Predict first. The mean rises from 14 to 17.33 mm, the median stays 14 mm, and the SD jumps from 2 to 7.57 mm.
Use mean(close_mm + 10) and sd(close_mm + 10) to find out what changes if every plant had grown 10 mm more. The mean becomes 24 mm and the SD stays 1 mm, because the plants still differ from each other by the same amounts.
Divide close_mm by 10 to convert to centimetres and find out the new mean, variance and SD. You get 1.4 cm, 0.01 cm² and 0.1 cm: the mean and SD are divided by 10, the variance by 100. The plants are not less variable; only the unit changed. A check like this is useful when your code converts units.







Hint: use the units to check yourself





Adding a constant moves the centre but leaves every deviation unchanged. Dividing lengths by ten divides the mean and SD by ten, and the variance by one hundred because its unit is squared. ?var and ?sd describe the functions and their na.rm argument for missing values.

title: Day 12 — How much do the plants differ?
text:
Another lab: percentage yield
Your teacher may choose this context instead of task 2 above. In an organic synthesis, each run is one attempt to make a product. In data/organic-recovery.csv, theoretical_mass_g is the most product a run could give from its starting materials, and isolated_mass_g is the dry product actually collected, both in grams. Runs started from different amounts, so you compare the percentage yield, 100 × isolated / theoretical, rather than grams.
Use mean(), var() and sd() to find out how much the yield of the standard protocol varies between runs:

organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
standard_runs <- filter(organic, protocol == "standard")
mean(standard_runs$yield_percent)
var(standard_runs$yield_percent)
sd(standard_runs$yield_percent)

Run Y01 gives 100 × 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%. The six standard runs have a mean yield of 68.67%, a variance of 18.67 squared percentage points and an SD of 4.32 percentage points. A change from 62% to 70% is 8 percentage points, not an 8% increase. Repeat the summaries for protocol == "modified": mean 77.00%, SD 3.74 percentage points.

title: Day 12 — How much do the plants differ?
text:
A second class’s data
The second class’s file, data/seedlings-transfer.csv, has 18 plants, nine per group. Do their treated plants also vary more than their controls? Start day12-transfer.R with its own library() lines, import and growth calculation.

Find T01 and check its growth by hand (15.0 mm), so you know the subtraction is the right way round.
Use group_by(treatment) and summarise() with n(), mean(), median(), var() and sd() to find out the centre and spread of each group, and save the table as output/day12-transfer-summaries.csv. Control: n 9, mean 13.66 mm, median 12.9 mm, SD 2.53 mm. Treated: n 9, mean 17.87 mm, median 17.1 mm, SD 1.94 mm. Here the treated plants grew more but varied less, the opposite of the first study, so a larger mean does not come with a larger SD.
Add a column growth_cm = growth_mm / 10 and summarise it again to find out which numbers change with the unit. Means and SDs are divided by 10 and variances by 100, and the treated group still has the larger mean and the smaller SD.

title: Day 12 — How much do the plants differ?
text:
Check your understanding






Which spread is larger in the main study, and what does it describe?





The treated SD (4.87 mm) is larger than the control SD (3.19 mm). It describes how much individual treated plants differ from each other. How precisely we know a group’s mean is a different question, which comes on day 14.









Does a larger SD mean the measurements were careless?





Not necessarily. Plants really differ, and measurement noise adds to that. The SD shows how much the values vary, not why they vary.



Keep: day12-variation.R and day12-transfer.R with your notes in comments. Next: summarise groups while still showing individuals.

title: Day 13 — Summarising groups without hiding the plants
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 13 — Summarising groups without hiding the plants
text:
Today’s question
A bar chart of two group means cannot tell a reader how many plants are behind each bar, how much they varied, or whether one unusual plant pulled a mean up. Today you make a small table with one row per group and a figure that shows every plant together with its group mean, so a reader gets both.
Start day13-groups.R in the project root:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

Save today: day13-groups.R, output/growth-summary.csv and output/growth-summary.png.

title: Day 13 — Summarising groups without hiding the plants
text:
One row per group
Use group_by() and summarise() to find out the number of plants, mean, median and SD of growth in each treatment group:

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_plants = n(),
            n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
            mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")
group_summary

group_by(treatment) makes the next step work separately within each treatment, and summarise() returns one row per group. The names left of = become the column names. n() counts rows, that is plant records, while sum(!is.na(growth_mm)) counts the growth values that are actually there (! means “not”). .groups = "drop" returns an ordinary table.



treatment
n_plants
n_observed
mean_mm
median_mm
sd_mm




control
12
12
15.28
15.65
3.19


treated
12
12
21.49
20.85
4.87



group_summary has two rows that describe groups; seedlings still has the 24 plants. You need both: the plants for the figure, the summary for the means.

title: Day 13 — Summarising groups without hiding the plants
section: Plants and means in one figure
text:
Plants and means in one figure

group_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 13),
             alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = group_summary, aes(x = treatment, y = mean_mm),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 18, size = 4, colour = "darkred") +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)",
       caption = "Small dots: individual plants. Red diamonds: group means.") +
  theme_minimal()
group_plot

The first geom_point() draws one dot per plant from seedlings. position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0) moves dots a little sideways so they do not hide each other, but never up or down, so every dot stays at its measured growth. The second geom_point() takes its data from group_summary and draws the means as red diamonds; inherit.aes = FALSE tells it to use its own x and y instead of looking for growth_mm, which the summary table does not have.
The figure shows what the table cannot: the groups overlap, one treated plant grew only 12.2 mm, and two treated plants grew about 30 mm. If you add whiskers, say what they show. Mean ± SD describes how plants vary; a confidence interval, which comes in week 4, describes how uncertain a mean is. Points and means without whiskers are a good choice for today.

title: Day 13 — Summarising groups without hiding the plants
text:
Histograms
A histogram cuts the growth axis into intervals, called bins, and counts the plants in each. Use one to find out the shape of each group’s growth values:

ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = growth_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 4, boundary = 0, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ treatment, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Change in seedling length (mm)", y = "Number of plants") +
  theme_minimal()

facet_wrap(~ treatment, ncol = 1) draws one panel per group, stacked on the same growth axis so the panels can be compared. With 4 mm bins, most control plants fall between 12 and 20 mm, and most treated plants between 20 and 24 mm, with two treated plants in the 28–32 mm bin. With only 12 plants per group the shape changes noticeably when you change the bin width.

title: Day 13 — Summarising groups without hiding the plants
section: Saving the table and the figure
text:
Saving the table and the figure

write_csv(group_summary, "output/growth-summary.csv")
ggsave("output/growth-summary.png", plot = group_plot, width = 6, height = 4)

The CSV holds the numbers and the PNG holds the picture; until you save them, both exist only in R’s memory. Find the two files in your file manager and open them outside RStudio.

title: Day 13 — Summarising groups without hiding the plants
text:
Group summaries for the seedlings

Use filter() and mean() to find out whether the control mean in group_summary matches the plants it came from. You should get 15.28 mm.
Use the same summary code on output/seedlings-cleaned.csv from day 11 (add growth_mm if it is not there) to find out how the missing P06 shows up. Control has n_plants 12 but n_observed 11, and a mean of 15.21 mm instead of 15.28 mm, because a different set of plants contributed. This is why the table keeps both counts.
Change the histogram’s binwidth to 2 and then to 6 and find out which features stay the same. At every width the treated values sit higher than the controls and the two treated plants near 30 mm stand apart; smaller peaks and gaps appear or vanish with the bin width, so do not describe them.
Write a caption for output/growth-summary.png that a reader could check without the code: the unit (one plant), the outcome and its unit, what dots and diamonds mean, and n. For example: “Seven-day growth (mm) of 24 individually potted seedlings, 12 per group. Dots are plants; red diamonds are group means.”







Hint: keep the two tables apart





write_csv(group_summary, "output/growth-summary.csv") saves the summary, while ggsave("output/growth-summary.png", plot = group_plot, width = 6, height = 4) saves the plot. If a layer complains about a column it cannot find, use names() on the table that layer uses.

title: Day 13 — Summarising groups without hiding the plants
text:
Another lab: percentage yield
Your teacher may choose this instead of task 2 above. In data/organic-recovery.csv each row is one independent synthesis run. Calculate yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g, as on day 12, then use group_by(protocol) and summarise() to find out the number of runs, mean yield and SD for each protocol. Both protocols have six runs; the standard mean is 68.67% (SD 4.32 percentage points) and the modified mean 77.00% (SD 3.74). Plot the runs with a mean marker as above, with the y-axis labelled “Isolated product yield (%)”, and save output/organic-yield-summary.csv and output/organic-yield-summary.png.

title: Day 13 — Summarising groups without hiding the plants
text:
A second class’s data
Make the same table and figure for data/seedlings-transfer.csv (18 plants, nine per group) in a new script, day13-transfer.R, with its own library() lines, import and growth calculation.

Use group_by() and summarise() to make transfer_summary with n, mean, median and SD, and save it as output/day13-transfer-summary.csv. Use nrow() to find out how many rows transfer and transfer_summary have: 18 plants and 2 groups. You should get means of 13.66 mm (control) and 17.87 mm (treated).
Draw the plants with a mean marker from transfer_summary, with a caption that says n = 9 per group, and save it as output/day13-transfer-points.png. Does any control plant grow more than a treated plant? Yes: three control plants (15.9, 16.3 and 17.4 mm) grew more than the smallest treated plant (15.0 mm).
Restart R and rerun the script to find out whether it rebuilds both files on its own.

title: Day 13 — Summarising groups without hiding the plants
text:
Check your understanding






Why show individual dots as well as the means?





The dots show how many plants there are, how much they vary, where unusual values lie and how much the groups overlap. A higher mean does not mean every treated plant grew more than every control plant.









The summary table has two rows. Are they two new observations?





No. Each row describes a group of 12 plants. The 24 plants stay in seedlings, and that is the table any later analysis uses.



Keep: day13-groups.R, output/growth-summary.csv, output/growth-summary.png and your caption. Next: replicates and uncertainty.

title: Day 14 — How many independent plants do we have?
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 14 — How many independent plants do we have?
text:
Today’s question
Would measuring one plant ten times tell you as much about other plants as measuring ten different plants? A thesis that counts the ten readings as ten plants looks far more certain than the experiment can support. Today you learn to count the independent units in a design, and you use a short simulation to see how much a mean changes from one sample of plants to the next.
Save today: day14-sampling.R in the project root and output/day14-design-notes.txt.

title: Day 14 — How many independent plants do we have?
text:
The experimental unit
The experimental unit is the thing that independently received a treatment. In the seedling study each plant grows in its own pot and was randomly allocated to control or treated (see the data dictionary), so the unit is one plant, and there are 24 of them, 12 per group. Each plant was measured twice, but the two lengths become a single growth value.
Another plant is a biological replicate: it tells you how plants respond. Measuring the same plant again is a technical replicate: it tells you how repeatable your measurement is. Three ruler readings of P01 can show how well you measure, but they are still one plant. In the same way, 100 cells from one mouse are one mouse, and ten time points from one culture are one culture.

title: Day 14 — How many independent plants do we have?
text:
When plants share a tray
Suppose the nutrient had been given to whole trays instead: one tray of twelve control plants and one tray of twelve treated plants. Then each group received a single treatment decision, and anything special about a tray, such as a warmer spot on the bench, is mixed up with the treatment. The independent unit is the tray, so there is one per group, however many plants are measured. Only more trays, not more plants per tray, would fix this.

title: Day 14 — How many independent plants do we have?
section: Spread among plants and spread among means
text:
Spread among plants and spread among means
The SD from day 12 describes how much individual plants differ. A different question is how much the mean would change if you repeated the experiment with new plants. That spread is called sampling uncertainty, and it becomes smaller when the mean is based on more independent plants, while the plants themselves stay just as variable.

title: Day 14 — How many independent plants do we have?
text:
Simulating many experiments
We cannot repeat the experiment hundreds of times, but R can imitate it. The supplied code treats the 24 measured growth values as a small “population” and draws many samples from it. Save it in day14-sampling.R and run it unchanged:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
population_mm <- seedlings$growth_mm
set.seed(14)
means_4 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(population_mm, size = 4, replace = TRUE)))
means_16 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(population_mm, size = 16, replace = TRUE)))
sampling <- data.frame(mean_mm = c(means_4, means_16),
                       sample_size = rep(c("4 plants", "16 plants"), each = 400))
ggplot(sampling, aes(x = mean_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ sample_size, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean growth in one simulated sample (mm)",
       y = "Number of simulated samples") +
  theme_minimal()
sd(population_mm)
sd(means_4)
sd(means_16)

sample(population_mm, size = 4, replace = TRUE) draws 4 values, and replace = TRUE allows the same value to be drawn twice. mean() turns that sample into one mean, and replicate(400, ...) repeats the whole thing 400 times. set.seed(14) fixes the random draws so that everyone gets the same result.
Each value in the histogram is the mean of one simulated sample, not a plant. The 24 plants vary with an SD of 5.13 mm. The means of 4 plants vary with an SD of 2.44 mm, and the means of 16 plants with an SD of only 1.24 mm: four times as many plants roughly halves the spread of the means. The SD of the means is what is later called the standard error.



Repeated sample means from samples of sixteen plants cluster more tightly than means from samples of four. The source values are the same in both panels.

title: Day 14 — How many independent plants do we have?
section: Counting units and reading the simulation
text:
Counting units and reading the simulation

For each design below, write in output/day14-design-notes.txt how many measurements there are and how many independently treated units, completing “We have … measurements, but … independently treated units”:

the seedling study; (b) one plant per treatment, each measured with a ruler twelve times; (c) two trays of twelve plants with the treatment given per tray;
one synthesis run whose product is weighed twelve times. For each, say what the repeated measurements can tell you.

Use sd(means_4) and sd(means_16) to find out how much more stable a mean of 16 plants is than a mean of 4. You should get 2.44 and 1.24 mm, while sd(population_mm) stays 5.13 mm, because the plants did not become more alike.
Change the seed to 25 and rerun to find out whether the result depends on the particular random draws. The exact values change (2.54 and 1.30 mm), but means of 16 plants still vary about half as much as means of 4. Then set the seed back to 14.
Change replicate(400, ...) to replicate(1000, ...) for means_16 to find out whether more repetitions make the means more stable. The SD stays about the same (1.24 mm): more repetitions give a smoother histogram, but only a larger sample size narrows it. Neither adds a measured plant.







Answer check for task 1






24 growth values from 24 plants: 24 units, 12 per group. (b) 24 readings from 2 plants: 1 unit per group; the readings show how repeatable the ruler is.
24 growth values from 2 trays: 1 unit per group; the plants show how plants within a tray vary. (d) 12 masses from 1 run: 1 unit; the weighings show how repeatable the balance is.

title: Day 14 — How many independent plants do we have?
text:
A second class’s data
Use the 18 growth values in data/seedlings-transfer.csv as a new small population, in a new part of day14-sampling.R. Both groups are combined because the question is about sample size, not treatment.

Import the file, calculate growth_mm, then set the seed to 14 and make means_3 and means_12 with size = 3 and size = 12. Use sd() to find out how much means of 3 and of 12 plants vary. You should get 1.69 and 0.83 mm, while the 18 plants themselves vary with an SD of 3.08 mm.
Put both sets of means in one table with the data.frame() pattern above, save it as output/day14-transfer-sampling.csv, and draw the two histograms on the same axis to see the difference.
A supervisor offers you a choice: measure each of two plants twenty more times, or grow ten more plants. Which tells you more about the mean growth of plants under these conditions? Write two sentences in your design notes. The ten plants, because the mean of more independent plants is more stable; extra readings of two plants only show how well you measure those two.

title: Day 14 — How many independent plants do we have?
text:
Check your understanding






Is a precise mean enough?





No. If every plant was measured 5 mm too long, or all plants grew in one unusually sunny tray, a large sample gives a very stable mean in the wrong place. A narrow histogram of means shows that the sampling is repeatable, not that it measures the right thing.









What do the 400 values in means_16 represent?





400 simulated sample means, each from 16 values drawn from the same 24 plants. They are not 400 new plants.



Keep: day14-sampling.R and output/day14-design-notes.txt. Next: write a descriptive report.

title: Day 15 — A short descriptive report
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 15 — A short descriptive report
text:
Today’s question
You send your supervisor a figure and the line “treated plants grew more”. The replies come back: which data file, how many plants, what are the dots, and can I rerun it? Today you write one short report that answers all of these: it states the question, shows the data checks, the summary table and the figure, says in words what they show, and rebuilds itself from the saved data.
Save a new file, descriptive-report.Rmd, in the project root, next to data/. You may copy the structure of your day 10 report and then rewrite its text. The study is described in the data dictionary; the data are simulated, and the nutrient formulation is not specified.
Make one report today. If your teacher chooses the organic-yield context below, make organic-report.Rmd instead.
Save today: descriptive-report.Rmd (or organic-report.Rmd) and its HTML.

title: Day 15 — A short descriptive report
text:
The parts of the report
A short report needs four parts, in this order:

Question: one or two sentences on what you want to find out.
Data and methods: the input file, what one row is (one plant), the outcome and its unit, the checks you made, and how growth was calculated.
Results: a table with n, mean, median and SD per group, and a figure of the individual plants with the group means.
Interpretation: what the numbers show, in plain words, and what they cannot show yet.

Use the complete file data/seedlings.csv. If your teacher asks you to use the repaired day 11 data instead, include the repair code, say so in the methods, and use 23 usable growth values in every count.

title: Day 15 — A short descriptive report
text:
Data and methods
Use anyDuplicated(), count() and sum(is.na()) to find out, inside the report, whether the file has one row per plant, two groups and complete lengths:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
anyDuplicated(seedlings$plant_id)
seedlings |> count(treatment)
sum(is.na(seedlings$initial_mm))
sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm))
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

anyDuplicated() gives 0 when no ID is repeated (a positive number would be the position of the first repeat). You should find 12 plants per group and no missing lengths, so the methods can say: “24 plants, 12 per group, no missing lengths; growth is final minus initial length in mm.”

title: Day 15 — A short descriptive report
text:
Results
Reuse the day 13 summary, printed as a neat table with knitr::kable():

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
            mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(group_summary, digits = 2,
             caption = "Observed growth and variation by treatment; lengths in mm.")

The table is calculated when the report renders, so if the data change, the table changes with them. Below it, add the day 13 figure of individual plants with red diamonds for the means, with a caption that names the unit, the symbols and n. The SD in the table describes how plants vary; this report has no confidence intervals.

title: Day 15 — A short descriptive report
text:
Writing the interpretation
Describe three things: how the group means differ, how much plants vary within each group, and how much the groups overlap. For the complete data:

Treated seedlings grew a mean of 21.5 mm and controls 15.3 mm (12 plants each). Treated plants also varied more (SD 4.9 mm against 3.2 mm), and the two groups overlap: the smallest treated plant grew 12.2 mm, less than most controls.

Check each number against your table before you write it. “Every treated plant grew more” would be false, as the figure shows. How uncertain the 6 mm difference is, and whether chance could produce it, is the question of week 4, so end with that as the limitation.

title: Day 15 — A short descriptive report
text:
Rendering from a fresh session
Restart R (Session → Restart R) and run this in the R Console, not in a chunk inside the report:

rmarkdown::render("descriptive-report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")

The report must then load its own packages, read its own data and create every object, because nothing from your earlier session is available. Because the .Rmd is in the project root, data/seedlings.csv points to the right file, and output_dir = "reports" puts the HTML in reports/. A report must never contain its own render command.






Hint: the render fails with “object not found” or “file not found”





“Object not found” means the report uses something that only existed in your Console; add the code that creates it to the report. “File not found” usually means the .Rmd is not in the project root or the path points to a personal folder such as Downloads. Read the first error message and the chunk name it gives.

title: Day 15 — A short descriptive report
Day 15 — A short descriptive report
text:
Revising your report

Close RStudio, open the HTML in a browser, and find out whether a reader can find the question, the input file, the unit, the outcome with its unit, the meaning of the symbols, and the main limitation. Add a sentence or a label for anything missing.
Replace two numbers in your results text with inline R, so they are calculated when the report renders: for example We measured `r nrow(seedlings)` plants. renders as “We measured 24 plants.” Render to find out whether they appear; the object must be created earlier in the report.
Rewrite these weak sentences if your draft has anything like them: “The results were good” (name the pattern and its size), “The treated group had more error” (“treated plants varied more, SD 4.9 mm”), “The computer removed the bad values” (say which value changed and which record supported it).
Copy the project folder to a new location and render there to find out whether the report depends on anything outside it. Record what failed, what you changed and the result of the rerun in reports/day15-revision.txt.

title: Day 15 — A short descriptive report
text:
A second class’s data
Write a second, shorter report, transfer-description.Rmd, in the project root, about the 18 plants in data/seedlings-transfer.csv. Start from your report’s structure, but replace the import, every object name, number, caption and sentence, because the new data tell a different story.

Use the same checks to find out whether the file is complete: 18 rows, 9 per group, no missing lengths.
Make the table and figure. You should get control: mean 13.66 mm, median 12.9 mm, SD 2.53 mm; treated: mean 17.87 mm, median 17.1 mm, SD 1.94 mm.
Write the interpretation. This time the treated plants varied less than the controls, so a sentence copied from your first report would be wrong. Render from a fresh session and note in reports/day15-revision.txt where the HTML ended up.

title: Day 15 — A short descriptive report
text:
Check your understanding






What makes a limitation useful?





It is specific. “The sample is small” says little. “Each group has 12 plants, the groups overlap, and this report describes the sample without estimating how uncertain the difference between the means is” tells the reader what to be careful about.









The report renders only while your objects are in the Environment. What is wrong?





The report uses objects created in the Console. Put the code that creates them in the report, restart R and render again.



Keep: descriptive-report.Rmd or organic-report.Rmd, its HTML, and the data it needs to render. Next: from description to a comparison.

title: Quiz: A difference between groups
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Control mean growth is 15.28 mm and treated mean growth is 21.49 mm. Calculate treated minus control from these rounded means. What does a positive sign mean?






Hint





State the subtraction order before calculating.









Answer





\(21.49-15.28=6.21\) mm (about 6.22 mm from unrounded data). A positive sign means greater mean growth in the treated sample.




Q2. Twelve plants per treatment are measured initially and finally. How many independent growth values are there per treatment: 12 or 24?






Hint





The two measurements belong to the same plant and yield one growth value.









Answer





12. Initial and final measurements are combined into one final-minus-initial growth value per plant.




Q3. Some control plants grew more than some treated plants. Does that force the two sample means to be equal?






Hint





Individual overlap and equality of group means are different properties.









Answer





No. Groups can overlap and still have different means. Use the observations to describe overlap and calculate the group means separately.




Q4. Which is the null hypothesis for the planned two-sided comparison?

Every plant has identical growth.
The two population mean growths are equal.
The treatment must increase growth.







Hint





The hypothesis concerns population means, and a two-sided question allows both directions of difference.









Answer





(ii). The alternative allows either population mean to be larger. Individual plants may vary under either hypothesis.




Q5. The new class has a smaller sample mean difference than the first class. Does the difference alone establish that the treatment stopped working? What else do you need?






Hint





An estimate varies across samples and conditions.









Answer





No. Consider sampling uncertainty, observed variability, sample size, and study conditions. A sample difference alone does not determine its uncertainty or establish a universal treatment effect.

title: Quiz: Welch t-test
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Which study matches the independent groups used in this lesson?

The same plants measured before and after treatment.
Separate plants randomly allocated to treated and control groups.
Several leaves taken from one plant in each group.







Hint





Identify the unit that received treatment independently.









Answer





(ii). The independent unit is a plant. Measurements on the same plant are related; many leaves from one plant do not supply many independently treated plants.




Q2. Mean growth is 21.49 mm in treated plants and 15.28 mm in controls. What difference does t.test(treated, control) estimate, and in what units?






Hint





Subtract the second group’s mean from the first group’s mean.









Answer





Treated minus control: \(21.49 - 15.28 = 6.21\) mm using the rounded means. The difference from the full data is about 6.22 mm.




Q3. A treated-minus-control 95% confidence interval is [2.70, 9.73] mm. What interval and two-sided p-value would result from reversing the vector order?






Hint





Negate both endpoints, then put the lower endpoint first. The equal-means question is the same in either direction.









Answer





The interval is [−9.73, −2.70] mm. The two-sided p-value is unchanged.




Q4. Which statement correctly interprets a 95% confidence interval for a mean difference?

It contains 95% of individual plants’ growth values.
Its procedure covers the true mean difference in about 95% of repeated experiments under the assumptions.
Every value inside it has the same probability of being the true difference.







Hint





The interval describes uncertainty in a population mean difference.









Answer





(ii). The coverage statement concerns repeated use of the procedure. The interval is not an individual-growth range, and it does not give equally probable values of the fixed population difference.




Q5. The p-value is 0.0015. Does this mean there is a 0.15% probability that the treatment has no effect? What does the p-value describe?






Hint





Begin with “If the equal-means model and its assumptions held …”.









Answer





No. If the equal-means model and assumptions held, a two-sided t statistic at least this extreme would occur with probability about 0.0015. The p-value does not assign a probability to the hypothesis or measure biological importance.




Q6. For the same observations, will a 99% confidence interval be wider or narrower than the 95% interval? Will the group means change?






Hint





A higher coverage target requires more room around the same estimate.









Answer





Wider. The observed group means stay the same; only the interval level changes.

title: Quiz: Paired measurements
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Plants D1, D2, D3 have before readings 5, 8, 6 and after readings 7, 9, 9 in the same order, in µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. Calculate their changes and mean change.






Hint





Subtract before from after for each matching identifier.









Answer





Changes are 2, 1, 3; mean change is 2 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. These are three independent pairs, not six independent plants.




Q2. Which function call estimates after minus before for matched plants?

t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)
t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)
t.test(after, before, paired = FALSE)







Hint





Both the pairing argument and vector order matter.









Answer





(i). (ii) estimates the reverse direction; (iii) treats the two vectors as independent groups.




Q3. Independently sorting the before and after columns preserves their means. Does that make the resulting paired test valid?






Hint





Pairing carries subject identity, which is more information than two means.









Answer





No. Sorting columns separately destroys the original plant matching. The mean difference can remain unchanged while the SD of within-plant changes and the confidence interval change. Move complete rows together.




Q4. A 95% interval for mean change is [−0.48, 4.48] in the stated rate units. Does it prove no change, or contain 95% of individual changes?






Hint





The interval describes uncertainty in a mean change under the assumptions.









Answer





Neither. It spans zero and both positive and negative mean changes; the small dataset does not resolve direction at this interval level. It is not an individual-change range or proof of equivalence.




Q5. All plants are measured before, then after changing light. A paired test gives a small p-value. Why is light alone still not established as the cause?






Hint





What else changes between the first and second reading?









Answer





Elapsed time, acclimation, measurement order, or equipment drift may contribute. The test addresses mean change; a suitable comparison and design addressing order effects are needed to isolate causes.

title: Quiz: Calibration and unknown samples
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. Known concentration is in mg/L; the measured response is absorbance. Which formula fits the calibration used here?

lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l, data = standards)
lm(concentration_mg_l ~ absorbance, data = standards)







Hint





The response is left of ~; the predictor is right of it.









Answer





(i). Prepared concentration is the predictor and absorbance the response. The unknown concentration is later estimated by rearranging that fitted line.




Q2. For absorbance = 0.04 + 0.065 * concentration_mg_l, estimate concentration from an in-range reading of 0.30. What does the slope mean?






Hint





Rearrange to (reading - intercept) / slope.









Answer





\((0.30-0.04)/0.065 = 4\) mg/L. The slope is an increase of 0.065 absorbance per mg/L increase in concentration.




Q3. A standard has observed absorbance 0.30 and fitted absorbance 0.28. What is its residual, and where is its point relative to the line?






Hint





Residual = observed − fitted.









Answer





The residual is +0.02 absorbance, so the point lies above the fitted line. It is a signal-scale difference, not a concentration.




Q4. Measured standard signals span 0.024–0.525. Unknown X1 reads 0.270 and X2 reads 0.700. Which gets a supported inverse estimate, and how should the other appear in the saved table?






Hint





Check the measured signal range before inverting.









Answer





X1 is in range. Retain X2’s ID and reading with an out-of-range flag and a missing concentration estimate. A suitable new measurement is needed.




Q5. A new sample is diluted from 1.00 mL to 10.00 mL total volume. Its new in-range reading corresponds to 7.40 mg/L. Estimate the original concentration assuming no measured substance is lost or reacts.






Hint





Multiply the diluted estimate by final total volume / original-sample volume.









Answer





\(7.40\times(10.00/1.00) = 74.0\) mg/L using the rounded estimate. This uses a measured dilution and stated volumes; it does not validate a different sample’s out-of-range reading.

title: Quiz: A biological association
text:
Exercises · Lecture slides
Try each question before opening its hint or answer.

Q1. A dry-mass-on-leaf-area line has slope 4.11, with mass in mg and area in cm². Give the slope units and interpretation.






Hint





A slope is change in response divided by change in predictor.









Answer





4.11 mg/cm². Within the observed range, an additional 1 cm² of area is associated with about 4.11 mg greater fitted mean dry mass.




Q2. For mass_mg = 9.48 + 4.11 * area_cm2, calculate fitted mass at 8 cm². Must an individual leaf at that area have exactly this mass?






Hint





Insert 8 into the fitted equation; distinguish a mean relationship from an individual measurement.









Answer





\(9.48+4.11\times8 = 42.36\) mg. No: individual masses vary around the fitted relationship, and the fitted line also has uncertainty.




Q3. Areas were observed from 2.96 to 14.68 cm². Is the intercept 9.48 mg a measured mass of a zero-area leaf? Is prediction at 80 cm² supported by this range?






Hint





Both zero and 80 are outside the observed predictor range.









Answer





No to both. The intercept positions the fitted line over the observed range; zero-area mass is not measured. A prediction at 80 cm² extrapolates far beyond the evidence.




Q4. A18 changes the slope when omitted, but has no documented error. What belongs in the main analysis, and what does the omitted-point fit show?






Hint





Influence and invalidity are different questions.









Answer





Retain A18 in the main fit. The separate fit is a sensitivity check showing how much this observation influences the line; influence alone does not justify removal.




Q5. If area is converted from cm² to mm² by multiplying by 100, what happens to the 4.11 mg/cm² slope and fitted masses?






Hint





The same physical area has a numeric value 100 times larger in mm².









Answer





The slope becomes 0.0411 mg/mm². The intercept and fitted masses stay the same apart from numerical rounding.




Q6. Leaf area was measured rather than randomly assigned. Which statement is supported by the fitted line?

Larger leaves tended to have greater dry mass in this sample.
Adding 1 cm² causes every leaf to gain 4.11 mg.
Area is the only influence on mass.







Hint





Association is a pattern among observed variables; causation needs design and subject knowledge.









Answer





(i). Age, species, environment, and other factors may influence both measurements. The observational line alone establishes neither causation nor a complete explanation of mass.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
text:
Review questions from the week. Use the stated design, units, and comparison direction. See the statistics reference for definitions.
Topic quizzes:

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
text:
1. Interpret the direction and interval
For independent seedlings, the estimated treated-minus-control mean growth difference is 6.22 mm, with a 95% confidence interval from 2.70 to 9.73 mm. What quantity is this interval describing? Is it a range for 95% of the plants?






Answer





It describes uncertainty in the population mean difference, under the model assumptions and in the stated treated-minus-control direction. It is not a range containing 95% of individual plants. A 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed true quantity in about 95% of repeated samples when its assumptions hold.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 2. What does the p-value condition on?
text:
2. What does the p-value condition on?
Does a p-value of 0.0015 mean a 0.15% probability that the null hypothesis is true, or prove that a 6 mm difference matters biologically?






Answer





Neither. It describes the probability, under the null model and its assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed. It is not the probability of the hypothesis. Biological importance needs the effect’s size, units, uncertainty, organism, and purpose. The test cannot repair dependent units.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
text:
3. Pair by identity
The same ten plants were measured before and after increasing light. Why should the analysis use within-plant differences? Could independently sorting the two measurement columns improve their pairing?






Answer





The two readings belong to each same plant, so calculate after minus before within matching IDs. There are ten independent pairs, not twenty independent plants. Sorting columns independently destroys that identity and does not improve pairing. The fixed before/after order also leaves a time/order limitation.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 4. Invert the calibration in the stated direction
text:
4. Invert the calibration in the stated direction
The fitted line is approximately absorbance = 0.03957 + 0.06489 × concentration_mg_l. For an in-range absorbance of 0.310, what formula estimates concentration?






Worked answer





Rearrange to concentration = (0.310 - 0.03957) / 0.06489, giving about 4.17 mg/L. Use full fitted coefficients in code. We fitted absorbance as the measured response to known concentration; reversing the regression is a different fit. The inverse calculation is a point estimate, not full calibration uncertainty.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 5. A diluted reading is new evidence
text:
5. A diluted reading is new evidence
An unknown’s original reading is above the measured standards. Can you simply report the line’s extrapolated concentration? If a new in-range reading gives 7.40 mg/L after 1.00 mL was diluted to 10.00 mL total, what is the original estimate?






Answer and check





Flag the original as outside range rather than treat extrapolation as a supported result. A new in-range diluted measurement permits a stated correction: 7.40 × (10.00 / 1.00) ≈ 74.0 mg/L, using rounded numbers. The dilution assumes no measured material was lost or reacted. It does not validate another old out-of-range reading without its own new measurement.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
text:
6. Slope units and causal limits
A fitted dry-mass-versus-leaf-area slope is about 4.11. Dry mass is in mg and area in cm². What are the slope’s units, and what claim is not established by this observational fit?






Answer





The units are mg per cm²: fitted change in dry mass for a one-cm² increase in area. The sample association does not establish that experimentally changing area would cause this mass change. Inspect residuals and the measured range, and avoid extrapolating far beyond observed leaf areas.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
text:
7. Reversing the contrast
A treated-minus-control95% interval is2.70 to9.73 mm. What is the control-minus-treated interval? What happens to the two-sided p-value?






Answer and reasoning





The reversed interval is−9.73 to−2.70 mm. Reverse the endpoint order as well as their signs. The two-sided p-value is unchanged because the equal-means question and observations are the same. Clearly label the reported direction.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
text:
8. Different confidence levels, same observations
With identical data and model, would a99% interval normally be narrower or wider than a90% interval? Does changing the interval level alter the observed means?






Answer and reasoning





The99% procedure gives the wider interval to target greater long-run coverage. The sample means do not change. Retain the confidence level chosen for the main analysis.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 9. What if the smaller study has a narrower interval?
text:
9. What if the smaller study has a narrower interval?
The transfer study has 9 plants per group instead of 12, yet its interval is narrower. Must R have failed?






Answer and reasoning





No. Interval width also depends on observed variability and model assumptions. The transfer study has lower observed group spread. When several features differ, sample size alone does not determine the ordering of interval widths.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
text:
10. Pairing checked only by means
Independently sorting before and after columns preserves their separate means. Does that validate the paired analysis?






Answer and reasoning





No. It destroys subject identity and can alter the spread of within-subject changes while preserving their average. In the actual ten-plant file the correct and artificial pairings have the same mean change but very different SDs and intervals. Sort complete rows together or match by recorded identity.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 11. A new instrument gives two unknown readings
text:
11. A new instrument gives two unknown readings
Transfer standards cover measured signals0.024–0.525. X1 reads0.270 and X2 reads0.700. Which gets an inverse estimate, and what should happen to the other record?






Answer and reasoning





X1 is within the measured range and estimates about 2.48 mg/L using the new fitted coefficients. X2 remains in the output with its reading, an out-of-range flag, and no supported concentration estimate. A suitable new measurement is required.

title: Week 4 revision — comparisons and fitted lines
section: 12. A unit conversion changes a slope
text:
12. A unit conversion changes a slope
A mass-on-area slope is4.11 mg/cm². Area is converted to mm² by multiplying by 100. What happens to slope and fitted masses?






Answer and reasoning





The slope becomes about 0.0411 mg/mm², a factor of 100 smaller numerically. The intercept and fitted masses remain the same apart from rounding. The biological association did not become weaker merely because the predictor unit changed. A line through formula-calculated values is also not independent empirical evidence.



Return to association practice, or continue to how a computer works.

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
Today’s question
A colleague sends you a single-cell RNA-seq table: 30,000 genes measured in 100,000 cells. Will it open in R on your laptop? To answer that you need a rough picture of what is inside a computer, and a way to estimate how much memory a dataset needs before you load it.
Save your code as data-size.R in the project root and your answers in reports/data-size.txt. Write each estimate down before R gives you the real value, so you can see how close you were.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
1. The parts of your computer








Part
What it does
In this course




CPU (processor)
Carries out calculations. It has a few cores, each able to work on its own task.
Runs R.


RAM (memory)
Fast, temporary working space. Emptied when a program closes or the computer turns off.
Holds the objects in R’s Environment pane.


Disk (SSD)
Slower, permanent storage. Usually much larger than RAM.
Holds saved files: CSVs, scripts, reports.


GPU (graphics processor)
Thousands of simple cores doing the same small calculation at once.
Not needed. Used for images, video and deep learning.



An installed program is a file on disk. When you start it, the operating system creates a process: a running copy that uses CPU and RAM. Closing the window ends the process; the program stays installed.
How much RAM, disk and how many cores does your own laptop have? Look it up and write it in reports/data-size.txt:

Windows: Settings → System → About. Read “Installed RAM”. Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) → Performance shows CPU cores and disk size.
Mac: Apple menu → About This Mac. Read “Memory”. For disk size, Apple menu → System Settings → General → Storage.

Use parallel::detectCores() in the R console to find out how many cores R can see. parallel is a package that comes with R, and :: uses one function from it without loading the whole package. The answer counts logical cores, which can be twice the number printed on the box.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
section: 2. How much memory does R use?
text:
2. How much memory does R use?
Open Task Manager (Windows: Processes tab) or Activity Monitor (Mac: Memory tab) and find the R process, called rsession or R (on Windows it may sit inside RStudio’s entry). Note how much memory it uses. Then make one million random numbers in the R console with x <- rnorm(1000000) and look again: the process has grown by roughly 8 MB, because the numbers now sit in RAM. rm(x) removes the object and gc() (“garbage collection”) tidies up memory R no longer needs.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
section: 3. Objects in RAM, files on disk
text:
3. Objects in RAM, files on disk
Everything in R’s Environment pane is in RAM. It disappears when R closes or restarts. Only what you save to disk survives.
Load the seedlings with seedlings <- readr::read_csv("data/seedlings.csv") and the object appears in the Environment pane. Restart R (Session → Restart R) and the pane is empty, because the object was in RAM, while data/seedlings.csv is still in the Files pane, because it is on disk. This is why we render reports from saved files in a fresh session: a result that exists only in RAM cannot be repeated, not even by you tomorrow.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
section: 4. How many bytes is a number?
text:
4. How many bytes is a number?
A byte is 8 bits and can hold one of 256 patterns (0–255). Sizes use 1 kB = 1,000 bytes, 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes, and 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes.
One number in R takes 8 bytes. That gives a quick estimate for any table of numbers:
\[\text{RAM} \approx \text{rows} \times \text{numeric columns} \times 8 \text{ bytes}\]
For example, 1,000,000 rows × 10 columns × 8 bytes = 80,000,000 bytes = 80 MB. R also needs working space for copies and calculations, so plan for roughly 2–3 times the object: here about 160–240 MB free RAM.
Use object.size() to find out how much memory one million numbers take:
x <- rnorm(1000000)
object.size(x)
format(object.size(x), units = "MB", standard = "SI")
format(..., units = "MB", standard = "SI") converts bytes to MB with 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes. You should get 8,000,048 bytes, about 8 MB: 8 bytes per number plus a small fixed overhead.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
5. File size versus object size
A CSV stores numbers as text: one byte per character. The value 25.7, is 5 characters, so 5 bytes on disk, while the same number takes 8 bytes in R. A long value such as 23.172052685196473, takes 19 bytes as text. So a CSV can be smaller or larger than its object in R.
Use file.size("data/seedlings.csv") to find out how much disk space the seedling table takes, and object.size(seedlings) to find out how much memory it takes once loaded. The file is 592 bytes, but the object is a few thousand bytes, because for a tiny table R’s bookkeeping (column names, types, row information) is larger than the 96 measurements themselves. The 8-byte rule is for large tables, where the data dominate.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
6. A larger table
Real experiments are much bigger than 24 plants. Simulate a table of 100,000 rows and 10 numeric columns of measurements, rounded to one decimal:
set.seed(21)
n <- 100000
big <- data.frame(matrix(round(rnorm(n * 10, mean = 20, sd = 4), 1), ncol = 10))
dim(big)
head(big)
set.seed(21) makes the random numbers the same for everyone. matrix(..., ncol = 10) arranges the numbers into 10 columns, and data.frame() turns them into a table with columns X1 to X10.
Estimate with the 8-byte rule how much memory big needs, then use object.size(big) to find out whether you were right. Next, estimate how large the table will be as a CSV: most values look like 19.3, four characters plus a comma or line ending. Save it and use file.size() to check:
library(readr)
write_csv(big, "output/big-measurements.csv")
file.size("output/big-measurements.csv") / 1e6






Answer check





Estimate: 100,000 × 10 × 8 = 8,000,000 bytes = 8 MB, and R reports 8.0 MB. CSV: about 100,000 × 10 × 5 = 5,000,000 bytes; the real file is 4.79 MB because some values, such as 9.8, are only three characters. Here the CSV is smaller than the object, so a file of a given size can need more RAM than its size suggests.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
7. Text columns
Most real tables also have an identifier for each sample. Add one, a unique text value per row, and use object.size() and file.size() to find out what it costs in memory and on disk:
big$sample_id <- sprintf("S%06d", 1:n)
head(big$sample_id)
object.size(big$sample_id)
object.size(big)
write_csv(big, "output/big-measurements.csv")
file.size("output/big-measurements.csv") / 1e6
sprintf("S%06d", 1:n) writes the numbers 1 to 100,000 as text with six digits: S000001, S000002, ….
On disk each ID adds 8 characters (7 plus a comma), so expect about 0.8 MB more. In RAM every different text value is stored separately with its own bookkeeping, about 64 bytes per ID here.






Answer check





The ID column alone uses 6.4 MB in R; the whole object grows to 14.4 MB. The CSV grows only to 5.59 MB. A column of repeated labels such as treated / control is cheap (about 8 bytes per row), because R stores each different text value once. Many unique text values are expensive.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
8. DNA as text
dna <- readLines("data/dna.txt")
nchar(dna)
file.size("data/dna.txt")
bases <- strsplit(dna, split = "")[[1]]
table(bases)
readLines() reads the one line of text and nchar() counts its 40 letters, so the file is 41 bytes: 40 letters plus the line ending. strsplit() separates the letters ([[1]] takes the first result) and table() counts them: A 11, C 9, G 9, T 11. The sequence is invented teaching data.
The human genome is about 3.1 billion letters. How large is it as a text file? Then use object.size(dna) and object.size(bases) to find out what splitting the sequence into separate letters costs in R, and estimate the human genome stored that way.






Answer check





As text: 3.1 × 10⁹ bytes ≈ 3.1 GB. One string in R is 152 bytes; the 40 separate letters are 592 bytes. At 8 bytes per letter the genome would need 3.1 × 10⁹ × 8 ≈ 25 GB: more than most laptops have. Genome software therefore stores sequences compactly and reads them piece by piece.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
9. Images
A grayscale image is a table of brightness values. Our tiny teaching image has 8 × 8 pixels on a 0–255 scale (0 is black, 255 is white), so each pixel fits in one byte in an image file.
pixels <- as.matrix(read_csv("data/pixels.csv", show_col_types = FALSE))
dim(pixels)
pixels
sum(pixels > 100)
plot.new()
rasterImage(as.raster(pixels / 255), 0, 0, 1, 1)
as.matrix() turns the all-number table into a grid, sum(pixels > 100) counts the 24 bright pixels (each TRUE counts as 1), and the last two lines draw the grid as an image.
A microscope camera image is often 2048 × 2048 pixels. How large is one such image as an 8-bit file (1 byte per pixel), and as numbers in R (8 bytes per pixel)? How much RAM would 100 images from a time-lapse experiment need in R? Use R as a calculator, for example 2048 * 2048 * 8 / 1e6 for MB.






Answer check





2048 × 2048 = 4,194,304 pixels. As a file: about 4.2 MB. In R: about 33.6 MB. One hundred images in R: about 3.4 GB. A colour image has three values per pixel (red, green, blue), so three times as much.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
section: 10. Will the single-cell table fit on your laptop?
text:
10. Will the single-cell table fit on your laptop?
The table has one number per gene and cell, so 30000 * 100000 * 8 / 1e9 gives its size in GB: 24 GB before any working space, more than a 16 GB laptop has in total, and the operating system, browser and RStudio need RAM too.
When R needs more RAM than is free, one of two things happens:

The computer swaps: it moves parts of RAM to the much slower disk. Everything crawls, including the mouse and other programs.
R stops with an error such as cannot allocate vector of size …, or the R session crashes and the Environment is lost.

So estimate first, and do not try it on your laptop. If 2–3 times the estimate is close to or above your RAM, load fewer rows or columns, use a format that stores data more compactly, or use a bigger computer. Tomorrow we use a remote computer with more RAM and cores.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 21 — how a computer works, and how big is your data?
text:
Check your understanding
Complete reports/data-size.txt with:

your laptop’s RAM, cores and disk size;
each prediction and the value R gave (sections 4–9);
one sentence on whether the single-cell table fits on your laptop, and why.


You restart R. Which of these survive: the object big, the file output/big-measurements.csv, the script data-size.R (saved)?
