A CSV of 2,000,000 rows and 5 numeric columns. Roughly how much RAM does the loaded table need, and how much free RAM would you want?
Your colleague says “the CSV is only 500 MB, so it needs 500 MB of RAM”. Why might that be wrong in both directions?
Does a GPU help with today’s R work?







Short answers






The file and the saved script survive (disk). The object big is gone (RAM).
2,000,000 × 5 × 8 = 80,000,000 bytes = 80 MB; plan for about 160–240 MB free.
Short rounded numbers take fewer bytes as text than in R, so the object can be larger. Long decimals take more bytes as text, so it can be smaller. Unique text columns cost much more in RAM. Then add working space.
No. R’s ordinary calculations run on the CPU. GPUs matter for image analysis and deep learning.




Keep: data-size.R, output/big-measurements.csv, and reports/data-size.txt.
Before you finish: restart R and run data-size.R from the top. Check that your saved numbers match. Next: Day 22 — work on a remote computer.
crumbs: 21. How a computer works; data size

title: Day 22 — the same workflow on a remote computer
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 22 — the same workflow on a remote computer
text:
Why a bigger computer?
On Day 21 you estimated that a single-cell table of 30,000 genes × 100,000 cells needs about 24 GB of RAM, more than a 16 GB laptop has. Universities and research centres therefore run shared Linux computers with far more RAM and CPU cores, which you log in to over the network. The analysis is the same R and the same project; what changes is which computer runs it and where the files are.
Today’s question: you render a report on the remote computer. Where is it, and how do you get it back to your laptop?
Keep a short log, reports/remote-log.txt, of which computer and folder each file is in. Never write passwords or login codes in it.






Remote connection details are pending



HPC2N or another Linux environment will be used. The hostname, account route, authentication, remote desktop, transfer method, permitted execution location, and supported R application will be provided separately. Use those instructions for remote work. Until access is available, do the local rehearsal below and mark the connection tasks pending.

title: Day 22 — the same workflow on a remote computer
section: 1. Two computers, two sets of files
text:
1. Two computers, two sets of files
A path names a place on one particular computer. Your laptop and the remote computer each have their own disk, so a folder called course project on each of them holds two separate copies that do not update each other:
Laptop                         Remote Linux computer
course project                 course project (a separate copy)
  data/seedlings.csv              data/seedlings.csv
  report.Rmd                     report.Rmd
  report.html                    report.html
          -- supported transfer -->
          <-- supported transfer --
There are two ways in. SSH gives you a terminal on the remote computer, with the same shell commands as Day 3, and a remote desktop shows its screen in a window. Neither copies files for you. The service guide will say whether both see the same home folder.

title: Day 22 — the same workflow on a remote computer
section: 2. Which computer and folder am I in?
text:
2. Which computer and folder am I in?
Connect with the SSH command from the service guide, in Ubuntu on Windows or Terminal on Mac. Its general form is ssh your-course-username@the-provided-host, with both placeholders replaced from the guide. Then use hostname to find out which computer answered, and pwd to find out which folder you are in there:
hostname
pwd
ls
Write both answers in your log. Make a practice folder with mkdir -p introcomputing-practice, then type exit. You are back in your laptop’s shell, and pwd now shows a laptop folder. Reconnect and use ls to find out whether the practice folder is still there: it is, because it was saved on the remote disk and exit only ends the connection.

title: Day 22 — the same workflow on a remote computer
section: 3. Does R on the remote computer see the project?
text:
3. Does R on the remote computer see the project?
Transfer the course ZIP with the supported upload method, extract it, and open its .Rproj in the provided R application. Then, in the remote R console, use file.exists() to find out whether R can see the seedling data:
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")
You should get the remote project folder and TRUE. If you get FALSE, R is looking in the wrong folder: check getwd() and look for an extra folder level created during extraction, rather than typing a path from your laptop.

title: Day 22 — the same workflow on a remote computer
section: 4. Rendering remotely and getting the report back
text:
4. Rendering remotely and getting the report back
Open report.Rmd and render it in the provided R application. If R is set up in the remote shell, the teaching team may instead ask you to run this from the project root:
Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd")'
Rscript starts a fresh R process and renders the saved document, the same fresh-session idea as restarting R. The HTML now exists only on the remote disk, so download it to a folder on your laptop that you can name, and open that copy in your browser. Write the remote path, the laptop path, and the direction of the transfer in your log. If the laptop folder is empty, the render probably did not fail: find the HTML on the remote computer first, then check where the transfer put it.

title: Day 22 — the same workflow on a remote computer
section: Local rehearsal while remote access is pending
text:
Local rehearsal while remote access is pending
Copy the whole extracted course folder to a folder called introcomputing-rehearsal, open that copy’s .Rproj, and repeat sections 3 and 4 there: getwd(), file.exists(), render, and find the HTML. This checks that the project works wherever it is copied. Write “local rehearsal only” in your log, with the remote steps still to do.

title: Day 22 — the same workflow on a remote computer
section: 5. Did the algae table arrive complete?
text:
5. Did the algae table arrive complete?
data/algae.csv holds dry biomass (mg) of 24 separately grown algae cultures, 12 reference and 12 supplement; culture A19 spilled before weighing (see data/README.md). Before copying, write reports/transfer-plan.txt with the source computer and project path, the destination computer and project path, and the file you will move.
Then use nrow() and is.na() to find out whether the copy holds every culture and every available measurement. Run the same lines in the source project and in the destination project:
library(readr)
algae <- read_csv("data/algae.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(algae)
sum(!is.na(algae$biomass_mg))
algae$biomass_mg[algae$culture_id == "A19"]
Both copies should give 24 cultures, 23 measurements, and NA for A19. Write a short reports/transfer-receipt.txt in the destination copy with the date, the destination path, and these three results, then bring the receipt back to the source project with the supported transfer.

title: Day 22 — the same workflow on a remote computer
text:
6. Which copy is the latest?
You now have two files called transfer-receipt.txt. In a disposable copy, change the returned receipt to say “second revision”, save it, and reopen both copies. The other copy is unchanged, because each copy is a separate file on its own disk. Equal names, and even equal file sizes, do not mean equal contents; for small text files, open both and read them, or in R use identical(readLines("first-path"), readLines("second-path")) with your real paths.
Finish with reports/transfer-audit.txt: source, destination, the three checks, which receipt is the latest, and which remote steps are still pending.






Hint: the file exists, but R cannot find it





Check which computer R is running on, then getwd(), then the actual path beneath that folder. An extra folder created during extraction is the most common cause. Keep report paths relative to the project root.

title: Day 22 — the same workflow on a remote computer
text:
Check your understanding

Does exit delete the files you saved remotely?
You rendered remotely, but local Downloads is empty. Did the render fail?
Can R on the remote computer read your laptop’s data/ folder without a transfer?







Short answers






No. It ends the connection; saved files stay on the remote disk, subject to the service’s storage policy.
Probably not. The output is on the remote computer until you transfer it.
No. Each computer reads its own disk, so the files must be transferred.




Keep: reports/remote-log.txt, reports/transfer-plan.txt, both receipts, and reports/transfer-audit.txt.
Before you finish: mark any steps still waiting for remote access, and end the remote session as the service guide describes. Next: Day 23 — a small integrated study.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text:
Today’s question
Duckweed is a small aquatic plant that floats as tiny leaf-like fronds. In our simulated study, twenty flasks started with equal amounts of duckweed; ten were randomly given extra nutrients and ten were controls. After seven days the dry biomass in each flask was weighed. How much more biomass did the nutrient flasks produce, and how certain is that difference?
Today you answer this on your own, from the raw file to a rendered report, using what you learned in weeks 2–4. The flask is the independent unit: the fronds in one flask share its water and nutrients. One nutrient flask, F17, was spilled before weighing, so its biomass is missing. The full design is in data/README.md.
If your teacher chooses the organic-laboratory study instead, skip to The organic alternative and do that one only.
Save today: duckweed-report.Rmd and its HTML, reports/study-decisions.txt, algae-transfer.R and reports/algae-transfer.txt.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text:
A plan before the code
Before writing code, write five lines in reports/study-decisions.txt: the question, the independent unit, the outcome and its units, what you will do with the missing F17, and the direction of the comparison (nutrient minus control). These decisions shape every later step, and writing them first keeps the code and the text in agreement.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: Is the file what the design says?
text:
Is the file what the design says?
Use Save As on the root report.Rmd to create duckweed-report.Rmd, replace the title and the seedling text, and load the data:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
duckweed <- read_csv("data/duckweed.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(duckweed)
Use count(duckweed, treatment) to find out how many flasks are in each group, anyDuplicated(duckweed$flask_id) to find out whether any flask appears twice, and sum(is.na(duckweed$biomass_mg)) to find out how many flasks have no biomass. Write each result in the report as a sentence, for example “20 flasks, 10 per group, no duplicates; F17 has no biomass because it was spilled.”






Answer check





20 rows, 10 control and 10 nutrient, anyDuplicated() returns 0, and one missing biomass value (F17). The biomass values run from 19.8 to 46.2 mg.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: How much biomass is in each group?
text:
How much biomass is in each group?
Use group_by() and summarise() to find out the number of flasks with a measurement, the mean and the SD in each group. Then plot every flask:
available <- duckweed |>
  filter(!is.na(biomass_mg))
available holds the 19 flasks with a measurement, while duckweed keeps F17’s row. Make an individual-point plot of available with treatment on the x-axis and biomass_mg on the y-axis, with the label “Dry biomass after seven days (mg)”, and state in the caption that F17 is missing.






Hint and answer check





In summarise(), use n_available = sum(!is.na(biomass_mg)), mean_mg = mean(biomass_mg, na.rm = TRUE) and sd_mg = sd(biomass_mg, na.rm = TRUE). For the plot, reuse the week 3 point plot with horizontal jitter only.
Control: 10 flasks, mean 32.28 mg, SD 5.70 mg. Nutrient: 9 flasks, mean 39.63 mg, SD 4.79 mg. The groups overlap: nutrient flask F11 (31.7 mg) is below most controls, and control F08 (19.8 mg) is low but has no recorded error.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: How large is the nutrient effect?
text:
How large is the nutrient effect?
The flasks are independent and were randomly allocated, so the Welch test from day 17 fits. Use t.test() to find out the nutrient-minus-control difference and its 95% confidence interval:
nutrient <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "nutrient")
control <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "control")
comparison <- t.test(nutrient$biomass_mg, control$biomass_mg)
comparison
Nutrient comes first, so the result is nutrient minus control.






Answer check





Difference 7.35 mg (39.63 − 32.28), 95% CI 2.27 to 12.44 mg, p = 0.0072. The whole interval lies above zero, so the nutrient flasks produced more biomass on average.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text:
Writing the result
Write a paragraph with the direction and size of the difference in mg, the number of flasks in each group, the confidence interval and p-value, and one limitation, such as the missing F17 or the small size of the study. Use an inline result, for example `r round(comparison$conf.int[1], 2)`, for at least one number, so the text updates itself when the data change.
A classmate wrote this draft. Find what is wrong with it before you write yours:

“There were 20 biomass results. The nutrient plants all grew more, and the group SD is the error in the treatment effect. The p-value tells us the probability that nutrients work.”







What is wrong





There are 20 flasks but 19 measurements, because F17 is missing. The groups overlap, so only the mean is higher, not every flask. The SD describes how much single flasks vary; the uncertainty of the difference is the confidence interval. The p-value is calculated assuming no difference: it says how surprising the data would be if nutrients had no effect, not how likely it is that they work.



Save the report, restart R and render. Before you finish, check:

Can a reader find the question, the flask as the unit, and why there are 19 values?
Do the plot, the table and the text give the same numbers?
Does the sign of the difference agree with the order in t.test()?
Does the report run without anything typed in the Console first?

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text:
The organic alternative
Do this study instead of the duckweed report if your teacher selects it. Twelve synthesis runs, procedures that make a chemical product, were randomly assigned a standard or a modified collection protocol, six each. For each run, the file gives the maximum possible product mass (theoretical_mass_g) and the dry product actually collected (isolated_mass_g). Runs started at different scales, so grams cannot be compared directly, but the percentage yield can:
yield (%) = 100 × isolated mass (g) / theoretical mass (g)
Question: which protocol collected a larger percentage of the possible product? Save the report as organic-study.Rmd; if you made organic-report.Rmd on day 15, keep it and use Save As.
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
organic <- organic |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
Check Y01 by hand: 0.62 g of 1.00 g possible is 62%. Then use group_by() and summarise() to find out the mean yield and SD in each protocol, and plot every run. Each run is one independent unit; weighing a product three times would still be one run. Save a summary CSV and the plot in output/ with names starting organic-. A descriptive comparison is all this study needs: there is no test today. Write a result paragraph and render.






Answer check





Six runs per protocol, no missing values. Standard: mean 68.67%, SD 4.32 percentage points. Modified: mean 77.00%, SD 3.74. The modified protocol collected 8.33 percentage points more on average. That is a difference of percentage points, not an 8.33% relative increase. Purity was assumed, not measured, so a higher yield says nothing about how pure the product is.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text:
A new dataset: algae cultures
Can you apply the same steps to data you have not seen before? In data/algae.csv, 24 algae cultures were grown separately and randomly given a reference or a supplement treatment, twelve each, and harvested after seven days. Culture A19 was spilled before weighing. The outcome is dry biomass in mg.
Write a short script, algae-transfer.R, that imports the file and uses the same functions as above to find out:

how many cultures have a measurement in each group;
the mean and SD of biomass in each group, and the supplement-minus-reference difference;
whether every supplement culture produced more than every reference culture (make an individual-point plot).

Save the summary and plot in output/ with names starting algae-transfer, and write a short result paragraph in reports/algae-transfer.txt. Restart R and run the script from the top. Day 24 will turn it into a report that someone else can reproduce.






Answer check





24 unique cultures; 12 reference and 11 supplement measurements, with A19 kept as NA. Reference: mean 28.20 mg, SD 7.26 mg. Supplement: mean 33.92 mg, SD 3.37 mg. Supplement minus reference: +5.72 mg. Not every supplement culture is higher: the largest single value, 41.7 mg, is reference culture A11. Putting 0 for A19 would wrongly lower the supplement mean to 31.09 mg.



Leave with: duckweed-report.Rmd (or organic-study.Rmd) and its HTML, reports/study-decisions.txt, algae-transfer.R, and reports/algae-transfer.txt. Note anything that failed.
Next: Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report.

title: Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report
section: Can someone else get the same report?
text:
Can someone else get the same report?
Your supervisor, a lab partner, or you next year should be able to open your project and get exactly the same report. Today you find out whether that works: you render the report from a fresh R session, pack the project into a ZIP, and open it as the receiver would, in a new place.
Use the report from day 23. The examples use the duckweed study (duckweed-report.Rmd and data/duckweed.csv; design in data/README.md): 20 flasks, 10 per group, with F17 spilled before weighing. For the organic alternative, substitute organic-study.Rmd and data/organic-recovery.csv throughout.
Save today: the corrected report and its HTML, a tested report-share-v2.zip, algae-brief.Rmd with its HTML, and reports/reproduction-log.txt, where you note what you tested and what you found.

title: Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report
section: Does the report tell a reader what they need?
text:
Does the report tell a reader what they need?
Read your report as someone who was not in the room, and use it to find out whether the nutrient flasks grew more. A reader should be able to find the question, that each flask is one independent unit, why there are 9 nutrient values and not 10 (F17), the units, which group is subtracted from which, and your conclusion. They should also be able to tell SD (spread among flasks) from the confidence interval (uncertainty in the difference). The numbers to expect: 10 control flasks with mean biomass 32.28 mg and 9 nutrient flasks with 39.63 mg.
Replace any leftover notes such as “insert result here” with your interpretation.

title: Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report
section: Does it render from a fresh R session?
text:
Does it render from a fresh R session?
Save the .Rmd, choose Session → Restart R, and click Knit without running anything in the Console first. Restarting empties R’s memory, so the report must now import, calculate and plot everything itself, just as it will on someone else’s computer. If rendering stops, read the first error and the chunk it names, and fix one thing at a time:








Error
Usual cause
Repair




object 'duckweed' not found
The import was only run in the Console
Put the import in a chunk before it is used


could not find function
A package was only loaded in the Console
Add its library() call to the setup chunk


cannot open file
A personal path such as C:/Users/…, or a missing file
Use data/duckweed.csv and keep that file in the project


Old text disagrees with new numbers
A result was typed by hand
Check the sentence, or use an inline result

title: Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report
section: Packing the project as a ZIP
text:
Packing the project as a ZIP
A ZIP is one file that holds a whole folder, which makes it the simplest way to hand a project to someone or to submit it. First make the folder complete, then pack it.
Use the file manager to create report-share outside your working project, for example in Documents, and copy in:
report-share/
├── introcomputing.Rproj
├── duckweed-report.Rmd
├── duckweed-report.html
├── README.txt
├── data/
│   ├── duckweed.csv
│   └── README.md
└── output/
    └── README.txt
The .Rmd and the CSV are the analysis; the HTML lets someone read the result without R; data/README.md describes the study. Include output/ if your report saves a figure there. In README.txt, write that the data are simulated, which file to render, the packages it needs (readr, dplyr, ggplot2, rmarkdown, knitr), and what one row of the CSV is.
Then, in a shell, go to the folder that contains report-share and pack it:
zip -r report-share-v1.zip report-share/
unzip -l report-share-v1.zip
-r packs the folder with everything inside it, and unzip -l lists what went in: check that the .Rmd, data/duckweed.csv and the README are there. The ZIP is saved beside report-share, not inside it; a ZIP inside the folder it packs would pack an old copy of itself next time. Give every new ZIP a new name (-v1, -v2): re-running zip on an existing name updates it and can keep files you have since deleted.






Hint: Windows with Ubuntu





Copy report-share into your Ubuntu workspace with File Explorer before running zip. The Windows and Ubuntu copies are separate and do not update each other, so after any edit in Windows, copy again before zipping. Copy the finished ZIP back to a normal Windows folder before the receiver test below, because RStudio runs in Windows.

title: Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report
section: Does it work in a new location?
text:
Does it work in a new location?
Listing the ZIP shows names, not whether the report works. Extract it into a new, empty folder, as the receiver would, and use it to find out whether the report comes out the same:
unzip report-share-v1.zip -d receiver-v1
ls receiver-v1
ls shows only report-share: extraction keeps the packed folder, so it adds one level, and the report is at receiver-v1/report-share/duckweed-report.Rmd. Open receiver-v1/report-share/introcomputing.Rproj (the project name in RStudio’s corner tells you which copy you are in), restart R and Knit.
You should see the same counts (10 and 9 flasks), the same means (32.28 and 39.63 mg) and the same conclusion. Point positions in a jittered plot may shift slightly between computers. If numbers differ, record sessionInfo() in your log: it lists the R and package versions.






Hint: the project opens, but the data are missing





Look at the actual extracted folder tree. The .Rproj file does not contain any data, and a shortcut to your original data folder does not travel with the ZIP. Copy the CSV itself into report-share/data/ and pack again under a new name.

title: Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report
section: Correcting a ZIP you already made
text:
Correcting a ZIP you already made
Your receiver test will probably show something to improve, such as a unit missing from the README. A ZIP is a snapshot of the folder at the moment you made it, so use this correction to find out what happens to the copies you already have.

Edit README.txt in your ordinary report-share folder, for example by adding “Biomass is dry mass in mg per flask.”
Open receiver-v1/report-share/README.txt. It still has the old text, and so does report-share-v1.zip.
Pack again as report-share-v2.zip, extract it to receiver-v2, and check that the new sentence is really there. Add one line to the README saying what changed in v2.

A ZIP on the same laptop as the original is a way of sharing, not a backup: if the laptop is lost, both are gone. Put a copy of the finished project on the supported separate storage as well, and write in your log where it is.

title: Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report
section: What does a successful render tell you?
text:
What does a successful render tell you?
Use two disposable copies of report-share to find out which mistakes stop a report and which do not.

In the first copy, rename data/duckweed.csv to duckweed-missing.csv, restart R and Knit. Rendering stops with an error naming the file, because the report can no longer find its input. Restore the name and check that the means are back to 32.28 and 39.63 mg.
In the second copy, replace your sentence about F17 with “All 20 flasks had a measured biomass.” and Knit. The report renders without complaint, although the sentence contradicts the data: only 19 flasks were weighed. (Organic route: “The percentage yield shows that the product is pure.”)

R can tell you that a file is missing, but not that a sentence is wrong. A report that renders still needs a reader who checks its claims against the numbers. Note both cases in your log, and delete the disposable copies so the false sentence cannot end up in what you share.

title: Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report
section: A second report: the algae memo
text:
A second report: the algae memo
On day 23 you analysed data/algae.csv in algae-transfer.R: 24 cultures, 12 per group, with A19’s biomass missing. Turn it into a small report and use the same steps to find out whether it reproduces.

Create algae-brief.Rmd at the project root with a short question, the import, the group summary, one plot of individual cultures, and a sentence on the missing A19. Use inline R for the counts, so they come from the data.
Restart R and Knit. You should see 12 reference cultures with mean 28.20 mg and 11 supplement cultures with mean 33.92 mg.
Pack algae-share (the .Rproj, algae-brief.Rmd, its HTML, data/algae.csv, data/README.md and a README) as algae-share-v1.zip, extract it into a new folder, and Knit there. The counts and means should match step 2. If they do not, compare the input and code before suspecting rounding: 33.91818 and 33.92 are the same mean, 34.32 would be a different one.

title: Day 24 — Reproduce and share your report
text:
Check your understanding






Why can a report work after “Run All” but fail for someone else?





It may use objects created only in the Console, a personal file path, or files that are not in the ZIP. Restarting R and rendering in a new folder finds these.









You fixed the README after making report-share-v1.zip. Does v1 contain the fix?





No. A ZIP is a snapshot. Make a newly named ZIP, extract it into a new folder, and check the fix there.









Is a ZIP on the same disk a backup?





No. If the disk is lost, the ZIP is lost with it. Keep a copy on separate supported storage.









The report renders in a fresh folder. Is its conclusion therefore correct?





It shows that the saved source and data make the same report on this computer. Whether the design and conclusion are sound is a separate question for the reader.



Next: consolidation and error recovery.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
text: Lecture slides · Quiz · Weekly revision

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
text:
Today’s question
In a later lab course or thesis project, someone will hand you a data file and ask what it shows. Can you find the files, check them, make a figure, explain the result and produce a report that someone else can render, without the course telling you each step? Today you practise exactly that on familiar data, using the reference pages whenever you need them.
Start with the station where you feel least sure. Over the day, do stations 1–3, then the A11 investigation and the handover.
Save today: recovery.R, reports/final-investigation.txt, a tested handover package, reports/next-lab.txt and reports/readiness-review.txt.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Station 1: finding and inspecting lab files
text:
Station 1: finding and inspecting lab files
Download a fresh copy of lab-data.zip. In your shell, list the archive, extract it into a new folder and read its README. Then use grep -F treated on the sample manifest, piped into wc -l, to find out how many samples were treated; predict the number before you run it. Save the matching lines as treated-samples.txt, and finally pack the extracted folder into a new ZIP placed outside it.






Hint and answer check





The commands from days 3–4 are enough: pwd, ls, cd, unzip -l, unzip … -d …, less, grep -F, wc -l and zip -r; see the terminal reference. The manifest has two treated records; the header line does not match. > writes only to treated-samples.txt; the manifest itself is unchanged.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
text:
Station 2: repairing a broken analysis
This code is meant to calculate the mean growth of the seedlings, but it contains several errors:
seedling <- read_csv("seedlings.csv")
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm + initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$Growth_mm)
Write a working version in recovery.R in your project root. Use P01 to find out whether your repaired growth calculation is right: it started at 25.7 mm and ended at 44.3 mm. Then save a labelled plot of growth by treatment.






A working repair





library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- seedlings |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$growth_mm)
P01 grew 18.6 mm. The original had no library() calls, a path without data/, two different object names (seedling and seedlings), addition instead of subtraction, and Growth_mm with a capital G, which R treats as a different name. The fourth error is the dangerous one: code that adds instead of subtracts runs without any error message, which is why checking one row by hand matters.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
text:
Station 3: explaining results
Answer each question in one or two sentences, then compare with the answers.

One treated plant has 100 cells measured, and so does one control plant. Are there 100 replicates per group?
Two groups have the same mean, but one has twice the SD. What do their observations look like?
A missing biomass value is replaced by zero. What happens to the group mean?
A treatment-minus-control estimate is 3 mm with a 95% interval from −2 to 8 mm. Does this show that the treatment has no effect?
An unknown sample reads a higher absorbance than the highest calibration standard. What should happen before its concentration is reported?
Leaf mass rises with leaf area. Would enlarging a leaf add the same mass?







Answers






No. There is one treated and one control plant; the cells inside a plant share its treatment, so they are not independent replicates.
The values in the second group are spread much more widely around the same centre.
The mean drops, because zero is an invented, very low value. Leave it as NA and report one fewer measurement.
No. The interval includes zero but also effects in both directions up to 8 mm, so the study cannot tell. Report it as inconclusive.
Flag it as above the range; dilute the sample and measure it again.
Not necessarily. Area was measured, not changed, and older or better-lit plants may have both larger and heavier leaves.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
text:
Station 5: the remote computer
If remote access works, repeat day 22: log in, find out which computer and folder you are in, locate a supplied file, disconnect, reconnect and find it again, then copy one output to your laptop. If access is still pending, note it in your readiness review as a skill still to practise.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
text:
Is A11 a mistake?
In the algae data from days 23–24, reference culture A11 has the largest biomass of all, 41.7 mg. A high value like this is tempting to remove. Find out whether there is a reason to remove it, and how much it changes the result. Record each step in reports/final-investigation.txt.

Without using “recent files”, find your project, algae-transfer.R, algae-brief.Rmd, data/algae.csv and the HTML, and write their paths.
Read the algae section of data/README.md. It records that A19 was spilled, and says nothing wrong about A11, so A11 belongs in the primary result.
Use your summary code on all available measurements to find out the supplement-minus-reference difference. Label it “primary, all available measurements”.
Make a separate object without A11 and repeat the calculation to find out how much this one culture moves the difference:

algae_without_a11 <- filter(algae, culture_id != "A11")

In a copy of algae-brief.Rmd, add a limitations paragraph that separates three things: A19 is missing, A11 is high but recorded, and the study is small and simulated. Render it and check that the main figure and numbers still use all available measurements.







Answer check





Primary: reference 28.20 mg (12 cultures), supplement 33.92 mg (11), difference 5.72 mg. Without A11: reference 26.97 mg (11 cultures), difference 6.95 mg. The supplement mean does not change, because A11 is a reference culture. Report the primary result; if you show the second one, label it “A11 omitted without evidence of error”.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Can someone else follow your instructions?
text:
Can someone else follow your instructions?
Write a short README.txt for your report: the question, where the raw data are, what one row means, what blank cells mean, which file to render and what the result should look like. For the organic study, include the yield formula.
Then test it. Pack the project, extract it into a new folder, and follow only your README: open the .Rproj, restart R, render, and find the main result and a limitation in the HTML. If something is unclear, fix the README or the report, make a new, clearly named package and test that one too. A copy you edited in one place, for example on Windows, does not update a copy already packed or moved elsewhere; use the version checks from day 22.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: What will you take to your next lab?
text:
What will you take to your next lab?
Save reports/next-lab.txt with your own workflow for a new dataset: where raw data go, how to open the project, which checks to make, how to choose a figure, and how to render and back up the report. Add the questions you would ask a lab teacher first, such as “What was randomly assigned?” and “What do blank cells mean?”
Finally, save reports/readiness-review.txt: three things you can now do reliably, two that need more practice, and one concrete practice task for each of those two. List remote login and file transfer as pending if you have not used the real service.
Leave with: recovery.R, reports/final-investigation.txt with the primary and A11-omitted results, a tested handover package, reports/next-lab.txt and reports/readiness-review.txt. Keep the reference pages and your project for later lab courses.

title: Why biologists need computing
Why biologists need computing
text:
Spreadsheets change your data



Type the gene symbol SEPT2 into Excel and it becomes the date 2 September. MARCH1 becomes 1 March.
This happened in published papers: about one in five papers with Excel gene lists had damaged names (Ziemann et al., 2016).
In 2020 the gene-naming committee gave up and renamed the genes (SEPT2 → SEPTIN2, MARCH1 → MARCHF1).





A spreadsheet converts the gene symbols SEPT2, MARCH1 and DEC1 into dates, while TP53 is unchanged.




This is a real and well-documented problem: Zeeberg et al. first described it in 2004, Ziemann, Eren and El-Osta quantified it in Genome Biology in 2016, and a follow-up in 2021 found it had not improved. The point is not that Excel is evil, but that a spreadsheet silently guesses what you meant, and the guess is stored instead of your data. A plain-text file read by R stores exactly what is in it.

title: Why biologists need computing
section: Spreadsheets lose data without telling you
text:
Spreadsheets lose data without telling you



In October 2020, England’s public health agency left out nearly 16,000 positive COVID-19 tests from its daily reports.
Lab results were collected in an old .xls spreadsheet format, which holds at most 65,536 rows. Everything after that row was dropped.
No error message. Contact tracing of those people was delayed.





Lab CSV files are loaded into an .xls template; rows beyond row 65,536 are dropped without an error.




Widely reported at the time (Public Health England, 25 September to 2 October 2020). The lesson for us: a tool that quietly truncates, rounds, or reformats is dangerous precisely because it does not complain. In this course we always check counts after loading data: how many rows did we expect, how many do we have?

title: Why biologists need computing
text:
Biological data are getting big

Bar chart on a log scale: 24 seedlings and a plate-reader run fit in a spreadsheet; a single-cell experiment, a microscopy image, a sequencing run and the human genome exceed the old .xls and the .xlsx row limits.
A modern spreadsheet stops at about 1 million rows. One sequencing run gives around a billion reads; one microscope image has millions of pixels.
These data need code, and sometimes a bigger computer than your laptop. Week 5 shows how to estimate when.


Each step on the x-axis is a factor of ten. Our seedling table is tiny on purpose so we can see every value. But the same skills — a table in a plain-text file, read by code, checked, plotted, summarised — are what scale to the data students will meet in genetics, microbiology, imaging and their thesis. The sizes are rough orders of magnitude.

title: Why biologists need computing
section: Clicks leave no record; code does
text:
Clicks leave no record; code does

Raw data flow through code, checks and results into a report; changing anything and re-running updates every number and figure.
A supervisor asks: “how did you get this number?” With clicks, you cannot show it. With code, the answer is the code.
Fix one wrong value in the raw data, re-run, and every figure and table updates.


This is the course’s central habit: the raw data stay untouched, every step from raw file to report is written down as code, and the report is rebuilt from scratch to prove it still works. Students will render their first report in week 2 and test that someone else can re-run it in week 5.

title: Why biologists need computing
text:
The five weeks








Week
Question
You will




1 Files and the terminal
What is in our data files, and where are they?
Tell plain text from Word/Excel files, use paths and a terminal, meet R


2 R and reports
How much did the seedlings grow?
Import a table, calculate, plot, and render an R Markdown report


3 Variation
How much do individual plants differ?
Check data quality, summarise groups, understand SD and replicates


4 Comparisons and lines
Did the treatment work? How do two measurements relate?
Estimate a difference with uncertainty, analyse pairs, fit a line


5 Bigger data and reproducibility
Can someone else repeat our analysis?
Estimate data size, use a remote computer, run a small study, reproduce it




Keep this brief; the sidebar on the course website follows the same structure. Point out that week 1 starts with files rather than R because every later step begins with finding and reading a file correctly.

title: Why biologists need computing
text:
Summary

Spreadsheets silently change data (gene names into dates) and lose it (the COVID row limit).
Biological data are growing far beyond what a spreadsheet can hold.
Code keeps a complete, re-runnable record from raw data to report.
This course teaches that workflow from the very first file.

Before Day 1: install the software via the Getting started pages and download the course files.
Next (Day 1, kinds of files): plain text versus Word and Excel files, and why it matters for your data.

If installation is not finished, that is fine; Day 1 starts in the file manager and a text editor. Encourage students to bring installation problems to the first session rather than struggling alone.

title: Folders and paths
Folders and paths
text:
A project is a tree



The course project folder contains data, output and reports; seedlings.csv is inside data and notes.txt inside reports.



data and reports are neighbours; their parent is the project folder.
The project folder is where every route in this project starts.


Open the project in the file manager and walk the tree. Project root means the starting folder of this project, not the top of the whole disk. Turn on View, Show Path Bar in Finder; show the address bar in File Explorer.

title: Folders and paths
section: A path names each folder on the route
text:
A path names each folder on the route



The path /home/anna/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv drawn as a chain of folders from the top of the disk to the file.


Windows writes the same idea as C:\Users\anna\Documents\...\data\seedlings.csv.

Read the path left to right, opening one folder per part. Show a real path: Windows “Copy as path”, Mac right-click with Option, “Copy as Pathname”. Paste it into a text editor. Usernames will differ from anna.

title: Folders and paths
text:
Absolute and relative paths


Absolute: from the top of the disk.
/Users/anna/Documents/
  introcomputing-course/
  data/seedlings.csv
Relative: from an agreed folder, here the project folder.
data/seedlings.csv




The same relative path works from the project folder but points to a missing folder from inside reports.



The folder a program starts from is its working directory.

From inside reports, data/seedlings.csv asks for reports/data/seedlings.csv, which does not exist. The file did not move; the starting point changed. Tomorrow pwd prints the terminal’s working directory.

title: Folders and paths
text:
Going up to the parent



The route from reports to data first goes up to the project folder, then down into data.


From reports, data is a neighbour: go up to the parent, then down.

Trace it with the file manager: open reports, go up, enter data. In the terminal tomorrow, “up one level” is written as two dots, so the relative path from reports is ../data/seedlings.csv. Mention the notation but do not drill it today.

title: Folders and paths
section: Relative paths work on every computer
text:
Relative paths work on every computer



Anna’s and Ben’s absolute paths differ by username, but from the project folder both use data/seedlings.csv.


That is why our R code will say data/seedlings.csv.

Ask: if you email your R code with an absolute path to a classmate, what happens? It fails, because their username differs. The relative path assumes only that the project folder is intact and that R starts in it.

title: Folders and paths
section: Moving a folder changes the path
text:
Moving a folder changes the path



Moving map-a into map-b changes the path to note.txt from practice/map-a/note.txt to practice/map-b/map-a/note.txt; the contents stay the same.


Any route written before the move must be updated.

This is the independent task: students create map-a and map-b in practice, write routes, predict, move, and correct. Copying would leave the old route valid and create a second file.

title: Folders and paths
text:
Saved work is on disk



Before closing, the edited note is in working memory; after closing, only the saved note on disk remains.


Unsaved text is in memory and disappears when the program closes. Saved work stays on disk.

Demonstrate on a practice copy: add a sentence, save, close, reopen; then add one, close with Don’t save, reopen. Some editors autosave or restore drafts; what counts is the saved file. Hardware details come later in the course.

title: Folders and paths
text:
Different computers, different folders



Laptop storage, local Ubuntu storage on Windows, and a remote Linux home folder are separate places.


A path is a place on one computer. A file is elsewhere only after you copy it there.

Windows students will have a separate Ubuntu home folder for the terminal exercises. Later a remote Linux computer has its own folders. A cloud folder may synchronise; a remote desktop does not. A second copy on the same laptop is not a backup.

title: Folders and paths
text:
Check yourself

From the project folder, what is the path to yesterday’s note?
From inside reports, what does data/seedlings.csv point to?
Why does C:\Users\anna\... fail on Ben’s laptop?
You close the editor without saving. What is in the file?


Answers: 1 reports/day01-notes.txt; 2 a data folder inside reports, which does not exist; 3 his username and folders differ; 4 the last saved version.

title: Folders and paths
text:
Summary

A project is a tree; the project folder is the starting point.
A path lists the folders on the route to a file.
Absolute paths start at the top of the disk; relative paths start at the working directory.
Relative paths inside a project work on every computer.
Moving a folder changes the path, not the file. Saved work is on disk.

Next (Day 3, the terminal): the same folders, navigated by typing commands.
Now: open the Day 2 exercises. Leave with reports/day02-map.txt and the practice folder.

Students who cannot find yesterday’s files or explain a relative path need help before the terminal day.

title: Unzip and inspect laboratory data
Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
What is in the archive?


unzip -l lab-data.zip
unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data
cd lab-data
less README.txt

-l lists without unpacking.
-d lab-data names the folder to unpack into.
The ZIP stays as it was. Press q to leave less.





Extracting lab-data.zip creates a folder of ordinary files: README, the samples.tsv manifest, four measurement files and field notes, while the archive itself stays.




First copy the browser download into ~/introcomputing-shell with the file manager (explorer.exe . on Ubuntu/Windows, open . on Mac); Downloads is not the terminal’s workspace. Read the README aloud: four pots, lengths in mm after seven days. If unzip asks to replace files, answer n and extract to a fresh folder name.

title: Unzip and inspect laboratory data
section: The manifest links samples to files
text:
The manifest links samples to files


head -n 3 samples.tsv
wc -l samples.tsv

One header line names the columns: sample_id, treatment, file.
wc -l prints 5: header + 4 samples.
Columns are separated by tabs (TSV).





The manifest has one header line and four sample lines, each pointing to a measurement file.




Ask before running wc -l: how many lines? Students often say 4. The header is not a sample. A CSV is the same idea with commas.

title: Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
Which samples were treated?



grep prints only the lines that contain treated: S03 and S04.


grep -F treated samples.tsv
grep prints the lines that contain the text. -F means plain text, not a pattern. Answer: S03 and S04.

The header and the control lines are not printed. Point out that grep does not know about columns; it just looks for the letters t-r-e-a-t-e-d anywhere on the line. We test that limit in two slides.

title: Unzip and inspect laboratory data
section: Count with a pipe, save with >
text:
Count with a pipe, save with >


grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt

| passes grep’s lines to wc -l: 2.
> writes them into a new file. The manifest is unchanged.
> replaces what was in the file. Never write to the input: > samples.tsv can empty it.





Four sample lines go into grep, two matching lines come out, and wc -l counts 2.




Open treated-samples.txt with less: two lines and no header. Ask which file changed (only the new one). Do not demonstrate input = output on real files; just explain the danger.

title: Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
grep matches text, not meaning



In a copy where S01 is labelled untreated, grep -F treated selects S01 as well as S03 and S04.


If S01 were labelled untreated, the count would be 3: untreated contains treated. Look at the lines selected, not only at the number.

Students make this trap file themselves in the exercises, on a copy (search-trap.tsv). The real manifest still gives 2. This is the main reason to print the lines before counting.

title: Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
Are the treated seedlings longer?


head measurements/S03.csv
head measurements/S01.csv



Sample
Group
Length (mm)




S01
control
32.1


S02
control
35.2


S03
treated
42.4


S04
treated
39.8



Both treated pots are longer. Two pots per group is a hint, not yet a result.




Lengths of the four seedlings after seven days: controls S01 32.1 and S02 35.2 mm, treated S03 42.4 and S04 39.8 mm.




The file column of the manifest gives each path. Units come from the README, not from the file. With so few pots we cannot conclude much; the 24-plant dataset in week 2 and the comparisons in week 4 address the question properly.

title: Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
Work on a copy



cp makes a second file in working/, mv renames that copy, and the original samples.tsv is untouched.


mkdir working
cp samples.tsv working/samples-copy.tsv
mv working/samples-copy.tsv working/manifest-practice.tsv
cp copies, mv renames or moves. Both silently replace an existing file with the same name.

Ask which files exist after each line. The original stays; only the copy is renamed. Students then write working/observations.txt with today’s answers.

title: Unzip and inspect laboratory data
section: When a listed file is missing
text:
When a listed file is missing



The manifest lists measurements/S04.csv, but the folder has S04-renamed.csv.
head measurements/S04.csv fails: No such file or directory.
Look inside: it contains S04,39.8. Now you know it is S04 and can restore the name with mv.
If the contents did not tell you, ask the lab group rather than guess.





The manifest expects measurements/S04.csv while the folder holds S04-renamed.csv, whose contents still say S04 and 39.8.




In the exercise students rename the file themselves in a copied folder (received-check), so they know the cause. The point: a manifest says what should be there; check that the files really are.

title: Unzip and inspect laboratory data
text:
Summary

unzip -l to look, unzip -d to unpack into a named folder.
The manifest has 5 lines: a header and 4 samples.
grep -F picks lines by text: 2 treated, S03 and S04. Check the lines, not just the count.
| passes output on; > saves it and replaces the destination.
Work on copies; the original data stay untouched.

Next (Day 5, meet R): open the course project in RStudio and run a first calculation and plot.
Now: open the Day 4 exercises. Leave with treated-samples.txt, working/manifest-practice.tsv and working/observations.txt.

An optional exercise repeats the same commands on an organic-laboratory inventory (which samples are labelled ester? O02 and O03). Make sure everyone can find their extracted lab-data folder before leaving.

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
text:
Why write the steps down?



A spreadsheet shows results but not how they were made; a script lists every step and can be run again.



In a spreadsheet you see the answers, not which cells were typed, sorted or pasted.
A script is a text file of instructions. Anyone can read it and run it again, and get the same result.


Many published analyses cannot be repeated because they were done by clicking. Nobody, including the author, can say exactly which steps were taken. The script is the record. This is not “spreadsheets are bad”; they are fine for looking at data.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
text:
R as a calculator


In the Console, after the > prompt:
37 - 20
37 / 20

[1] 17 and [1] 1.85. [1] just numbers the first value printed.
17 mm is the growth. 1.85 is a ratio with no unit: the plant ended 1.85 times as long.
Both calculations are correct. Pick the one that answers your question.





The plant is 20 mm initially and 37 mm finally; the growth is 17 mm.




Ask students to predict both results before running. A calculation can be right and still answer the wrong biological question. Ratios of two lengths in the same unit have no unit.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
text:
Give a result a name


# Lengths in millimetres
initial_mm <- 20
final_mm <- 37
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm

Read <- as “store this under this name”.
The name now appears in the Environment pane.
# starts a comment for people; R ignores it.
Capitals matter: Growth_mm is a different name.





A calculation is stored in a named object in memory, while the script on disk holds the instructions.




Write this in a new script, File → New File → R Script, saved as day06.R in the project folder. Run each line with Run (Ctrl+Enter / Cmd+Enter). Putting the unit in the name (_mm) is a habit that prevents mistakes later.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: A stored result does not update itself
text:
A stored result does not update itself


final_mm <- 39
growth_mm      # still 17
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm      # now 19

A name holds a value, not a live formula as in a spreadsheet cell.
Change an input, then rerun the lines that use it.
Safest: run the whole script from the top.





After the final length changes, the stored growth stays 17 until the subtraction is run again.




Ask for a prediction before printing growth_mm the first time. This is the most common source of “but I changed it!” confusion in the first weeks.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Saved script versus objects in memory
text:
Saved script versus objects in memory

Saving the script writes instructions to disk. It does not run them.
Running a line creates objects in memory. It does not save the script.
Restart R (Session → Restart R): the objects are gone, the saved script is not.
So after reopening, run the script from the top. Everything it needs must be in it.

Test it today: save day06.R, restart R, run all lines. Does growth_mm come back?

This is the same disk versus memory distinction from week 1. Unsaved editor changes may be recoverable, but do not rely on it. A script that works only after some unrecorded Console typing is not a complete record.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
text:
Several plants in one name


initial_mm <- c(20, 22, 19)
final_mm <- c(37, 40, 34)
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm

c() combines values into a vector.
R subtracts position by position: 17, 18, 15 mm.
This is right only if both vectors list the same plants in the same order.





Three plants each have an initial and a final length, giving three growth values.




Work through the second plant: 40 − 22 = 18. R does not know which plant is which; it only matches positions.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
text:
Summarise and compare


mean(growth_mm)
length(growth_mm)
growth_mm > 16
plant_id <- c("P01", "P02", "P03")


mean() gives 16.67 mm; length() gives 3 plants.
growth_mm > 16 gives TRUE TRUE FALSE: yes/no answers, not new measurements.
Text goes in quotes. "20" is text, 20 is a number.
mean(plant_id) makes no sense: IDs are labels, not measurements.


A function is a name followed by brackets: mean(...). Run ?mean to open its help page.

Read the help’s Description and Examples, not every option. Plant IDs contain digits but are still labels; storing them as text keeps R from treating them as numbers.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Wrong order, wrong answer, no warning
text:
Wrong order, wrong answer, no warning


final_wrong <- c(34, 37, 40)
final_wrong - initial_mm

Gives 14, 15, 21 instead of 17, 18, 15.
Same values, same length, so R raises no error.
Only you know which plant each position belongs to. Keep the order matched.





Reordering one vector changes which initial and final lengths are paired.




Equal lengths are necessary but do not prove matching plants. From Day 7 we keep both lengths in the same row of a table, which protects the pairing.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: Convert the values, not only the label
text:
Convert the values, not only the label


growth_cm <- growth_mm / 10
mean(growth_mm)   # 16.67
mean(growth_cm)   # 1.667

Dividing by 10 converts mm to cm. Store it under a new name ending _cm.
Renaming an object or an axis to “cm” without dividing would be wrong by a factor of 10.





A growth of 18.6 mm relabelled as cm is wrong; converted it becomes 1.86 cm.




Keep the original values. A changed label does not change the numbers. The figure uses plant P01 from the course data (18.6 mm).
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
section: The same habit for a lab calculation
text:
The same habit for a lab calculation


mass_g <- 0.2922
molar_mass_g_mol <- 58.44
volume_l <- 100 / 1000
amount_mol <- mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol
1000 * amount_mol / volume_l   # 50 mmol/L

Every input has a name with its unit.
Each step can be checked on its own.





Mass divided by molar mass gives amount; amount divided by volume gives concentration, 50 mmol/L.



Doubling the mass gives 100 mmol/L; doubling the volume gives 25 mmol/L.

A mole is a unit of chemical amount; molar mass is grams per mole. All values are supplied; no chemistry background is needed. The alternative ratio exercise is a product yield: 100 × 0.62 g / 1.00 g = 62%.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
text:
When something goes wrong

object 'growth_mm' not found: check the spelling and capitals, then run the line that creates it.
A + prompt instead of >: R is waiting for the rest of a line. Check quotes and brackets, or press Esc.
An old result: did you rerun the lines after changing an input?
Lost track? Restart R and run the script from the top.


Teach checking the dependency (which line creates this object?) instead of running random lines until the error goes away.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Let R keep track of the calculation
text:
Summary

A script is a saved list of instructions; it can be read and run again.
<- stores a value under a name. The value does not update itself when inputs change.
c() makes a vector; R calculates position by position, so the order must match.
Units belong in names and comments; converting means changing the values.
Restart R and run the script from the top to check it is complete.

Next (Day 7, import): read a whole table of measurements from a file instead of typing values.
Now: open the Day 6 exercises. Leave with day06.R: the four-plant example with comments about units, which runs from the top after a restart.

The exercises extend to a fourth plant (21 to 39 mm) and offer a ratio or product-yield choice, then a stale-value and concentration exercise in day06-extended.R.

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Growth is a new column, not an edit
text:
Growth is a new column, not an edit


library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings,
  growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

P01: 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm. P02: 8.0 mm.
The CSV on disk is unchanged; the table in R gains a fifth column.





A growth column is calculated from each plant’s final and initial lengths, keeping the original columns.




Save in day08.R. mutate() looks for final_mm and initial_mm inside the table and returns a new table, which we assign back to seedlings. Ask students to check P02 by hand. Growth is change; final_mm is size: a plant can start large and grow little. A negative growth would deserve checking, not deletion.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
text:
Which plants? Which columns?


control_plants <- filter(seedlings,
  treatment == "control")
growth_table <- select(seedlings,
  plant_id, treatment, growth_mm)

filter() keeps rows (plants): control_plants has 12 rows.
select() keeps columns (variables): growth_table is 24 × 3.
== asks “is it equal?”; <- stores. Do not mix them up.





Treated rows are kept by filtering, then only the ID and growth columns are kept by selecting.




Predict the row and column counts before running each line. Quotes mark the text label “control”; it must match the spelling in the data exactly.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Read the steps from left to right
text:
Read the steps from left to right


longer_control <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "control") |>
  filter(growth_mm > 15)
nrow(longer_control)   # 7

|> (the pipe) passes the table on to the next step.
Read it as: take seedlings, then keep controls, then keep growth above 15 mm.
7 of the 12 control plants grew more than 15 mm.





Filtering keeps whole rows; selecting keeps whole columns.




The pipe is a convenience for writing steps in order; it does not change what they do. When something goes wrong, run the chain one step at a time.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: A plot maps columns to positions
text:
A plot maps columns to positions


size_plot <- ggplot(seedlings,
    aes(x = initial_mm, y = final_mm,
        colour = treatment)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Initial seedling length (mm)",
       y = "Final seedling length (mm)",
       colour = "Treatment") +
  theme_minimal()
size_plot




Final against initial length for the 24 seedlings, coloured by treatment.



aes() says which column goes where. Each point is one plant. + adds a layer; labs() gives axis names with units.

Read the axes before the pattern. Colour shows a group label, not a measurement. This plot is about final size; it does not show growth directly, and it cannot show that starting longer causes ending longer.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Pick the plot that answers your question
text:
Pick the plot that answers your question



Same plants, same x-axis, different y-axis.
Left: final length. Plants that started long tended to end long.
Right: growth. Here, plants that started long tended to grow less.
“Bigger at the end” is not “grew more”. Read the y-axis label before you interpret.





For the transfer study, initial length against final length (left) and against growth (right).




These panels use the 18-plant transfer study, which students work with in the exercises. The question decides the plot: for a treatment effect on growth, growth belongs on the y-axis.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
text:
Show every plant’s growth


growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings,
    aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(
    width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 8)) +
  labs(x = "Treatment",
       y = "Change in seedling length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot

Jitter spreads points sideways so they don’t hide each other. height = 0: no value moves up or down.





Growth of each seedling by treatment; the two groups overlap.




Ask: what is one dot? (one plant). What does higher mean? (more growth, mm). Do the groups overlap? (yes: control 8.0 to 18.7 mm, treated 12.2 to 30.8 mm). Treated values tend to be higher; whether that is more than chance is a question for week 4. seed = 8 makes the sideways spread the same every time.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Jitter must never change a measurement
text:
Jitter must never change a measurement



Without and with horizontal jitter: the same growth values, spread sideways so that overlapping points become visible.



Sideways spread makes hidden points visible. The number of points and their heights stay the same.
Never add vertical jitter, and never drop points to make a plot look tidier.


Transfer-study data. In the exercises students change only the width and confirm the y values are unchanged.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Save files other programs can open
text:
Save files other programs can open
ggsave("output/seedling-growth.png", plot = growth_plot,
       width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 150)
write_csv(growth_table, "output/seedling-growth.csv")

growth_plot is an object in memory. ggsave() writes a PNG image to disk.
write_csv() writes a table to disk. An image is not a table, and vice versa.
Both overwrite a file with the same name without asking. Use clear names; never write into data/.
Open both files from the file manager to check they exist.


The output/ folder is part of the supplied project. If saving fails, check getwd() and dir.exists(“output”).
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Worked example: the same steps on new data
text:
Worked example: the same steps on new data


transfer <- read_csv("data/seedlings-transfer.csv",
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
nrow(transfer)                       # 18
treated <- filter(transfer, treatment == "treated")
nrow(treated)                        # 9


T01: 40.3 − 25.3 = 15.0 mm. Check one plant by hand.
Adding a column keeps all 18 plants.
Change the names, labels and file names; the steps stay the same.


Then plot growth by group and save as output/transfer-... so nothing from the main study is overwritten.

This is day08-transfer.R in the exercises. Compare with the main study: what changed (object names, row counts, file names), what stayed the same (operations).
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Calculate a variable, then show the observations
section: Same steps for a lab calculation
text:
Same steps for a lab calculation


dilutions <- read_csv("data/dilutions.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(stock_volume_ml =
           target_mmol_l * final_volume_ml /
           stock_mmol_l,
         possible_by_dilution =
           target_mmol_l <= stock_mmol_l)

D01–D03 need 2.5, 5 and 10 mL stock.
D04 needs 100 mL for a 50 mL final volume: impossible. Keep the row and flag it.





Calculated stock volume against final volume for four dilution requests; D04 needs more stock than its final volume.




A stock is a solution of known concentration; dilution adds solvent up to a final total volume. D04’s target, 200 mmol/L, is above its stock, 100 mmol/L. A formula can produce a number for a request that cannot be carried out. The organic-yield alternative uses the same mutate step: Y01 yield = 100 × 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%.

Step
Function
What to check

mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

Keep rows

crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
text:
Four sections, four jobs



Question and data: what was asked, what was measured, what one row is.
Methods: how the file was read and how growth was calculated.
Results: a labelled figure and a few calculated facts.
Interpretation: what the pattern is, how much plants vary, one limitation.





A report leads from the data through an analysis to a readable result.



Every sentence should be backed by the data, a figure or the study description.

Save report.Rmd as first-report.Rmd in the project root. Students already have most of the code from Days 8 and 9.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Question and data: what was measured?
text:
Question and data: what was measured?



24 seedlings in separate pots; 12 randomly allocated to a nutrient treatment, 12 controls.
Length measured at the start and after seven days, in mm.
One row = one plant. Two lengths of the same plant are not two plants.
Simulated teaching data: say so.





Separate control and treated pots; each plant is its own independent unit.




All of this comes from data/README.md, not from R. The nutrient formulation is unspecified; do not invent one.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
text:
Methods: biology first, code underneath

“Growth was calculated as final minus initial length for each plant, in mm.”

That tells a reader more than “we used mutate()”. The code still belongs in the report so the calculation can be rerun:
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
nrow(seedlings)                    # 24
sum(is.na(seedlings$growth_mm))    # 0
range(seedlings$growth_mm)         # 8.0 30.8
Simple checks like these tell the reader the data are complete: 24 plants, nothing missing.

The range describes these 24 plants, not all seedlings in nature, and is sensitive to a single unusual plant. Keep library() calls in the first chunk.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Results: a figure the reader can read
text:
Results: a figure the reader can read



One dot = one plant. Say so in the caption.
y-axis: change in length (mm). Not final size.
Every plant shown, so the reader sees the spread, not only a summary.
The figure answers the question; one good figure beats three unexplained ones.





Growth of each seedling by treatment; values vary within both groups and the groups overlap.




If students also made the initial-versus-final plot on Day 8, ask which figure answers “did treated plants grow more?”. Keep the second only if it answers a stated question.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Interpretation: say what you see, and no more
text:
Interpretation: say what you see, and no more







Sentence
OK?




“Growth varied among plants in both groups.”
Yes: visible in the figure


“Treated plants tended to grow more, but the groups overlap: control 8.0–18.7 mm, treated 12.2–30.8 mm.”
Yes: describes these data


“Every treated plant grew more than every control.”
No: P17 (treated) grew 12.2 mm, less than many controls


“The treatment works.”
Not yet: we have not measured how uncertain the difference is (week 4)



End with one limitation, e.g. a small simulated study, or no uncertainty assessed yet.

Ask students which sentence in their own draft is closest to the last row, and rewrite it. “The graph shows a difference” is vague: say what is higher, by roughly how much, and with how much overlap.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: A unit slip runs without warning
text:
A unit slip runs without warning



Relabelling the axis “cm” without dividing by 10 makes P01’s 18.6 mm into “18.6 cm”.
R gives no error: it does not know units.
Check together: the values, the column name (_mm), the axis label and the text.





P01’s growth of 18.6 mm only relabelled as cm is wrong; converted it is 1.86 cm.




The same check as Day 6: conversion changes values, not only labels. A reader trusts the axis label.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
text:
Make the project portable



Paths start from the project folder: data/seedlings.csv, not a personal path such as C:/Users/anna/Desktop.
The .Rmd stays in the project folder; the HTML can go to reports/.
Then the whole folder can move to another place or person and still work.





The whole project moves to a new location and the report still finds data/seedlings.csv.




The .Rproj file sets the working folder; it does not contain the data. Personal absolute paths are the most common reason a report fails on someone else’s computer.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Your first biological report
section: Test it like a stranger would
text:
Test it like a stranger would


Restart R, then in the Console:
rmarkdown::render("first-report.Rmd",
                  output_dir = "reports")

Fails? Fix the source, not the Console.
Then copy the project to another folder, open that .Rproj, and render again.





A copied project keeps the report and its data folder together and is tested with a fresh render.




A successful fresh render shows the report is reproducible here; it does not show the interpretation is right. On Windows, use the native project in Documents, not a copy inside Ubuntu.

title: Your first biological report
section: Read the HTML as the reader
text:
Read the HTML as the reader
Open the HTML in a browser, without the source. Can you find:

the question, and what one plant (one row, one dot) is?
the input file and the units?
how growth was calculated, and what the y-axis shows?
the main pattern, the overlap, and one limitation?

Anything missing: add it to the .Rmd and render again. Never edit the HTML.

The extended exercise turns this into a revision log, reports/report-revision.txt: issue, correction, evidence the corrected report reruns.

title: Your first biological report
text:
Then: a second, smaller brief


Pick one table and write laboratory-brief.Rmd with the same four sections:

18-plant transfer study: T01 grew 15.0 mm; 9 plants per group.
Or solutions.csv: calculated concentrations of 50, 100 and 150 mmol/L for each solute.





Individual growth values in the transfer study overlap between the groups.



Same skills, new data: check every number and every sentence against this table, not the old one.

For solutions, rows are calculation cases, not independent experimental units; concentrations follow from a supplied formula, not from measured variation among plants. The leaf-mass scatter plot (leaf-first-look.R) is a further optional transfer.

Summary







Section
What it must contain

Question; 24 plants, 12 per group, random allocation; one row = one plant; units; simulated


Methods
