crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: An average is not every plant
text:
About this lecture
You write in a lab report: “control seedlings grew 15.3 mm on average.” A reader cannot tell whether every plant grew about 15 mm, or whether some grew 8 mm and others nearly 19 mm. Those are very different biological pictures: one unusual plant, or a treatment that makes plants more variable, would be invisible. How do we describe both the typical value and how much plants differ?

The mean and median describe the centre; one unusual value moves them differently.
Deviations from the mean lead to the variance (squared units) and the standard deviation (SD, original units).
Adding a constant or changing units changes the numbers in predictable ways, which makes a useful check.
The SD describes how much individual plants vary. It is not the uncertainty of the mean (Day 14) and does not tell you why plants vary.

This is a concept day with small hand calculations; centre and spread are used in every later day.

Ask students to imagine two seed batches with the same mean growth: one uniform, one with a few plants that hardly grew. A breeder, a field ecologist or a reviewer would care about that difference. Today’s numbers are the tools to say it.

title: An average is not every plant
section: The problem: same mean, different plants
text:
The problem: same mean, different plants



Group A: 13, 14, 15 mm. Group B: 8, 14, 20 mm.
Both means are 14 mm.
In A plants are alike (SD 1 mm); in B they differ a lot (SD 6 mm).
Reporting only “mean 14 mm” makes the two groups look identical.

A description needs a centre and a spread.




Two toy growth groups share a mean of 14 millimetres; one set of dots is tightly clustered and the other widely spread.




Give students a moment to read the axis before naming SD. A larger spread is not automatically sloppy work: organisms really differ, and measurement noise also contributes. We need words and numbers for both centre and spread.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Mean and median: two ways to describe the centre
text:
Mean and median: two ways to describe the centre


uneven_mm <- c(10, 10, 10, 100)
mean(uneven_mm)     # 32.5
median(uneven_mm)   # 10

Mean: add all values, divide by how many. Every value pulls on it.
Median: the middle of the sorted values (average of the two middle ones if n is even).
Change 12, 14, 16 to 12, 14, 26 mm: the mean moves from 14 to 17.33 mm; the median stays 14 mm.
Neither is wrong. A large value is checked against the source and kept if real.





Changing one value from 16 to 26 millimetres moves the group mean, shown as a diamond, from 14 to 17.33 millimetres.




Ask for predictions before showing the numbers. The changed set also has variance 57.33 mm² and SD 7.57 mm, against 4 mm² and 2 mm before: one value changes spread a lot. This is sensitivity reasoning, not permission to remove a real large value. Day 11’s rule still holds: only source evidence justifies a change.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Spread starts with deviations from the mean
text:
Spread starts with deviations from the mean



Take three growth values: 12, 14, 16 mm. Their mean is 14 mm.
Each deviation is value minus mean: −2, 0, +2 mm.
Deviations carry the measurement’s units.
Adding them gives 0, always: positives and negatives cancel. So the plain average deviation cannot measure spread.
Squaring removes the sign: 4, 0, 4.





Growth values 12, 14 and 16 millimetres have deviations of minus 2, 0 and plus 2 millimetres from their mean of 14 millimetres.




Work through the three numbers slowly on the board. Students do this by hand in the exercises and then check with R. The cancellation is a property of the mean, not a coincidence of this example.

title: An average is not every plant
text:
Variance and standard deviation


For 12, 14, 16 mm:

Squared deviations: 4 + 0 + 4 = 8 mm².
Divide by n − 1 = 2: variance = 4 mm².
Square root: SD = 2 mm.


Variance is in squared units (mm²), hard to picture.
SD is back in mm, the same units as the plants, so it can be read next to the mean.
Dividing by n − 1 rather than n is the convention for estimating spread from a sample; R uses it.





A two-millimetre deviation squared gives four square millimetres; the square root of the variance returns to millimetres.




No derivation of n − 1 is needed; say that with small samples, dividing by n tends to underestimate population spread. SD is not an error bar for the mean, and it does not mean every plant lies within one SD of the mean.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Let R do the arithmetic, and check it by hand
text:
Let R do the arithmetic, and check it by hand
growth_mm <- c(12, 14, 16)
deviations_mm <- growth_mm - mean(growth_mm)   # -2  0  2
sum(deviations_mm^2) / (length(growth_mm) - 1) # 4, by the formula
var(growth_mm)                                 # 4   (mm²)
sd(growth_mm)                                  # 2   (mm)

Predict each result before running it. If R disagrees with your hand calculation, find out why.
var() and sd() use n − 1, as on the previous slide.
R prints numbers without units. You add mm or mm² when you write them down.


Ask students to predict 14, 4 and 2 before running. Their task is not memorising function names: it is choosing the quantity that answers their question and labelling it correctly.

title: An average is not every plant
text:
Worked example: our control plants


seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
control <- filter(seedlings,
                  treatment == "control")
mean(control$growth_mm)    # 15.28
median(control$growth_mm)  # 15.65
var(control$growth_mm)     # 10.18 (mm²)
sd(control$growth_mm)      # 3.19  (mm)

The 12 control plants grew from 8.0 to 18.7 mm; none grew exactly 15.28 mm.
Treated plants: mean 21.49 mm, SD 4.87 mm: higher centre and more spread.





The twelve control growth values spread along one axis from 8 to 18.7 millimetres, with a vertical line at their mean of 15.28 millimetres.




We switch to the complete, clean seedlings.csv today, not yesterday’s deliberately incomplete export; say this explicitly. Load readr and dplyr first, as in the practical. The mean is a summary, not an observed “average plant”. Report with units and sensible rounding: 15.3 mm, SD 3.2 mm.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Shifts and unit changes: a built-in check
text:
Shifts and unit changes: a built-in check


Start with 13, 14, 15 mm (mean 14, SD 1).

Add 10 mm to every value: mean becomes 24 mm, SD stays 1 mm. Moving all plants together does not change how they differ.
Convert to cm (÷ 10): mean 1.4 cm, SD 0.1 cm, variance ÷ 100 (mm² → cm²).
The smaller SD in cm is a different unit, not less variable plants.
If a shift changes your SD, there is a mistake in the code.





The same three values shown in millimetres, shifted by ten millimetres, and converted to centimetres: the centre moves, the spread only changes with the unit.




In code: mean(close_mm + 10), sd(close_mm + 10), and the same with close_mm / 10. For 12, 14, 16 the variance 4 mm² becomes 0.04 cm² and the SD 2 mm becomes 0.2 cm. Variance scales with the square of the conversion factor. This is a units check, not a new method.

title: An average is not every plant
section: What the SD does not tell you
text:
What the SD does not tell you


In a second class’s study, treated plants have the larger mean (17.87 vs 13.66 mm) but the smaller SD (1.94 vs 2.53 mm).

Centre and spread are separate facts; one does not predict the other.
A larger SD can come from biology (plants really differ) or measurement noise. The SD alone cannot say which.
The SD is about individual plants, not about how precisely we know the mean. That is Day 14.





In the transfer study, treated plants have a higher mean growth than controls but their points are less spread out.




In the main study the treated group had both the larger mean and the larger SD; here it is the other way round, so students should use the actual values. A claim such as “the group with the larger SD has the worse technique” goes beyond what the SD shows. The transfer data: data/seedlings-transfer.csv, 9 plants per group, T01 grew 15.0 mm.

title: An average is not every plant
section: Same tools in another lab: percentage yield
text:
Same tools in another lab: percentage yield
An organic synthesis run gives 0.62 g of dry product when at most 1.00 g was possible.
yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g = 62%

Six standard-protocol runs: mean yield 68.67%, SD 4.32 percentage points.
A change from 62% to 70% is 8 percentage points, not an 8% relative increase.
Runs used different starting amounts, so raw grams would answer a different question.
A higher yield alone does not show higher purity or a better method in general.


This is a transfer choice from data/organic-recovery.csv, an alternative to the treated-group step in the practical, not extra compulsory work. Collected material is assumed pure in this simplified calculation. Variance is 18.67 squared percentage points.

title: An average is not every plant
text:
Report centre and spread together
Good: “Control seedlings grew a mean of 15.3 mm (SD 3.2 mm, median 15.7 mm, n = 12 plants).”

Name the quantity (seven-day growth), the unit, n, the centre and the spread.
Calculate with full precision; round only the numbers you display. Six decimals from R are not six decimals of ruler precision.
If you convert units, change the mean, SD, variance units and axis labels together.








Misreading
Better




“The average plant grew 15.3 mm.”
The mean is a summary; individual plants grew 8.0 to 18.7 mm.


“The SD is the error of the mean.”
The SD describes plant-to-plant variation.




A table with correct numbers but wrong unit labels is still a misleading report. The ordering of group means and the relative spread stay the same under a positive unit conversion; that is a good check.

title: An average is not every plant
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Mean
Sum ÷ n; pulled by unusual values (12, 14, 26 → 17.33)


Median
Middle of the sorted values; less affected by one extreme (stays 14)


Deviation
Value − mean; deviations always sum to 0


Variance
Sum of squared deviations ÷ (n − 1); squared units (mm²)


SD
√variance; original units (mm); describes spread among individuals


Shift / unit
+ constant moves the mean only; ÷ 10 divides mean and SD by 10, variance by 100


Seedlings
Control 15.28 mm (SD 3.19); treated 21.49 mm (SD 4.87), n = 12 each


Limits
SD does not identify its cause, and is not uncertainty in the mean



Next (Day 13, group summaries): calculate these summaries for every group at once, and plot them without hiding the individual plants.
Now: open the Day 12 exercises. Leave with day12-variation.R and a short interpretation of centre and spread with units.

Ask: what would stay the same if every measurement increased by 10 mm? What changes when mm become cm? Keep the by-hand three-number example before moving to the full dataset.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
text:
About this lecture
A thesis student treats three plants, measures a leaf on each plant ten times, and writes n = 30 in the methods. The examiner replies: “You have three plants. n = 3.” With n = 30 every later result looks far more certain than the experiment can support. Which measurements count as independent evidence, and how precisely does a mean describe the population?

The experimental unit is the thing that independently received the treatment: here, a plant in its own pot.
Technical replicates (re-measuring the same plant) check the measurement; biological replicates (more plants) tell us about plants.
The SD describes how plants vary; a sampling distribution shows how much a mean would vary between repeated samples.
A precise estimate can still be wrong if the sampling or measurement is biased.

This is a reasoning day, supported by a short supplied simulation. Days 16–18 rely on counting independent units correctly.

Inflated n from technical replicates or from many cells of one animal is one of the most common reasons manuscripts and theses are sent back. Students should leave able to say, for any design, “we have many measurements, but the number of independently treated units is …”.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: The problem: more rows, not more plants
text:
The problem: more rows, not more plants



Six ruler readings of P01 are six numbers about one plant.
They tell you how repeatable the measurement is (technical replicates).
They tell you nothing about how other plants respond. For that you need more plants (biological replicates).
Same trap: 100 cells from one mouse, ten time points from one culture, one product batch weighed twelve times.





Six separate ruler readings all refer to the same plant, P01.




Ask: if P01 happened to be an unusually vigorous plant, would six more readings reveal that? No. Technical repeats are useful, for example to check a new measuring method, but they are a different kind of information. The organic analogue is repeatedly weighing one collected product batch: one run, not twelve.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: The experimental unit: what was treated independently?
text:
The experimental unit: what was treated independently?



In our study, each plant has its own pot and was randomly allocated to control or treated.
Ask: could this plant get control while its neighbour gets treatment? If yes, it is a separate unit.
So the seedling study has 24 units, 12 per group, even though each plant was measured twice (initial and final).
Initial and final lengths become one growth value per plant.





Twelve separate pots, each with its own plant and its own treatment allocation, illustrate individual plants as independent units.




Physical separation alone does not prove independence; the design description in data/README.md states independent allocation and handling. Students should get the unit from the study description, not from counting rows.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: When the tray is the unit
text:
When the tray is the unit


Suppose instead the treatment was given to whole trays: one tray of control plants, one tray of treated plants.

Many plants per tray, but only one treatment decision per group.
Any tray effect (warmer spot, more light) is mixed up with the treatment.
Counting 24 independent plants would overstate the evidence. No statistical test can repair this; only more trays can.





Two trays of six plants each; tray A receives control and tray B receives the treatment, so plants within a tray share one treatment unit.




This is a schematic counterexample, not the course experiment. Ask how many treatment assignments occurred, not how many measurements fill the spreadsheet. With several trays per treatment, the tray becomes the unit of analysis.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
text:
Count the independent units








Design
Measurements
Independent units




24 plants in separate pots, randomly allocated
24 growth values
24 plants (12 per group)


1 plant per treatment, measured 12 times each
24 readings
1 plant per group


2 trays of 12 plants, treatment given per tray
24 growth values
1 tray per group


1 synthesis run, product weighed 12 times
12 masses
1 run




The independent units decide what the data can say about other plants or runs.
Write it as: “We have many measurements, but our number of independently treated units is ….”


Go through each row with the class before revealing the last column. Ask in which design technical repeats would still be useful: for example, checking that the ruler reading is repeatable before starting the real experiment.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
text:
Two kinds of spread



SD among plants: how much individual plants differ. It does not shrink with more plants; plants are as variable as they are.
Sampling uncertainty: how much the mean would change if we took a new sample of plants. This does shrink with more independent plants.
Read the horizontal axis: individual values, or means?





Three histograms on one scale: individual growth values are widely spread, means of four draws less so, and means of sixteen draws cluster tightly.




This figure is generated from the course values with a fixed illustrative random generator; exact bins need not match the R demonstration. The concept is the narrower distribution of means from larger samples. Distinguish SD among means from SD among the plants within one sample.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: A simulation: draw many samples, compute many means
text:
A simulation: draw many samples, compute many means
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
population_mm <- seedlings$growth_mm          # 24 values used as a toy population
set.seed(14)                                  # makes the random draws repeatable
means_4 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(population_mm, size = 4, replace = TRUE)))
means_16 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(population_mm, size = 16, replace = TRUE)))
sd(population_mm); sd(means_4); sd(means_16)  # 5.13  2.44  1.24

sample(..., size = 4, replace = TRUE) draws 4 values; a value may be drawn twice.
replicate(400, ...): repeat “draw a sample, take its mean” 400 times.
The result is 400 means, not 400 new plants. The 24 recorded plants never change.


Load readr, dplyr and ggplot2 first, and keep the block in day14-sampling.R as in the practical; the practical also plots the two sets of means. Students are not asked to write loops or a sampling algorithm; they need to understand source, draw size, replacement, repetitions and seed. This is a teaching demonstration with a toy population, not a new experiment or a claim about nature.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Larger samples give more stable means
text:
Larger samples give more stable means



Each bar counts simulated sample means.
Means of 4 plants: SD 2.44 mm. Means of 16 plants: SD 1.24 mm.
Four times as many plants → the spread of means roughly halves.
The plants themselves still vary with SD 5.13 mm. More plants make the mean more stable, not the plants more alike.





Histograms of 400 simulated sample means: means of sixteen draws cluster more tightly than means of four draws from the same fixed source values.




The SD of the means approximates what is later called the standard error. Change the seed to 25 in the practical: exact numbers change, the relationship between sample size and spread stays. Choosing a convenient seed is not evidence for anything.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Simulation settings are not sample size
text:
Simulation settings are not sample size


Three settings, three meanings:

Draw size (size = 12): plants in each simulated sample. Changes how much the means vary.
Repetitions (100 vs 1000): how many means we look at. Gives a smoother picture, same width.
Seed: which random sequence. Exact values change; the pattern does not.

None of them adds a measured plant.




Histograms of 100 and 1000 simulated means, each from samples of twelve draws, have the same width; more repetitions only smooth the picture.




Compare 100 and 1000 repeats, each using 12 draws. More repetitions do not create more measured plants or narrow the distribution the way a larger independent sample size does. Avoid trying seeds until a pretty plot appears.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Precise is not the same as correct
text:
Precise is not the same as correct



If every measurement is 5 mm too high (a misread ruler, one unusually sunny tray), means of 40 plants are tightly clustered, in the wrong place.
More readings or more plants from the same biased source make the estimate narrower, not truer.
Another ruler reading fixes measurement noise; another independent, representative unit addresses the biology.





Means of four draws from the correct source are widely spread around the true mean; means of forty draws from a source shifted by 5 millimetres cluster tightly around the wrong value.




This schematic uses a known 5 mm shift for illustration; it does not diagnose bias in the course study. A narrow histogram describes the sampling process precisely, not whether that process answers the biological question.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
section: Same idea, new source: the second class
text:
Same idea, new source: the second class


transfer <- read_csv("data/seedlings-transfer.csv",
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
set.seed(14)
means_3 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(
  transfer$growth_mm, size = 3, replace = TRUE)))
means_12 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(
  transfer$growth_mm, size = 12, replace = TRUE)))
sd(means_3); sd(means_12)   # 1.69  0.83

18 recorded plants (SD 3.08 mm) as a toy source.
Means of 3 draws vary about twice as much as means of 12.





Histograms of simulated sample means from the transfer source: means of 12 draws vary less than means of 3 draws.




The transfer source combines both groups only to illustrate sampling; it is not a treatment comparison or a confidence interval. Students keep the two results in separate objects and save them as output/day14-transfer-sampling.csv.

title: What counts as independent evidence?
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Experimental unit
What independently received the treatment; seedling study: 24 potted plants


Technical replicate
Re-measuring the same material; checks the measurement, not the biology


Biological replicate
Another independent unit; informs how plants (or runs) respond


Shared trays
Treatment per tray → the tray is the unit; a test cannot repair the design


SD among plants
Spread of individuals (5.13 mm); does not shrink with more plants


Sampling uncertainty
Spread of means: 2.44 mm (n = 4) vs 1.24 mm (n = 16)


Simulation settings
Draw size changes precision; repetitions and seed do not add plants


Precision vs bias
A narrow distribution can sit in the wrong place



Next (Day 15, descriptive report): put the checked data, summaries, figure and an honest statement of the units and limits into one report that renders from scratch.
Now: open the Day 14 exercises. Leave with day14-sampling.R, your replicate diagrams and a short explanation of what was repeated and what increased the independent information.

Design question to end with: measure each of two plants twenty more times, or obtain ten additional independent plants? For a population mean, the ten plants, assuming comparable measurements; checking measurement repeatability first can still be useful.

title: What difference are we estimating?
text:
About this lecture
Your descriptive report says treated seedlings grew more on average. Your supervisor asks: “More than what, by how many millimetres, measured how, and could the set-up itself have produced that?” Before any statistical test, a comparison has to be defined: the outcome, the units, the direction, and which plants count as independent. What exactly are we comparing, and what can the design support?

Name the question, outcome, unit and direction (treated − control) before calculating.
Look at the plants first: a difference in means is not a claim about every plant.
Check the design: independent groups or paired measurements? Plants or shared trays?
A sample difference is one estimate; another experiment would give another number.

Week 4 is about comparisons. Today defines the comparison; Day 17 adds how uncertain it is.

Motivate from the reader’s side: every results section in biology compares groups, and the first thing a careful reader checks is what was compared, in which direction, and on how many independent units. Students prepare comparison.Rmd today; Day 17 adds a confidence interval and p-value to the same file.

title: What difference are we estimating?
text:
The question and the design


Does the nutrient treatment change seven-day seedling growth?

Outcome: growth = final − initial length, in mm, one value per plant.
Unit: one plant in its own pot; 12 + 12, randomly allocated.
Direction: treated − control. A positive number means treated plants grew more.
Random allocation comes from the study description, not from the order of rows in the file.





Twelve control and twelve treated seedlings in separate pots represent independent random allocations.




The course data are simulated (data/README.md). Each plant is measured twice, but its two lengths are reduced to one growth value, so it contributes one observation. Writing the plan before the output exists prevents choosing a direction or an outcome after seeing which looks best. Students save it as output/day16-plan.txt.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Choose the outcome that answers the question
text:
Choose the outcome that answers the question



Left: initial lengths. Controls started slightly larger (mean 23.0 mm vs 21.9 mm).
Right: growth over seven days, the outcome for our question.
Final length alone would mix starting size with growth.
A starting difference is worth noting as a limitation; adjusting for it is beyond this course.





Initial lengths and seven-day growth shown separately for control and treated plants; growth is the outcome for the treatment question.




Random allocation means a starting difference like this is due to chance, but with 12 plants per group it can still be noticeable. Ask students which quantity answers “does treatment change growth?” before computing any summaries.

title: What difference are we estimating?
text:
Start with the observations


seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings,
    aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(
    width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 16)) +
  labs(x = "Treatment group",
       y = "Growth over the study period (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()

The treated group sits higher, but the groups overlap.
The largest control (18.7 mm) grew more than the smallest treated plant (12.2 mm).
So “every treated plant grew more” is false, even if the treated mean is higher.





Individual growth values for 12 control and 12 treated plants; the groups overlap although treated plants tend to be higher.




Ask students what one dot represents and whether any value contradicts the documented measurement process. There is no known source error in this complete table; keep all valid measurements. Overlap does not mean the means are equal, and separated means do not mean every pair of plants differs. Save with ggsave(“output/day16-growth.png”, growth_plot, width = 6, height = 4).

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: Compute the difference in the stated direction
text:
Compute the difference in the stated direction


treated <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "treated") |>
  pull(growth_mm)
control <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "control") |>
  pull(growth_mm)
observed_difference <- mean(treated) - mean(control)
observed_difference   # 6.22

pull() takes one column out as a plain vector of 12 numbers.





The treated mean of 21.49 millimetres exceeds the control mean of 15.28 millimetres by 6.22 millimetres.



Control 15.28 mm, treated 21.49 mm.
Treated − control = 6.22 mm: a number with units and a sign.



Load readr, dplyr and ggplot2 first, as in the practical. These vectors are exactly what Day 17’s t.test(treated, control) uses, so the direction carries over. Ask students to read the result aloud: “treated plants grew on average 6.22 mm more than controls”.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: The sign comes from the subtraction, not the name
text:
The sign comes from the subtraction, not the name



mean(treated) - mean(control) = +6.22 mm.
mean(control) - mean(treated) = −6.22 mm.
Same plants, same experiment: only the description changes.
Calling an object treatment_effect does not fix its sign. State the direction in words next to the number.
A report that says one direction and computes the other is wrong.





The same two group means produce +6.22 mm as treated minus control and −6.22 mm as control minus treated.




If a result comes out negative unexpectedly, print mean(treated) and mean(control) separately before concluding anything about the biology. Neither direction is wrong when it is labelled; we chose treated − control in advance and keep it.

title: What difference are we estimating?
text:
Independent groups or pairs?



Today: different plants in each group (P01 control, P13 treated). The groups are independent.
Day 18: the same plant measured before and after a change (L01 before, L01 after). Those readings form a pair and must stay together.
Two columns in a table do not make a pair; the same individual does.
Within one plant, initial and final are already combined into growth, so each plant gives one value.





On the left, two different plants belong to separate groups; on the right, the same plant measured twice forms a pair.




Pairing requires matching subject identity, not matching row positions. Getting this wrong changes the analysis: a paired design needs the within-plant differences, which comes on Day 18.

title: What difference are we estimating?
text:
Plants or shared trays?


Imagine all treated plants shared one tray and all controls another.

The plants are still measured, but there is only one treatment assignment per group.
A warmer or brighter tray would look exactly like a treatment effect.
Counting 24 independent plants would overstate the evidence. No test can repair this; only more independent trays.
Our study allocated plants individually, so the plant is the unit.





A hypothetical layout in which tray A receives control and tray B receives treatment, so each tray is one shared treatment unit.




This is the Day 14 counterexample, not the course study. Other things that weaken a comparison: biased allocation, recording mistakes, one dominating questionable value, or an outcome that does not answer the question. If a real design looks unsuitable, asking for advice is a good outcome; deleting genuine values until a test “works” is not.

title: What difference are we estimating?
text:
Another sample, another difference


transfer <- read_csv("data/seedlings-transfer.csv",
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
transfer |> group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mm = mean(growth_mm),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm),
            .groups = "drop")

Second class: 9 plants per group; control 13.66 mm, treated 17.87 mm.
Treated − control = 4.21 mm, not 6.22 mm.
Different plants and conditions give a different estimate. That alone is not evidence that the treatment “failed”.





Transfer study growth values: treated plants have a higher mean, and the observed treated-minus-control difference is 4.21 millimetres.




Students analyse this in transfer-comparison.Rmd with the same direction, and save output/day16-transfer-summary.csv. Confirm 18 rows, 9 per group, no missing values. The two simulated studies differ in values, spread and sample size; descriptive work cannot settle why their differences differ.

title: What difference are we estimating?
section: What we can say today, and what remains open
text:
What we can say today, and what remains open
Results paragraph: “Treated seedlings grew a mean of 21.49 mm (SD 4.87) and controls 15.28 mm (SD 3.19), 12 plants each: a difference of 6.22 mm (treated − control). Growth overlapped between the groups.”
Still open: would another set of plants give a similar difference, or could chance alone produce 6 mm?

The null hypothesis for Day 17: the population mean growth is the same under both conditions.
Two-sided: a difference in either direction counts. We decide this now, before seeing a test.
A p-value will say how surprising our data are if the means were equal. It is not the probability that the treatment works, and not the size of the effect.


Students should have a meaningful results paragraph before Day 17; the test adds an interval and p-value to it but does not replace it. The within-group SDs describe plants; uncertainty in the difference is a different quantity that also depends on sample size.

title: What difference are we estimating?
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Plan first
Question, outcome (growth, mm), unit (potted plant), direction (treated − control), before calculating


Outcome
Growth answers the question; initial length is a possible limitation (23.0 vs 21.9 mm)


Observations
Plot the plants; groups overlap, so a mean difference is not “every plant”


Difference
21.49 − 15.28 = 6.22 mm; the sign comes from the subtraction order


Independent vs paired
Different plants are independent; the same plant twice is a pair (Day 18)


Design
Shared trays → the tray is the unit; a test cannot repair the design


One estimate
Another study gave 4.21 mm; samples vary


Open question
Is 6.22 mm larger than chance variation could produce? (Day 17)



Next (Day 17, Welch test): how uncertain is the 6.22 mm difference? We add a confidence interval and a p-value, using the same treated and control vectors and the same direction.
Now: open the Day 16 exercises. Leave with comparison.Rmd, its rendered HTML, and output/day16-growth.png.

Ask students to read their difference aloud with units and direction. Today’s report should already be scientifically intelligible without any test.

title: The same plant measured twice
The same plant measured twice
section: The problem: twenty readings, ten plants
text:
The problem: twenty readings, ten plants



data/paired.csv: ten plants, each measured before and after the light was increased (µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹).
Before readings range from 5.20 to 8.81: plants differ from each other.
Yet almost every line goes up by a similar amount.
The two readings of one plant are not independent: a high plant before is likely high after.

Question: how large is the change within a plant?




Each of ten plants has a line from its before reading to its after reading; starting levels differ, but every line rises.




Point at the lowest and highest starting plant. The differences between plants are larger than many of the changes. If we treat the 20 readings as two separate groups, that plant-to-plant variation hides the change we care about. This is the motivation for the whole day. The data are simulated teaching data.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Pair by identity, not by position
text:
Pair by identity, not by position



plant_id says which two readings belong together.
In paired.csv each row holds one plant’s before and after, so the pair is already kept together.
If the readings came in two files, match them by ID before subtracting. Ten rows in each file is not enough.
Sorting the whole table is safe: rows move together. Sorting one column on its own breaks the pairs.





Plant identifiers connect before and after readings even when the two lists are in different orders.




The diagram imagines two lists in different orders to make the point visible. With the course file this cannot happen, but students will meet two-file data in lab courses (for example a plate-reader export before and after treatment). Ask: what would go wrong if you subtracted row 1 from row 1 here?

title: The same plant measured twice
text:
One change per plant



Three example plants show their after-minus-before change: L01 +1.08, L02 +4.17, L03 +1.31.



Change = after − before for the same plant. Positive means the rate went up.
L01: 6.95 − 5.87 = +1.08. L02: 11.92 − 7.75 = +4.17. L03: 10.12 − 8.81 = +1.31.
Each plant is its own reference, so differences in starting level drop out.


Do one subtraction on the board. Insist on writing the direction in words (“after minus before”) before any code is run; the sign of every later number depends on it. Units stay µmol CO2 m-2 s-1.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: In R: check the pairs, then compute the change
text:
In R: check the pairs, then compute the change
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
paired <- read_csv("data/paired.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
anyDuplicated(paired$plant_id)        # 0: every plant appears once

paired <- paired |>
  mutate(change_umol_m2_s = after_umol_m2_s - before_umol_m2_s)
mean(paired$change_umol_m2_s)         # 1.983

anyDuplicated() returns 0 when no identifier is repeated: ten rows, ten plants.
The new column holds one change per plant; L01’s should be +1.08. Check one by hand.
The mean change is 1.983 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹.


These are the object and column names used in the practical page and paired-report.Rmd. Have students run it and compare L01 with the hand calculation before going further.

title: The same plant measured twice
text:
Look at the ten changes



All ten changes are positive, from +1.08 to +4.17.
Mean change 1.983; SD of the changes 1.02.
The dashed line is no change.
L02 changed much more than the others. That alone is not an error: keep it.





Each point is one plant’s after-minus-before change, all above the dashed zero line.




The y-axis is the change, not the after reading. This is the plot students save as change_plot in the practical. A large valid value must not be removed because it is inconvenient; there is no recording note saying L02 is wrong.

title: The same plant measured twice
text:
The paired t-test
paired_comparison <- t.test(paired$after_umol_m2_s,
                            paired$before_umol_m2_s,
                            paired = TRUE)
paired_comparison








R prints
Value
Meaning




mean difference
1.983 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹
Estimated mean change, after − before


95 percent confidence interval
1.255 to 2.711 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹
Uncertainty in the mean change


t, df
6.16, 9
df = 10 pairs − 1


p-value
0.00017
How surprising, if the true mean change were zero




paired = TRUE matches position 1 with position 1, and so on. That is why the rows must hold true pairs.
The same numbers come from t.test(paired$change_umol_m2_s, mu = 0): a paired test is a test of the changes against zero. It is one analysis, not two pieces of evidence.
The interval is about the mean change; individual plants changed from 1.08 to 4.17.


First vector after, second before, so the estimate is after minus before. Ten independent units, not twenty. Run the one-sample version live and show that estimate, interval and p agree to the last digit. Do not present the second call as confirming evidence.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Why not use Day 17’s Welch test?
text:
Why not use Day 17’s Welch test?



Treating before and after as two separate groups gives the same estimate, 1.98, but an interval of 0.74 to 3.23.
That interval is wider because plant-to-plant differences stay in the calculation.
The paired analysis removes them: each plant is compared with itself.
The design decides which test to use, not which result looks better.





The paired interval 1.25 to 2.71 is narrower than the 0.74 to 3.23 interval from wrongly treating the readings as two separate groups.




Welch on the two columns: t.test(after, before) without paired = TRUE gives 0.74 to 3.23, p about 0.004. It is not wrong arithmetic, it answers a question about two separate groups of plants that this study does not have. Conversely, two unrelated groups can never become paired by putting them side by side.

title: The same plant measured twice
text:
Pitfall: sorting the columns separately



Sorting before and after one column at a time matches the smallest with the smallest, not plant with plant.
The mean change is still 1.983: means cannot detect the mistake.
But the SD of the changes drops from 1.02 to 0.50, and p shrinks to about 0.0000006.
A smaller p after breaking the pairs is not better evidence; it is a wrong analysis.





Left: correct within-plant pairings cross each other. Right: matching by rank gives parallel lines that connect readings from different plants.




In the practical, students build this deliberately as a separate object, wrong_sorted, and keep paired unchanged. Ask why mean(after) − mean(before) equals mean(after − before) yet tells us nothing about whether the pairs were preserved. The uncertainty depends on the spread of the true within-plant changes.

title: The same plant measured twice
section: Pitfall: few pairs leave much uncertainty
text:
Pitfall: few pairs leave much uncertainty



Illustrative example: three plants, before 5, 8, 6 and after 7, 9, 9.
Changes +2, +1, +3: all positive, mean 2.
95% interval for the mean change: −0.48 to 4.48 (p ≈ 0.07).
With three pairs we cannot even be sure of the direction. That is not proof of no effect: report the uncertainty.





Three observed changes of 1, 2 and 3 have a mean of 2, but the 95 percent interval for the mean change runs from about −0.48 to 4.48 and includes zero.




These are supplied illustrative values (plants D1–D3), not a measured dataset; students put them into paired-transfer.Rmd. Keep this example separate from the ten-plant study; do not pool them. More independent plants is what narrows the interval.

title: The same plant measured twice
text:
What the design cannot show



Every plant was measured before, then after. Light changed, but time also passed: acclimation, time of day or instrument drift could contribute.
There is no group of plants measured twice without a light change.
A small p-value does not separate light from time.
Better design: add plants measured twice under unchanged light, and use more plants.





Plants are measured in lower light and later in higher light; light and elapsed time change together.




Distinguish three improvements: more independent plants gives more pairs and a narrower interval; repeat readings of one plant only tell us about measurement repeatability; a control group measured twice separates light from time. These are different fixes for different limitations.

title: The same plant measured twice
text:
Write the result
“Across 10 plants, photosynthesis rate was on average 1.98 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ higher after the light was increased than before (95% CI 1.25 to 2.71; paired t-test, p ≈ 0.0002). Light and measurement order changed together, so the change cannot be attributed to light alone.”







Misreading
Better




“We had 20 observations.”
10 plants, each measured twice: 10 pairs.


“Most plants changed by 1.25 to 2.71.”
The interval is for the mean change; plants changed by 1.08 to 4.17.


“Light caused the increase.”
Light and time changed together; no unchanged-light group.


“Sorting the columns gave a smaller p, so it is better.”
Sorting destroyed the pairs; the result is invalid.




Have students write their own sentence before revealing this one. Precision: two or three significant digits is enough in prose; keep the full numbers in R.

title: The same plant measured twice
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Paired design
Each unit measured twice; the unit, not the reading, is independent (10 plants, not 20 readings)


Identity
Match readings by plant_id; never sort one column on its own


Change
after − before per plant; the direction is a choice you write down first


Paired t-test
t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE) = one-sample test of the changes against 0


Estimate and CI
Mean change 1.98, 95% CI 1.25 to 2.71 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹; about the mean change


Why pair
Removes plant-to-plant differences: narrower than treating the columns as two groups


Few pairs
Three pairs: CI −0.48 to 4.48; uncertain, not “no effect”


Design limit
Fixed before/after order: light and time are mixed; a test cannot separate them



Next (Day 19, calibration): a straight line that turns an instrument reading into a concentration.
Now: open the Day 18 exercises. Make paired-report.Rmd with the ID check, the change plot, the paired test and a limitation; save output/day18-changes.png and render.

Ask: could a reader of your report tell what counted as one independent pair? The exercises also include the matching check with the wrong_sorted object and the three-plant paired-transfer.Rmd.

title: A line through biological measurements
A line through biological measurements
section: Not a calibration: nobody set the leaf area
text:
Not a calibration: nobody set the leaf area



Day 19: we prepared the concentrations; only absorbance was measured.
Today: both area and dry mass were measured on leaves as they were found. Nothing was assigned.
Plant age, light, water or species could affect both measurements.
So the line can describe how they go together, not show that changing one changes the other.
One leaf per plant: 18 independent plants.





Three leaves of different sizes, each from a different plant; area and dry mass are measured and no treatment is assigned.




This is an observational study. If we had 18 leaves from a single plant, they would share that plant’s conditions and would not be 18 independent units. Emphasise the change of meaning, because the R code will look identical to yesterday’s.

title: A line through biological measurements
text:
Plot first



x: leaf area (cm²); y: dry mass (mg). Mass is the variable we want to explain.
Larger leaves tend to be heavier: a clear positive association.
But the points scatter around the line: leaves of similar area differ in mass.
Observed areas: 2.96 to 14.68 cm².





Leaf dry mass rises with leaf area across 18 plants, with scatter around a fitted straight line.




Read the axes before the trend. Ask: is there any sign of curvature, or of one point far from the rest? Note the minimum and maximum area; they will matter for predictions.

title: A line through biological measurements
text:
Fit the line in R
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
leaves <- read_csv("data/leaf-mass.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
leaf_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_cm2, data = leaves)
coef(leaf_fit)
#>   (Intercept) leaf_area_cm2
#>      9.476606      4.110117

Same lm() as Day 19: response (mass) on the left of ~, area on the right.
Line: fitted mass ≈ 9.48 + 4.11 × area.
The intercept, 9.48 mg, is the fitted mass at zero area, far outside the data. It positions the line; it is not a leaf.


The intercept has the units of the response (mg). Zero area is not a biologically meaningful leaf, and it lies well below the smallest observed area of 2.96 cm2.

title: A line through biological measurements
text:
The slope has units



Slope 4.11 mg per cm²: in these plants, a leaf with 1 cm² more area had on average about 4.11 mg more fitted dry mass.
Not 4.11 %, not 4.11 cm², and not a promise for every leaf.
Units change the number, not the biology: with area in mm² the slope is 0.0411 mg per mm², and every fitted mass is the same.





Along the fitted line, a step of one square centimetre in area corresponds to about 4.11 milligrams of fitted dry mass.




1 cm2 = 100 mm2, so the slope per mm2 is the slope per cm2 divided by 100. In the practical students fit both versions and check that max(abs(fitted(leaf_fit) - fitted(unit_fit))) is essentially zero. A smaller number in other units is not a weaker association.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Residuals: what the line leaves out
text:
Residuals: what the line leaves out



Residual = observed − fitted mass, in mg.
A17 lies 8.4 mg below the line; A14 lies 6.3 mg above it.
Points on both sides of zero, no clear curve: a straight line is a reasonable summary here.
The plot cannot show independence. That comes from how the plants were sampled.





Residuals of the 18 leaves scatter on both sides of zero, mostly within about 5 milligrams, without a curved pattern.




In the practical, students pick one leaf, compute observed minus fitted by hand and compare with residuals(leaf_fit). A residual has a sign: positive means heavier than the line predicts at that area. A small sample gives only a rough check of the model.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Predictions: inside the observed range only
text:
Predictions: inside the observed range only



At 8 cm²: 9.48 + 4.11 × 8 ≈ 42.36 mg, a fitted mean. Single leaves of that size scatter around it.
At 25 cm² the formula gives 112 mg, and at 80 cm² 338 mg. No leaf that large was measured.
The relation may bend or change beyond the data. A longer line is not more evidence.





The fitted line covers observed areas up to about 15 square centimetres; a dashed extension into a shaded region without observations is unsupported.




coef(leaf_fit)[1] + coef(leaf_fit)[2] * 8 gives 42.36. Same range rule as for U3 in the calibration yesterday: calculable is not supported.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Pitfall: one point can move the line
text:
Pitfall: one point can move the line



A18 is the largest leaf and sits at the end of the range, where a point has most influence.
Refit without A18, in a separate object: slope 4.065 instead of 4.110 mg per cm². A small change.
A18 has no recorded error, so it stays in the main result.
A sensitivity check asks “does my conclusion depend on one point?”. It is not a way to pick the line you like.





The fitted line for all 18 plants and a labelled sensitivity line without A18 almost coincide.




Code: without_a18 <- leaves |> filter(plant_id != “A18”); sensitivity_fit <- lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_cm2, data = without_a18). Report the full-data fit as the result and the sensitivity check, labelled, as a check. An exclusion needs evidence from the records, not a tidier plot.

title: A line through biological measurements
text:
Write what the data support
“Across 18 plants, leaves with larger area had greater dry mass: within the observed range (2.96 to 14.68 cm²), each additional 1 cm² was associated with about 4.11 mg more fitted dry mass. The study was observational, so this does not show that increasing leaf area would increase mass.”







Claim
Supported?




“Larger leaves tended to have more dry mass in this sample.”
Yes, a description of the association.


“Adding 1 cm² of area causes 4.11 mg extra mass.”
No: nothing was manipulated; other factors vary too.


“Every 8 cm² leaf weighs 42.36 mg.”
No: that is a fitted mean; leaves scatter by several mg.


“A 30 cm² leaf will weigh about 133 mg.”
No: far outside the observed areas.




Showing that area affects mass would need a different design and biological knowledge, not a different lm() call. Ask students to write their own sentence first, using the hint pattern in the practical.

title: A line through biological measurements
section: Week 4: the question chooses the method
text:
Week 4: the question chooses the method










Design
Day
Output




Two independent groups
16–17
Mean difference, Welch CI


Same unit measured twice
18
Mean within-unit change, paired CI


Prepared standards → reading
19
Calibration line, inverse estimate


Two measured variables
20
Slope with units, residuals



Name the unit, the outcome and its units before choosing a function.




Three sketches: two independent groups lead to a mean difference, paired measurements to a within-unit change, and a scatter of two measurements to a slope and residuals.




In the practical, students write this as a comparison sheet for future labs. The transfer exercise relates initial and final length in seedlings-transfer.csv: an association question, which is different from the treatment comparison on the same file. Not a menu to pick whichever test gives a small p-value.

title: A line through biological measurements
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Observational data
Both variables measured, nothing assigned: the line describes, it does not show cause


Fit
lm(dry_mass_mg ~ leaf_area_cm2, data = leaves): mass ≈ 9.48 + 4.11 × area


Slope
4.11 mg per cm² of fitted mean mass; 0.0411 mg per mm² is the same line


Intercept
Fitted mass at area 0, outside the data; not a measured leaf


Residual
Observed − fitted mass (mg); look for curvature or a point far away


Prediction
Fitted mean, only within 2.96–14.68 cm² (8 cm² → 42.36 mg)


Sensitivity
Without A18: slope 4.065; keep A18 in the main result


Choosing a method
Design and question first: groups, pairs, calibration or association



Next (Day 21, how a computer works and how big data are): from the analysis to the machine that stores and processes the data.
Now: open the Day 20 exercises. Make association-report.Rmd with the plot and line, the slope in a sentence with units, the residual plot and a labelled A18 check; save output/day20-leaf-line.png and render.

The exercises add the unit-conversion check, the transfer-association.Rmd on seedling lengths, and the week 4 comparison sheet.

title: One workflow, two computers
text:
About this lecture
Yesterday’s single-cell table needs about 24 GB of RAM; your laptop has 16 GB or less. Research groups solve this by logging in to a bigger, shared Linux computer and running the same R analysis there. But then there are two computers, each with its own files. You rendered a report remotely: where is it, and how do you get it back?
Today you will:

connect to a remote computer and find out which computer and folder you are in;
copy a project there, check that the copy is complete, and render a report;
bring the result back and keep a short record of what is where.

This is a hands-on day. The remote service details (host, login, transfer method) will be supplied separately; until then you rehearse locally. On Day 23 you run a small study from question to report.

Link back to Day 21: estimate first, and if the data do not fit, use a bigger computer. HPC2N or another Linux environment will be used; do not invent hostnames or login steps. Students only need to understand the ideas today and practise on the real service when the guide is issued.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Two computers, two sets of files
text:
Two computers, two sets of files



The laptop and the remote computer each have their own disk.
Both may contain a folder called course project with a report.Rmd. They are separate copies.
A filename means little without saying which computer and which folder.





A laptop and a remote computer each hold their own separate course-project folder.




Ask where a browser download normally lands. Then ask whether logging in to a remote desktop changes that. It does not. Two identically named folders on different computers do not synchronise.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Two ways in: a terminal or a desktop
text:
Two ways in: a terminal or a desktop



SSH gives a terminal on the remote computer: the same shell commands as Day 3.
A remote desktop shows the remote computer’s screen in a window.
Neither one copies files for you.
The service guide will say whether both see the same home folder.





SSH and remote desktop lead to the same remote environment through two different interfaces.




The general SSH form is ssh your-course-username@the-provided-host; replace the placeholders from the service guide when it is issued. Host-key checks and authentication follow that guide. Never write passwords or login codes in notes or logs.

title: One workflow, two computers
text:
Which computer? Which folder?
After connecting, run in the remote shell:
hostname   # which computer answered?
pwd        # which folder am I in on that computer?
ls         # what is in that folder?

Write the answers in reports/remote-log.txt. A large service may have several computers with different names.
exit ends the connection and returns you to your laptop’s shell. Run pwd again: now it shows a laptop folder.


Demonstrate only on the approved environment. Then make a practice folder with mkdir -p introcomputing-practice, cd into it, exit, reconnect, and find it again. Saved files belong to the disk, not to the terminal window.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Leaving does not delete your files
text:
Leaving does not delete your files



exit closes the session (the connection), not the remote disk.
Reconnect, cd to the folder, and the saved files are still there.
Same idea as Day 21: closing a process empties its RAM; saved files stay on disk.
Whether a running program keeps running after you leave depends on the service.





Ending an SSH session closes the connection while the saved project remains in storage.




Ask: if R was running a long analysis in that session, does it continue after exit? Not necessarily: the service guide will explain how to run work that keeps going. Today we only work interactively.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Moving files: a transfer makes a copy
text:
Moving files: a transfer makes a copy



Uploading or downloading creates a second copy in a named place.
Before transferring, write down the source, the destination, and the direction.
Editing one copy afterwards does not change the other.
Transfer the whole project (ZIP), not single files, so relative paths still work.





A deliberate transfer copies a report between laptop and remote storage.




Use the service’s supported upload/download method; if scp turns out to be the route, its exact syntax belongs in the service guide. Extract the ZIP on the remote side and open its .Rproj, exactly as on Day 1.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Check the copy before you analyse
text:
Check the copy before you analyse


In the remote R console:
getwd()
file.exists("data/algae.csv")
algae <- readr::read_csv("data/algae.csv",
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(algae)                      # 24
sum(!is.na(algae$biomass_mg))    # 23
algae$biomass_mg[algae$culture_id == "A19"]  # NA
Same checks on both computers, same answers: 24, 23, NA.




Twenty-four separate culture records, with one unavailable supplement measurement, A19.




data/algae.csv: 24 separately grown cultures, 12 reference and 12 supplement, harvested once; A19 spilled before weighing, so its biomass is unavailable (NA, not zero). FALSE from file.exists means R did not find that path from its working directory: check computer, project and folder before typing an absolute laptop path. Matching counts are good evidence but do not prove every value matches.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Render remotely, then bring the result back
text:
Render remotely, then bring the result back



Open the remote project and render report.Rmd in the provided R application.
If R is set up in the remote shell, from the project root: Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd")'
Download the HTML into a folder you can name, and open that copy.
To recalculate later you need the source and the data, not only the HTML.





Source and data are transferred in, the report is rendered remotely, and the output is transferred back.




Rscript starts a fresh R process and renders the saved document: the same fresh-session idea as restarting R. Run it only on the permitted execution host named in the service guide. On Windows, keep using native RStudio locally; the Rscript line is for a configured remote shell.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: The report is missing on my laptop
text:
The report is missing on my laptop
The report rendered remotely, but local Downloads is empty. Before rendering again, check:

Where did rendering write the HTML on the remote computer?
Was that file actually transferred?
Which destination folder received it?
Which copy did the browser open?

An empty Downloads folder does not mean the render failed. Rendering again only makes another copy in the same unexpected place.

Ask students to answer before showing the list. Distinguish three different failures: the calculation failed, the transfer did not happen, or the result is somewhere other than where you looked. Avoid making final2.html, final3.html while the real problem is location.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Plan the copy before you make it

title: One workflow, two computers
text:
Same filename, different contents



Two copies of receipt.txt can hold different versions.
Change one copy, save it, and reopen both: the other copy does not change.
Open the saved files and compare the text before deciding which copy to send.





Two files named receipt.txt contain a first and a second revision.




Demonstrate with a disposable receipt, not raw data. Keep both versions until you know which is which, rather than deleting an unfamiliar folder.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: An unsaved edit has not travelled
text:
An unsaved edit has not travelled



What you see in an editor can differ from the saved file.
A transfer copies the saved file.
Save, close, reopen, then transfer.
Likewise, editing report.Rmd does not change an old HTML until you render again.





A changed editor buffer and the saved receipt contain different revisions until the file is saved.




This is the RAM/disk split from Day 21 again: the editor buffer is in RAM, the file on disk. Some editors autosave or restore unsaved text, so the test is the saved file.

title: One workflow, two computers
section: Equal size is not equal contents
text:
Equal size is not equal contents



version 1 and version 2 have the same number of characters, so the same file size.
Equal row counts are a useful check, but two tables can have equal sizes and different values.
For small text files, open both and read them; in R, identical(readLines(a), readLines(b)).





Two notes with different version text occupy the same number of character positions.




Yesterday file.size counted bytes; here that is exactly why it is not enough: one character per byte, and the same number of characters. Replace a and b with the real paths of the two copies. No hashing theory needed.

title: One workflow, two computers
text:
Summary







Idea
Key fact




Why remote
data larger than laptop RAM need a bigger computer (Day 21)


Two computers
each has its own disk; same folder names are separate copies


SSH / remote desktop
a terminal or a screen on the remote computer; neither copies files


hostname, pwd, exit
which computer, which folder; leave without deleting saved files


Transfer
makes a copy; name source, destination and direction


Checks
repeat nrow, available counts and named records after copying; equal size ≠ equal contents


Missing result
find it on the remote side, then check the transfer and destination



Next (Day 23, mini-study): plan and analyse a small biological study from question to report.
Now: Open exercises · Quiz. Leave with reports/remote-log.txt, reports/transfer-plan.txt, the receipt and the audit. Until access details arrive, do the local rehearsal and mark the remote steps pending.

A local rehearsal checks portable paths and project structure; connecting, authenticating and transferring still need practice on the real service once the guide is issued.

title: Reproduce and share your report
Reproduce and share your report
section: The problem: it works on my screen

title: Reproduce and share your report
section: Source and result have different jobs
text:
Source and result have different jobs



Input data and the R Markdown source together produce the HTML result.



The HTML is for reading. It cannot be re-run on new data.
The .Rmd plus the CSV is the recipe. That is what makes the result repeatable.
Share both; keep the source as the master copy.


Ask: when next month’s flasks arrive, which file do you edit? The .Rmd, then Knit. Someone who only receives the HTML can read the result but not check or extend it.

title: Reproduce and share your report
text:
Test 1: restart R, then Knit
Session → Restart R, then Knit without running anything in the Console. The report must now import, calculate and plot by itself.








Error
Usual cause
Repair




object 'duckweed' not found
Import only run in the Console
Put the import in a chunk before it is used


could not find function
Package loaded only in the Console
Add library() to the setup chunk


cannot open file
Personal path, or file not in project
Use data/duckweed.csv and keep the file


Old text, new numbers
Result typed by hand
Check the sentence, or use inline R



Read the first error and the chunk it names. Fix one thing, then Knit again.

Demonstrate with a report whose import line has been run only in the Console: works before restart, fails after. Restarting does not delete saved files; it only empties memory. Expected duckweed values after a correct render: 10 control flasks, mean 32.28 mg; 9 nutrient flasks, mean 39.63 mg (F17 spilled).

title: Reproduce and share your report
text:
What the receiver needs


Copy into a new report-share folder outside your project:

introcomputing.Rproj
duckweed-report.Rmd and its HTML
data/duckweed.csv and data/README.md
output/ if the report saves there
a README.txt: data simulated, file to render, packages needed

The .Rproj contains no data; a shortcut is not a copy.




The share folder holds the project file, report source and HTML, the data and its dictionary, an output folder and a README.




For the organic alternative: organic-study.Rmd and data/organic-recovery.csv. Leave out credentials, session files and unrelated work. The README is what a supervisor reads first: what the data are and how to get the report.

title: Reproduce and share your report
section: Pack the folder as a ZIP
text:
Pack the folder as a ZIP



report-share and report-share-v1.zip sit side by side in Documents; zip -r packs the folder into the ZIP next to it.


zip -r report-share-v1.zip report-share/
unzip -l report-share-v1.zip
Run this from the folder that contains report-share, so the ZIP is saved beside it, not inside it. -r packs everything inside; unzip -l checks what went in. Use a new name for every ZIP.

A ZIP inside the folder it packs would be packed into the next ZIP. Re-running zip with an existing name updates that archive and can keep files you have since deleted, so new names (v1, v2) are simpler. Windows students: copy report-share into Ubuntu first, and copy the finished ZIP back to Windows for the RStudio test.

title: Reproduce and share your report
section: Test 2: open it as the receiver would
text:
Test 2: open it as the receiver would


unzip report-share-v1.zip -d receiver-v1

Extraction keeps the packed folder: one extra level.
Open receiver-v1/report-share/introcomputing.Rproj, restart R, Knit.
Expect the same counts (10 and 9) and means (32.28 and 39.63 mg).





Extracting into receiver-v1 adds a level: the report is at receiver-v1/report-share/duckweed-report.Rmd.




Check the project name in RStudio’s corner: it is easy to Knit the original by mistake. Jittered point positions may move slightly between computers; numbers should not. If they differ, save sessionInfo() in the log: it lists R and package versions.

title: Reproduce and share your report
section: Two fresh starts test different things
text:
Two fresh starts test different things



Restarting R tests for hidden objects; moving the project to a new folder tests for missing files and personal paths.



Restart R finds objects that only lived in memory.
New folder finds missing files and paths that point back to your original.
Together they are the closest you can get to the receiver’s computer on your own laptop.


Restarting in the original folder can still find a file via a personal absolute path. Moving the project but keeping the session can hide a missing import. Both together catch both. A different computer can still differ in software versions.

title: Reproduce and share your report
text:
A ZIP is a snapshot



You fix the README after making v1. Neither v1.zip nor receiver-v1 changes.
Make report-share-v2.zip, extract to receiver-v2, and check the fix is there.
A new name is not proof. Open the file.
Add a line to the README saying what changed in v2.





After the folder is edited, report-share-v1.zip still holds the old README while a newly made v2 contains the edit.




The same applies to separate copies on Windows and Ubuntu: they do not update each other. Revise, recopy, repack, retest.

title: Reproduce and share your report
text:
Sharing is not backup



A share folder and its ZIP on the same laptop are lost together; a copy on separate supported storage survives.


A ZIP next to the original protects against nothing if the laptop is lost, stolen or broken. Keep a copy of the project on the supported separate storage, and note where.

Ask students to say where their backup is. If the university storage is not set up for them yet, they should say so in the log rather than count a second folder on the same disk as a backup.

title: Reproduce and share your report
text:
It renders ≠ it is right


In two disposable copies:

Rename data/duckweed.csv: Knit stops with an error naming the file.
Write “All 20 flasks had a measured biomass.”: Knit succeeds, but only 19 were weighed.

R notices a missing file. It cannot notice a wrong sentence. A reader has to check claims against the numbers.




Running successfully and being scientifically supported are separate: a report can run and still make an unsupported claim.




After restoring the file name, check that the means are back to 32.28 and 39.63 mg; an absent error message is not the same as the right result. Delete the disposable copies so a deliberately false sentence never ends up in the shared ZIP.

title: Reproduce and share your report
section: A source edit does not update the HTML
text:
A source edit does not update the HTML



The source has been revised but the HTML still shows the old version until the report is rendered again.


After any change, Knit again and open the new HTML. Compare numbers at sensible precision: 33.91818 and 33.92 mg are the same mean; 34.32 mg is a different analysis.

A browser tab with a familiar title may be the old file. The numbers come from the algae data (supplement mean 33.91818 mg), which students package as algae-brief in the exercises. A difference beyond rounding means checking input, exclusions and code, not the number of digits.

title: Reproduce and share your report
text:
Summary







Check
What it finds




Restart R, then Knit
Objects and packages that existed only in the Console


Extract the ZIP into a new folder, then Knit
Missing files and personal paths


Make v2 and check the fix in a new extraction
Old snapshots sent by mistake


Copy on separate storage
Protection against losing the laptop


Read the claims against the numbers
Wrong sentences that render without error



Next (Day 25, consolidate): the whole workflow once more, from files to a shared report.
Now: open the Day 24 exercises. Leave with a tested report-share-v2.zip, algae-brief.Rmd with its HTML, a backup copy, and reports/reproduction-log.txt.

The exercises use the day-23 report (duckweed or organic), then repeat the procedure for the algae memo: 12 reference cultures, mean 28.20 mg; 11 supplement cultures, mean 33.92 mg (A19 missing). Formative practice, not graded.
